Its restriction over \(D\) is restricted, and \(R\to D\) is a nilpotent coefficient thickening by (DRD.13). The full lift comparison (DRD.8) therefore gives its unique restricted lift, with every coherent path. Hence \[ \mathcal Z_H^{\mathrm{restr}}(X)(R) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathcal Z_H^{\mathrm{restr}}(X)(B) \mathop{\times}_{\mathcal Z_H^{\mathrm{restr}}(X)(C)} \mathcal Z_H^{\mathrm{restr}}(X)(D). \tag{DRD.17} \] This is infinitesimal cohesiveness on the stated full DG coefficient squares. It follows from finite projective frame gluing and stable operator-image lifting, without essential surjectivity for the gluing of all unbounded modules.

Figure 3.29. The uniform bound and all-coefficient comparison are (DRD.1)–(DRD.5). The scalar triangle and its nilpotent consequences are (DRD.6)–(DRD.11). Finite projective frame gluing and the two point-functor comparisons are (DRD.12)–(DRD.17). The lower examples retain the sharp \(SL_2\) bound, the bi-infinite module obstruction and all the higher projective-line coefficient directions.

3.125. A sharp projective-line operator calculation

Exercise 3.CH. Let \(H=SL_2\), and put \(A=\Lambda_{\mathbf C}(a,b,c)\), with all three generators closed of degree minus one. On the standard representation take \[ U=\begin{pmatrix}c&a\\ b&-c\end{pmatrix}. \tag{DRD.18} \] Compute \(U^2,U^3,U^4\). Decide whether \(u^2=0\) is a valid replacement for the uniform bound (DRD.2).

Solution 3.CH. Use \(a^2=b^2=c^2=0\) and \(ba=-ab\), \(ca=-ac\), \(cb=-bc\). Matrix composition uses these graded-commutative scalar products. Direct multiplication gives \[ U^2=\begin{pmatrix}ab&-2ac\\2bc&-ab\end{pmatrix}, \qquad U^3=3abc\,I_2,\qquad U^4=0. \tag{DRD.19} \] For example the top-left cubic entry is \(abc-2acb=3abc\), and the bottom-right one is \(2bca+abc=3abc\); the off-diagonal cubic entries contain repeated generators. The exterior basis makes \(ab\) and \(abc\) nonzero. Thus \(U^2\ne0\) and \(U^3\ne0\). Here \(\dim\mathfrak{sl}_2=3\), so \(u^4=0\), or \(v^2=0\), is exactly the uniform bound and is sharp on this representation. The associative square \(u^2\) is retained throughout.

3.126. A full unbounded module-gluing counterexample

Exercise 3.CI. Let \(k=\mathbf C\), \(B=D=k\), and \(C=k\oplus k\eta\), with \(|\eta|=-1\), \(d\eta=0\), \(\eta^2=0\). Both maps to \(C\) are the unit. Compute \(R=B\times_C D\). Exhibit a nonzero object of \[ \operatorname{Mod}_B \mathop{\times}_{\operatorname{Mod}_C}\operatorname{Mod}_D \tag{DRD.20} \] that is not the scalar restriction of any \(R\)-module.

Solution 3.CI. The scalar triangle (DRD.12) puts all cohomology of \(R\) in degree zero. Its degree-zero algebra has the constant class and the relative interval class \(\eta\,dt\); the latter has square zero. Thus \[ R\simeq k[\epsilon]/\epsilon^2,\qquad |\epsilon|=0. \tag{DRD.21} \] This is an equivalence of DG algebras: a connective DG algebra with cohomology only in degree zero is equivalent to its ordinary cohomology algebra.

Take the zero-differential complex \(V=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}k e_n\), with \(|e_n|=n\). The degree-zero map \(T:V\to V[1]\), \(e_n\mapsto e_{n+1}\), is an isomorphism. On \(C\otimes V\), the \(C\)-linear degree-zero map \[ \phi(e_n)=e_n+\eta e_{n+1} \tag{DRD.22} \] is invertible, with inverse subtracting the second term. It supplies the transition for the nonzero pair \((V,V,\phi)\) in (DRD.20).

The unit pair is \((k,k,\mathrm{id}_C)\). Its full mapping complex to this pair is the fibre of \[ V\oplus V\longrightarrow C\otimes V=V\oplus V[1], \qquad (v,w)\longmapsto(v-w,-Tw). \tag{DRD.23} \] The displayed map is an isomorphism: the inverse sends \((x,y)\) to \((x-T^{-1}y,-T^{-1}y)\). Its fibre is therefore zero. If this nonzero pair were the restriction of an \(R\)-module \(M\), full faithfulness would identify this mapping complex with \(\operatorname{RHom}_R(R,M)=M\), forcing \(M=0\). Full faithfulness for all modules here follows directly from (DRD.12): use scalar adjunction in the three mapping complexes and tensor that triangle with the target \(M\). Restriction of the zero module is zero, a contradiction. This is a failure of essential surjectivity for all unbounded modules. It does not contradict finite projective gluing (DRD.14); \(V\) is unbounded in both directions and is not finite projective.

3.127. An unbounded coefficient algebra with infinitely many higher point groups

Exercise 3.CJ. Let \(X=\mathbf P^1\), \(H=\mathbf G_m\), and \(A=\mathbf C[z]\), \(|z|=-2\), \(dz=0\). Compute the whole framed restricted point space. Show directly that its finite representation values lie in \(\mathscr I_{\mathbf P^1}\), including along representatives of all its higher homotopy groups.

Solution 3.CJ. The actual free-generator comparison is \[ \mathcal Y_{\mathbf G_m}^{\mathrm{restr}}(\mathbf P^1)(A) =\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Mod}_{\mathbf C}}(\mathbf C[1],A). \tag{DRD.24} \] Its mapping complex is \(A[-1]\). There is one component, and \[ \pi_{2r-1}=\mathbf C z^r\quad(r\geq1),\qquad \pi_{2r}=0\quad(r\geq1). \tag{DRD.25} \] For the odd-dimensional group indexed by \(2r-1\), an iterated interval representative sends the degree-minus-one generator to \[ z^r\,dt_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dt_{2r-1}. \tag{DRD.26} \] Its total degree is \(-2r+(2r-1)=-1\), it is closed, and restriction to every boundary face is zero. Successive relative interval integrations give \(z^r\). The polynomial interval contraction of Solution 3.CA, applied in each direction, identifies these with exactly the groups in (DRD.25).

On a representation of weight \(m\in\mathbf Z\), \(u\) acts by \(m\alpha\), where \(\alpha\) is the odd scalar coefficient of the point or path. Its square is zero, so localization at \(v=u^2\) vanishes. This holds on every displayed higher representative and every coherent coefficient simplex. Thus the ind-target comparison retains all the infinitely many higher point groups; no bound on the negative cohomology of \(A\) has been introduced.

Effective derived ind-affine charts additionally require a compact connective cotangent calculation and effectivity beyond these comparisons. RSE.37–RSE.38 and NTR.16 give the subsequent restricted projector and Hecke-lisse image; GFP.55–GFP.56 give its original-complex ind-regularity and nilpotent-support containment. GZR.33 gives equality with all independent nilpotent support over the complex numbers. Extension to the other geometric ground fields retains its requirements. This uses more than the infinitesimal comparison above.

The deformation framework is discussed in AGKRRV, The stack of local systems with restricted variation and geometric Langlands theory with nilpotent singular support, “Establishing deformation theory” and “Calculating the (co)tangent spaces.” The scalar square (DRD.12), finite projective gluing (DRD.14), stable-image lifting (DRD.7) and full Postnikov comparison supply the arguments used above.

3.128. The adjoint de Rham complex on the full coefficient algebra

Retain a smooth projective connected complex curve \(X\), a point \(x\), and a connected reductive complex group \(H\). Let \(A\) be any connective commutative complex DG algebra, and let \(F\) be a restricted point over \(A\). By (DRD.4)–(DRD.5), its actual operator realization is a flat \(H\)-torsor \(P\). Write \(E=\operatorname{ad}(P)\), with its adjoint connection. Put \[ \begin{aligned} C_F&=R\Gamma_{\mathrm{dR}}(X_A,E),\\ e_x&:C_F\longrightarrow E_x,\qquad K_F=\operatorname{fib}(e_x). \end{aligned} \tag{DCT.1} \] The evaluation first forgets the one-form term and then evaluates the bundle at \(x\). All complexes retain their internal coefficient degrees.

Here is a finite, base-change-compatible construction. The two-affine computation and divisor construction (DCA.1)–(DCA.5) give finite projective two-term models for \(R\Gamma(E)\) and \(R\Gamma(E\otimes\Omega_X^1)\), in relative degrees zero and one. The connection is \(A\)-linear, although it is not \(\mathcal O_X\)-linear. It induces a map between these actual global complexes. Its fibre is \[ C_F= \operatorname{fib}\!\left( R\Gamma(X_A,E)\xrightarrow{\nabla_{\rm ad}} R\Gamma(X_A,E\otimes\Omega_X^1)\right). \tag{DCT.2} \] Equivalently, totalize the two affine Čech columns and the two de Rham terms. There are finitely many columns, even when \(A\) is unbounded to the left. The one-form term contributes one additional relative degree. Therefore \[ \begin{gathered} C_F\text{ is perfect of relative Tor amplitude }[0,2],\\ C_F\otimes_A^{\mathbf L}A' \simeq C_{F_{A'}} \quad\text{for every connective }A',\\ R\Gamma_{\rm dR}(X_A,E\otimes_A^{\mathbf L}M) \simeq C_F\otimes_A^{\mathbf L}M \quad\text{for every }A\text{-module }M . \end{gathered} \tag{DCT.3} \] For the last two assertions, tensor each affine term of the finite Čech/de Rham complex. Derived tensor commutes with its finite fibres. The finite projective models identify the resulting maps as well as their objects. Thus these statements apply to nonflat coefficient changes and unbounded modules; no replacement by \(H^0(A)\) occurs.

3.129. Linearizing the whole split square-zero lift space

Let \(M\) be a connective \(A\)-module and \(A\oplus M\) the split square-zero algebra. There is a distinguished lift of \(P\) with connection, obtained by scalar extension along the splitting \(A\to A\oplus M\). Denote the space of full flat-torsor lifts, with their specified reduction to \(P\), by \(\operatorname{Def}^{\rm dR}_F(M)\). We prove \[ \operatorname{Def}^{\rm dR}_F(M) \simeq \Omega^\infty\bigl((C_F\otimes_A M)[1]\bigr). \tag{DCT.4} \] Here \(\Omega^\infty\) denotes the underlying mapping space of a complex; its \(i\)-th homotopy group at zero is its cohomology in degree \(-i\).

Choose an affine étale torsor-trivializing cover and its whole nerve. The full DG Jacobian calculation (DCA.15) identifies based infinitesimal \(H\)-points with \(\Omega^\infty(\mathfrak h\otimes M)\). This is a calculation of mapping complexes, not only of ordinary points: the smooth Koszul presentation has a contractible pivot Jacobian block, leaving the projective differential module. In every mapping simplex, products of two corrections vanish. Comultiplication becomes addition and conjugation becomes the adjoint action. Étale charts lift uniquely because their entire Jacobian block is invertible. Consequently the same cover and its compatible refinements compute the lift problem.

The bundle part of this computation is (DCA.16). Include the connection coefficients using the actual transformation identity (DCA.7). Write a transition correction as \((1+a_{ij})g_{ij}\), and a connection correction as \(\theta_i\). Multiplication and the connection identity, modulo the square-zero ideal, give \[ \delta a=0,\qquad \delta\theta-\nabla_{\rm ad}a=0. \tag{DCT.5} \] For precision, the second equality follows by expanding \(\operatorname{Ad}(1+a)\beta_i-d_X(1+a)(1+a)^{-1}\): its change is \([a,\beta_i]-d_Xa=-\nabla_{\rm ad}a\). Choose the change of lifted frame \(1-\gamma_i\). It acts by \[ a\longmapsto a+\delta\gamma,\qquad \theta\longmapsto\theta+\nabla_{\rm ad}\gamma. \tag{DCT.6} \] Thus the equations, changes of frames and their composition are the additive total complex of \(E\otimes_A M\to E\otimes\Omega_X^1\otimes_A M\). With Čech degree \(q\), its Čech/de Rham differential is \(\delta+(-1)^q\nabla_{\rm ad}\); the internal DG differential uses the same total-complex sign rule.

This also identifies every higher path. Indeed (DCA.15) and (DCA.7) apply to the full simplicial free-algebra mapping model, with all faces and degeneracies. After subtracting the split origin, its correction nerve is additive in every degree. Its normalized cochains are exactly the displayed total complex, shifted by one for descent objects. The polynomial interval homotopy satisfies \(dh+hd=1-\mathrm{ev}_0\), by integration, as in Solution 3.CA. Apply it successively in the mapping interval directions: based \(i\)-loops are the degree-\(-i\) cocycles of that shifted complex, modulo the boundaries furnished by the next interval homotopy. The same contraction identifies compositions with addition. This proves the equivalence of the full additive mapping spaces, not a truncation to an ordinary cocycle groupoid. Étale descent and the finite Čech comparison (DCA.2) identify that totalization with \((C_F\otimes_A M)[1]\). This proves (DCT.4).

3.130. Framing and the universal cotangent module

Now give \(F\) its specified \(H\)-frame at \(x\). Thus \(E_x=\mathfrak h\otimes A\). The framed prestack is the actual fibre of the evaluation map to \(BH\), as in (RSP.9)–(RSP.10). At the fibre torsor, the split lift space of \(BH\) is \(\Omega^\infty((E_x\otimes_A M)[1])\), by the same additive kernel calculation: \(BH\) is the classifying space of \(H\), so it adds one descent degree. The evaluation on lift spaces is \(e_x[1]\). Therefore the full framed lift space is \[ \operatorname{Def}^{\rm fr}_F(M) \simeq \Omega^\infty\bigl((K_F\otimes_A M)[1]\bigr). \tag{DCT.7} \] For the restricted prestack the comparison is identical. The map \(A\oplus M\to A\) is a nilpotent coefficient thickening. Apply the full Cartesian lift comparison (DRD.8), and then take the actual frame fibre. It identifies the restricted and full framed spaces, with every specified reduction and path. In particular (DCT.7) computes the derivative of the genuine restricted prestack.

Dualizing (DCT.1), set \[ \begin{aligned} L^{\rm fr}_F &=K_F^\vee[-1]\\ &\simeq\operatorname{fib}\!\left( \mathfrak h^\vee\otimes A \xrightarrow{\,e_x^\vee\,}C_F^\vee\right). \end{aligned} \tag{DCT.8} \] The shifts follow from \(K_F^\vee=\operatorname{cofib}(E_x^\vee\to C_F^\vee)\). Finite duality gives, naturally for every connective \(M\), \[ \operatorname{Def}^{\rm fr}_F(M) \simeq\Omega^\infty \operatorname{RHom}_A(L^{\rm fr}_F,M). \tag{DCT.9} \] This natural square-zero mapping property is the cotangent module assertion. It includes the higher lift groups, and is compatible with every coefficient map. Without a frame, the same argument gives \[ L^{\rm unfr}_F=C_F^\vee[-1],\qquad L^{\rm unfr}_F\longrightarrow L^{\rm fr}_F \longrightarrow\mathfrak h^\vee\otimes A . \tag{DCT.10} \] The last triangle is also the cotangent triangle of the \(H\)-frame torsor.

3.131. Compactness, connectivity and the coadjoint comparison

Both \(C_F\) and \(E_x\) are perfect, so (DCT.8) is perfect and compact. We prove its sharper relative Tor bound \[ L^{\rm fr}_F\text{ has Tor amplitude }[-1,0]. \tag{DCT.11} \] First pass to any residue field \(\kappa\) of \(H^0(A)\); (DCT.3) identifies the fibre with the same connection complex. It has cohomology only in degrees zero through two. The map \[ H^0(C_{F_\kappa}) \longrightarrow (E_x)_\kappa \quad\text{is injective}. \tag{DCT.12} \] Indeed it is evaluation of a horizontal map from the unit connection to the adjoint connection. The fibre functor on the ind-connection heart is exact and conservative by (RSP.2). Such a functor is faithful: the image of a morphism has zero fibre only when that image object is zero. This applies also after the ordinary field coefficient extension; the underlying complex connection is an ind-connection by (DRD.4). Thus a horizontal section with zero fibre is zero.

Duality over \(\kappa\) makes the degree-zero map \((E_x)_\kappa^\vee\to H^0(C_{F_\kappa}^\vee)\) surjective. Since \(C_{F_\kappa}^\vee\) has degrees \([-2,0]\), the fibre in (DCT.8) has degrees \([-1,0]\). To pass from these residue calculations to the relative assertion, use the finite projective model of (DCT.2). Locally the cone in (DCT.8) has finite free relative generators in degrees \(-1,0,1\). Vanishing of degree-one residue cohomology makes the degree-zero-to-degree-one differential surjective modulo the corresponding maximal ideal. Invert a nonzero maximal minor; lift its inverse in the connective DG algebra. Gaussian elimination splits off that contractible degree-zero/degree-one block. Remove all degree-one generators. The remaining model has only relative degrees \(-1,0\), so tensoring it with any ordinary coefficient module has precisely that Tor range. These neighbourhoods cover the coefficient spectrum. This is the same finite pivot cancellation used in (CSD.4), applied to the two upper degrees. It proves (DCT.11). As \(A\) is connective, \(L^{\rm fr}_F\) itself is connective.

There is an intrinsic tensor description of the second term in (DCT.8). Write \((\mathscr I_X)_A=\operatorname{Mod}_A(\mathscr I_X)\), and let \(\mathbf1_A\) be its tensor unit. For every \(A\)-module \(M\), dualizability of the adjoint value, the full operator embedding and the finite Spencer/Čech calculation give \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{RHom}_{(\mathscr I_X)_A} (F(\mathfrak h^\vee),M\otimes_A\mathbf1_A) &\simeq C_F\otimes_A M\\ &\simeq\operatorname{RHom}_A(C_F^\vee,M). \end{aligned} \tag{DCT.13} \] The first comparison moves the dualizable coadjoint value across Hom and computes Hom from the unit by (RSC.2); (DCT.3) permits every \(M\). Thus, on this coadjoint value, \(C_F^\vee\) is the module of coinvariants, namely the module corepresenting maps to constants. The map from \(\mathfrak h^\vee\otimes A\) is the dual of the actual fibre evaluation. Formula (DCT.8) therefore agrees with this coinvariant formulation without assuming a tensor-lift theorem in place of its proof.

All these identifications commute with nonflat scalar change: use (DCT.3), finite duals and the actual evaluation map. They also respect frame changes and tensor equivalences of \(F\); these act on the adjoint connection and on its evaluation, so they induce the same coherent maps on the fibre and its dual. This supplies the cotangent modules as a natural full DG family. Compactness here concerns the actual \(A\)-module, not merely its geometric fibres.

Figure 3.30. The actual proper complex and full lift comparison are (DCT.1)–(DCT.7). The cotangent and frame triangles are (DCT.8)–(DCT.10). Finite cancellation proves (DCT.11); the coadjoint corepresenting property is (DCT.13). The lower panels show the constant and unipotent dimensions, the nonzero second-order obstruction and the full unbounded coefficient example.

3.132. Constant connections in every genus

Exercise 3.CK. At the trivial framed \(H\)-connection, compute \(L^{\rm fr}_F\) over every connective \(A\). Give its virtual rank and compare its projective-line value with (RSC.28).

Solution 3.CK. For the constant connection, \[ C_F=\mathfrak h\otimes_{\mathbf C} R\Gamma_{\rm dR}(X,\mathbf C)\otimes A . \tag{DCT.14} \] The trivial connection has \(H^0=\mathbf C\), and (RSC.6) gives \(H^2=\mathbf C\). Riemann–Roch in the earlier curve lesson gives \(\chi(\mathcal O_X)-\chi(\Omega_X^1)=2-2g\); the finite two-row complex (DCT.2) has that Euler characteristic. Hence \(\dim H^1_{\rm dR}=2g\). Choose bases and split this finite complex over the field. The evaluation is the identity on its degree-zero summand and zero on its positive-degree cohomology. Removing that summand gives the noncanonical, base-change-compatible expression \[ \begin{aligned} K_F&\simeq (\mathfrak h\otimes A)^{2g}[-1] \oplus(\mathfrak h\otimes A)[-2],\\ L^{\rm fr}_F&\simeq (\mathfrak h^\vee\otimes A)^{2g} \oplus(\mathfrak h^\vee\otimes A)[1]. \end{aligned} \tag{DCT.15} \] The splitting depends on the chosen complex-vector-space bases; (DCT.8) is canonical. Its virtual rank is \[ (2g-1)\dim H . \tag{DCT.16} \] For \(g=0\), \(L^{\rm fr}_F=\mathfrak h^\vee\otimes A[1]\). This is exactly the cotangent module of the free algebra \(\operatorname{Sym}_{\mathbf C}(\mathfrak h^\vee[1])\) at its zero point: a derivation is specified freely on that degree-minus-one generator module. Its mapping complex into \(M\) is \(\mathfrak h\otimes M[-1]\), including its higher groups. The projective-line direction has not disappeared because its ordinary point space is a point.

3.133. A nonsemisimple elliptic example

Exercise 3.CL. On an elliptic curve, choose its two commuting fundamental loops and the rank-two monodromy \[ U=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad V=I_2, \qquad H=GL_2 . \tag{DCT.17} \] Compute the framed tangent and obstruction dimensions at this restricted point.

Solution 3.CL. This finite complex local system is an actual restricted point by the full connection comparison and tensor reconstruction in (RSC.2)–(RSC.5), (TBF.2)–(TBF.7). The one-vertex torus cell complex for its adjoint local system is \[ \begin{gathered} \mathfrak{gl}_2 \xrightarrow{d_0}\mathfrak{gl}_2\oplus\mathfrak{gl}_2 \xrightarrow{d_1}\mathfrak{gl}_2,\\ d_0(X)=(DX,0),\quad d_1(P,Q)=DQ, \quad D=\operatorname{Ad}(U)-1 . \end{gathered} \tag{DCT.18} \] These differentials come by transporting along the four edges of the torus fundamental square; \(V=1\) kills its other two terms. A reversal of the oriented two-cell changes the last sign and not the calculation. The full connection/sheaf comparison of (RSC.2) identifies this with the adjoint de Rham complex.

For \(X=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), multiplication gives \[ DX=\begin{pmatrix}c&d-a-c\\0&-c\end{pmatrix}. \tag{DCT.19} \] Thus \(D\) has rank two and kernel \(\mathbf C I_2+\mathbf C E_{12}\). The three cohomology dimensions of (DCT.18) are \(2,4,2\). Evaluation is the inclusion of this two-dimensional horizontal kernel in the four-dimensional fibre. The fibre triangle (DCT.1) consequently gives \[ \dim H^0(K_F[1])=4-2+4=6,\qquad \dim H^1(K_F[1])=2 . \tag{DCT.20} \] Equivalently the framed deformation complex is the two-term complex \(\mathfrak{gl}_2^{\,2}\xrightarrow{(P,Q)\mapsto DQ}\mathfrak{gl}_2\) in degrees zero and one. Removing degree zero of the adjoint complex is justified by its actual evaluation isomorphism on the one-vertex degree-zero cochains. At the trivial rank-two point the same map is zero, so the dimensions are instead eight and four. In both cases the virtual dimension is four, as (DCT.16) requires.

3.134. Connectivity does not remove the obstruction

Exercise 3.CM. Let \(H=SL_2\) on an elliptic curve and \(R_2=\mathbf C[\epsilon]/\epsilon^2\). Put \(X_0=E_{12}\), \(Y_0=E_{21}\). The two loop matrices \(1+\epsilon X_0\), \(1+\epsilon Y_0\) commute over \(R_2\). Determine whether this framed restricted point lifts to \(R_3=\mathbf C[\epsilon]/\epsilon^3\).

Solution 3.CM. Both matrices have determinant one. Their associated finite free \(R_2\)-local systems, viewed as complex local systems with commuting \(R_2\)-action, give a restricted flat torsor by the full finite connection comparison and regular Hopf reconstruction. In every finite associated representation the underlying complex dimension is finite, so it lies in \(\mathscr I_X\).

Any lifted matrices have the form \[ M_1=1+\epsilon X_0+\epsilon^2P,\qquad M_2=1+\epsilon Y_0+\epsilon^2Q . \tag{DCT.21} \] Their difference of products is \[ M_1M_2-M_2M_1 =\epsilon^2[X_0,Y_0] =\epsilon^2 \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\ne0 . \tag{DCT.22} \] The terms \(P,Q\) cancel, so no choices, including choices enforcing determinant one, can make the lifts commute. A framed flat-torsor lift would give commuting monodromy matrices; it therefore does not exist. This is a genuine degree-one obstruction of the framed deformation complex. A perfect connective cotangent complex of amplitude \([-1,0]\) permits this obstruction; it does not assert ordinary smoothness. The nilpotent lift comparison (DRD.8) says that a full lift, when present, is restricted, and does not assert existence of every full lift.

3.135. Unbounded coefficients and all higher derivative groups

Exercise 3.CN. At the trivial framed point take \(A=\mathbf C[z]\), \(|z|=-2\), \(dz=0\). Let \(M=A\), so the split extension is \(A[\epsilon]/\epsilon^2\), with \(|\epsilon|=0\). Compute the entire space of framed lifts reducing to that point.

Solution 3.CN. Equations (DCT.9) and (DCT.15) give the additive mapping complex \[ \operatorname{RHom}_A(L^{\rm fr}_F,A) \simeq(\mathfrak h\otimes A)^{2g} \oplus(\mathfrak h\otimes A)[-1]. \tag{DCT.23} \] Taking cohomology in degree \(-i\) yields \[ \begin{aligned} \pi_{2r}\operatorname{Def}^{\rm fr}_F(A) &=(\mathfrak h^{\,2g})z^r &&(r\ge0),\\ \pi_{2r-1}\operatorname{Def}^{\rm fr}_F(A) &=\mathfrak h\,z^r &&(r\ge1). \end{aligned} \tag{DCT.24} \] For \(i=0\) the first line denotes the additive set of components; positive homotopy groups are taken at the split origin. Choose the same degree-one de Rham cocycles as in Solution 3.CK. For a component of their coefficient complex, a \(2r\)-loop is represented by \(z^r\,dt_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dt_{2r}\) multiplying that deformation component. On the degree-one framed-obstruction summand of the tangent complex, a \((2r-1)\)-loop uses \[ z^r\,dt_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dt_{2r-1}. \tag{DCT.25} \] Its coefficient degree is minus one; the tangent generator has degree one, so its total degree is zero, as required for a point in the shifted mapping complex. Iterated relative interval integration recovers \(z^r\) in each case. The additive correction construction of §3.129 converts these cochains into actual coherent split lifts. Every degree in (DCT.24) is thus retained on the full unbounded coefficient algebra.

The compact connective cotangent module and infinitesimal comparisons do not alone construct effective derived ind-affine stages. That representability assertion additionally requires such stages and an identification of their whole convergent point functor. RSE.37–RSE.38 and NTR.16 give the subsequent restricted projector and Hecke-lisse image; GFP.55–GFP.56 give its original-complex ind-regularity and nilpotent-support containment. GZR.33 gives equality with all independent nilpotent support over the complex numbers. Extension to the other geometric ground fields retains its requirements. This uses more than the compact cotangent calculation above.

For the tensor-coinvariant formulation, see AGKRRV, The stack of local systems with restricted variation and geometric Langlands theory with nilpotent singular support, “Calculating the (co)tangent spaces.” The actual arguments here are the proper finite model (DCT.2), full square-zero linearization (DCT.4)–(DCT.7), nilpotent comparison (DRD.8) and finite duality (DCT.8)–(DCT.13).

3.136. A finite pointed model of the curve

Let \(X\) be a smooth projective connected complex curve, with \(x\in X(\mathbf C)\), and let \(H\) be a connected reductive complex group. All DG coefficient algebras are connective, without a lower cohomological bound.

The compact smooth manifold \(X^{\rm an}\) has a finite good cover. Here are the needed constructions. A coordinate ball has a smooth nonnegative bump supported in a larger coordinate ball and positive on a prescribed smaller closed ball: in rescaled coordinates use \(\exp(-1/(1-|z|^2))\) inside the unit ball and zero outside. Every derivative at the boundary vanishes, since it is a polynomial in \((1-|z|^2)^{-1}\) times that exponential, and \(e^t\geq t^m/m!\) for every \(m\). Compactness gives finitely many such smaller balls covering \(X^{\rm an}\). Dividing their bumps by their positive sum gives a finite subordinate smooth partition. Weighted Euclidean coordinate metrics give a positive smooth metric. Each weighted term extends smoothly by zero because its support lies in its chart.

Theorem B.5 of Riemannian connections and convex neighbourhoods proves arbitrarily small strongly convex neighbourhoods, with smoothly varying unique globally minimizing segments. Choose finitely many \(U_i\) covering \(X^{\rm an}\). Every nonempty intersection \(U_\sigma=\bigcap_{i\in\sigma}U_i\) is contractible: contract it to a point by those segments. The segment is the same in every \(U_i\), by global minimizing uniqueness, and therefore stays in the intersection.

Let \(N\) be the finite nerve. Form \[ T=\left(\coprod_{\varnothing\ne\sigma\in N} U_\sigma\times\Delta^\sigma\right)\big/\text{face identifications}, \qquad X^{\rm an}\xleftarrow{p}T\xrightarrow{q}|N|. \tag{RBC.1} \] Both arrows are homotopy equivalences. For \(p\), use a subordinate partition \((\phi_i)\) with closed supports inside \(U_i\). The section sends \(y\) to \((y,(\phi_i(y)))\); interpolate the simplex weights linearly to obtain a homotopy from \(1_T\) to this section followed by \(p\). This is continuous in the quotient: locally the indices of possibly nonzero \(\phi_i\) all contain that neighbourhood, so on each face the homotopy is a map into the larger face given by their union.

For \(q\), filter by the nerve skeleta. Its \(d\)-th step attaches \(U_\sigma\times\Delta^d\) along \(U_\sigma\times\partial\Delta^d\). Projection of this pair to \((\Delta^d,\partial\Delta^d)\) is a homotopy equivalence, since \(U_\sigma\) is contractible. The boundary inclusion has the homotopy extension property: the usual simplex boundary collar, times \(U_\sigma\), supplies it. Gluing preserves these equivalences. Explicitly, replace each attachment by its double mapping cylinder; collapse its cylinder using that collar. Homotopy inverses on the three pieces extend across the cylinder, and the same extension glues their inverse homotopies. This proves the gluing assertion and, by finite induction, the assertion for \(q\). Consequently \[ (X^{\rm an},x)\simeq(K,k), \qquad K\text{ a finite connected pointed CW complex}. \tag{RBC.2} \] Choose the partition to equal one at \(x\) on a selected cover member, by the same bump construction; this fixes the nerve vertex. A maximal tree in the finite one-skeleton can be collapsed to give one vertex. Collapsing is a homotopy equivalence: contract the tree and extend the contraction over the cells using their boundary collars. Thus \(K\) may have one vertex. No classification of surfaces or assertion about a contractible universal cover is needed.

3.137. The full ind-target inside derived local systems

Write \(\mathcal L(K)=\operatorname{Fun}(K,\operatorname{Mod}_{\mathbf C})\), with pointwise tensor and colimits. The bounded finite-connection comparison (RSC.2)–(RSC.3) gives \[ \mathscr L_X\simeq\operatorname{Fun}(K,\operatorname{Perf}_{\mathbf C}). \tag{RBC.3} \] We specify its derived content. On a contractible good-cover intersection, the constant sheaf has cohomology \(\mathbf C\) in degree zero and zero otherwise. This is Theorem 1.3 of Sheaf cohomology and singular cohomology on manifolds, applied to the displayed contraction. Thus constant finite complexes have their full complex-vector-space Hom complexes there. A bounded complex with locally constant finite cohomology is locally such a constant complex: trivialize its cohomology and lift its finite truncation attachments using these same Hom complexes. The finite-cover descent used here has an explicit inverse. For two opens \(U,V\), glue complexes with a specified intersection equivalence by the fibre of \(Rj_{U*}M_U\oplus Rj_{V*}M_V\to Rj_{U\cap V,*}M_{U\cap V}\). Restricting to \(U\) or \(V\) cancels the identical intersection summand and recovers the prescribed complex. Open restriction is exact and preserves injective sheaves, since extension by zero is an exact left adjoint, so these restriction and derived-pushforward comparisons follow on actual injective resolutions. The same fibre triangle and adjunction compute the full mapping complexes, proving fullness on all paths. This also gives the inverse gluing equivalences. Finite iteration handles the cover, and local boundedness on its finitely many members is a uniform bound. Thus descent identifies this category with the limit of the constant diagram \(\operatorname{Perf}_{\mathbf C}\) on the nonempty intersections. This limit is the functor category from the nerve's homotopy type: its objects are the compatible objects, equivalences and all higher comparisons. The full connection/sheaf comparison in (RSC.2) identifies the operator Hom complexes with these sheaf Hom complexes. The injective and mapping models used here are Theorem 2.3, Lemma 3.2 and Theorem 4.1 of Injective modules, flasque sheaves and bounded-below derived functors. This proves (RBC.3), including compositions and higher paths.

A perfect-stalk local system is compact in \(\mathcal L(K)\). To prove this, attach the finitely many cells. Functors out of a cell pushout are a pullback of functor categories. Their Hom complex is the corresponding finite fibre of the Hom complexes on the old skeleton, the cell and its attaching sphere. On a cell it is Hom from a finite-dimensional perfect complex and commutes with colimits. Induct first on dimension for the spheres, and then on the number of top-dimensional cells. Finite fibres of complexes commute with colimits, so the same is true on \(K\).

The comparison is tensor-compatible: on flat bundles the tensor product of horizontal sections is the horizontal comparison, and finite cones extend it to the bounded DG category. The full Yoneda/free-action bar argument of (GSL.9), now on these actual compact objects, extends (RBC.3) to a full continuous symmetric monoidal embedding \[ \mathscr I_X\hookrightarrow\mathcal L(K). \tag{RBC.4} \] On bounded objects it is the given comparison; on ind-objects it is their colimit. Fullness follows by computing maps first from a compact bounded object and then from its colimit presentation. Tensor agrees on bounded objects and extends by colimits in both variables.

Internal scalar actions give \[ \operatorname{Mod}_A(\mathscr I_X) \hookrightarrow \operatorname{Mod}_A(\mathcal L(K)) \simeq\operatorname{Fun}(K,\operatorname{Mod}_A). \tag{RBC.5} \] The last equivalence simply places the action maps and their whole free-action bar at each point, with their coherent transports. It preserves all module and tensor mapping spaces. This does not identify \(\mathscr I_X\) with every object of \(\mathcal L(K)\); on the projective line the distinction in (RSC.23) remains.

3.138. An actual affine Betti target

The full Hopf torsor reconstruction (TBF.2)–(TBF.5), with no connection imposed, identifies right t-exact continuous tensor functors \(\operatorname{Rep}(H)\to\operatorname{Mod}_A\) with the entire space \(BH(A)\). Finite representation values are finite projective: they and their duals are connective, so the residue criterion (CSD.4) applies. The regular Hopf algebra then constructs their actual faithfully flat torsor and every tensor transformation.

Tensor functors into the right side of (RBC.5) are such functors point by point, with their transports. Framing at \(x\) therefore gives the full space \[ \mathcal Y_{\rm B}(A) =\operatorname{Map}_*((K,k),(BH(A),*)). \tag{RBC.6} \] It is a derived affine functor. The one-skeleton with one vertex gives \(H^m\), where \(m\) is the number of one-cells. A \(d\)-cell, \(d\geq2\), replaces a previous affine functor \(V\) by \[ V\times_{\Omega^{d-2}H}\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf C . \tag{RBC.7} \] Indeed based maps from the attaching sphere into \(BH(A)\) are \(\Omega^{d-2}H(A)\); based maps from the disk are contractible. Attaching maps can be based: move their selected boundary point to \(k\) along a path and extend that homotopy using the sphere's point inclusion and its boundary collar. Homotopic attaching maps give equivalent cell pushouts. Iterated based loops of an affine functor are affine, by their successive derived self-fibres. Thus all the finitely many fibres (RBC.7) are affine. Write \[ \mathcal Y_{\rm B}=\operatorname{Spec}B, \qquad B\text{ connective}. \tag{RBC.8} \] These are derived fibre products, not ordinary solution sets. Their maps and every higher relation are the ones induced by the actual cell attachments. The construction is a presentation of the based mapping functor, so changing the finite model changes neither that functor nor its comparisons.

3.139. Nilpotent lifting in the Betti target

Equations (DRD.4), (RBC.4) and (RBC.5) give a full embedding of the actual framed restricted functor \(\mathcal Y^{\rm restr}\) into \(\mathcal Y_{\rm B}\). Its image is the tensor functors whose finite representation values lie in the full ind-image.

For every \(D\to A\) with surjective \(H^0(D)\to H^0(A)\) and nilpotent kernel, it has the full lift comparison \[ \mathcal Y^{\rm restr}(D)\simeq \mathcal Y^{\rm restr}(A) \times_{\mathcal Y_{\rm B}(A)}\mathcal Y_{\rm B}(D). \tag{RBC.9} \] Here is the argument in this target. For a derived square-zero extension, tensor its scalar triangle with each finite associated local system. Its two outer objects lie in the full stable continuous ind-image, so its middle object does too. All scalar actions, tensor maps and coherent paths lift through that full embedding.

For an ordinary nilpotent ideal \(J\), finite projective coefficient fibres make the local system coefficient-flat. Its finite \(J\)-filtration has subquotients \((J^a/J^{a+1})\otimes E_{D/J}\). These lie in the ind-image, so their finite extension does. On a bounded connective DG base, the cohomology layers are \(H^r(D)\otimes_{H^0(D)}E_{H^0(D)}\), naturally for all transports; finite truncation dévissage applies. Finally take all bounded Postnikov truncations. Fullness lifts their compatible paths, (RSP.5) reconstructs the restricted point, and the affine functor (RBC.8) recovers the same full point because maps from \(B\) preserve the inverse limit of coefficient algebras. This proves (RBC.9) without a lower bound on \(D\).

In particular, an ambient point is restricted precisely when its ordinary reduction is: \[ \mathcal Y^{\rm restr}(A)\simeq \mathcal Y^{\rm restr}(H^0A) \times_{\mathcal Y_{\rm B}(H^0A)}\mathcal Y_{\rm B}(A). \tag{RBC.10} \] This concerns the restricted ind-image. It is not an equivalence of all algebraic de Rham and Betti families; unrestricted variable de Rham monodromy need not have coefficients in the original algebraic parameter ring.

3.140. The ordinary coefficient stages are closed in this ambient

Put \(R=H^0(B)\). Write \(\Gamma=\pi_1(K,k)\). Its one-cell loops generate the group. To verify this using the finite nerve, subdivide a loop finely enough that each source vertex star maps into one target vertex star. Such a subdivision exists by compactness and uniform continuity. Assign those target vertices to the source vertices. On each source edge the assigned vertices belong to a common target simplex, since their open stars meet at its image. Linear interpolation inside that simplex homotopes the loop to the resulting edge path, fixing its base vertex. A finite spanning tree then expresses every edge path in the finitely many non-tree edge loops. On ordinary coefficients \(BH(A)\) is a one-type, so the higher cells impose no further conditions on based maps. Thus \[ (\operatorname{Spec}R)(A)=\operatorname{Hom}(\Gamma,H(A)). \tag{RBC.11} \] Its coordinate ring is the quotient of \(\mathcal O(H^m)\) by the finitely many coordinate equations saying that the finitely many relator words equal one. In particular \(R\) is a finitely generated, Noetherian complex algebra; the polynomial Noetherian proof is supplied in §3.113.

Let \(Y_E=\operatorname{Spec}S_E\) be a coefficient stage of (SCI.6). Its coordinate generators \(x_{i\alpha}\) are the coefficients in a fixed basis of \(E\) of the images of the faithful matrix-entry/determinant-inverse generators \(q_i\) of \(\mathcal O(H)\). Choose finitely many \(\gamma_w\in\Gamma\) whose evaluations on \(E\) are injective, by the finite-evaluation proof in §3.97. A linear left inverse gives constants \(c_{\alpha w}\) with \[ x_{i\alpha} =\sum_w c_{\alpha w} \bigl(q_i(\rho(\gamma_w))\bigr). \tag{RBC.12} \] Each \(\gamma_w\) is a finite word in the chosen generators and their inverses. Its matrix entries and determinant inverses are regular polynomial expressions in the corresponding \(H^m\) coordinates. Thus every generator of \(S_E\) lies in the image of \(R\), and \[ R\twoheadrightarrow S_E,\qquad J_E=\ker(R\to S_E). \tag{RBC.13} \] This proves a closed immersion on all ordinary rings, including nonreduced ones. The Hopf coefficient reconstruction proves that the map is the original SCI map, not a different point parametrization. No assumption that \(E\) is a subalgebra is made. Each \(J_E\) is finitely generated, and \(E\subset E'\) gives \(J_{E'}\subset J_E\).

3.141. Explicit derived Koszul neighbourhoods

Fix \(E\), and lift generators of \(J_E\) to closed degree-zero elements \(f_1,\ldots,f_r\) in a semifree nonpositive commutative DG model of \(B\). For \(N\geq1\) put \[ B_{E,N}=B[\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_r],\qquad |\eta_i|=-1,\quad d\eta_i=f_i^N, \qquad T_{E,N}=\operatorname{Spec}B_{E,N}. \tag{RBC.14} \] The generators are graded-commutative. This is the derived base change of the Koszul resolution for the regular sequence \(t_1^N,\ldots,t_r^N\) in the polynomial algebra \(\mathbf C[t_1,\ldots,t_r]\). Its exactness follows by successively separating the monomials of exponent below \(N\) in each variable: multiplication by the next power is injective in the preceding quotient, and its two-term Koszul complex has precisely that quotient as degree-zero cohomology.

For \(N'\geq N\) the actual algebra map \[ B_{E,N'}\longrightarrow B_{E,N},\qquad \eta_i\longmapsto f_i^{N'-N}\eta_i \tag{RBC.15} \] commutes with the differential and composes as the exponents add. Moreover \[ H^0(B_{E,N})=R/(f_1^N,\ldots,f_r^N). \tag{RBC.16} \] A closed immersion of connective derived affines is characterized by a surjection on degree-zero coordinate rings, equivalently a closed immersion on ordinary truncations; this is the standard definition in Lurie, Derived Algebraic Geometry, Definition 5.3.1. Consequently these transitions are closed immersions. Such a map need not be a monomorphism of full DG point spaces; the nullhomotopies below are part of its derived data.

3.142. The whole unbounded formal-completion functor

Let \(\widehat{\mathcal Y}_E(A)\) be the full subspace of \(\mathcal Y_{\rm B}(A)\) where the image of \(J_E\) in \(H^0(A)\) is nilpotent. This property is invariant under paths and defines a union of components. We prove \[ \operatorname*{colim}_{N}T_{E,N} \simeq\widehat{\mathcal Y}_E \quad\text{on all connective DG algebras}. \tag{RBC.17} \] Fix an ambient point \(z:B\to A\). The fibre of \(T_{E,N}(A)\) over \(z\) is the product of the spaces of nullhomotopies of the closed elements \(z(f_i)^N\). This follows from the actual free generator and differential in (RBC.14), or from its derived polynomial pushout. A nonempty fibre is a torsor for \[ \prod_{i=1}^r\Omega^\infty(A[-1]). \tag{RBC.18} \] If all \(z(f_i)\) are nilpotent in \(H^0(A)\), choose \(n_0\) with \(z(f_i)^{n_0}=0\) there for every \(i\). This also makes the whole generated ideal nilpotent: every product of \(r(n_0-1)+1\) generators repeats one at least \(n_0\) times. All \(N\geq n_0\) have nonempty fibres. The maps on differences of nullhomotopies are multiplication by \(z(f_i)^{N'-N}\), by (RBC.15). Thus on every homotopy group, including the difference group of components, they are zero whenever \[ N'-N\geq n_0. \tag{RBC.19} \] This bound works in every negative degree of \(A\). The transition on the torsor itself is affine; no compatible choice of origins is being assumed. Any two components become equal after that transition, and every positive homotopy class becomes zero after it. The fibre colimit is therefore contractible. If the ideal is not nilpotent, no fibre is nonempty. The case \(r=0\) gives a point fibre throughout.

For clarity, filtered colimits of these spaces preserve the fibres and their homotopy groups: a finite simplicial sphere, a horn or a homotopy uses finitely many simplices and relations, all of which occur together at one filtered stage. The same finite-data argument proves commutation with finite homotopy limits. Hence the fibre calculation proves (RBC.17) as a natural equivalence of entire spaces, not just of components. It also proves that different choices of lifted generators present the same full completion.

3.143. Coherent filtered assembly of the affine stages

Allow all finite choices in (RBC.14). Let \(\mathcal C\) be the full infinity-category over \(\mathcal Y_{\rm B}\) on these \(T_{E,N}\). Its objects and mapping spaces form a small category after fixing a set of models. Every map in it induces a quotient map on \(H^0\): both rings are quotients of \(R\), and a map over \(\operatorname{Spec}B\) must be the identity on their common images of \(R\). Thus every transition in \(\mathcal C\) is a closed immersion.

This category is filtered, including coherent cones. Given a diagram indexed by a finite simplicial set, choose \(E'\) containing the finitely many coefficient coalgebras of its vertices. For each vertex \(T\), the image of \(J_{E'}\) in \(H^0(T)\) is nilpotent, since it is contained in the image of that vertex's \(J_E\), whose finite generating powers vanish. Formula (RBC.17), evaluated on the full coordinate algebra of \(T\), gives \[ \operatorname*{colim}_{N} \operatorname{Map}_{/\mathcal Y_{\rm B}}(T,T_{E',N}) \simeq * . \tag{RBC.20} \] Take the finite homotopy limit describing compatible cones to all the vertices, arrows and higher simplices of the diagram. By the finite-data argument above, its colimit in \(N\) is the limit of point spaces and hence is contractible. It has a point at some stage. That point is a full coherent cone in \(\mathcal C\). This proves filteredness in its infinity-categorical sense; passing only to the homotopy category would not give this conclusion.

3.144. Effective framed derived charts and the actual quotient

Each \(\widehat{\mathcal Y}_E\) lies in the restricted functor. Indeed quotient \(H^0(A)\) by the nilpotent image ideal of \(J_E\). The resulting ordinary point lies in \(Y_E\), and (RBC.9) lifts it back to the specified ambient point over \(A\). Conversely, a restricted ordinary reduction factors through a single \(Y_E\) by SCI, so it lies in this completion. Therefore \[ \mathcal Y^{\rm restr} =\operatorname*{colim}_E\widehat{\mathcal Y}_E \ \subset\ \mathcal Y_{\rm B}. \tag{RBC.21} \] Both sides here are full unions of ambient components on every coefficient algebra, so the equality retains their whole higher spaces.

Each stage has a contractible space of lifts to the restricted functor, by its full embedding in the ambient. These factorizations therefore assemble coherently over the entire category \(\mathcal C\). The affine presentation is \[ \operatorname*{colim}_{T\in\mathcal C}T \xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal Y^{\rm restr}. \tag{RBC.22} \] Here is its full effectivity check. Evaluation on an affine commutes with colimits of prestacks, and taking a fibre over an ambient point commutes with the filtered colimit by the finite-limit argument above. A restricted point factors through some completion and then through an affine \(T_{E,N}\), by (RBC.17), so that fibre is nonempty. Any finite collection of lifts, comparisons or simplicial homotopies can be put in a common completion by enlarging \(E\). Its affine targets have contractible fibre colimit by (RBC.20). This argument also allows the chosen source affine as an extra vertex: its ambient point lies in the same completion, so the identical finite-limit cone argument applies. It makes any two lift components equal and contracts every finite sphere of lift choices. Thus the fibre of (RBC.22) is contractible over every restricted point. It is empty over all other points, since every stage is restricted. This proves the equivalence on arbitrary unbounded connective algebras.

The original frame action and frame descent now give \[ \mathcal Z_H^{\rm restr}(X) \simeq[\,\mathcal Y^{\rm restr}/H\,], \qquad \mathcal Y^{\rm restr}\longrightarrow\mathcal Z_H^{\rm restr}(X) \text{ the actual }H\text{-frame torsor}. \tag{RBC.23} \] This is (RSP.9)–(RSP.10) on the actual full DG point functor. Its pullback to any affine is the faithfully flat frame scheme already constructed there. The ind-affine frame presentation is therefore effective, rather than a presentation only of ordinary or bounded coefficient points. The chosen individual Koszul generator tuples need not be \(H\)-stable; (RBC.23) uses the intrinsic action on the whole framed functor and does not assert equivariance of each chosen stage.

3.145. Finiteness of the derived stages

The algebra \(B\) and every \(B_{E,N}\) are compact as connective commutative DG algebras: \[ \operatorname{Map}_{\rm CAlg}(B_{E,N},\operatorname*{colim}_j A_j) \simeq\operatorname*{colim}_j \operatorname{Map}_{\rm CAlg}(B_{E,N},A_j) \quad(j\text{ filtered}). \tag{RBC.24} \] First, the coordinate algebra of the smooth finite-type group \(H\) is compact. Cover it by finitely many principal standard smooth charts. The full Koszul/Jacobian construction in (DCA.15) makes each chart, and each of its finite principal intersections, a finite derived polynomial presentation with inversions. Such a presentation is compact. A free generator in degree \(-a\) has mapping space \(\Omega^\infty A[-a]\), which commutes with filtered coefficient colimits by the finite-data argument of §3.142. Finite cell attachments impose finite homotopy fibres, so the same holds after finitely many of them. Inversion is the finite presentation \(st=1\). Its Koszul resolution is exact because the relevant Jacobian block is invertible.

For a map from a filtered coefficient colimit to \(H\), pull these finitely many chart functions back to the coefficient spectrum. Their finite principal cover, including a finite equation expressing the unit in their ideal, descends to one coefficient stage. The chart maps and their overlap comparisons then descend by compactness of those chart presentations. Descent uses only finitely many homotopy limits: for two opens it is a pullback, and induction on the number of opens expresses a finite cover using its finitely many intersections. The same reasoning applies to any finite sphere or homotopy of maps. This proves compactness of \(\mathcal O(H)\).

Finite colimits of compact algebras are compact, since maps out of them are finite limits and filtered colimits of spaces commute with those. The construction (RBC.7) and iterated loop fibres therefore proves compactness of \(B\). Adjoining the finitely many generators and differentials in (RBC.14) proves (RBC.24).

In particular the stages are almost of finite type in the following explicit sense: \[ H^0(B_{E,N})\text{ is finite type over }\mathbf C,\qquad H^{-a}(B_{E,N})\text{ is a finite }H^0(B_{E,N})\text{-module} \quad(a\geq0). \tag{RBC.25} \] For the cohomology assertion, the relative semifree construction in §3.158 supplies a resolution by nonpositive free commutative DG generators. It is the filtered union of its finite cell subalgebras: the differential of a generator uses finitely many earlier ones, and the closure of a finite set is finite. Indeed an infinite finitely branching dependency tree would have an infinite descending branch, contradicting the well-founded cell order. Compactness makes the identity factor through one such finite subalgebra, so the algebra is a homotopy retract of it. A finite cell algebra has a Noetherian polynomial ring in its degree-zero generators; each fixed negative degree is a finite module over that ring, because there are only finitely many monomials of that total negative degree. Kernels, images and cohomology are finite, and the degree-zero boundary ideal acts trivially on cohomology. For a retract, apply the retraction to finitely many cohomology generators and their coefficients; their images generate over the retracted degree-zero ring. This proves (RBC.25).

The stages also have the precise cotangent bound. At their universal point \(A=B_{E,N}\), equation (RBC.9) identifies the split derivatives of the restricted and Betti functors. The affine cotangent module \(L_{B/\mathbf C}\otimes_B A\) is therefore (DCT.8), of Tor amplitude \([-1,0]\). This identification is of actual connective modules: apply their natural derivation comparisons to every connective ideal \(M\), as in (DCT.9). Adjoining the generators \(\eta_i\) has relative cotangent module \(A^r[1]\), since a relative derivation is freely specified on those degree-minus-one generators. Restriction of derivations gives the cotangent triangle \(L_{B/\mathbf C}\otimes_B A\to L_{A/\mathbf C}\to A^r[1]\). Both outside terms are perfect of Tor amplitude \([-1,0]\); hence so is the middle term. Thus each displayed derived affine stage is quasi-smooth. This concerns the derived stages themselves, not merely their ordinary truncations.

Figure 3.31. The three open discs form a local good-cover model; the global finite complex uses the complete cover of the curve, as in (RBC.1)–(RBC.5). The Betti and coefficient maps are (RBC.6)–(RBC.13). The explicit thickenings, full unbounded comparison and coherent filtered presentation are (RBC.14)–(RBC.25). The last panel shows the exact homotopy-nilpotent example (RBC.37)–(RBC.40), including its nonzero one-step maps and uniform two-step homotopy.

3.146. Projective-line and elliptic line-system charts

Exercise 3.CO. Compute the framed presentation for \(H=\mathbf G_m\) on the projective line and on an elliptic curve. Give an explicit filtered affine presentation in the elliptic case, including its derived mapping data.

Solution 3.CO. The usual stereographic formula identifies \(\mathbf P^1(\mathbf C)\) with the sphere: on its finite chart use \((2\operatorname{Re}z,2\operatorname{Im}z,|z|^2-1)/(1+|z|^2)\), with infinity at the north pole. The inverse stereographic formulas give its two continuous inverse charts. The sphere is a disk with its boundary collapsed, so its framed mapping functor is the derived loop of \(\mathbf G_m\). The identity-point resolution gives \[ B_{\mathbf P^1}=\mathbf C[\xi],\qquad |\xi|=-1,\quad d\xi=0,\quad \xi^2=0 . \tag{RBC.26} \] Its ordinary truncation is already a point. The restricted functor is this entire derived affine, in agreement with (RSC.28).

For an elliptic curve, its complex points are a compact connected commutative real Lie group of dimension two. Its invariant vector fields are complete: local flow existence has a uniform time on finitely many charts covering the compact manifold, and repeated continuation gives every real time. Their commuting flows give a homomorphism \(\mathbf R^2\to X(\mathbf C)\) with invertible differential at zero. Its image is an open subgroup, hence is the whole connected group, and its kernel \(\Lambda\) is discrete. The local inverse makes this map a covering map, with the fibres the translates of \(\Lambda\).

For completeness, discreteness of a subgroup implies that its bounded subsets are finite: an accumulating bounded sequence would give nonzero pairwise differences tending to zero. Choose a shortest nonzero vector \(a\), if one exists. Projection of \(\Lambda\) to the perpendicular line is discrete. Otherwise reduce the parallel coordinates of vectors with perpendicular projections tending to zero modulo \(\mathbf Za\); the resulting vectors lie in a fixed bounded rectangle, contradicting finiteness. If that projection is nonzero, choose \(b\) with its least positive projection, and reduce its parallel coordinate modulo \(a\). Subtracting an integer multiple of \(b\) from any vector leaves zero perpendicular projection, since a positive remainder smaller than this minimum is impossible. The remaining vector is an integer multiple of \(a\), by the minimal length on its line. Thus \(\Lambda\) has rank at most two. Compactness of \(\mathbf R^2/\Lambda\) rules out ranks zero and one, since an unbounded linear coordinate would descend. Hence \(\Lambda\) is a rank-two lattice. Its fundamental parallelogram gives the one-vertex torus CW model with commutator relator.

The commutator of line monodromies is identically one. Its derived fibre is consequently \[ B_{\rm ell}=\mathbf C[u^{\pm1},v^{\pm1},\xi], \qquad |\xi|=-1,\quad d\xi=0,\quad\xi^2=0. \tag{RBC.27} \] For ordinary \(A\), restrictedness says that the image of \(\mathbf C[u^{\pm1},v^{\pm1}]\) is finite-dimensional over the original \(\mathbf C\). This is equivalent to each of the two commuting units satisfying a complex polynomial: reduce all powers to the finitely many monomials below their degrees; negative powers reduce as well because the units' annihilating polynomials have nonzero constant terms after removing zero factors. Factor these polynomials into their nonzero complex roots. Bezout idempotents separate the finitely many root pairs \((\lambda,\mu)\). On each piece the differences \(u-\lambda,v-\mu\) are nilpotent. The proof of (RBC.17) uses only a finitely generated ordinary ideal, so it also applies directly to each root-pair ideal. Thus an explicit filtered presentation uses finite disjoint unions of \[ \begin{gathered} \operatorname{Spec}\left( \left(\mathbf C[u^{\pm1},v^{\pm1}] /((u-\lambda)^N,(v-\mu)^N)\right)[\xi]\right),\\ (\lambda,\mu)\in(\mathbf C^\times)^2 . \end{gathered} \tag{RBC.28} \] The displayed ordinary quotient is used with its full derived mapping spaces. Its polynomial powers form a regular sequence, so an explicit cofibrant presentation over (RBC.27) is \[ B_{\rm ell}[\eta_u,\eta_v],\qquad d\eta_u=(u-\lambda)^N,\quad d\eta_v=(v-\mu)^N, \quad|\eta_u|=|\eta_v|=-1. \tag{RBC.29} \] Thus their nullhomotopies are retained. The ordinary clopen decomposition also retains the full DG coefficient: for an idempotent \(e\in H^0(A)\), choose a closed lift \(a\); the map \(A\to A[a^{-1}]\times A[(1-a)^{-1}]\) is an equivalence, since on every cohomology group it is the splitting by \(e,1-e\). Finite iteration handles all root pairs. Equations (RBC.17) and (RBC.22) therefore identify the entire framed functor, including all negative coefficient directions, with the disjoint union of these formal neighbourhoods carrying the additional generator \(\xi\).

3.147. Surplus stage homotopies and the unbounded limit

Exercise 3.CP. In the elliptic example take \(A=\mathbf C[z]\), \(|z|=-2\), \(dz=0\), and the point \(u=\lambda,v=\mu,\xi=0\). Compute its positive homotopy groups in the full restricted functor. For \(N\geq2\), compute the extra groups at the corresponding point of (RBC.29), and explain their transition.

Solution 3.CP. The unit space of \(A\) is the union of the invertible components of \(\Omega^\infty A\), since a polynomial generator can be inverted exactly when its degree-zero cohomology class is a unit. It therefore has the same positive homotopy groups as this additive mapping space: at a chosen unit the groups are \(H^{-i}(A)\), with multiplication by that unit identifying the tangent coordinates. The free odd generator has mapping complex \(A[-1]\). Thus the chosen full component has \[ \pi_{2r}=\mathbf C^2z^r,\qquad \pi_{2r-1}=\mathbf Cz^r \quad(r\geq1), \qquad \pi_0\text{ one point}. \tag{RBC.30} \] These are the full component's groups, not the derivative's set of first-order components.

For the stage, use the homotopy fibre of the power map \[ (\mathbf G_m(A))^2\longrightarrow(\Omega^\infty A)^2,\qquad (u,v)\longmapsto((u-\lambda)^N,(v-\mu)^N). \tag{RBC.31} \] Its maps on all positive homotopy groups at this point are zero. An even \(2r\)-loop of one unit has representative \(\lambda+z^r\,dt_1\cdots dt_{2r}\); its difference from \(\lambda\) squares to zero, so its \(N\)-th power is zero for \(N\geq2\). The same holds for the other coordinate; the odd groups of the source and target vanish. The fibre long exact sequence, together with the independent \(\xi\)-factor, gives \[ \pi_{2r}T_N(A)=\mathbf C^2z^r,\qquad \pi_{2r-1}T_N(A)=\mathbf C^3z^r\quad(r\geq1). \tag{RBC.32} \] The two additional odd generators are represented by sending \(\eta_u\) or \(\eta_v\) to \(z^r\,dt_1\cdots dt_{2r-1}\) while both unit coordinates are constant. Under \(N\to N'>N\), formula (RBC.15) multiplies them by the positive power of \(u-\lambda\) or \(v-\mu\), and kills them. The unit loops and the \(\xi\)-loops remain. Their colimit is exactly (RBC.30). Thus the affine stage fibres need not be contractible before the filtered colimit, and the unbounded comparison cannot be replaced by discarding higher stage paths.

3.148. A variable character and a restricted polynomial family

Exercise 3.CQ. On the elliptic curve compare the line family \((u,v)=(s,1)\) over \(\mathbf C[s^{\pm1}]\) with the \(SL_2\)-family \[ U=1+bE_{12},\qquad V=1+cE_{12} \quad\text{over }\mathbf C[b,c]. \tag{RBC.33} \] Which lies in the restricted functor?

Solution 3.CQ. The line family does not: its coefficient image contains the linearly independent Laurent monomials \(s^n\), so it is not finite-dimensional over \(\mathbf C\). Nilpotence does not alter this conclusion because the parameter ring is reduced. It is an ordinary point of the full Betti ambient which belongs to no SCI stage or formal completion of one. Every complex specialization is a restricted point; testing those points alone therefore fails to detect this family.

For the matrix family, \(E_{12}^2=0\), and for every pair of integers \[ U^mV^n=1+(mb+nc)E_{12}. \tag{RBC.34} \] The formula for negative integers follows from \((1+bE_{12})^{-1}=1-bE_{12}\). Thus the coefficient functions of the faithful matrix generators lie in the finite subcoalgebra \[ E=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbf C}\{1,m,n\} \subset C_{\mathbf Z^2}. \tag{RBC.35} \] Here \(m,n\) are the two additive functions on the group; their coproducts are primitive and their antipodes are their negatives. The determinant is one, so its inverse coefficient is constant. All the Hopf equations hold by actual multiplication of \(U,V\), and SCI places the family in one finite coefficient stage. This is a restricted family over an infinite-dimensional, reduced parameter ring. Restricted variation does not mean a finite parameter ring or an isotrivial framed family.

3.149. An exact nilpotence threshold

Exercise 3.CR. Let \(A=\mathbf C[\epsilon]/\epsilon^3\), choose nonzero \(\lambda,\mu\), and take \[ u=\lambda(1+\epsilon),\qquad v=\mu(1+2\epsilon),\qquad \xi=0. \tag{RBC.36} \] Find the least common exponent \(N\) for the stage in (RBC.28), and the dimension of its coefficient image over the original complex field.

Solution 3.CR. The squares of the two differences are respectively \(\lambda^2\epsilon^2\) and \(4\mu^2\epsilon^2\), which are nonzero. Their cubes vanish. Thus the least \(N\) is exactly three. Since the target is ordinary, (RBC.29) has no additional choices of degree-minus-one coefficient and no higher mapping paths; its factorization at \(N=3\) is the actual ordinary quotient factorization. The coefficient image contains \(\epsilon=\lambda^{-1}u-1\) and hence \(\epsilon^2\), so it is all of \(A\), of dimension three over \(\mathbf C\). This is the finite-image condition with the nilpotents included.

3.150. A homotopy-nilpotent coefficient with infinitely many layers

Exercise 3.CS. For the formal completion of the affine line at zero, use \(B=\mathbf C[f]\) and the unbounded DG algebra \[ \begin{gathered} A=\mathbf C[t,z]\otimes\Lambda(s,\theta),\\ |t|=0,\quad |z|=-2,\quad |s|=|\theta|=-1,\\ ds=t^2,\quad dt=dz=d\theta=0 . \end{gathered} \tag{RBC.37} \] Map \(f\) to \(t\). Show that \(t\) is nilpotent in cohomology but not in the DG algebra, give compatible nullhomotopies for all \(N\geq2\), and determine whether any stage fibre is already contractible.

Solution 3.CS. Multiplication by \(t^2\) is injective on \(\mathbf C[t,z]\), in each degree. Its two-term Koszul complex with generator \(s\), tensored with \(\Lambda(\theta)\), therefore gives \[ H^*(A)= \bigl(\mathbf C[t]/t^2\bigr) \otimes\mathbf C[z]\otimes\Lambda(\theta). \tag{RBC.38} \] In the underlying graded algebra \(t^N\ne0\) for every \(N\), so strict nilpotence would be false. Nevertheless the stage maps have the compatible representatives \[ \eta_N\longmapsto t^{N-2}s,\qquad d(t^{N-2}s)=t^N . \tag{RBC.39} \] They commute exactly with (RBC.15). Relative to these origins each fibre is \(\Omega^\infty A[-1]\). In even homotopy degree \(2r\), including degree zero, its difference group has basis \(\theta z^r,t\theta z^r\); in odd degree \(2r+1\) it has basis \(z^{r+1},tz^{r+1}\). Thus no stage fibre is contractible. A one-step transition multiplies by \(t\) and is nonzero on each displayed first basis vector. A two-step transition is chain-nullhomotopic, uniformly on the whole complex: \[ d(s\,a)+s\,da=t^2a \qquad(a\in A). \tag{RBC.40} \] The sign follows from \(|s|=-1\). This kills every homotopy group and every difference of components after the same two steps, in all infinitely many coefficient degrees. The fibre colimit is a point, exactly as (RBC.17) requires. This example uses homotopy nilpotence rather than replacing the coefficient model by a strictly truncated algebra.

The framed derived ind-affine presentation and actual full frame quotient are (RBC.22)–(RBC.23), with finite-type derived stages as in (RBC.24)–(RBC.25). RSE.37–RSE.38 and NTR.16 give the subsequent restricted projector and Hecke-lisse image; GFP.55–GFP.56 give its original-complex ind-regularity and nilpotent-support containment. GZR.33 gives equality with all independent nilpotent support over the complex numbers. Extension to the other geometric ground fields retains its requirements. This uses more than the framed presentation above.

For the ind-representability framework see AGKRRV, The stack of local systems with restricted variation and geometric Langlands theory with nilpotent singular support, “Proof of ind-representability.” The effective derived presentation here uses the finite Betti construction, the SCI closed coordinate maps and the explicit Koszul and coherent filtered arguments (RBC.14)–(RBC.22).

3.151. Full restricted embeddings and spaces of isomorphisms

Continue over the complex numbers, with the same smooth projective connected curve, base point and connected reductive group \(H\). Write \(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}\) for the actual restricted stack, \(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm B}\) for the full Betti stack and \(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm dR}\) for the full de Rham stack of §§3.84–3.95. Every affine coefficient algebra is connective and may be unbounded below. The functors \[ i_{\mathrm B}:\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}\longrightarrow\mathcal Z_{\mathrm B}, \qquad i_{\mathrm dR}:\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}\longrightarrow\mathcal Z_{\mathrm dR} \tag{RDI.1} \] are full embeddings of point spaces. For the first, (RBC.4)–(RBC.5) embed the full scalar-action category into derived local systems. For the second, the compact full operator comparison in §3.96 embeds the finite-lisse ind-category into the full operator category. Internal scalar actions retain fullness: the action maps, their module bar and their mapping complexes are computed in the full target, and every term whose underlying object belongs to the ind-image belongs to that image. Tensor diagrams are limits of these full mapping diagrams. Consequently their spaces of tensor functors and tensor equivalences are full as well.

This reasoning also applies without a chosen frame. Alternatively, trivialize both frame torsors on a common faithfully flat cover. Fullness there is (RBC.10) for the Betti target and (DRD.4)–(DRD.7) for the operator target. The full descent of (RSP.8)–(RSP.10) identifies the totalizations of their isomorphism spaces, including all higher paths. Thus for every \(z,w\in\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}(A)\), \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Isom}_{\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}(A)}(z,w) &\simeq \operatorname{Isom}_{\mathcal Z_{\mathrm B}(A)}(i_{\mathrm B}z,i_{\mathrm B}w)\\ &\simeq \operatorname{Isom}_{\mathcal Z_{\mathrm dR}(A)}(i_{\mathrm dR}z,i_{\mathrm dR}w). \end{aligned} \tag{RDI.2} \] These equivalences are natural in the points and in all coefficient maps. They do not identify arbitrary Betti and algebraic de Rham families. Only the two full images of the restricted functor are being compared.

More generally, a full embedding \(i:T\to S\) of space-valued prestacks has a Cartesian square \[ \begin{CD} T @>{i}>> S\\ @V{\Delta_T}VV @VV{\Delta_S}V\\ T\times T @>{i\times i}>> S\times S . \end{CD} \tag{RDI.3} \] Evaluate on any affine. The fibre over a pair of points of \(T\) is their entire path space in \(S\), and fullness identifies it with their path space in \(T\). This proves the square on spaces, so also on every higher simplex. No assertion about the injectivity of a map on ordinary isomorphism classes would suffice.

3.152. The affine restricted diagonal and an explicit fibre algebra

The affine full de Rham diagonal is (CSD.19). Its base change in (RDI.3) proves that \(\Delta_{\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}}\) is affine. There is also an explicit Betti description. Set \[ Y_{\mathrm B}=\operatorname{Spec}B,\qquad \mathcal Z_{\mathrm B}=[Y_{\mathrm B}/H],\qquad \mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}=[Y_{\mathrm r}/H], \tag{RDI.4} \] where (RBC.8) and (RBC.23) give the actual whole point functors. Use the left action \(h\cdot y\), and orient an isomorphism from \(y_1\) to \(y_2\). Pulling the quotient diagonal back to \(Y_{\mathrm B}\times Y_{\mathrm B}\) gives the affine map \[ Y_{\mathrm B}\times H\longrightarrow Y_{\mathrm B}\times Y_{\mathrm B}, \qquad (y,h)\longmapsto(y,h\cdot y). \tag{RDI.5} \] Indeed an isomorphism between the two trivialized \(H\)-torsors is multiplication by one \(h\); compatibility of its maps to \(Y_{\mathrm B}\) is precisely the specified path from \(h\cdot y_1\) to \(y_2\). All paths in that compatibility are retained by the derived fibre product.

For framed restricted \(A\)-points \(y_1,y_2\), the diagonal fibre therefore has coordinate algebra \[ D_{y_1,y_2} = A\underset{B\otimes_{\mathbf C}B}{\otimes^{L}} \bigl(B\otimes_{\mathbf C}\mathcal O(H)\bigr). \tag{RDI.6} \] The second algebra map is the pullback of (RDI.5), and the first is the pair \((y_1,y_2)\). Derived tensor products of connective algebras are connective, by the nonpositive relative semifree construction in §3.158. Hence this is an actual derived affine in the coefficient convention of the lesson.

For general unframed \(z,w\), one may trivialize their frame torsors faithfully flatly and descend (RDI.6). The descent here is effective on algebras, not merely on sets: its underlying complexes descend by (RSP.6)–(RSP.8), and multiplication, unit and every coherent relation descend by the same full mapping-space comparison. Its descended relative spectrum is the diagonal fibre because this is true after the conservative cover. In particular \[ \operatorname{Spec}D_{z,w} \simeq \operatorname{Spec}A \underset{\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}\times\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}}{\times} \mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}. \tag{RDI.7} \] The algebra is independent of the chosen trivializations: its maps to any connective algebra represent the intrinsic space (RDI.2). Changes of frames and their higher comparisons are therefore identified by algebra Yoneda. For every coefficient map \(A\to A'\), including nonflat ones, \[ D_{z,w}\otimes_A^L A' \simeq D_{z_{A'},w_{A'}}. \tag{RDI.8} \] This follows either by associative derived tensor in (RDI.6) and descent, or by base change of the Cartesian square (RDI.7). These are natural equivalences of algebras, not just of their degree-zero cohomology.

3.153. The actual quasicoherent diagonal algebra and adjunction

Let \(\mathcal D_{\mathrm r}\) be the Cartesian quasicoherent algebra on the actual product \(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}\times\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}\) whose value at \((A,z,w)\) is \(D_{z,w}\). Equation (RDI.8) is its scalar compatibility. The general affine-map construction and inverse in (CSD.21)–(CSD.23) give \[ \begin{gathered} \mathcal D_{\mathrm r} \simeq(\Delta_{\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}})_* \mathcal O_{\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}},\\ \operatorname{QCoh}(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}) \simeq \operatorname{Mod}_{\mathcal D_{\mathrm r}} \bigl(\operatorname{QCoh}(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}\times\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r})\bigr). \end{gathered} \tag{RDI.9} \] Here are the maps explicitly. From a quasicoherent object on the diagonal, evaluate it on each actual affine fibre \(\operatorname{Spec}D_{z,w}\) and retain its full module structure. In the other direction, a point \(S=\operatorname{Spec}C\to\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}\) gives a lift of its diagonal pair and hence an algebra map \(D_S\to C\). Send the corresponding \(D_S\)-module \(M_S\) to \[ M_S\otimes_{D_S}^L C . \tag{RDI.10} \] The first inverse comparison is quasicoherent pullback to this lift. On the universal affine fibre the other inverse is the cancellation \[ (M_A\otimes_A^L D_A) \underset{D_A\otimes_A^L D_A}{\otimes^L}D_A \simeq M_A\underset{D_A}{\otimes^L}D_A \simeq M_A . \tag{RDI.11} \] In the first term the first \(D_A\)-action is the given one on \(M_A\), the second comes from scalar extension, and the last algebra map multiplies the two copies. The augmented free-module bar proves the associative cancellation on arbitrary unbounded modules and all mapping complexes. Thus these are coherent inverse functors.

Under (RDI.9), diagonal pullback is free module formation and diagonal pushforward is the forgetful functor. Their free/forgetful adjunction proves \[ \Delta_{\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}}^* \dashv(\Delta_{\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}})_*, \qquad (\Delta_{\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}})_* \text{ preserves all colimits}. \tag{RDI.12} \] Colimits of the Cartesian module data are computed pointwise; their transition functors preserve colimits by derived scalar extension. Forgetting a module therefore preserves these colimits. The same description gives arbitrary derived base change. If \(N\) is quasicoherent on the product and \(M\) is quasicoherent on the diagonal, associative tensor gives the full projection formula \[ N\otimes(\Delta_{\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}})_*M \simeq (\Delta_{\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}})_* \bigl(\Delta_{\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}}^*N\otimes M\bigr). \tag{RDI.13} \] This argument uses the actual product prestack. It requires no equivalence between its quasicoherent category and a tensor product of two global quasicoherent categories.

3.154. The Ran regular algebra on the restricted product

Use the full unital Ran category \(\mathcal R\), its regular algebra \(R_{\mathcal R}\), and the full de Rham spectral functor \(\mathsf L_{\mathrm dR}\) of §§3.84–3.92. Pullback along the actual map in (RDI.1) defines a continuous symmetric monoidal functor \[ \mathsf L_{\mathrm r} =i_{\mathrm dR}^*\mathsf L_{\mathrm dR}: \mathcal R\longrightarrow\operatorname{QCoh}(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}). \tag{RDI.14} \] For each affine restricted point this is the original universal coefficient functor, since its associated flat bundle is the full operator image of that same restricted point. The actual Ran comparisons for all finite-set maps, collisions, units and DG parameters are those of §§3.48–3.74 evaluated on this universal bundle. Pullback preserves their compositions and higher relations. Thus this definition does not replace the restricted target by the full target.

For any prestack \(T\), let \[ \mathrm{ext}_T: \operatorname{QCoh}(T)\otimes\operatorname{QCoh}(T) \longrightarrow\operatorname{QCoh}(T\times T), \qquad M\otimes N\longmapsto p_1^*M\otimes p_2^*N \tag{RDI.15} \] be the canonical continuous exterior functor; no equivalence is included in this notation. Then the actual product has the algebra identity \[ \mathrm{ext}_{\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}} \bigl((\mathsf L_{\mathrm r}\otimes\mathsf L_{\mathrm r}) (R_{\mathcal R})\bigr) \simeq\mathcal D_{\mathrm r}. \tag{RDI.16} \] To prove it with its multiplication and unit, first use the full-target algebra comparison (CSD.15)–(CSD.20) and (GSL.17). Exterior pullback is natural, so the left side of (RDI.16) is the pullback along \(i_{\mathrm dR}\times i_{\mathrm dR}\) of the full diagonal algebra. Its pullback to any affine pair is \(D_{i_{\mathrm dR}z,i_{\mathrm dR}w}\). By (RDI.2)–(RDI.3) and the affine base-change formula, this is \(D_{z,w}\), with its algebra structure. These are precisely the Cartesian values of \(\mathcal D_{\mathrm r}\). Their inverse maps are the natural affine algebra-Yoneda comparisons; hence they agree on all higher coefficient paths and glue.

One can also express this fibre algebra internally in the restricted ind-target. Put \[ Q_{z,w} =\operatorname{mult}(E_z\otimes E_w)(R_{\operatorname{Rep}(H)}) \in\operatorname{CAlg}(\operatorname{Mod}_A(\mathcal I_X)). \tag{RDI.17} \] The regular representation is a filtered union of finite representations, as in §3.78, so it has this actual ind-image. Constant scalar objects belong to \(\operatorname{Mod}_A(\mathcal I_X)\). Fullness of its operator embedding, including internal algebra actions, identifies all maps from \(Q_{z,w}\) to a constant algebra with the corresponding operator-algebra maps. The left adjoint \(L_A\) constructed by the whole free-algebra bar (CSD.9)–(CSD.11) consequently gives \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{CAlg}_A}(L_AQ_{z,w},C) &\simeq \operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{CAlg}(\operatorname{Mod}_A(\mathcal I_X))} (Q_{z,w},\underline C)\\ &\simeq \operatorname{Isom}^{\otimes} (E_w\otimes_A^LC,E_z\otimes_A^LC). \end{aligned} \tag{RDI.18} \] The coefficient \(C\) in this algebra adjunction need not be connective. The fixed restricted point extends its scalar action to \(C\), and the full module/algebra embeddings still compute these spaces. The last equivalence is the full regular-coend reconstruction (SDG.11)–(SDG.15), with the same target-dual orientation. Algebra Yoneda and (CSD.14) yield \[ D_{z,w}\simeq L_AQ_{z,w} \in\operatorname{CAlg}^{\leq0}_A . \tag{RDI.19} \] The entire algebra bar is essential; applying only the underlying linear coinvariant functor would omit its multiplication relations.

The product identity (RDI.16) is distinct from the additional equivalence \[ \operatorname{QCoh}(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}) \underset{\mathcal R}{\otimes} \operatorname{QCoh}(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}) \simeq\operatorname{QCoh}(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm r}). \tag{RDI.20} \] The relative tensor multiplication in (RDI.20) follows from the global quotient exterior comparison and the full regular-algebra identification proved in §§3.167–3.175. The geometric diagonal and its actual-product algebra in this section supply the input to those arguments. The nilpotent projector with its Hecke realization and regularity properties requires further geometric results. The corresponding Ran-diagonal and relative-tensor statements are treated separately in AGKRRV, The stack of local systems with restricted variation and geometric Langlands theory with nilpotent singular support, “Identification of the diagonal” and “Tensor products over representations versus quasicoherent sheaves.”

Figure 3.32. The full embedding square is (RDI.3). The framed fibre algebra and arbitrary derived base change are (RDI.6)–(RDI.8). The algebra on the actual product and its module adjunction are (RDI.9)–(RDI.13), and its Ran image is (RDI.16). The lower examples retain the degree-minus-two diagonal generator and the nonflat Koszul generator in (RDI.21)–(RDI.30).

3.155. A derived diagonal direction on the projective line

Exercise 3.CT. For \(X=\mathbf P^1\) and \(H=\mathbb G_m\), compute the automorphism fibre of the trivial restricted system. Compute its points and positive homotopy groups on \(A=\mathbf C[z]\), \(|z|=-2\).

Solution 3.CT. Equation (RBC.26) gives \(Y_{\mathrm r}=Y_{\mathrm B}=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf C[\xi]\), with \(|\xi|=-1\). Conjugation is trivial for the commutative group. Thus its automorphism fibre at the zero point is \(\mathbb G_m\) times the derived self-intersection of that point in \(Y_{\mathrm B}\). The semifree resolution \[ \bigl(\mathbf C[\xi,w],\ |\xi|=-1,\ |w|=-2,\ dw=\xi\bigr) \longrightarrow\mathbf C \tag{RDI.21} \] is a quasi-isomorphism: \(d(w^n)=n\xi w^{n-1}\), so all \(\xi w^{n-1}\) are boundaries and no positive power of \(w\) is a cycle. Division by \(n\) is legitimate in characteristic zero. Tensoring this resolution with the other copy of \(\mathbf C\) sets \(\xi=0\).
