At \(\psi:I\to J\), replace its parameter category by the transposed lisse coalgebra, and form \[ \mathcal R_{\mathscr I} =\operatorname*{colim}_{\psi:I\to J} \operatorname{Rep}(H)^{\otimes I}\otimes\mathscr I^{\otimes J}. \tag{HLA.23} \] For a transition \((\alpha,\beta)\) the coefficient functor is \(\operatorname{mult}^{\alpha}\otimes\delta_{\mathscr I}^{\beta}\). This is an actual presentable colimit: use the small-relations construction of §3.205 at one common sufficiently large \(\kappa\) for its small diagram of stage functors. The full DG Grothendieck strings retain every transition and higher composition; the specified colimit relations retain each entire stage. Formula (HLA.3) then says that a continuous functor out is exactly a coherent compatible family of continuous stage functors, on all transformation complexes. This construction does not require \(\delta_{\mathscr I}\) to preserve compact objects. Disjoint union of finite sets and exterior tensor of stages gives the continuous symmetric tensor on the colimit: tensor preserves colimits in each variable, and all associativity, symmetry and empty-set maps are the same stage maps and coherent strings.

Equation (HLA.22) gives the actual continuous strong symmetric monoidal functor \[ \begin{gathered} Q_{\mathrm{Ran}}:\mathcal R\longrightarrow\mathcal R_{\mathscr I},\\ \operatorname{ins}_{\psi}(\vec V\otimes N) \longmapsto \operatorname{ins}_{\psi}(\vec V\otimes t^{\otimes J}N). \end{gathered} \tag{HLA.24} \] No localization or fully faithful adjoint for this functor is inferred. Its definition uses all the transition maps of the full source Ran category, including the proper diagonal and projection maps.

Let \(\widehat{\mathrm H}_{\psi}^{\mathrm{Hl}}(\vec V;m)\) denote (HLA.15) with the factors collapsed by the fibres of \(\psi\), inserting units at unused coordinates. It lies in \(\mathcal M^{\mathrm{Hl}}\otimes\mathscr I^{\otimes J}\). The continuous stage operations \[ \begin{aligned} \Phi^{\mathscr I}_\psi(\vec V,Q;m) &=(\operatorname{Id}_{\mathcal M^{\mathrm{Hl}}} \otimes\operatorname{ev}_{\mathscr I^{\otimes J}})\\ &\qquad\bigl(\widehat{\mathrm H}_{\psi}^{\mathrm{Hl}}(\vec V;m)\otimes Q\bigr),\\ \Phi_\psi(\vec V,N;m) &\simeq\Phi^{\mathscr I}_\psi (\vec V,t^{\otimes J}N;m) \end{aligned} \tag{HLA.25} \] use the full evaluation pairing, with the indicated lisse and parameter factors paired coordinatewise. The second line is (HLA.19), extended by the entire exterior bar. It is natural on all unbounded parameters.

For a transition \((\alpha,\beta)\), coefficient collisions give the same multiplication of the lisse-valued Hecke factors as in (RA.8). Moving that multiplication through evaluation gives precisely \(\delta_{\mathscr I}^{\beta}\), by (HLA.20). Thus \[ \Phi^{\mathscr I}_{\psi_2} (\operatorname{mult}^{\alpha}\vec V, \delta_{\mathscr I}^{\beta}Q;m) \simeq\Phi^{\mathscr I}_{\psi_1}(\vec V,Q;m). \tag{HLA.26} \] The equality \(\psi_1=\beta\psi_2\alpha\) has the same variance as (RA.7). Tensor transpose respects all the coherence diagrams; the ambient full Hecke diagrams lift uniquely through (HLA.15). This proves every string comparison in (HLA.26). Apply the actual colimit (HLA.23) after tensoring its stages with \(\mathcal M^{\mathrm{Hl}}\). This gives \[ \begin{gathered} \Phi^{\mathscr I}:\mathcal R_{\mathscr I}\otimes\mathcal M^{\mathrm{Hl}} \longrightarrow\mathcal M^{\mathrm{Hl}},\\ \Phi|_{\mathcal M^{\mathrm{Hl}}} \simeq\Phi^{\mathscr I}(Q_{\mathrm{Ran}}\otimes\operatorname{Id}). \end{gathered} \tag{HLA.27} \] The operation is a continuous unital action. Disjoint unions use the actual independent-coordinate Hecke compositions and the product evaluation; their empty instance is the unit. All associativity and symmetry comparisons are the lifted full Hecke comparisons. This establishes the whole action factorization through the lisse-coefficient Ran category, rather than separate factorizations of isolated point operations.

3.213. The comparison with the restricted spectral category

The actual universal functor \(\mathcal E:\operatorname{Rep}(H)\to\mathcal A\otimes\mathscr I\) in (BLI.16) defines compatible continuous stage functors out of (HLA.23): multiply its coefficient factors along \(\psi\) and evaluate against the full \(Q\in\mathscr I^{\otimes J}\). The same transposition (HLA.20) proves their transition comparisons. Their full colimit gives \[ \begin{gathered} L_{\mathscr I}:\mathcal R_{\mathscr I}\longrightarrow\mathcal A,\\ L_{\mathscr I}(\operatorname{ins}_\psi(\vec V\otimes Q)) =\operatorname{ev}_{\mathscr I^{\otimes J}} (\mathcal E_\psi(\vec V),Q). \end{gathered} \tag{HLA.28} \] This functor is continuous strong symmetric monoidal. On exterior generators its tensor comparison is the symmetric tensor comparison of the universal functor and independent evaluation. Continuity and the full stage bars extend it to all coefficients; the same transition strings give all its coherences. The actual operator-coefficient identification in §3.199 and (HLA.19) identify its composite: \[ L_{\mathscr I}Q_{\mathrm{Ran}}\simeq\mathsf L. \tag{HLA.29} \] This is an equality of the actual full Ran coefficient functors, not merely of their values at ordinary points.

There is a precise conditional consequence. If \(L_{\mathscr I}\) is an equivalence, transport (HLA.27) to a unital \(\mathcal A\)-action on \(\mathcal M^{\mathrm{Hl}}\). The actual geometric idempotent lands there by (BLI.23). Apply (BLI.24) to this full subcategory and the actual composite (HLA.29); it gives \[ \begin{gathered} L_{\mathscr I}\text{ an equivalence}\\ \Longrightarrow\quad \Pi_{\mathrm r}|_{\mathcal M^{\mathrm{Hl}}}\simeq\operatorname{Id},\\ \operatorname{Im}_{\mathrm{full}}(\Pi_{\mathrm r}) =\mathcal M^{\mathrm{Hl}}. \end{gathered} \tag{HLA.30} \] The equivalence hypothesis is a separate spectral comparison theorem. Equations (HLA.23)–(HLA.29) construct its actual source and comparison map; they do not establish that hypothesis. GFP.55–GFP.56 prove original-field ind-regularity and nilpotent-support containment of the full Hecke-lisse category. GZR.31–GZR.33 give the independent nilpotent converse over the complex numbers in every genus. For the lisse-subcategory and spectral-decomposition framework, see The stack of local systems with restricted variation and geometric Langlands theory with nilpotent singular support, the subsection Complements: de Rham and Betti spectral actions.

Figure 3.38. Coreflection and coordinate intersection are (HLA.4)–(HLA.9). The full kernel, all-coordinate operations and Ran stability are (HLA.10)–(HLA.16). The precise coefficient pairing, transposed collision maps and coefficient action are (HLA.17)–(HLA.27). The spectral comparison and conditional image statement are (HLA.28)–(HLA.30). Solutions 3.DM–3.DO distinguish actual membership, compactness of the diagonal and full faithfulness.

3.214. Two independent torsion directions with unbounded coefficients

Exercise 3.DM. Work over \(R=\mathbf C[s,t]\), with the two independent torsion coreflectors. Put \[ \begin{gathered} C_s=\operatorname{fib}(\mathbf C[s]\to\mathbf C[s,s^{-1}]),\qquad C_t=\operatorname{fib}(\mathbf C[t]\to\mathbf C[t,t^{-1}]),\\ T=\mathbf C[z,z^{-1}],\quad |z|=-2,\qquad K=C_s\otimes_{\mathbf C}C_t\otimes_{\mathbf C}T,\\ Z=K\oplus(R[s^{-1}]\oplus R[t^{-1}])\otimes_{\mathbf C}T. \end{gathered} \tag{HLA.31} \] Compute the joint coreflection of \(Z\), the cohomology of \(K\), and whether \(Z\) itself belongs to either individual torsion image. Retain the actual derived tensor and every integer power of \(z\).

Solution 3.DM. Tensoring the two fibre triangles gives the total Čech complex \(R\to R[s^{-1}]\oplus R[t^{-1}]\to R[s^{-1},t^{-1}]\), in degrees zero, one and two. Its first map is the pair of restrictions and its second map is their difference; the composite is zero. The kernel at degree zero is zero. At degree one, two Laurent polynomials with equal image have only nonnegative powers in both variables and hence come from the same element of \(R\). Its last cokernel is the span of the monomials with both exponents strictly negative. Thus \[ H^{2-2r}(K) =\bigoplus_{a,b\geq1}\mathbf C\,s^{-a}t^{-b}z^r \quad(r\in\mathbf Z), \qquad H^j(K)=0\quad(j\text{ odd}). \tag{HLA.32} \] Tensor over the coefficient field is exact on complexes, so the Laurent-coefficient direct sum introduces no hidden derived terms. It has nonzero cohomology in arbitrarily positive and negative even degrees.

Write \(\Gamma_s(M)=C_s\otimes_{\mathbf C[s]}^LM\), and similarly for \(t\). They commute by tensor associativity with its actual symmetry maps. On \(K\), their counits are both equivalences, since localization in either variable is zero. On \(R[s^{-1}]\) the \(s\)-coreflection is zero, and on \(R[t^{-1}]\) the \(t\)-coreflection is zero. The other individual coreflections of these two summands are nonzero principal-part complexes. It follows that \[ \begin{gathered} \Gamma_s\Gamma_t Z\simeq\Gamma_t\Gamma_s Z\simeq K\ne0,\\ Z\notin\operatorname{Im}(\Gamma_s),\quad Z\notin\operatorname{Im}(\Gamma_t). \end{gathered} \tag{HLA.33} \] For example the localization of \(Z\) at \(s\) retains its nonzero \(R[s^{-1}]\otimes T\) summand, so the \(s\)-counit cannot be an equivalence. The corresponding argument applies at \(t\). Hence a nonzero joint coreflection is not a membership test. The criterion (HLA.8) requires every coordinate counit to be an equivalence, and then gives the full object, not merely a nonzero part.

3.215. The transposed diagonal on the projective line

Exercise 3.DN. On \(X=\mathbf P^1\), use the actual monoidal model (RSC.17)–(RSC.18): \[ \begin{gathered} \mathscr I_X=\operatorname{Mod}_E, \qquad E=\mathbf C[\eta]/(\eta^2),\quad |\eta|=2,\\ R=E\otimes E=\mathbf C[x,y]/(x^2,y^2),\quad |x|=|y|=2. \end{gathered} \tag{HLA.34} \] Identify \(\delta_{\mathscr I}(\mathbf1)\), decide whether it is compact, and compare it with \(\Delta_*\omega_X\). Explain what this says about compactness of the right adjoint \(g\).

Solution 3.DN. The monoidal product on \(\operatorname{Mod}_E\) is derived tensor over \(E\), and its pairing (HLA.17) is the underlying complex of that tensor. The full module bar therefore identifies its categorical self-duality with the usual module duality: evaluation is balanced tensor over \(E\), and coevaluation is the diagonal \(E\)-bimodule. Multiplication \(\operatorname{Mod}_R\to\operatorname{Mod}_E\) is extension along \(R\to E\), \(x,y\mapsto\eta\). Its transpose is restriction along this map, by the balanced evaluation formula on free generators and then all module bars. Consequently \(\delta_{\mathscr I}(\mathbf1)\) is the actual diagonal module \(E=R/(x-y)\).

It has an explicit full semifree resolution. Let \(P=\bigoplus_{n\geq0}Re_n\), \(|e_n|=n\), map \(e_0\) to \(1\in E\), and set \[ de_0=0,\qquad de_n= \begin{cases} (x-y)e_{n-1},&n\text{ odd},\\ (x+y)e_{n-1},&n\text{ even},\ n>0. \end{cases} \qquad P\xrightarrow{\sim}E. \tag{HLA.35} \] The differential has degree one, since the coefficients have degree two, and its square is zero because \((x-y)(x+y)=0\) in \(R\). To prove exactness, use the basis \(1,x,y,xy\). The kernel of multiplication by \(x-y\) is spanned by \(x+y,xy\), which is the ideal generated by \(x+y\). The other kernel is the ideal generated by \(x-y\). The augmentation kernel is that same latter ideal. Thus the alternating graded free resolution is exact. Each total cohomological degree has only finitely many terms, so this calculation also proves the asserted quasi-isomorphism of its total complex; no convergence of an infinite product is being used.

After derived scalar extension \(R\to\mathbf C\), \(x,y\mapsto0\), all displayed differentials are zero. Hence \[ E\otimes_R^L\mathbf C =\bigoplus_{n\geq0}\mathbf C[-n], \qquad H^n(E\otimes_R^L\mathbf C)=\mathbf C \quad(n\geq0). \tag{HLA.36} \] A perfect \(R\)-module would become a finite perfect complex over \(\mathbf C\), which has bounded cohomology. Thus this diagonal module is not perfect or compact, whereas the unit \(E\) is compact in \(\operatorname{Mod}_E\). The transposed coproduct does not preserve compact objects in this example.

The ambient diagonal object \(\Delta_*\omega_X\) is nonzero and supported on the diagonal in \(X^2\). It is not in the full image of \(\mathscr I_X^{\otimes2}\): objects in that image are ind-complexes of external finite connections, whose cohomology is locally constant on an analytic product ball, while this object vanishes off the diagonal and has a nonzero diagonal stalk. For the local-constancy assertion, trivialize the finite connections on such a ball and use the full local Spencer comparison; their maps and ind-colimits give complexes of constant vector spaces there. This is also the chartwise ind-regular comparison in §§3.55–3.56. The coalgebra comparison instead says precisely \[ (g\otimes g)(\Delta_*\omega_X) \simeq\delta_{\mathscr I}(\mathbf1)[-2]=E[-2] \quad\text{in }\operatorname{Mod}_R. \tag{HLA.37} \] The left-hand input is compact in the full operator category, since the normalized unit is compact and proper diagonal direct image preserves compact objects by (RN.5)–(RN.6). Its displayed image is not compact. In particular \(g\) cannot preserve all compact objects: otherwise \(g\otimes g\) would preserve the exterior compact generators and their finite-cell closure, hence every compact product object. This explains why the full presentation in (HLA.23) uses sufficiently large \(\kappa\)-compact objects, and why the ambient diagonal cannot simply be restricted to the lisse subcategory.

3.216. Idempotence alone does not prove full faithfulness

Exercise 3.DO. Let \(\mathcal C=\operatorname{Vect}\times\operatorname{Vect}\). Define continuous DG functors \[ \begin{gathered} L(U,V)=U,\qquad G(U)=(U,U),\\ F=GL,\qquad LG=\operatorname{Id},\quad F^2=F. \end{gathered} \tag{HLA.38} \] Does it follow that \(G\) is fully faithful, or that \(F\) is the identity on its full essential image? Compute full mapping complexes to decide.

Solution 3.DO. A map in \(\mathcal C\) is an independent pair. Thus \[ \begin{gathered} \operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal C}(G(U),G(V)) =\operatorname{RHom}(U,V)\oplus\operatorname{RHom}(U,V),\\ G(f)=(f,f). \end{gathered} \tag{HLA.39} \] For nonzero \(U=V=\mathbf C\), the degree-zero map \((\operatorname{Id},0)\) is not in the diagonal image. Hence \(G\) is not full. Its full essential image consists of pairs whose two components are isomorphic, but its maps include all independent pairs between such objects. On the particular endomorphism just found, \[ F(\operatorname{Id},0) =(\operatorname{Id},\operatorname{Id}) \ne(\operatorname{Id},0). \tag{HLA.40} \] There cannot even be a natural equivalence between this restriction of \(F\) and the identity: conjugating the nonzero projection \((\operatorname{Id},0)\) by an equivalence of its two components cannot turn it into an identity on both components. This example satisfies all three functor relations in (HLA.38) strictly and disproves the claimed inference from those relations alone. It is a categorical test of insufficient hypotheses, not a model for the geometric Hecke action. In (HLA.30), full membership, actual action factorization and the specified module natural maps are precisely the additional data that yield the identity on the full subcategory.

3.217. A local Koszul criterion from a residue cotangent fibre

The local model in §3.196 has a useful residue-fibre formulation. Suppose that \(A\) is a connective complex commutative DG algebra, with \[ \begin{gathered} R=H^0(A)\text{ finite type},\qquad H^{-j}(A)\text{ finite over }R\quad(j\geq0),\\ L_{A/\mathbf C}\text{ perfect},\qquad H^r(L_{A/\mathbf C}\otimes_A^L k(x))=0\quad(r\notin\{-1,0\}) \end{gathered} \tag{RSE.1} \] at a closed point \(x\). Then a principal neighbourhood of \(x\) has an actual finite exterior Koszul model.

Here is the construction, with only the displayed fibre bound as input. Choose a finite polynomial algebra \(P\to A\) surjective on \(H^0\). Add finite degree-minus-one generators whose differentials generate its kernel ideal, together with finite closed degree-minus-one generators hitting \(H^{-1}(A)\). Noetherian finiteness and the full semifree construction are those of §§3.158 and 3.196. Complete the resolution using cells of degrees at most minus two. In the residue cotangent fibre let \(W\) be its finite degree-minus-one generator space, let \(J\) be the image from degree minus two, and choose a constant complement \(U\). Finitely many degree-minus-two differentials span \(J\). They are literal polynomial syzygies \(\sum_j a_{\ell j}f_j=0\), because the only degree-minus-one monomials are the original generators.

Invert the determinant of their \(J\)-coefficient block. Those syzygies express the discarded differentials in terms of the ones belonging to \(U\). The finite Koszul algebra \(B_0=P_\Delta[U]\) has the same \(H^0\) as \(A_\Delta\). Its cotangent map at the point is the two-term complex \([U\to\mathbf C^{\dim P}]\) mapping to the full cotangent fibre. It has the same degree-zero cokernel and degree-minus-one kernel; every other target fibre cohomology vanishes by (RSE.1). The relative cotangent module is perfect and has zero residue fibre. Apply the identity-based local vanishing lemma (BLI.2), and shrink once more. The relative cotangent module is zero. The full first-difference criterion (BLI.4) then gives \[ A[f^{-1}]\simeq P'[\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_r],\qquad |\epsilon_i|=-1,\quad d\epsilon_i=g_i\in P',\qquad f(x)\ne0, \tag{RSE.2} \] where \(P'\) is a localization of the finite polynomial algebra. All maps are actual DG algebra maps. No regular-sequence hypothesis is imposed.

If the fibre hypothesis holds at every closed point, these principal opens cover the entire spectrum. Otherwise their closed complement would have a closed complex point by the proved Nullstellensatz. A finite subcover exists by quasi-compactness. The largest exterior length gives \[ H^j(A)=0\quad(j<-N_A) \text{ for one finite }N_A. \tag{RSE.3} \] If \(H^0(A)=0\), its unit is a boundary and the algebra is contractible, as in §3.197. Thus the empty case is included. The argument uses perfectness globally and the cotangent amplitude only at each chosen residue point; it does not assume a global Tor bound in advance.

3.218. Finiteness and perfect cotangent of the full Betti algebra

Let \(\mathcal Y_{\mathrm B}=\operatorname{Spec}B\) be the actual full framed Betti functor (RBC.6)–(RBC.8), constructed from the finite pointed good-cover model \(K\). Compactness of \(B\) as a connective commutative algebra is (RBC.24). In a semifree resolution, its identity factors through a finite cell subalgebra, by that compactness. Thus there are actual maps in the derived algebra category \[ B\xrightarrow{s}Q\xrightarrow{r}B, \qquad rs\simeq\operatorname{Id}_B, \qquad Q\text{ a finite cell algebra}. \tag{RSE.4} \] The finite-dependency argument in §3.145 ensures that the chosen cell subalgebra really is finite. The same Noetherian fixed-degree calculation there, followed by the cohomology retraction, gives \[ H^0(B)\text{ finite type over }\mathbf C,\qquad H^{-j}(B)\text{ finite over }H^0(B)\quad(j\geq0). \tag{RSE.5} \] Indeed a finite cell algebra has finitely many monomials of each fixed negative total degree over its degree-zero polynomial ring. Its kernels, images and cohomology are finite modules. The boundary ideal acts trivially on cohomology. Apply \(r\) to those finitely many module generators and their coefficients; the results generate over the retracted degree-zero ring. This proves the assertion for the full algebra, not just its restricted power stages.

Cotangent functoriality in (RSE.4) gives \[ L_{B/\mathbf C}\longrightarrow B\otimes_Q^L L_{Q/\mathbf C}\longrightarrow L_{B/\mathbf C}, \qquad\text{composite }\simeq\operatorname{Id}. \tag{RSE.6} \] For the first map, base-change the derivative of \(s\) along \(r\); the second is the derivative of \(r\). Their composite is the derivative of \(rs\). The middle module is perfect because a finite cell algebra has a finite free-cell cotangent module. Perfect modules are closed under retracts, so the full cotangent complex of \(B\) is perfect.

3.219. Closed complex points and their entire cotangent fibres

Every closed point of \(\operatorname{Spec}H^0(B)\) has residue field \(\mathbf C\). At such a point the associated functor sends a finite representation to a local system with finite-dimensional fibre in degree zero. All its transports have that same finite perfect fibre. The full bounded comparison (RBC.3) identifies these objects and all their maps with bounded finite-connection complexes. Hence its finite representation values, tensor maps and higher comparisons lift through the full embedding (RBC.4). The full representation bar extends that lift to every representation, and the chosen frame is retained. This proves \[ \mathcal Y^{\mathrm{restr}}(\mathbf C) \xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal Y_{\mathrm B}(\mathbf C). \tag{RSE.7} \] This is a statement about the original coefficient field. It does not say that every affine family has restricted variation. A variable ordinary character on an elliptic curve, as in §3.147 and Solution 3.DP below, distinguishes those assertions.

At each of these points use the full nilpotent lift comparison (RBC.9) on every connective square-zero ideal. It identifies the entire derivative of the full Betti functor with the restricted framed derivative. Equations (DCT.8)–(DCT.12) consequently give \[ L_{B/\mathbf C}\otimes_B^L\mathbf C \simeq K_F^\vee[-1],\qquad H^j(K_F^\vee[-1])=0\quad(j\notin\{-1,0\}). \tag{RSE.8} \] The shift is the actual framing shift: \(K_F\) is the fibre of the adjoint connection cohomology map to its value at the framed point. Its adjoint de Rham complex has degrees zero through two, and evaluation of a horizontal section is injective in degree zero. Dualizing its fibre removes the extra upper degree exactly as in §3.131. The comparison on all square-zero ideals proves an equality of full cotangent fibres, rather than just an equality of classical tangent spaces.

3.220. A bounded quasi-smooth full Betti ambient

Apply §§3.217–3.219 to \(B\). A finite principal-open cover has the actual local models \[ B[f_\alpha^{-1}] \simeq P_\alpha[\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_{r_\alpha}], \qquad |\epsilon_i|=-1,\quad d\epsilon_i\in P_\alpha. \tag{RSE.9} \] For each such algebra its cotangent module is the finite two-term Jacobian complex with free relative generators in degrees minus one and zero. It therefore has Tor amplitude \([-1,0]\). These localizations cover \(\operatorname{Spec}H^0(B)\), so localization of a tensor with any ordinary coefficient module detects vanishing outside those two degrees. Hence \[ L_{B/\mathbf C}\text{ is perfect of Tor amplitude }[-1,0]. \tag{RSE.10} \] The largest of the finitely many exterior lengths also proves \[ H^j(B)=0\quad(j<-N_B\text{ or }j>0) \quad\text{for some finite }N_B. \tag{RSE.11} \] Thus the actual full framed Betti affine is quasi-smooth, cohomologically bounded and almost of finite type. The argument does not use a classification of surfaces or a punctured-curve bouquet presentation. Products with the ordinary smooth group \(H^s\) remain bounded, since tensoring over the coefficient field with its ordinary coordinate algebra is flat. The full unframed Betti prestack is \(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm B}=[\mathcal Y_{\mathrm B}/H]\): forgetting the frame has the same actual faithfully flat frame torsor and whole action nerve as in (RBC.23), now for the full Betti functor.

3.221. Full derived local systems with arbitrary categorical coefficients

Write \(\mathcal L=\operatorname{Fun}(K,\operatorname{Mod}_{\mathbf C})\). Evaluation at the chosen point has a left adjoint \(a_x\), given by left Kan extension. Its fibre at a point \(y\) is the coefficient complex tensored with the chains of paths from \(x\) to \(y\). Since \(K\) is connected, evaluation is conservative, and it preserves all colimits because those are pointwise. The free-action bar of this adjunction has an extra unit degeneracy after evaluation. Its augmentation therefore becomes an equivalence there and hence is an equivalence in \(\mathcal L\). This proves the full module model \[ \mathcal L\simeq\operatorname{Mod}_{R_K},\qquad R_K=C_*(\Omega(K,x),\mathbf C). \tag{RSE.12} \] Here cohomological chains have nonpositive degrees; multiplication is actual loop composition with its full bar coherences. The same bar proves the mapping-complex comparison, so the assertion includes all derived actions. The object \(a_x(\mathbf C)\) is compact, since its Hom functor is evaluation, and it generates by that conservativity.

For any presentable \(\mathbf C\)-linear DG category \(\mathcal T\), the same free-action bars give \[ \mathcal T\otimes\mathcal L \simeq\operatorname{Mod}_{R_K}(\mathcal T) \simeq\operatorname{Fun}(K,\mathcal T). \tag{RSE.13} \] The first comparison identifies the free \(R_K\)-action in each variable; the relative tensor and free-forgetful bars have identical faces and contracting augmentations. The second uses the point-evaluation adjunction just described, now with values in \(\mathcal T\). It is valid without assuming \(\mathcal T\) dualizable. If \(\mathcal T\) is symmetric monoidal, the pointwise tensor has the loop-diagonal action on both sides, so this comparison retains the symmetric tensor and its unit.

The compact-generator dual construction (SUL.22) applies to \(\mathcal L\). Moreover (RBC.3)–(RBC.4) embeds \(\mathscr I\) fully with compact images: the finite-CW Hom proof in §3.137 supplies the required compactness. Its entire right adjoint is therefore continuous by the coend argument of (HLA.4). We obtain \[ i_\infty:\mathscr I\hookrightarrow\mathcal L, \qquad i_\infty\dashv g_\infty,\quad g_\infty i_\infty=\operatorname{Id}, \qquad \mathcal L\text{ dualizable}. \tag{RSE.14} \] All tensor extensions of this inclusion remain full, with the actual counit test, as in (HLA.6). No identification of the entire ind-category with its completion is used.

3.222. Regular frames and full categorical descent

We need an explicit change-of-frame construction. Let \(\mathcal C\) be a presentable symmetric monoidal DG category equipped with a continuous strong symmetric monoidal functor \(u:\operatorname{Rep}(H)\to\mathcal C\), and put \(S=u(\mathcal O(H))\). The regular algebra has left translation as a representation and the commuting right-translation coaction. Complete reducibility and evaluation at the identity give \[ \mathcal O(H)\simeq\bigoplus_{V\text{ simple}}V^\vee\otimes V, \qquad \mathbf C\longrightarrow\mathcal O(H) \xrightarrow{\lambda}\mathbf C, \quad\lambda(1)=1. \tag{RSE.15} \] To check the multiplicity, an equivariant map from a simple \(V\) to regular functions is determined by evaluation at the identity; its inverse takes a functional to its matrix coefficient. This proves the displayed decomposition from complete reducibility, including the matrix-coalgebra coactions. Projection to the trivial component is \(\lambda\); it is compatible with the commuting translation. Complete reducibility and its extension from the semisimple Lie algebra and central torus to the connected reductive group are proved in Lesson 2, §4.5, using the Weyl–Casimir and trace-form arguments of The Killing form and Cartan's criteria, Theorem 3.3, and Complete reducibility: Casimir elements and Weyl's theorem, §§2–4. Rational representations are filtered unions of their finite-dimensional subrepresentations, so the decomposition extends to them.

Applying \(u\) gives a retraction of \(\mathbf1_{\mathcal C}\to S\). Thus \(S\otimes-\) is conservative: every input and every morphism fibre is a retract of its tensor with \(S\). The regular torsor identity is \[ S\otimes S\simeq S\otimes_{\mathbf C}\mathcal O(H), \tag{RSE.16} \] with the first \(S\)-action and the right \(H\)-coaction. It is the image of the Hopf map corresponding to \((g,h)\mapsto(g,g^{-1}h)\), with its inverse. The antipode identities verify both composites; these are the full Hopf identities of (TBF.2)–(TBF.5).

There is an actual equivalence \[ \mathcal C\xrightarrow{\sim} (\operatorname{Mod}_S(\mathcal C))^H, \qquad c\longmapsto S\otimes c, \tag{RSE.17} \] where equivariance is the algebraic right-translation descent data. Here is a direct proof on the full categories. The matrix-coalgebra decomposition in (RSE.15) makes rational \(H\)-objects a sum of their isotypic components, also with coefficients in \(\mathcal C\): apply the coalgebra projections to the coaction and split the resulting orthogonal idempotents. Coassociativity and the counit identify their sum with the original object. Extracting the trivial component is consequently exact and continuous and commutes with tensoring by any independently trivially acted-on object.

For an equivariant \(S\)-module \(M\), take \(M^H\) and the natural map \(S\otimes M^H\to M\). After tensoring with an independent first copy of \(S\), (RSE.16) reduces this map to the ordinary Hopf-module identity over \(\mathcal O(H)\). Explicitly, if \(\rho(m)=\sum m_0\otimes m_1\), the projector onto invariant vectors is \(m\mapsto\sum\operatorname{ant}(m_1)m_0\). Coassociativity and the two antipode identities show that its coaction is trivial and that it fixes every invariant. Multiplication and the inverse map \(m\mapsto\sum m_1\otimes\operatorname{proj}(m_0)\) are inverse. These formulas are compositions of the actual action and coaction morphisms and therefore make sense in the coefficient category; they commute with differentials and all maps. Invariants commute with this independent base change by the preceding trivial-component calculation. Conservativity of \(S\otimes-\) proves the original map an equivalence. Conversely \((S\otimes c)^H=c\) by (RSE.15). These natural inverse functors prove (RSE.17), including full mapping complexes and the entire coaction nerve.

Finally the full free-module bar gives the symmetric monoidal framing identity \[ \operatorname{Vect}\underset{\operatorname{Rep}(H)}\otimes\mathcal C \simeq\operatorname{Mod}_S(\mathcal C). \tag{RSE.18} \] For \(\mathcal C=\operatorname{Rep}(H)\), (RSE.17) on the trivial regular torsor is the Hopf-module equivalence \(\operatorname{Mod}_{\mathcal O(H)}(\operatorname{Rep}(H))=\operatorname{Vect}\). Base-change its complete free \(\mathcal O(H)\)-module bar along \(u\). The resulting monad is \(S\otimes-\), and its free-forgetful augmentation identifies its entire category with \(\operatorname{Mod}_S(\mathcal C)\). This proves (RSE.18) on all objects and maps. A continuous strong symmetric monoidal functor from that category to a target \(\mathcal T\) is equivalently such a functor \(F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal T\) together with an algebra map \(F(S)\to\mathbf1_{\mathcal T}\). Relative tensor with that augmentation constructs it, and the same free bar proves uniqueness. The regular torsor identity turns this augmentation into a tensor trivialization \(F u(V)\simeq\underline V\otimes\mathbf1_{\mathcal T}\), and conversely the trivialization gives evaluation at the identity. Thus (RSE.18) has the actual universal property of a chosen frame.

3.223. The full framed Betti comparison

Construct \(\mathcal R_{\mathcal L}\) by the same finite-point DG relations as in §§3.205 and 3.212, using the coalgebra dual to the pointwise tensor of \(\mathcal L\). Its coefficient category is \(\mathcal L^\vee\); no self-duality defined by ordinary global sections is assumed. The full tensor universal property (SDG.4), with this duality in each parameter, identifies its continuous strong symmetric monoidal functors to \(\mathcal T\) with such functors \(\operatorname{Rep}(H)\to\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal L\). To verify the identification, transpose a one-point functor along evaluation and coevaluation. Transposing the collision relation gives its tensor comparison; the empty-point relation gives its unit. The finite-point bar supplies their associativity, permutation and higher comparisons. Conversely these comparisons define compatible functors on every finite-point term. Evaluation–coevaluation cancellation proves both composites on that entire bar. This argument uses the large-cardinal relation construction, and imposes no compact-preservation condition on the transposed collision maps.

Evaluation at the chosen point gives \(\operatorname{Rep}(H)\to\mathcal R_{\mathcal L}\). Let \(\mathcal R_{\mathcal L}^{\mathrm{fr}}\) be its framing by (RSE.18). For any target \(\mathcal T\), put \(D=\operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal T}(\mathbf1,\mathbf1)\), with its commutative algebra structure from tensoring endomorphisms of the unit. For every connective commutative algebra \(A\) there is an equivalence of spaces \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Fun}^{L,\otimes}(\operatorname{Mod}_A,\mathcal T) &\simeq\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{CAlg}}(A,D)\\ &\simeq\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{CAlg}}(A,\tau^{\leq0}D). \end{aligned} \tag{RSE.19} \] Indeed such a functor takes the free rank-one module to the unit and gives the displayed endomorphism map. Conversely that map makes the unit an \(A\)-module; the functor is \(M\mapsto M\otimes_A^L\mathbf1\). The entire free-module bar proves that these are inverse, including natural transformations and higher paths. Its relative tensor comparisons give the strong symmetric monoidal structure. For the second equivalence, a nonpositive semifree algebra resolution of \(A\) tests only the nonpositive good truncation of \(D\), including degree-zero cycles. The same assertion for its full simplicial mapping resolution proves the equivalence of spaces, not just their components.

By (RSE.13), a framed coefficient functor here is a tensor functor into \(\operatorname{Fun}(K,\mathcal T)\) whose value at the base point is \(V\mapsto\underline V\otimes\mathbf1\). Since \(K\) is connected, its transports are tensor automorphisms of this fixed functor. Mapping complexes between finite sums of the unit are the corresponding matrices over \(D\). The coefficient reconstruction (TBF.2)–(TBF.5) identifies their tensor automorphism group with \(H(\tau^{\leq0}D)\): the matrix-coordinate equations, inverse matrices and Hopf identities are the same equations in these endomorphisms. Their derived mapping resolutions give all paths and coherences. Thus \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Fun}^{L,\otimes}(\mathcal R_{\mathcal L}^{\mathrm{fr}},\mathcal T) &\simeq \operatorname{Map}_*(K,BH(\tau^{\leq0}D))\\ &=\mathcal Y_{\mathrm B}(\tau^{\leq0}D)\\ &=\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{CAlg}}(B,\tau^{\leq0}D). \end{aligned} \tag{RSE.20} \] All representations are included by their finite-representation bars. A frame fixes the tensor functor at the base point together with that identification; it is precisely the based mapping space, rather than an unframed quotient or its set of isomorphism classes.

Compare (RSE.19) for \(A=B\) with (RSE.20). The tautological framed Betti coefficient functor consequently induces an equivalence \[ \mathcal R_{\mathcal L}^{\mathrm{fr}} \xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Mod}_B. \tag{RSE.21} \] For completeness the representability argument gives an inverse without testing only affine scalar targets: take \(\mathcal T=\mathcal R_{\mathcal L}^{\mathrm{fr}}\) in the equivalence of functor spaces to produce an inverse on one side. Take \(\mathcal T=\operatorname{Mod}_B\) and use full faithfulness of the same equivalence to identify the other composite with the identity. Thus arbitrary categorical targets are essential in this argument.

3.224. Unframed Betti descent

Write \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm B}=\operatorname{QCoh}(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm B})\). The actual full frame quotient gives \[ \mathcal A_{\mathrm B} \simeq (\operatorname{Mod}_B)^H, \qquad\mathcal Z_{\mathrm B}=[\operatorname{Spec}B/H]. \tag{RSE.22} \] The notation on the right includes the algebraic action on \(B\), modules with compatible coaction, and the whole action nerve. It is not invariance under the abstract group of complex points. The universal framed coefficient functor descends along this nerve to \(\operatorname{Rep}(H)\to\mathcal A_{\mathrm B}\otimes\mathcal L\). Tensoring by \(\mathcal L\) commutes with these limits by its dualizability, so this descent retains the coefficient category. The universal property of §3.223 constructs the actual continuous strong symmetric monoidal comparison \[ L_{\mathrm B}:\mathcal R_{\mathcal L} \longrightarrow\mathcal A_{\mathrm B}. \tag{RSE.23} \]

Its framing is exactly (RSE.21), equivariantly for the entire algebraic \(H\)-action. To check this assertion, changing the frame multiplies the universal matrix coordinates by the regular Hopf coaction. On both sides the coaction is the matrix-coordinate map in (TBF.2)–(TBF.5). Repeating it \(s\) times gives the same maps over \(\mathcal O(H)^{\otimes s}\); the coproduct, counit and antipode give the same faces, degeneracies and inverse comparisons. The representing property (RBC.6) on every connective algebra identifies these maps on \(B\), and (RSE.19) identifies the induced functors on its modules. This verifies algebraic equivariance at all nerve levels, including derived paths.

Apply (RSE.17) to \(\mathcal R_{\mathcal L}\) and then use this equivariant framed equivalence. Together with (RSE.22) it proves \[ L_{\mathrm B}:\mathcal R_{\mathcal L} \xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal A_{\mathrm B}. \tag{RSE.24} \] The equivalence is on full unbounded DG categories, with their symmetric tensor structures. Every descent step was made on the actual frame nerve.

3.225. The supported kernel and all its residue generators

Let \(R=H^0(B)\) and let \(S\subset\operatorname{Spec}R\) be the union of the ordinary closed coefficient loci \(Z_E\) of §§3.138–3.146. This union is stable under specialization and under the frame action. The unbounded Koszul comparison (KTC.1)–(KTC.28) and the supported-union comparison (SUL.1)–(SUL.21) give the actual framed restricted category \(\mathcal T_S\subset\operatorname{Mod}_B\). Its continuous smashing coreflector is \(\Gamma_S=C_S\otimes_B-\). Write \(Q_S=\operatorname{cofib}(\Gamma_S\to\operatorname{Id})\). Its image is the kernel of \(\Gamma_S\).

The boundedness (RSE.11) supplies a finite Postnikov filtration of \(B\), as a \(B\)-module, with layers the \(R\)-modules \(H^{-j}(B)[j]\). For an arbitrary unbounded \(B\)-module \(M\), tensor that finite filtration with \(M\). Therefore \[ M\text{ is a finite extension of }i_*N_j,\qquad N_j=H^{-j}(B)[j]\otimes_B^L M\in\operatorname{Mod}_R, \quad 0\leq j\leq N_B, \tag{RSE.25} \] where \(i_*\) forgets the \(R\)-module structure along \(B\to R\). These \(N_j\) can be unbounded. No Postnikov convergence claim about \(M\) is used. Localization at each degree-zero generator commutes with \(i_*\); the finite Koszul fibres and their filtered unions consequently give \(Q_S i_*=i_*Q_S^R\).

The finite-type ring \(R\) is Noetherian of finite dimension. The complete residue-generation proof (FE.5) constructs \(R\) from all its residue fields by colimits and cones. Tensor that construction with any unbounded \(R\)-module \(N\). Each \(k(p)\otimes_R^L N\) is a complex of vector spaces over \(k(p)\), hence a sum of shifts of that field after splitting cycles and boundaries. Thus all these residue fields generate the full \(\operatorname{Mod}_R\). Their support tests are exact: \[ Q_S^R k(p)= \begin{cases}0,&p\in S,\\ k(p),&p\notin S.\end{cases} \tag{RSE.26} \] If \(p\in Z_E\), every defining generator vanishes on the field, so its Koszul local-cohomology functor is the identity there. If \(p\notin Z_E\), one defining generator is invertible, so that functor is zero. Taking the union proves both cases of (RSE.26). Empty or unit defining ideals give the same conclusions by the conventions of §3.158.

Apply \(Q_S\) to the finite extension (RSE.25), and then apply this residue construction to its \(R\)-module layers. We obtain the equality of full localizing subcategories \[ \ker(\Gamma_S:\operatorname{Mod}_B\to\mathcal T_S) =\operatorname{Loc}\{i_*k(p):p\notin S\}. \tag{RSE.27} \] Every generator on the right is killed by \(\Gamma_S\), proving the reverse inclusion as well. The finite filtration of the algebra is what makes the proof apply to all unbounded modules. Solution 3.DQ explains why that hypothesis cannot simply be dropped.

3.226. Categorical coefficients force restricted support

Suppose \(\Phi:\operatorname{Mod}_B\to\mathcal T\) is continuous strong symmetric monoidal. Its associated framed coefficient functor, under §3.223, has values in \(\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal L\). Assume that those values lie in the full subcategory \(\mathcal T\otimes\mathscr I\). We prove that \(\Phi\) kills (RSE.27).

Fix \(p\notin S\), put \(\kappa=k(p)\), and suppose the commutative algebra object \(A_p=\Phi(i_*\kappa)\) is nonzero. Its module category \(\mathcal T_p=\operatorname{Mod}_{A_p}(\mathcal T)\) has nonzero unit \(A_p\). The \(\kappa\)-action on that unit gives a strong symmetric monoidal functor \(j:\operatorname{Mod}_\kappa\to\mathcal T_p\). Free base change along \(\Phi\) factors exactly as \[ \operatorname{Mod}_B\longrightarrow\operatorname{Mod}_\kappa \xrightarrow{j}\mathcal T_p, \qquad M\longmapsto M\otimes_B^L\kappa \longmapsto\Phi(M)\otimes A_p. \tag{RSE.28} \] The identity follows from the full relative free-module bar, so it includes the algebra structure, tensor comparisons and every module map.

Every nonzero complex of \(\kappa\)-vector spaces contains a shift of \(\kappa\) as a retract: split its cycles, boundaries and a nonzero cohomology line. Consequently \(j\) is conservative. Since \(\mathcal L\) is dualizable, its tensor extension is also conservative: \[ \begin{array}{ccc} \operatorname{Mod}_\kappa\otimes\mathcal L&\xrightarrow{j\otimes\operatorname{Id}}&\mathcal T_p\otimes\mathcal L\\ \big\downarrow\scriptstyle\sim&&\big\downarrow\scriptstyle\sim\\ \operatorname{Fun}^L(\mathcal L^\vee,\operatorname{Mod}_\kappa) &\xrightarrow{j\circ-}& \operatorname{Fun}^L(\mathcal L^\vee,\mathcal T_p). \end{array} \tag{RSE.29} \] Indeed postcomposition with a conservative functor detects equivalences objectwise, also on the full subcategories of continuous functors. Both tensor identifications follow from the evaluation–coevaluation identities for a dualizable presentable category.

Let \(F_p\) be the actual framed Betti coefficient functor of the point \(p\). By (RSE.28), its image under (RSE.29) is the base change of the coefficient functor of \(\Phi\). This image lies in \(\mathcal T_p\otimes\mathscr I\) by the hypothesis. Apply the counit test for \(i_\infty\dashv g_\infty\). All functors in this adjunction are continuous, so that counit commutes with the independent base change \(j\). Conservativity in (RSE.29) shows, for every finite \(V\), \[ (\operatorname{Id}\otimes i_\infty g_\infty)F_p(V) \longrightarrow F_p(V) \text{ is an equivalence}. \tag{RSE.30} \] The entire coefficient functor therefore lifts through \(\operatorname{Mod}_\kappa\otimes\mathscr I\); fullness retains its tensor maps, frame and all higher paths. Its normalized finite-projective fibres and exact fibre functor were already those of the Betti point. Thus it is an actual restricted point over the ordinary field \(\kappa\), by (RBC.5) and (RSP.11).

The power-stage presentation (RBC.17)–(RBC.22) now forces \(p\in S\). More explicitly a point over an ordinary field in one of its finite power stages has each defining generator with a power equal to zero. In a field that generator is zero, so the point lies in the corresponding \(Z_E\). This contradicts \(p\notin S\). Hence \(\Phi(i_*k(p))=0\) for every such \(p\), and (RSE.27) proves \[ \Phi(\ker\Gamma_S)=0. \tag{RSE.31} \] The argument used membership in the original ind-connection category through its full counit. It did not replace that condition by regularity after an unspecified extension of the geometric ground field.

3.227. The actual restricted spectral equivalence

Put \(\mathcal A=\operatorname{QCoh}(\mathcal Z_H^{\mathrm{restr}}(X))\), and write \(L_{\mathrm r}=\mathsf L\) for the restricted Ran coefficient functor of (HLA.29). The quotient version of the supported-union equivalence identifies its restriction functor with \[ L_{\mathrm{Br}}:\mathcal A_{\mathrm B}\longrightarrow\mathcal A =(\mathcal T_S)^H,\qquad J\dashv L_{\mathrm{Br}},\qquad L_{\mathrm{Br}}J=\operatorname{Id}. \tag{RSE.32} \] Here \(J\) is the continuous full supported inclusion and the counit \(JL_{\mathrm{Br}}\to\operatorname{Id}\) has cofibres in \(\ker L_{\mathrm{Br}}\). The functor \(L_{\mathrm{Br}}\) is strong symmetric monoidal for the supported unit \(C_S\). Precomposition with it is fully faithful on continuous functor categories. Its essential image consists precisely of functors killing that kernel: if \(F\) kills the kernel, applying \(F\) to the counit identifies \(FJL_{\mathrm{Br}}\) with \(F\), so \(FJ\) is the required inverse construction. The identity \(L_{\mathrm{Br}}J=\operatorname{Id}\) proves uniqueness on all transformations. For strong symmetric monoidal functors the same statement holds: \(J\) preserves tensor products, and its unit map \(C_S\to\mathbf1_{\mathcal A_{\mathrm B}}\) has cofibres in the kernel. Applying \(F\) makes it an equivalence, supplying exactly the unital comparison of \(FJ\). All coherence diagrams are the ones inherited from \(F\) and this counit.

Let \(\Phi:\mathcal A_{\mathrm B}\to\mathcal T\) have coefficient functor in \(\mathcal T\otimes\mathscr I\). We must justify that the framed argument of §3.226 detects its whole unframed kernel. Let \(S_x\) be the regular frame algebra in \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm B}\) at the chosen point. The functor to \(\operatorname{Mod}_{\Phi(S_x)}(\mathcal T)\) is conservative, by the unit retraction (RSE.15). Framing \(\Phi\) gives \[ \Phi_{\mathrm{fr}}:\operatorname{Mod}_{S_x}(\mathcal A_{\mathrm B}) =\operatorname{Mod}_B \longrightarrow\operatorname{Mod}_{\Phi(S_x)}(\mathcal T). \tag{RSE.33} \] Its coefficients still lie in the tensor with \(\mathscr I\), since the frame extension is continuous. Section 3.226 shows that it kills the framed supported kernel. If \(M\in\ker L_{\mathrm{Br}}\), its frame pullback is in that kernel, because every defining Koszul fibre and filtered union commutes with frame pullback. Its image under (RSE.33) is the conservative frame extension of \(\Phi(M)\). Thus \(\Phi(M)=0\). This proves the unframed kernel assertion and the factorization of \(\Phi\) through (RSE.32).

Conversely every continuous strong symmetric monoidal functor \(\mathcal A\to\mathcal T\) has coefficient values in \(\mathcal T\otimes\mathscr I\), by the actual universal ind-connection coefficients (BLI.16). Write \(\mathfrak F_{\mathscr I}(\mathcal T)=\operatorname{Fun}^{L,\otimes}(\operatorname{Rep}(H),\mathcal T\otimes\mathscr I)\) and define \(\mathfrak F_{\mathcal L}(\mathcal T)\) by replacing \(\mathscr I\) with \(\mathcal L\). The functor spaces fit into a square \[ \begin{array}{ccc} \operatorname{Fun}^{L,\otimes}(\mathcal A,\mathcal T) &\longrightarrow& \mathfrak F_{\mathscr I}(\mathcal T)\\ \big\downarrow&&\big\downarrow\\ \operatorname{Fun}^{L,\otimes}(\mathcal A_{\mathrm B},\mathcal T) &\xrightarrow{\sim}& \mathfrak F_{\mathcal L}(\mathcal T). \end{array} \tag{RSE.34} \] Both vertical maps are fully faithful: the left one by (RSE.32), the right one by the tensored adjunction (RSE.14). Their essential images coincide by the framed kernel argument and the preceding converse. The bottom equivalence is (RSE.24). Hence the top arrow is an equivalence for every presentable symmetric monoidal \(\mathcal T\).

The full lisse-coefficient universal property (HLA.24)–(HLA.28) represents the top right space by \(\mathcal R_{\mathscr I}\). The top arrow is precisely precomposition with the actual map \(L_{\mathscr I}\) of (HLA.28): its universal coefficients are those of the same restricted point functor (RBC.5). Their comparison with the full Betti coefficients is the actual inclusion (RBC.4), and dualizability of \(\mathcal L\) retains the full frame descent. Thus it is that map, with its given tensor comparisons, which is an equivalence: \[ L_{\mathscr I}:\mathcal R_{\mathscr I} \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{QCoh}(\mathcal Z_H^{\mathrm{restr}}(X)), \qquad L_{\mathscr I}Q_{\mathrm{Ran}}\simeq L_{\mathrm r}. \tag{RSE.35} \] As in §3.223, take \(\mathcal T=\mathcal R_{\mathscr I}\) to obtain an inverse from the functor-space equivalence, and take \(\mathcal T=\mathcal A\) to identify the other composite with the identity by its full faithfulness. This proves the assertion on the full categories, not just a comparison on affine scalar-valued points. The exact composite with the original Ran functor is (HLA.29). No assertion about a general left-complete tensor category is used.

3.228. The full Hecke-lisse image of the geometric idempotent

Let \(\mathcal M\) be the full complex automorphic DG category used in §§3.209–3.213 and let \(\mathcal N=\mathcal M^{\mathrm{Hl}}\) be its full Hecke-lisse subcategory. Write \(\Pi=\Pi_{\mathrm r}\) and \(p_{\mathrm r}=p\) for the geometric functor and universal spectral object of §§3.188–3.189. Transport its continuous unital \(\mathcal R_{\mathscr I}\)-action (HLA.27) along (RSE.35). We obtain a continuous unital action \[ \Psi:\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal N\longrightarrow\mathcal N \tag{RSE.36} \] whose restriction along \(L_{\mathrm r}\) is the actual geometric Ran action by (HLA.29).

The geometric endofunctor \(\Pi\) of (UID.14) sends every object of \(\mathcal M\) to \(\mathcal N\), by (BLI.23). Its restriction to that subcategory is the action of the universal spectral object \(p_{\mathrm r}\). Equations (UID.7) and (RSE.36) therefore give the natural equivalence \[ \Pi|_{\mathcal N} \simeq\Psi(L_{\mathrm r}p_{\mathrm r},-) \simeq\Psi(\mathbf1_{\mathcal A},-) \simeq\operatorname{Id}_{\mathcal N}. \tag{RSE.37} \] All coefficient actions and Hecke comparisons here are those of the full unbounded categories, including unused coordinates. Landing in the full subcategory and (RSE.37) prove \[ \operatorname{EssIm}(\Pi)=\mathcal M^{\mathrm{Hl}}. \tag{RSE.38} \] This is equality with the full Hecke-lisse category. Original-complex full-image ind-regularity and nilpotent-support containment are GFP.55–GFP.56. GZR.33 identifies all independent nilpotent support over the complex numbers in every genus. The other geometric ground fields retain their separate requirements. A natural identity on the image has been constructed; no unit, counit or adjunction for the nonunital algebra \(p_{\mathrm r}\) is inferred from idempotence alone.

Figure 3.39. The framed comparison and full frame descent are (RSE.19)–(RSE.24). Boundedness of the ambient algebra and residue-field generation give the kernel test (RSE.25)–(RSE.31). Conservative categorical frames identify the exact functor in (RSE.35); its transported action and geometric image are (RSE.36)–(RSE.38). The bottom scope statement records the separate singular-support and regularity criteria.

3.229. Closed points and a varying character

Exercise 3.DP. In the elliptic rank-one character family of §3.147 fix the second monodromy to be one. Let \(R=\mathbf C[t,t^{-1}]\), let \(S\) be all its closed points, and let \(\kappa=\mathbf C(t)\). Compute the supported unit and the complementary kernel. Explain why every closed complex character is restricted although the universal character over \(R\) is not.

Solution 3.DP. A finite closed subset has defining equation \(f=\prod_\lambda(t-\lambda)\), up to powers and an invertible Laurent monomial. Its local-cohomology triangle is the fibre of \(R\to R[f^{-1}]\). The union over such subsets inverts every nonzero Laurent polynomial. Filtered colimits are exact, so \[ C_S=\operatorname{fib}(R\to\kappa),\qquad H^0(C_S)=0,\quad H^1(C_S)=\kappa/R, \qquad Q_SR=\kappa. \tag{RSE.39} \] The map is injective because \(R\) is a domain. At a closed point \(t=\lambda\), the one-dimensional coefficient space with monodromy \(\lambda\) is already a finite-dimensional complex representation. Thus it is restricted. The universal monodromy on \(R\), however, multiplies by \(t\), and the orbit of \(1\) contains all Laurent monomials. These are linearly independent over the original coefficient field, so this module is not locally finite. The ordinary original-field criterion (SCI.2)–(SCI.4) therefore excludes it. The generic fibre is excluded for the same reason: for any nonzero \(a\in\kappa\), \[ \{t^n a:n\in\mathbf Z\} \text{ is linearly independent over }\mathbf C. \tag{RSE.40} \] Multiplication by \(a^{-1}\) reduces a proposed finite relation to a Laurent-polynomial identity, whose coefficients are zero.

The prime ideals of this Laurent PID are its generic point and its closed maximal ideals, by factorization over \(\mathbf C\). Hence (RSE.27), or tensoring the triangle in (RSE.39) with any module, gives \[ \ker\Gamma_S=\operatorname{Loc}_R\{\kappa\}, \qquad\Gamma_S\kappa=0. \tag{RSE.41} \] All closed complex points being restricted therefore does not identify the full family with its restricted subfunctor. It does supply the residue cotangent tests of §3.219. The kernel argument of §3.226 also needs the generic residue field, which the closed-point tests alone would miss.

3.230. Bounded algebras and unbounded modules

Exercise 3.DQ. Let \(A=\mathbf C[t]\otimes\Lambda(\epsilon)\), where \(|\epsilon|=-1\) and \(d=0\). Give the finite algebra filtration used in §3.225 and explain why it handles an unbounded module. Contrast this with \(A_\infty=\mathbf C[z]\), \(|z|=-2\), whose only classical residue field is \(\mathbf C\).

Solution 3.DQ. Write \(R=\mathbf C[t]\) and \(i_*\) for restriction along the augmentation \(A\to R\). The ideal generated by \(\epsilon\) has square zero and is \(i_*R[1]\). The quotient is \(i_*R\). Thus the exact triangle of \(A\)-modules is \[ i_*R[1]\longrightarrow A\longrightarrow i_*R. \tag{RSE.42} \] It is split as a triangle of underlying \(R\)-complexes, but is not split as \(A\)-modules. Multiplication by \(\epsilon\) on the free module \(A\) is nonzero on cohomology; on the putative sum \(i_*R\oplus i_*R[1]\) it is zero. Tensor (RSE.42) over \(A\) with any unbounded \(M\). It expresses \(M\) as an extension of two restricted \(R\)-modules, \(R[1]\otimes_A^L M\) and \(R\otimes_A^L M\). These need not be bounded, and the argument has not truncated them. The all-degree residue construction over \(R\) applies directly to both, giving \[ \operatorname{Mod}_A =\operatorname{Loc}_A\{i_*k(p):p\in\operatorname{Spec}R\}. \tag{RSE.43} \]

For \(A_\infty\), the degree-zero ring is \(\mathbf C\), but the algebra has nonzero cohomology in every nonpositive even degree. Its nonzero localization \(A_\infty[z^{-1}]\) has zero derived fibre at \(\mathbf C\), because \(z\) becomes both zero and invertible there. The continuous localization functor kills \(\mathbf C\) and fixes this nonzero localized module. Therefore \[ \operatorname{Loc}_{A_\infty}\{\mathbf C\} \ne\operatorname{Mod}_{A_\infty}. \tag{RSE.44} \] This establishes the need for a genuine hypothesis in the all-unbounded residue-generation argument. In §3.225 that hypothesis is boundedness of the algebra, proved in §3.220, rather than boundedness of the module under study.

3.231. Conservative change to a nonzero category over a field

Exercise 3.DR. Let \(\kappa\) be a field and \(\mathcal T\) a presentable \(\kappa\)-linear symmetric monoidal stable category with nonzero unit. Prove conservativity of \(j(V)=V\otimes_\kappa\mathbf1\), including tensor extension by any dualizable presentable category. Give an unbounded example and show why the field hypothesis matters.

Solution 3.DR. In each degree of a complex choose a complement to boundaries inside cycles, and a complement to cycles in the whole vector space. The differential identifies the latter complement with the next degree's boundaries. The complex is the direct sum of its zero-differential cohomology and these contractible two-term pieces. This decomposition is valid without either degree bound. If cohomology is nonzero, choose a line in one of its degrees. The corresponding shift of \(\kappa\) is a retract of the complex. Applying \(j\) makes the same shift of the nonzero unit a retract. Thus \[ j(V)=0\ \Longrightarrow\ V=0, \qquad j\text{ detects equivalences by their cofibres}. \tag{RSE.45} \] For a dualizable presentable category \(\mathcal D\), the tensor–functor identifications of (RSE.29) identify \(j\otimes\operatorname{Id}_{\mathcal D}\) with postcomposition by \(j\). Apply (RSE.45) to each evaluation. It follows that \[ j\otimes\operatorname{Id}_{\mathcal D} \text{ is conservative}. \tag{RSE.46} \] For example the doubly unbounded complex \(\kappa[z,z^{-1}]\), \(|z|=-2\), is the sum of \(\kappa[2r]\) for \(r\in\mathbf Z\). Its image is the same sum of shifts of the unit and contains the unit as a retract, so it is nonzero.

Over \(R=\mathbf C[t]\), the nonzero category \(\operatorname{Mod}_{R[t^{-1}]}\) gives a counterexample. Its unit functor kills the nonzero module \(R/(t)\): tensor its free resolution \([R\xrightarrow{t}R]\) with \(R[t^{-1}]\), where the differential is invertible. Hence \[ (R/(t))\otimes_R^L R[t^{-1}]=0, \qquad R/(t)\ne0. \tag{RSE.47} \] The proof of §3.226 consequently passes to a residue field before using categorical conservativity. Nonvanishing of the target unit alone over a general ring would not justify that step.

3.232. The two proper-curve normalizations

Let \(X\) be the smooth projective connected complex curve used throughout this section. We retain the full unbounded operator category \(\mathcal D=\operatorname{Dmod}(X)\), the normalized ind-connection embedding \(i:\mathscr I\hookrightarrow\mathcal D\) and its continuous right adjoint \(g\). The two objects in §3.48 are distinct: \[ \begin{gathered} \mathbf k_X=\mathcal O_X[-1]=\omega_X[-2],\qquad \omega_X=\mathcal O_X[1]=i(\mathbf1),\\ p_{X,*}N=\operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal D}(\mathbf k_X,N). \end{gathered} \tag{NTR.1} \] The last identity is (GD.1), for arbitrary unbounded \(N\). Its finite Spencer calculation gives the de Rham form complex shifted by one. In contrast, Hom out of \(\omega_X\) shifts that same complex by minus one. The gap between these two functors is therefore two degrees.

For a compact finite-connection complex \(P\), the connection-dual Spencer calculation of §3.48 gives \[ \mathbb D_X(iP)\simeq i(P^\vee)[-2]. \tag{NTR.2} \] For a connection in degree zero this follows by applying the operator dual to its normalized shift \(P[1]\): the unshifted connection dual is \(P^\vee\), and dualization reverses the shift. The side-changing line is the one in §3.48. Finite cones and retracts extend this identity to every compact \(P\). Evaluation and coevaluation are the same signed Spencer maps, so the identity is natural on the full DG subcategory, not just on its objects.

The full operator pairing (SDG.1) is \((M,N)\mapsto p_{X,*}(M\otimes^!N)\). Apply its compact duality to \(iP\), and then (NTR.2). We obtain \[ \operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal D}(i(P^\vee),N) \simeq p_{X,*}(iP\otimes^!N)[-2]. \tag{NTR.3} \] This equality also follows directly from the finite connection Spencer resolution: tensoring the connection coefficient into \(N\) gives the same de Rham differential on both sides, and the two normalizations in (NTR.1) give the displayed shift. Thus it retains the actual operator actions and comparison maps for every unbounded \(N\).

The unit case is already an exact test: \[ \operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal D}(\omega_X,\omega_X) =\Gamma_{\mathscr I}(\mathbf1),\qquad p_{X,*}\omega_X\simeq\Gamma_{\mathscr I}(\mathbf1)[2]. \tag{NTR.4} \] The first complex is ordinary curve de Rham cohomology. The second is its shifted proper integral. They play different roles in transposing a coefficient functor.

3.233. The coreflector and the tensor transpose

Use the canonical tensor pairing (HLA.17) on \(\mathscr I\) and the full proper pairing (SDG.1) on \(\mathcal D\). The transpose of \(i\) for these specified pairings is \[ t:\mathcal D\longrightarrow\mathscr I, \qquad t(N)=g(N)[2]. \tag{NTR.5} \] Indeed, for every compact \(P\), adjunction and (NTR.3) give \[ \begin{aligned} \Gamma_{\mathscr I}(P\otimes tN) &\simeq\operatorname{RHom}_{\mathscr I}(P^\vee,gN)[2]\\ &\simeq\operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal D}(i(P^\vee),N)[2]\\ &\simeq p_{X,*}(iP\otimes^!N). \end{aligned} \tag{NTR.6} \] Every functor here is continuous in both variables. The full compact DG bars extend the identity from compact \(P\) to all \(P\); their enriched evaluation identifies all transformations and higher comparisons. This is the representing transpose under the actual dualities.

The right adjoint and its transpose satisfy different identities: \[ gi\simeq\operatorname{Id}_{\mathscr I}, \qquad ti\simeq[2]. \tag{NTR.7} \] The first is the unit of the fully faithful adjunction (HLA.4). The second follows from (NTR.5). In particular membership in the ind-connection image is tested by the original coreflector counit \[ igN\longrightarrow N, \qquad N\in i(\mathscr I) \ \Longleftrightarrow\ igN\longrightarrow N \text{ is an equivalence}. \tag{NTR.8} \] The coordinate intersections and full kernel constructions in §§3.206–3.209 use this adjunction. The integral pairing and coefficient coalgebra use \(t\). The shift does not change the full image subcategory, but it changes these maps and their unit normalizations.

3.234. All coordinate maps and the mixed diagonal kernel

The normalized inclusion \(i\) is strong symmetric monoidal. Transpose its multiplication and unit diagrams using (NTR.6). For every map \(\beta:J_2\to J_1\), including empty sets, we obtain \[ \begin{gathered} t^{\otimes J_2}(\Delta_\beta)_* \simeq\delta_{\mathscr I}^{\beta}t^{\otimes J_1},\\ \Gamma_{\mathscr I}t\simeq p_{X,*}. \end{gathered} \tag{NTR.9} \] The counit is the empty-fibre instance of the same transposed unit. Associativity and symmetry of the original tensor diagrams give the entire coalgebra coherence, by the evaluation–coevaluation triangles. No claim that \(i\) itself is a coalgebra map is needed.

Shifts add under exterior tensor. Writing the comparison solely with the coreflector gives the equivalent formula \[ g^{\otimes J_2}(\Delta_\beta)_* \simeq \delta_{\mathscr I}^{\beta}g^{\otimes J_1} [\,2(|J_1|-|J_2|)\,]. \tag{NTR.10} \] For composable coordinate maps the two cardinal differences add to the cardinal difference for their composite. Thus these shifts retain the same full string coherences. A bijection has shift zero. Projection to the point has shift two. The binary diagonal has \[ (g\otimes g)\Delta_* \simeq\delta_{\mathscr I}g[-2]. \tag{NTR.11} \]

Let \(K_{\mathcal D}=\Delta_*\omega_X\) be the full proper coevaluation kernel. Since \(g\omega_X=\mathbf1\), (NTR.11) shows that the canonical ind-connection coevaluation is the mixed restriction \[ K_{\mathscr I}=\delta_{\mathscr I}(\mathbf1) \simeq(g\otimes t)K_{\mathcal D} \simeq(t\otimes g)K_{\mathcal D}. \tag{NTR.12} \] The equality \(K_{\mathscr I}=\delta_{\mathscr I}(\mathbf1)\) follows by testing compact external objects: its pairing with \(P\boxtimes Q\) is \(\Gamma_{\mathscr I}(P\otimes Q)\), the diagonal representable functional. This is exactly the full enriched coend of (HLA.18). The mixed shift cancels the minus two in (NTR.11). Hence the actual Yoneda contractions give both triangles for (NTR.12).

3.235. The actual geometric action through the normalized comparison

The full lisse Ran category \(\mathcal R_{\mathscr I}\) is defined using the transposed tensor coalgebra of \(\mathscr I\), as in (HLA.23). The map out of the full operator Ran category uses its actual transpose: \[ \begin{aligned} Q_{\mathrm{Ran}}(\operatorname{ins}_{\psi}(\vec V\otimes N)) &=\operatorname{ins}_{\psi}(\vec V\otimes t^{\otimes J}N),\\ t^{\otimes J}N&=(g^{\otimes J}N)[2|J|]. \end{aligned} \tag{NTR.13} \] The transition squares are (NTR.9); all empty coordinates and compositions are included. Thus the full colimit gives a continuous strong symmetric monoidal functor. Its empty term is the actual unit, with no shift there.

Let \(\mathcal N=\mathcal M^{\mathrm{Hl}}\). The full Hecke operations on this category have ind-connection coefficients by (HLA.15). Pairing them against an arbitrary operator parameter uses (NTR.6), coordinate by coordinate. Therefore the full stage action satisfies \[ \Phi_\psi(\vec V,N;m) \simeq\Phi^{\mathscr I}_\psi (\vec V,t^{\otimes J}N;m). \tag{NTR.14} \] The actual Hecke collision maps transpose to the coalgebra maps in (NTR.9). Their finite-point strings give precisely the action factorization (HLA.27), with all unbounded parameters and every unused coordinate retained.

The abstract comparison \(L_{\mathscr I}\) is defined from the universal ind-connection coefficients and their canonical pairing. That construction and its equivalence (RSE.35) do not involve the operator coreflector. Applying (NTR.6) to those same universal coefficients identifies the actual composite \[ L_{\mathscr I}Q_{\mathrm{Ran}}\simeq L_{\mathrm r}. \tag{NTR.15} \] Here \(L_{\mathrm r}\) is the original restricted operator Ran coefficient functor. Transposition is natural on the complete coefficient functor, so the identity includes its tensor comparisons and all derived coefficient maps.

Transport the action through \(L_{\mathscr I}\). Equations (NTR.14)–(NTR.15), the landing theorem (BLI.23) and the unit comparison (UID.7) give \[ \Pi|_{\mathcal N}\simeq\operatorname{Id}_{\mathcal N}, \qquad\operatorname{EssIm}(\Pi)=\mathcal N. \tag{NTR.16} \] This proves the geometric action comparison with its full proper-curve normalization. GFP.55–GFP.56 give original-field ind-regularity and nilpotent-support containment. GZR.33 gives this identification over the complex numbers in every genus.

Figure 3.40. The coreflector and transpose are (NTR.5)–(NTR.8). Every coordinate shift is specified by (NTR.9)–(NTR.11); their mixed coevaluation is (NTR.12). These degree comparisons enter the actual coefficient functor and geometric action in (NTR.13)–(NTR.16). Solutions 3.DS–3.DU compute the nullary, binary and idempotence tests.

3.236. The projective-line counit in absolute degrees

Exercise 3.DS. For \(X=\mathbf P^1\), compare the absolute cohomological degrees of \(\Gamma_{\mathscr I}g\omega_X\) and \(p_{X,*}\omega_X\). Check the coalgebra counit for the transpose.

Solution 3.DS. The two-chart calculation (RSC.17) gives \(E=\mathbf C[\eta]/\eta^2\), \(|\eta|=2\), as the full endomorphism algebra of the ind-connection unit. By (NTR.1) and \(gi=\operatorname{Id}\), \[ \Gamma_{\mathscr I}g\omega_X=E,\qquad p_{X,*}\omega_X=E[2]. \tag{NTR.17} \] The first complex has cohomology in degrees zero and two. The second has cohomology in degrees minus two and zero. Thus \[ H^{-2}(E)=0,\qquad H^{-2}(E[2])=\mathbf C, \qquad E\not\simeq E[2]. \tag{NTR.18} \] This is a comparison of absolute degrees, not just parity or total dimension. Since \(t\omega_X=\mathbf1[2]\), the actual counit is \[ \Gamma_{\mathscr I}(t\omega_X) =\Gamma_{\mathscr I}(\mathbf1[2]) =E[2]=p_{X,*}\omega_X. \tag{NTR.19} \] It is the case \(J_2=\varnothing\), \(|J_1|=1\), of (NTR.9). Omitting this case would lose a necessary Ran transition.

3.237. Three restrictions of the projective-line diagonal

Exercise 3.DT. Let \(R=E\otimes E\), with its degree-two generators \(x,y\), and let \(K_{\mathcal D}=\Delta_*\omega_X\) for \(X=\mathbf P^1\). Compute its restrictions by two coreflectors, two transposes, and one of each. Determine compactness of the first image.

Solution 3.DT. The actual monoidal equivalence (RSC.18) identifies \(\delta_{\mathscr I}(\mathbf1)\) with the diagonal \(R\)-module \(E\), on which \(x=y=\eta\). Equations (NTR.5) and (NTR.11) give \[ \begin{gathered} (g\otimes g)K_{\mathcal D}\simeq E[-2],\qquad (t\otimes t)K_{\mathcal D}\simeq E[2],\\ (g\otimes t)K_{\mathcal D}\simeq E \simeq(t\otimes g)K_{\mathcal D}. \end{gathered} \tag{NTR.20} \] The alternating semifree resolution (HLA.35) has generator \(e_n\) in degree \(n\), with differentials alternating \(x-y\) and \(x+y\). Its exactness was proved in the basis \(1,x,y,xy\). Shift that complete resolution by minus two and tensor with the residue field \(x=y=0\). Every differential becomes zero, so \[ E[-2]\otimes_R^L\mathbf C \simeq\bigoplus_{n\geq0}\mathbf C[-n-2]. \tag{NTR.21} \] There is a one-dimensional cohomology group in every degree at least two. It is unbounded above, so the module is not perfect or compact. The same is true after any fixed shift. Meanwhile the original diagonal object is compact by proper coherent direct image. Consequently \[ \begin{gathered} (g\otimes g)\text{ does not preserve all compact objects},\\ g\text{ does not preserve all compact objects}. \end{gathered} \tag{NTR.22} \] For the second assertion, if \(g\) preserved compacts, its exterior square would preserve the compact external generators and their thick closure, which is the full compact product category. This would contradict the first assertion. The large-cardinal presentation used for the lisse Ran category remains necessary; a fixed cohomological shift does not fix compactness failure.

3.238. The membership projector is unshifted

Exercise 3.DU. Distinguish \(ig\) from \(it\). Test their squares on the normalized projective-line unit. Explain why the adjunction used for the full Betti inclusion in §3.221 is unchanged.

Solution 3.DU. Full faithfulness of \(i\) gives the actual unit and counit identities \[ (ig)^2\simeq ig,\qquad gi=\operatorname{Id}, \qquad ig\omega_X=\omega_X. \tag{NTR.23} \] All these are identities of continuous functors or their canonical adjunction maps. The shifted transpose instead satisfies \[ \begin{gathered} it=ig[2],\qquad(it)^2=ig[4],\\ it\omega_X=\omega_X[2],\qquad (it)^2\omega_X=\omega_X[4]. \end{gathered} \tag{NTR.24} \] The last two objects have different absolute cohomological degrees, because \(\omega_X=\mathcal O_X[1]\) is nonzero and bounded. They are not isomorphic. Thus \(it\) is not the membership coreflector. It is \(t\), however, that represents the proper integral pairing.

The full Betti inclusion \(i_\infty:\mathscr I\hookrightarrow\mathcal L\) in §3.221 is used with its actual right adjoint, characterized by \[ \begin{gathered} \operatorname{RHom}_{\mathscr I}(P,g_\infty L) \simeq\operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal L}(i_\infty P,L), \\ g_\infty i_\infty=\operatorname{Id}. \end{gathered} \tag{NTR.25} \] That proof tests membership by this adjunction, and does not identify it with the transpose under the proper operator integral. Its categorical residue-field and frame conservativity arguments use this unshifted counit. The abstract comparison (RSE.35) has the full unbounded scope stated there.

3.239. Reconstruction from the full Ran insertion adjoints

Use the actual full operator Ran category \(\mathcal R\) and its finite-point diagram of §3.46. Write \(\Xi\) for that entire indexing category, \(\psi:I\to J\) for an object, and \[ \mathcal C_\psi=\operatorname{Rep}(H)^{\otimes I} \otimes\operatorname{Dmod}(X^J),\qquad j_\psi:\mathcal C_\psi\longrightarrow\mathcal R, \qquad j_\psi\dashv r_\psi. \tag{CDK.1} \] The right adjoint exists by the full compact-generator module construction: on a compact \(P\) its value is the module \(\operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal R}(j_\psi P,-)\). The insertion preserves compact objects by (RN.11)–(RN.13), so these module values commute with colimits. Thus \(r_\psi\) is continuous. This assertion concerns the full operator diagram; it does not impose compact preservation on the transposed ind-connection diagram.

The compact duality in \(\mathcal C_\psi\) is representation duality tensored with proper operator duality. Denote it by \(d_\psi\). The actual insertion compatibility, including its evaluation maps, is (KG.19)–(KG.22): \[ (j_\psi P)^\vee\simeq j_\psi(d_\psi P) \quad(P\text{ compact}). \tag{CDK.2} \] Give each stage its tensor categorical self-duality: the representation pairing is ordinary invariant tensor, and the operator pairing is the full proper pairing (SDG.1) on \(X^J\). The canonical tensor self-duality of \(\mathcal R\) is the one of §3.186. On a compact \(P\), (CDK.2) and adjunction show that precomposition of the functional represented by \(M\) is the functional represented by \(r_\psi M\): \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{ev}_{\mathcal R}(j_\psi P,M) &=\operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal R}((j_\psi P)^\vee,M)\\ &\simeq\operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal C_\psi}(d_\psi P,r_\psi M)\\ &=\operatorname{ev}_{\mathcal C_\psi}(P,r_\psi M). \end{aligned} \tag{CDK.3} \] All functors are continuous; the compact bars extend this identity to the full categories and their maps. Consequently the dual of \(j_\psi\), under these specified dualities, is exactly \(r_\psi\). This uses the insertion's full compact-duality comparison, not an identification of the normalized ind-connection coreflector with a proper-integral transpose.

3.240. The coherent family comparison and its counit

The full Ran colimit universal property (RN.13) identifies continuous functors to \(\operatorname{Vect}\), including all transformation complexes, with coherent compatible stage functors. Apply the self-dualities in (CDK.3). This gives the actual DG category comparison \[ \mathcal R\xrightarrow{\sim} \lim_{\Xi^{\mathrm{op}}}\mathcal C_\psi, \qquad M\longmapsto(r_\psi M)_\psi. \tag{CDK.4} \] The transition at \(\alpha:\psi\to\chi\), whose stage functor is \(T_\alpha\), is its right adjoint \(T_\alpha^R\). To check this on the stages themselves, representation folds and unit insertions commute with finite representation duality. The coordinate functor is proper direct image, which commutes with the compact operator duality by the proper structure-map, external-product and closed-diagonal duality calculations of §§3.48–3.52. Their tensor product therefore satisfies \(d_\chi T_\alpha P=T_\alpha d_\psi P\) for compact \(P\). The calculation (CDK.3), with \(T_\alpha\) in place of \(j_\psi\), identifies its transpose with its right adjoint. All these identifications are adjunction mates of the actual coordinate comparisons, so they respect strings and their homotopies. The identity \(j_\psi=j_\chi T_\alpha\) gives \(r_\psi=T_\alpha^Rr_\chi\). The limit here means full coherent families, as in the path-bar construction of §3.46, rather than the diagram of homotopy categories. In particular \[ \operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal R}(M,N) \simeq\lim_{\Xi^{\mathrm{op}}} \operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal C_\psi}(r_\psi M,r_\psi N). \tag{CDK.5} \] One can check this last identity directly on the full coherent-family bar: a map is a family of component maps with its compatibility homotopies, then homotopies between those, and all higher simplex relations. This is the derived limit on the right. The full mapping-complex assertion in (RN.13) supplies precisely those relations.

There is a covariant \(\Xi\)-diagram of endofunctors. Its map at \(\alpha\) is \[ j_\psi r_\psi =j_\chi T_\alpha T_\alpha^Rr_\chi \xrightarrow{j_\chi\epsilon_\alpha r_\chi} j_\chi r_\chi. \tag{CDK.6} \] The adjunction counits give its full coherent composition maps. The insertion counits define an augmentation to the identity. For any \(M,N\), adjunction and (CDK.5) compute \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal R} (\operatorname*{colim}_{\Xi}j_\psi r_\psi M,N) &\simeq\lim_{\Xi^{\mathrm{op}}} \operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal C_\psi}(r_\psi M,r_\psi N)\\ &\simeq\operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal R}(M,N). \end{aligned} \tag{CDK.7} \] Under these identifications precomposition with the augmentation is the identity on the coherent family of maps. Indeed precomposing with (CDK.6) is, by the two adjunction triangles, applying \(T_\alpha^R\) to the component map. This is exactly the mapping transition in (CDK.5). Enriched Yoneda therefore proves the identity of actual continuous endofunctors \[ \operatorname*{colim}_{\Xi}j_\psi r_\psi \xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Id}_{\mathcal R}. \tag{CDK.8} \] This proof retains all unbounded objects and every higher comparison. It does not assert that one insertion is fully faithful or that an ordinary sum of stage objects is the identity.

3.241. The full regular kernel as an actual finite-point colimit

Let \(R_H\in\operatorname{Rep}(H)\otimes\operatorname{Rep}(H)\) be the regular representation coevaluation, with its two commuting group actions. It is the whole finite-representation coend of §3.42, not just its underlying vector space. The full stage coevaluation is \[ K_\psi^0=R_H^{\boxtimes I}\boxtimes (\Delta_{X^J})_*\omega_{X^J} \in\mathcal C_\psi\otimes\mathcal C_\psi. \tag{CDK.9} \] The representation triangles are the full Yoneda contractions, and the operator triangles are (SDG.3) on the product curve. Thus these are the actual stage dualities used in (CDK.3), with all proper shifts included.

The kernel corresponding to \(j_\psi r_\psi\) under \(\mathcal R\otimes\mathcal R\simeq\operatorname{Fun}^L(\mathcal R,\mathcal R)\) is \[ K_\psi=(j_\psi\otimes j_\psi)K_\psi^0. \tag{CDK.10} \] To verify it, apply the kernel to \(M\). Moving evaluation past the second insertion uses (CDK.3), leaving \(j_\psi\) applied to the stage evaluation–coevaluation triangle on \(r_\psi M\). The result is \(j_\psi r_\psi M\), naturally on the entire DG category.

Transport the counit maps (CDK.6) through this full kernel equivalence. They define the actual transition maps on the \(K_\psi\). On a coordinate transition they are the adjunction counit of the specified proper coordinate direct image and coefficient fold, with the duality comparisons of (KG.19). On a string they are their composed adjunction mates, so they retain every simplex relation. This specifies a coherent diagram of kernels, not merely a list of isomorphism classes.

The kernel equivalence is continuous, and the identity kernel for the canonical tensor self-duality is the actual regular algebra object \(R_{\mathcal R}\) of (KG.23). Applying (CDK.8) yields the object identity \[ R_{\mathcal R} \simeq\operatorname*{colim}_{\psi\in\Xi} (j_\psi\otimes j_\psi) \bigl(R_H^{\boxtimes I}\boxtimes (\Delta_{X^J})_*\omega_{X^J}\bigr). \tag{CDK.11} \] All transition maps are the ones just constructed. The identity concerns this underlying kernel with its coherent presentation; it does not replace the separately constructed algebra multiplication by an unproved termwise multiplication. It also does not reduce the compact-DG coend (KG.23) to the bare set of inserted generators: the insertion adjoints and their entire mapping-family limit were essential to (CDK.8).

3.242. Contracting against the actual restricted coefficients

Put \(\mathcal A=\operatorname{QCoh}(\mathcal Z_H^{\mathrm{restr}}(X))\). Write \(\mathcal E\) for its actual universal coefficient functor (BLI.16). At \(\psi:I\to J\), let \[ \begin{gathered} \mathcal E_\psi= (\operatorname{mult}_{\mathcal A}^{J}\otimes\operatorname{Id}) \mathcal E^{\otimes J}\operatorname{mult}^{\psi}: \operatorname{Rep}(H)^{\otimes I}\longrightarrow \mathcal A\otimes\mathscr I^{\otimes J},\\ B_\psi=(\operatorname{Id}\otimes i^{\otimes J}\mathcal E_\psi) (R_H^{\boxtimes I}). \end{gathered} \tag{CDK.12} \] Here the independent spectral factors of \(\mathcal E^{\otimes J}\) are multiplied in \(\mathcal A\), and empty coefficient fibres use the tensor unit. The resulting single \(\mathcal A\)-factor is reordered to the last position. Thus \(B_\psi\) belongs to \(\operatorname{Rep}(H)^{\otimes I}\otimes\operatorname{Dmod}(X^J)\otimes\mathcal A\). In the second expression \(\mathcal E_\psi\) is applied to the second representation factor, leaving the first unchanged.
