Write \[ F=df_x:k^n\to k^m,\qquad B=\operatorname{Hess}_x\!\left(\sum_{a=1}^m\eta_a f_a\right), \qquad L=T_{(x,\xi)}C. \tag{RTM.3} \] The matrix \(B\) is symmetric; here the coordinate coefficients \(\eta_a\) are held fixed when taking the Hessian. Differentiating the actual cotangent pullback, including its change with the source point, gives \[ E:=T_dD_C =\{(v,\alpha):(v,F^t\alpha+Bv)\in L\}. \tag{RTM.4} \] This is equality of tangent spaces of the scheme fibre product, obtained by its dual-number test. It does not replace a nonreduced fibre by its reduction. The other tangent map is \[ dq_d(v,\alpha)=(Fv,\alpha),\qquad W=dq_d(E). \tag{RTM.5} \] Use the symplectic convention \(\omega=d\theta=d\xi\wedge dx\). For \((v,\alpha),(w,\beta)\in E\), symmetry cancels the two Hessian terms and gives \[ \begin{aligned} &\omega_X\bigl((v,F^t\alpha+Bv),(w,F^t\beta+Bw)\bigr)\\ &\hspace{12mm}=\alpha(Fw)-\beta(Fv)\\ &\hspace{12mm}=\omega_Y\bigl((Fv,\alpha),(Fw,\beta)\bigr)=0. \end{aligned} \tag{RTM.6} \] The last equality is the isotropy of \(L\). Hence \(W\) is isotropic. The nondegenerate symplectic pairing identifies the annihilator of a subspace of dimension \(r\) with a space of dimension \(2m-r\); since an isotropic subspace is contained in its annihilator, \(r\le m\). Thus \[ \dim W\le m. \tag{RTM.7} \] This argument proves the tangent-dimension bound without assuming that \(D_C\) itself is smooth or reduced. The injectivity in (RTM.2) is used in the next step.

3.281. A quadratic target test is transverse on the source

The symmetric-graph construction (IS.1)–(IS.2), applied to \(W\subset T_yY\oplus T_y^*Y\), supplies a symmetric form \(Q:T_yY\to T_y^*Y\) such that \[ W\cap\operatorname{graph}(Q)=0. \tag{RTM.8} \] In the chosen target coordinates \(z\), set \[ g(z)=\sum_a\eta_a z_a+\tfrac12\sum_{a,b}Q_{ab}z_az_b, \qquad h=g\circ f. \tag{RTM.9} \] Then \(g(y)=h(x)=0\), \(dg_y=\eta\), and \(dh_x=\xi\). The chain rule with its second-derivative term is \[ H:=\operatorname{Hess}_x h=B+F^tQF. \tag{RTM.10} \] Suppose \((v,Hv)\in L\). Taking \(\alpha=QFv\) puts \((v,\alpha)\) in \(E\), and \[ dq_d(v,\alpha)=(Fv,QFv) \in W\cap\operatorname{graph}(Q). \tag{RTM.11} \] It is zero by (RTM.8). Injectivity in (RTM.2) then makes \(v=0\). Since both tangent spaces have dimension \(n\), we have proved the full transversality statement \[ \operatorname{graph}(dh)\pitchfork C \quad\text{at }(x,\xi). \tag{RTM.12} \] The term \(B\) cannot be omitted. Even when \(df_x=0\), it can be the entire nondegenerate source Hessian.

The conclusion is independent of the coordinate calculation. The schemes \(D_C\), its projection \(q\), and its tangent kernel are intrinsic. In any coordinates (RTM.4) differentiates those same maps, and the symplectic identity (RTM.6) differentiates the same canonical one-forms. The chosen quadratic polynomial depends on the coordinates, as permitted by this existence theorem; the resulting intrinsic graph is transverse to the original component.

3.282. Finite simultaneous choices and an étale Morse normal form

The good forms \(Q\) form a nonempty Zariski-open subset of the affine space of symmetric forms. Indeed the linear map \((v,\alpha)\mapsto\alpha-QFv\) on \(E\) must be injective. In fixed bases this means that at least one maximal minor is nonzero, a polynomial open condition; (RTM.8) proves nonemptiness. Consequently the same \(Q\) can work for finitely many smooth Lagrangian components satisfying (RTM.2): intersect their finitely many nonempty opens. The parameter space is an affine space over an infinite field, so the product of their nonzero minor polynomials is nonzero and has a nonvanishing value. No assertion about an arbitrary infinite family of components follows.

Suppose now that \(C=T_S^*X\) near the point, for a smooth locally closed subvariety \(S\) of dimension \(d\). In adapted coordinates \((a,b)\), \(S=\{b=0\}\). Its conormal tangent imposes \(\delta b=0\) and \(\delta\xi_a=0\). Thus (RTM.12) says exactly \[ d(h|_S)_x=0,\qquad \det\operatorname{Hess}_x(h|_S)\ne0. \tag{RTM.13} \] Here is the algebraic local normal form, including its coordinate extension. In the local ring of \(S\), choose parameters \(a\). Criticality puts \(h|_S\) in their squared ideal, so after symmetrizing its coefficients, \[ h|_S=a^t A(a)a,\qquad A(a)^t=A(a), \qquad \det A(0)\ne0. \tag{RTM.14} \] After a constant change of basis over the algebraically closed field, take \(A(0)=1\). To diagonalize over the local ring, pivot on the first diagonal entry, a unit, and subtract its multiples from the other rows and the same multiples from the columns. This cancels the first off-diagonal row and column and leaves a smaller symmetric matrix with invertible constant term. Induction gives \(A=T^t\operatorname{diag}(u_1,\ldots,u_d)T\), with \(T\) invertible and each \(u_i(0)=1\). Adjoin the chosen roots \(r_i^2=u_i\), \(r_i(0)=1\). The derivative \(2r_i\) is a unit, so these are étale local extensions; the square-zero lifting follows explicitly by replacing a lift \(r\) by \(r+(u-r^2)/(2r)\). The coordinates \[ w=\operatorname{diag}(r_i)T a, \qquad h|_S=\sum_{i=1}^{d}w_i^2 \tag{RTM.15} \] have invertible differential at the point. Here is the relative lifting check. Smoothness of \(S\) first lifts a point across a square-zero extension. An error in the desired \(w\)-values can then be corrected uniquely by its tangent vector, since the displayed Jacobian is invertible. The same argument applied to the difference of two lifts proves uniqueness. Finite presentation makes this a formally étale coordinate map, using the definitions and chart lifting in Smooth morphisms, §1. For complex varieties its local analytic branch is a coordinate chart. The choice of roots and ordered coordinates is retained; it does not canonically orient the resulting vanishing-cycle line.

3.283. The bounded coefficient and its exact cycle degree

Now work on complex varieties with complexes of complex vector spaces as coefficients. Use the perverse-normalized cycle convention \[ \Phi_hF=\operatorname{Cone}(i^*F\to\psi_hF)[-1]. \tag{RTM.16} \] Consider the actual local sheaf model \(F=j_*M_S[d]\), where \(j:S\hookrightarrow X\) is closed on the chosen neighbourhood and \(M\) is a bounded coefficient complex, constant there. This is an assumption on the local object, not an assertion that every sheaf with a given characteristic component has this form on an ordinary neighbourhood. For a local system, restrict to a coordinate neighbourhood where it is constant, retaining its fibre.

We give the quadratic calculation with its unit. On the universal cover of the punctured parameter, write \(\lambda=r e^{i\theta}\) with a lifted argument. In a small ball of \(\mathbb C^d\), the fibre \(\sum w_i^2=\lambda\) has coordinates \(e^{-i\theta/2}w=u+iv\), satisfying \[ |u|^2-|v|^2=r,\qquad u\cdot v=0, \qquad r+2|v|^2<\epsilon^2. \tag{RTM.17} \] Put \(s=u/\sqrt{r+|v|^2}\). Then \(s\in S^{d-1}\), \(v\in s^\perp\), and \(|v|^2<(\epsilon^2-r)/2\). Scaling \(v\) to zero and replacing \(u\) by \(\sqrt{r+t^2|v|^2}s\) gives a deformation retraction, preserving the lifted parameter. Its parameter half-plane is contractible. These retractions commute with shrinking the ball on their zero sections. The ordinary-cover section complexes and their constant-section unit are therefore \[ \psi_{\sum w_i^2}(M)_0 \simeq R\Gamma(S^{d-1};M),\qquad M\longrightarrow R\Gamma(S^{d-1};M). \tag{RTM.18} \] The constant-coefficient section and homotopy comparisons here are the singular-cochain resolution in Sheaf cohomology and singular cohomology on manifolds, §1. The reduced sphere complex is \(M[1-d]\): for \(S^0\) its unit is the diagonal into \(M\oplus M\); for higher spheres the two contractible hemisphere cover and its equatorial intersection give this formula inductively by the section Mayer–Vietoris triangle. The finite free sphere complex retains the same maps after tensoring with any bounded \(M\). Consequently \[ \operatorname{Cone}\bigl(M\to R\Gamma(S^{d-1};M)\bigr) \simeq M[1-d]. \tag{RTM.19} \] For the local closed embedding, sections of the direct image on an open set are the sections on its intersection with \(S\). The same statement holds on the pulled-back covering space and at the zero fibre. Thus the nearby section complexes, their central units, and their cones are precisely those of the restricted function on \(S\). Combining this comparison, its degree, (RTM.16), and the input shift \([d]\) gives \[ (\Phi_h j_*M_S[d])_x \simeq M\otimes\mathfrak o_{h,S}. \tag{RTM.20} \] The one-dimensional line \(\mathfrak o_{h,S}\) is in degree zero. The chosen ordered Morse coordinates identify it with the reduced sphere orientation coefficient; changing the coordinates carries this line by the induced orientation map. It has not been given an artificial canonical basis. In particular (RTM.20) is nonzero exactly when \(M\ne0\).

Deck translation changes the half-angle by \(\pi\), hence acts on the real sphere by \(s\mapsto-s\). Its degree is \((-1)^d\): extend it to the linear map \(-1\) of the oriented real \(d\)-ball and use the boundary orientation. Thus the coefficient-line monodromy is \[ T_{h,S}=(-1)^d\operatorname{Id}. \tag{RTM.21} \] For \(d=0\), the punctured inverse image of the point model is empty. Its nearby cycle is zero, and the cone followed by \([-1]\) is \(M\), so (RTM.20) holds directly with degree zero and identity monodromy. No negative-dimensional sphere is used. These calculations agree with Quadratic cycles and the holomorphic microsupport test, §§1–2.

3.284. The actual open Hecke stratum and the reduced-fibre input

The geometric fibre hypothesis can be checked before imposing a chosen source characteristic component. Work on the smooth open relative-position stratum of a reduced bounded Hecke support, after pulling back a smooth output-bundle-and-curve chart. This is a smooth finite-type scheme, by the finite-jet orbit and frame construction in §3.32; no independent input frame is added to its fibre. Let \(f\) be its output-and-point map and \(p_1\) its smooth input-bundle map.

We first identify the fibre equation on the open stratum; source membership alone would not identify this scheme fibre. Fix the output bundle and its Higgs field \(A_2\), and write the loop lattices as in (HG.1): \(L_2=\mathfrak g[[u]]\) and \(L_1=\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}L_2\). The vertical tangent for the input-bundle-and-point map is the actual orbit tangent \(L_1/(L_1\cap L_2)\), (AS.3). For its representative \(X\), take \((a_1,a_2,b)=(0,X,0)\) in (HG.4)–(HG.5). The input bundle is fixed, the output deformation has principal part \(X\), and (HG.3) evaluates its covector as \(\operatorname{Res}\langle A_2,X\rangle\). Thus the vanishing equation on every vertical orbit tangent is exactly that this residue be zero.

The field \(A_2\) already annihilates \(L_2\), by its regularity. Annihilation of the displayed orbit quotient is therefore equivalent to annihilation of \(L_1+L_2\). Under the invariant perfect residue pairing the annihilator of \(L_2\) is \(L_2du\): pairing a series with each opposite Laurent monomial tests every negative coefficient. Invariance gives the annihilator of \(L_1\) as \(L_1du\). Consequently the orbit equations say precisely that \(A_2\) is regular also in the input lattice. These are equalities of coefficient equations over every algebra, not only field points. Only finitely many negative root coefficients occur on the bounded orbit, as in the finite-jet proof of (AS.2); the remaining regular coefficients already annihilate all relevant integral tangents.

The output field on the complement and its now regular input-disc expression glue uniquely to an input global Higgs field, by the full gluing comparison (HG.8)–(HG.9). The residual one-dimensional vertical direction for the input-bundle map is movement of the point. Equation (HG.13) says that its remaining vanishing equation is exactly the prescribed moving-point residue. In the chosen output chart, covectors pulled from the output stack annihilate the additional frame directions; these impose no new condition and do not add an input-frame fibre. Hence the fixed-target cotangent fibre is the compatible-Higgs fibre with this residue equation, as a functor on coefficient algebras and therefore as its representing scheme.

At the cocharacter modification in §§3.26–3.29, the compatible-Higgs fibre with the output Higgs field fixed is an isolated reduced point on this bounded support, by (AS.6) and (HG.9). For this output-fixed assertion use the inverse modification and the opposite Schubert bound, as in the last paragraph of §3.26; its disc Higgs field has the same Levi invertibility. The residue equation is a further closed condition satisfied at that point. Its fibre is therefore the same reduced point near the modification. In particular its tangent is zero.

For any further smooth Lagrangian source component \(C\) in this image, imposing membership in \(C\) is another closed condition. Its tangent kernel therefore satisfies \[ \ker(dq_d|_{T_dD_C})=0, \qquad \eta=(\xi_2,\xi_x),\qquad \xi_x\ne0. \tag{RTM.22} \] This verifies the hypothesis of (RTM.12) on this chart whenever that smooth Lagrangian component is given. The quadratic test has exactly the prescribed first derivative, including its nonzero curve component; only its Hessian is varied. Its curve partial derivative remains invertible on a neighbourhood of the target point, since its value there is nonzero. The proof concerns the open stratum of the actual reduced bounded kernel support. It does not discard nilpotent parameters from a scheme fibre or assert that the full unbounded Grassmannian is reduced.

If the actual cycle complex has an isolated nonzero point summand, the proper-image comparison with its full stated hypotheses in (IS.9)–(IS.11) carries that summand to the output: \[ \Phi_gRf_*F \simeq i_{y,*}V\oplus R(F), \qquad V\ne0. \tag{RTM.23} \] Equations (RTM.12)–(RTM.20) calculate \(V\) for the bounded conormal local model. Identifying a general source object with that model microlocally, and proving that the specified cycle functor retains that microlocal comparison, are additional requirements for applying this calculation to an arbitrary object.

Figure 3.44. Equations (RTM.4)–(RTM.7) retain the changing cotangent pullback and its symmetric Hessian term. The quadratic graph and injective projection give source transversality in (RTM.8)–(RTM.12). The conormal model has the degree-zero coefficient and monodromy in (RTM.20)–(RTM.21). The quadratic and cubic fibres in Solutions 3.EE–3.EF distinguish a reduced point from a length-two scheme with the same reduced support. Solution 3.EG retains a nonzero source conormal and its negative monodromy. Free further reading on the isolated-test framework is Arinkin–Gaitsgory–Kazhdan–Raskin–Rozenblyum–Varshavsky, Appendix H.

3.285. Finite tests and full-category support

The simultaneous-choice statement of §3.282 is finite. An unbounded object's cohomological support can involve arbitrarily many closed components, without a single common neighbourhood isolating all their tests. The point-fibre calculation (RTM.22) does not supply that neighbourhood. Nor does a bounded coefficient calculation prove perverse exactness or the completion description for the actual full-category cycle functor.

The lower-bound deduction still needs precisely the microlocal coefficient comparison, its compatibility with cycles and characteristic support, the t-exact full-category extension in (IS.7)–(IS.8), and the relevant generic-point or geometric-field comparisons. The algebraic regular-holonomic and whole-D-module assertions remain distinct. The conditional enhanced field-test argument (ESG.34)–(ESG.35) likewise retains its point-detection hypothesis. These requirements cannot be replaced by set-theoretic isolation or by the matrix computation alone. Free further reading is The stack of local systems with restricted variation and geometric Langlands theory with nilpotent singular support, Appendix H, at the regular-holonomic scope stated there.

3.286. Exercise and solution: the quadratic ramification fibre

For the cycle calculations in the next three exercises take \(k=\mathbb C\). Their scheme-fibre and tangent computations are valid over every algebraically closed characteristic-zero field.

Exercise 3.EE. Let \(f:\mathbb A^1_z\to\mathbb A^1_t\), \(t=z^2\), and take \(C\) to be the source zero section. At \(z=0\), fix a target covector \(\eta\ne0\). Compute the scheme fibre, \(E\), \(W\), the pulled-back Hessian and the normalized cycle of the constant perverse input.

Solution 3.EE. The codifferential equation and its fixed-target fibre are \[ 2z\eta=0, \qquad k[z]_{(z)}/(2\eta z)=k. \tag{RTM.24} \] It is a reduced point. Here \(F=0\), \(B=2\eta\), and \(L\) is the horizontal source tangent. Formula (RTM.4) gives \[ E=\{(0,\alpha)\},\qquad W=\{(0,\alpha)\}\subset T_0\mathbb A^1\oplus T_0^*\mathbb A^1. \tag{RTM.25} \] Every symmetric graph is transverse to this vertical line. For \(g(t)=\eta t+qt^2/2\), the source function is \(\eta z^2+qz^4/2\), whose Hessian is \(2\eta\). Its nondegeneracy comes entirely from \(B\), not from \(F^tQF\). For the input \(k_{\mathbb A^1}[1]\), the normalized cycle is one line in degree zero, with monodromy minus one by (RTM.20)–(RTM.21). Equivalently its nearby unit is the diagonal into the two sheets, and the quotient is their signed difference. The finite map is proper, so the explicit finite-map computation (IS.12) gives the same cycle on the target.

3.287. Exercise and solution: cubic isolation is not reduced isolation

Exercise 3.EF. Replace the preceding map by \(t=z^3\), keeping the same component and nonzero target covector. Show that the fibre is set-theoretically isolated but the tangent hypothesis fails. Decide whether this refutes vanishing-cycle detection itself.

Solution 3.EF. This time \[ 3\eta z^2=0, \qquad k[z]_{(z)}/(3\eta z^2)\simeq k[z]/(z^2). \tag{RTM.26} \] Its length is two and its tangent is one-dimensional. At zero both \(F\) and \(B\) vanish, so \(E\) consists of all \((v,\alpha)\). The tangent projection has \[ \ker dq=\{(v,0)\},\qquad \operatorname{Hess}_0(g\circ f)=0 \quad\text{for every quadratic }g. \tag{RTM.27} \] Thus no such target test has a nondegenerate source Hessian. Replacing the fibre by its reduction would falsely erase exactly this obstruction.

Nevertheless a small nonzero fibre has three points and a small source disc is contractible. For constant perverse input the actual normalized cycle is \[ k^3/k(1,1,1), \qquad \dim=2, \quad\text{in degree zero}. \tag{RTM.28} \] Monodromy is the cyclic permutation of the three sheet coordinates on this quotient. This is the full diagonal-unit calculation (IS.12) with \(m=3\). It is nonzero. The example refutes a reduced-fibre-free Morse assertion; it does not refute the more general isolated-cycle theorem.

3.288. Exercise and solution: a nonzero source conormal

Exercise 3.EG. On \(X=\mathbb A^2_{s,t}\), let \(S=\{s=0\}\), \(C=T_S^*X\), and \(f(s,t)=s+t^2\). Fix \(\eta=1\) at zero on the target line. Compute \(E\), the quadratic test and its cycle on \(j_*k_S[1]\). Explain why the support-restricted map is proper even though \(f\) is not.

Solution 3.EG. The source covector is the nonzero normal \(ds\). At that point, \[ F=(1,0),\quad B=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}, \quad L=\{((0,v_t),(\beta_s,0))\}. \tag{RTM.29} \] The tangent condition is \(v_s=0\) and \(2v_t=0\); \(\alpha\) is free. Hence \(E=\{(0,\alpha)\}\), the projection is injective and its image is the vertical target line. In fact the fixed-target scheme fibre is cut out by \(s=0\), \(s+t^2=0\) and \(2t=0\), so is the reduced point, on all coefficient tests.

Take \(g(y)=y\). Then \(h=s+t^2\), and its restriction to \(S\) is \(t^2\). The chosen coordinate \(t\) identifies the Morse line and gives \[ (\Phi_h j_*k_S[1])_0\simeq k, \qquad\text{degree }0,\qquad T=-1. \tag{RTM.30} \] The restriction \(f|_S:t\mapsto t^2\) is finite, with free coordinate algebra of rank two over the target, so is proper. In contrast the full fibre of \(f\) is an affine line, hence the ambient map is not proper. Indeed the affine line is not universally closed: the closed set \(uv=1\) in \(\mathbb A^1_u\times\mathbb A^1_v\) has nonclosed image \(\mathbb A^1_u\setminus\{0\}\) under projection. This violates a defining property of properness after base change. The source object is carried by the closed support \(S\); its direct image is exactly the direct image through this finite restriction. The same two-sheet diagonal quotient therefore computes the target cycle. Both the nonzero input conormal \(ds\) and the output covector \(dy\) have been retained.

3.289. Finite projective operator resolutions on an affine chart

Let \(U=\operatorname{Spec}R\) be a smooth pure-dimensional affine complex variety of dimension \(d\), and put \(A=\Gamma(U,\mathcal D_U)\). Use left modules and the order filtration. The principal-parts and symbol proofs in Differential operators and the Weyl algebra, §§3–5, give \[ F_0A=R,\qquad S=\operatorname{gr}A =\operatorname{Sym}_R\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbf C}(R). \tag{IAC.1} \] The ring \(S\) is Noetherian and regular of dimension at most \(2d\): on a finite open cover its derivation module is free, so it is polynomial of rank \(d\) over a regular coordinate ring. The regular-local and polynomial arguments are proved in Regular local rings, Theorem 2.2 and Proposition 3.3. The Ext test for the last syzygy is Projective dimension and the Auslander–Buchsbaum formula, Theorem 1.3.

We retain a global projective last term. For a finite \(S\)-module take \(2d\) finite free surjections and kernels. At every prime the last kernel is projective by those regular-local bounds and the syzygy test. It is finite projective globally: choose a finite principal cover with dual bases, clear denominators in the corresponding factorizations of its identity through finite free modules, and take a linear combination using powers of the covering functions that generate the unit ideal. This factors its identity through one finite free module.

For a finite graded projective symbol module \(P\), put \(S_+=\bigoplus_{n>0}S_n\). A degree-zero part of an ungraded splitting is a graded splitting. Hence \(Q=P/S_+P\) is a finite graded projective \(R\)-module, with only finitely many nonzero degrees. Lift each \(Q_j\) to \(P_j\) by \(R\)-projectivity. The map \(S\otimes_RQ\to P\) is an isomorphism: its cokernel has zero reduction modulo \(S_+\), so its least nonzero degree would contradict that equality; the surjection splits by graded projectivity, and its kernel vanishes by the same argument. This is the full graded argument of Holonomic D-modules and duality, Lemma 3.0, without shrinking the base to make \(Q_j\) free.

Now take a finite \(A\)-module \(M\) with its bounded-below good filtration. Lift symbol generators to get strict finite filtered free surjections, and repeat on their filtered kernels \(2d\) times. Strictness follows by successively lowering order; boundedness below terminates the process. Noetherianity of \(S\) keeps all symbol kernels finite. The terminal symbol is a graded projective \(P\) as above. Lift the maps \(Q_j\to P_j\) to its filtered terminal kernel \(K\) using \(R\)-projectivity. This gives \[ \bigoplus_j A\otimes_RQ_j\longrightarrow K, \qquad\operatorname{gr}\text{ of this map is }S\otimes_RQ\xrightarrow{\sim}P. \tag{IAC.2} \] Leading-order reduction makes the map surjective; a nonzero kernel element would have a nonzero leading symbol in the zero symbol kernel. Thus it is an isomorphism. Each induced term is finite projective over \(A\), since induction takes an \(R\)-linear split summand of a finite free module to an \(A\)-linear split summand. We obtain a global finite projective resolution \[ 0\to P_{2d}\to P_{2d-1}\to\cdots\to P_0\to M\to0. \tag{IAC.3} \] The final term need not be free. Finite truncation triangles then make every bounded coherent \(A\)-complex perfect. The case \(d=0\) uses the projective symbol module itself and needs no nonzero resolution length.

3.290. The actual affine ind-regular category and its t-structure

The affine module comparison is at the full operator level. For an \(A\)-module \(N\), sheafify its \(R\)-module. A derivation acts on a localization by the Leibniz formula \(\theta(n/f^r)=\theta(n)/f^r-r\theta(f)n/f^{r+1}\). The principal-parts localization of §3 of the operator lesson identifies this with the actual restricted differential operators. Conversely global sections of a quasicoherent operator module recover its module over \(A\). On free operator modules these are inverse on multiplication, unit and every module-action map. The complete free-module bar therefore gives the inverse comparison on arbitrary unbounded modules and mapping complexes. This is a module-category comparison, including all higher maps.

Let \(\mathscr C_U=D^b_{\mathrm{rh}}(\mathcal D_U)\), with the full mapping complexes of (RH.1), and put \[ \mathscr R_\infty(U)=\operatorname{Ind}\mathscr C_U \hookrightarrow\operatorname{Mod}_A. \tag{IAC.4} \] All objects of \(\mathscr C_U\) are perfect by (IAC.3), hence compact in the full affine category. Thus the displayed functor is fully faithful: for filtered presentations its mapping complex is exactly \[ R\operatorname{Hom}\bigl(\operatorname*{colim}_ic_i, \operatorname*{colim}_jc'_j\bigr) =\lim_i\operatorname*{colim}_jR\operatorname{Hom}_A(c_i,c'_j). \tag{IAC.5} \] Its image is the localizing regular subcategory. This supplies a global affine projective verification of the embedding in (RH.3)–(RH.5).

Bounded regular holonomic complexes are closed under their standard truncations. On the ind-category the truncations are \[ \tau^{\le b}\operatorname*{colim}_ic_i =\operatorname*{colim}_i\tau^{\le b}c_i, \qquad \tau^{\ge b}\operatorname*{colim}_ic_i =\operatorname*{colim}_i\tau^{\ge b}c_i. \tag{IAC.6} \] To check the t-structure directly, take the colimit of each bounded truncation triangle. Orthogonality follows from compactness of the bounded terms: maps from a filtered colimit in the lower half to one in the shifted upper half are a limit of colimits of contractible mapping spaces. The triangles and this orthogonality characterize the truncations, so they do not depend on the filtered presentation. The affine embedding is t-exact because standard module truncations commute with exact filtered colimits. The heart consists of ind-objects of regular holonomic modules. No equivalence with the derived category of that heart has been asserted.

Each such heart object is a filtered union of its coherent regular holonomic subobjects. Start with its filtered presentation by regular holonomic modules and replace every map to the colimit by its image. The kernel in a coherent source is coherent by Noetherianity of \(A\), and its quotient is regular by the composition-factor Serre proof in Regular singularities, §5.2. Thus every image is coherent regular holonomic. Filteredness puts any two images inside a third, and their union is the whole colimit. This gives actual heart subobjects, rather than merely a presentation by complexes.

3.291. An all-target mapping bound

If a compact \(c\in\mathscr C_U\) has a finite projective complex in degrees \([r,s]\), then for any \(Z\in\operatorname{Mod}_A^{\le b}\), including an unbounded-below object, \[ R\operatorname{Hom}_A(c,Z)\in D(\mathbf C)^{\le b-r}. \tag{IAC.7} \] Represent \(Z\) by its actual upper-truncated complex. The ordinary Hom from this finite projective source computes derived Hom: a finite induction on the projective source terms sends acyclic targets to acyclic Hom complexes. Every term above degree \(b-r\) is zero. This proves the bound against the entire target complex. It is stronger than a calculation only against modules in degree zero.

An exact functor whose values on heart objects have degrees in a fixed interval \([a,b]\) has, on bounded objects, the bound \[ T(D^{[p,q]})\subset D^{[p+a,q+b]}. \tag{IAC.8} \] Finite Postnikov triangles prove it. For a continuous ind-extension the same inequalities hold on arbitrary objects, by the filtered truncation formulas (IAC.6). This extension uses a fixed functor bound; it does not require a single projective-resolution range for all compact generators.

3.292. Recovery by the lower-truncation tower

For an object \(E\) define its actual inverse tower by \[ E_n=\tau^{\ge -n}E, \qquad E_{n+1}\longrightarrow E_n. \tag{IAC.9} \] The fibre of \(E\to E_n\) is \(\tau^{\le -n-1}E\). A compact test \(c\), represented in degrees \([r,s]\), therefore has \[ \operatorname{fib}\bigl(R\operatorname{Hom}(c,E)\to R\operatorname{Hom}(c,E_n)\bigr) \in D(\mathbf C)^{\le -n-1-r}. \tag{IAC.10} \] For each fixed mapping degree the transition maps eventually become isomorphisms, compatibly with the augmentation from \(E\).

We retain the derived inverse limit. For a countable tower of complexes \(V_n\), it is \[ \lim_nV_n=\operatorname{fib}\left( \prod_{n\ge0}V_n\xrightarrow{1-\mathrm{shift}} \prod_{n\ge0}V_n\right). \tag{IAC.11} \] Here is a resolution proof. In diagrams on the ordered inverse tower, take the direct sums of the representable diagrams in degrees minus one and zero, mapping each generator to itself minus its successor. Evaluation at an index gives the finite-support telescoping resolution of the constant coefficient: a nonzero finite sequence has a final nonzero entry, so the first map is injective, and summing entries identifies its cokernel with the constant coefficient. The representables are projective evaluation objects. Applying the derived mapping functor to this resolution gives (IAC.11), including its augmentation.

Products of vector spaces are exact, so cohomology commutes with these products. For an eventually constant inverse system the product-difference map is surjective: after an index where the transitions are invertible, solve \(u_n-t_nu_{n+1}=v_n\) forwards, then solve through the finite initial segment backwards. Its kernel is the stable value. The long exact sequence of (IAC.11) therefore computes every cohomology of the limit as that stable value. Applying this to (IAC.10), and using preservation of limits by representable mapping functors, proves \[ E\xrightarrow{\sim}\lim_n\tau^{\ge -n}E \quad\text{in }\mathscr R_\infty(U). \tag{IAC.12} \] The compact tests detect the cone. Their stabilization indices may depend on the compact test and the mapping degree. Neither a common bound over all tests nor preservation of arbitrary limits by the affine embedding is used.

3.293. Continuous extensions and the specified tower

Let \(T_0\) be an exact t-exact functor between the bounded small categories defining two such ind-categories. Its continuous extension is t-exact by (IAC.6). In particular its actual truncation comparison is \[ T\tau^{\ge -n}E\simeq\tau^{\ge -n}TE. \tag{IAC.13} \] If the target satisfies (IAC.12), then \(TE\) is the limit of these terms. More generally, an exact continuous functor of finite t-amplitude also satisfies \[ TE\xrightarrow{\sim}\lim_nT(\tau^{\ge -n}E). \tag{IAC.14} \] Indeed its value on the fibre \(\tau^{\le -n-1}E\) has upper degree tending to minus infinity. For an affine ind-regular target, test this fibre by (IAC.7), and apply the same stabilized product-difference argument. For a vector-space target it is the argument of (IAC.11) directly.

Suppose a bounded functor has a natural splitting \(T_0=P_0\oplus Q_0\). Ind-extension retains its inclusion and projection identities, since finite sums commute with colimits. For t-exact summands, or finite-amplitude summands in the scope just proved, the tower comparison gives \[ TE\simeq PE\oplus QE \simeq\left(\lim_nP\tau^{\ge-n}E\right) \oplus\left(\lim_nQ\tau^{\ge-n}E\right). \tag{IAC.15} \] This proves the required completion calculation on these actual ind-categories. It does not assert that a continuous t-exact functor preserves every inverse limit.

3.294. Both closed-point adjoints within the regular category

Fix a closed complex point \(i:\{x\}\hookrightarrow U\). On the regular ind-category there are continuous adjunctions \[ i^*:\mathscr R_\infty(U)\rightleftarrows \operatorname{Vect}:i_* , \qquad i_*\dashv i^!. \tag{IAC.16} \] Here \(i_*V=\delta_x\otimes V\), with the ordinary closed-point delta in degree zero. It is the intrinsic point object of (SPT.24) in this scheme case. The right adjoint is the actual full-operator point functor restricted to the regular category. The left adjoint is the continuous extension of the bounded regular ordinary inverse image. Its scope is the regular category.

For completeness, the full mapping adjunctions extend as follows. On bounded regular inputs they are the actual closed-support adjunctions under (RH.2), with the units and counits of the four-map comparison there. The image of a finite point complex under \(i_*\) is compact by (IAC.3); the ordinary inverse image of a bounded regular object is a finite point complex. Compactness therefore extends the bounded identities to an arbitrary filtered target. Mapping out of a filtered source is a derived limit, so the same identities extend to every source and all mapping complexes. This proves (IAC.16) on the actual ind-categories.

There is a natural comparison \[ \theta_E:i^!E\xrightarrow{\sim}i^*i_*i^!E \longrightarrow i^*E, \tag{IAC.17} \] where the last arrow is \(i^*\) of the right-adjunction counit. It is not asserted to be an equivalence for every \(E\).

The point functors have uniform finite t-amplitude on this chart. Resolve \(\delta_x\) as in (IAC.3). Hom from its resolution gives amplitude \([0,2d]\) for \(i^!\). On a bounded regular module, coherent duality has degrees \([-d,d]\), by Lemma 3.0 of the duality lesson. Bounded ordinary inverse image is \(\mathbb D_{\mathrm{pt}}i^!\mathbb D_U\), with the actual duality comparison. Finite point duality reverses the resulting interval \([-d,3d]\). Hence the safe bounds, also valid on all ind-inputs by (IAC.8), are \[ i^!:D^{[p,q]}\longrightarrow D^{[p,q+2d]}, \qquad i^*:D^{[p,q]}\longrightarrow D^{[p-3d,q+d]}. \tag{IAC.18} \] The duality formula was used on bounded inputs to obtain the bound. On ind-inputs \(i^*\) is its continuous extension; no dualization of an arbitrary infinite coefficient complex is required.

3.295. A heart object with an isolated point part

Call a heart object \(A\) admissible at \(x\) if it is a filtered union of coherent regular holonomic heart subobjects \(A_\lambda\) whose closed carriers have \(x\) as an isolated component, or avoid \(x\) on a neighbourhood. The bounded closed-support decomposition (IS.6), transported by the full bounded comparison (RH.2), is \[ A_\lambda\simeq i_*V_\lambda\oplus B_\lambda, \qquad x\notin\operatorname{supp}(B_\lambda). \tag{IAC.19} \] The point complex \(V_\lambda\) is in degree zero, since it is a summand of a heart object and closed point extension is t-exact. Every derived map between a point object and a bounded object carried by a disjoint closed set is zero in both directions, by closed-support restriction. The decomposition is therefore natural in all bounded morphisms, even when their two disjoint carriers differ. Passing to the filtered system gives the actual point and away parts.

Both point functors commute with this filtered union. On a bounded away term they vanish, and on \(i_*V_\lambda\) their natural comparison is the identity. Thus \[ i^!A\xrightarrow{\theta_A,\ \sim}i^*A \simeq\operatorname*{colim}_\lambda V_\lambda \quad\text{in degree zero}. \tag{IAC.20} \] No single closed carrier or neighbourhood is required for the whole filtered union.

3.296. The actual retract on an unbounded object

Let \(E\in\mathscr R_\infty(U)\) be arbitrary unbounded, with every \(H^mE\) admissible at \(x\). A finite-amplitude exact functor whose values on these heart objects are in degree zero has \[ H^m(TE)\simeq T(H^mE) \qquad(T=i^*,i^!). \tag{IAC.21} \] Here is the convergence argument without a derived-heart assertion. Bounds (IAC.18) show that a fixed output degree depends on a finite window of input truncations; choose its endpoints farther than those amplitude bounds. The two omitted tails have zero cohomology in that degree and in its adjacent degrees. On the finite window, apply the finite Postnikov filtration. Each heart term has only one output degree by (IAC.20), so its finite filtration spectral sequence has only that row and yields (IAC.21). All comparisons are the functor's truncation maps, and hence are natural.

Applying (IAC.21) to the natural map (IAC.17), every cohomology map is (IAC.20). Consequently \[ \theta_E:i^!E\xrightarrow{\sim}i^*E. \tag{IAC.22} \] Let \(\varepsilon_E:i_*i^!E\to E\) be the right-adjunction counit and \(\eta_E:E\to i_*i^*E\) the left-adjunction unit. Define \[ u_E=\varepsilon_E, \qquad r_E=i_*(\theta_E^{-1})\eta_E, \qquad r_Eu_E=\operatorname{Id}_{i_*i^!E}. \tag{IAC.23} \] To check the last identity, naturality of the left unit identifies \(\eta_E\varepsilon_E\) with \(i_*\theta_E\), since that unit is the identity on objects in the fully faithful image of \(i_*\). Thus the composite is exactly the displayed identity. In particular \[ e_E=u_Er_E,\qquad e_E^2=e_E, \qquad E\simeq i_*i^!E\oplus\operatorname{cofib}(u_E). \tag{IAC.24} \] This is a natural projector on the full subcategory of such \(E\). It is an identity of actual maps and mapping complexes. If some heart piece has a nonzero point component, (IAC.21) gives \[ H^m(i^!E)\ne0, \qquad i_*i^!E\ne0. \tag{IAC.25} \] This is the isolated-point retract needed for a proper-image argument, with no cohomological boundedness requirement on \(E\).

3.297. The extension of bounded algebraic cycle functors

For a regular function on a separated finite-type complex variety, the bounded constructible normalized nearby and vanishing cycles are t-exact at the algebraic scope of Nearby and vanishing cycles, §5, Theorem 5.1. That proof uses its actual cyclic-cover comparison in Proposition F.1, bounded constructibility in Theorem G.4 and its resolution appendices, and the proved principal affine-open perverse bounds. It does not use the unrestricted holomorphic or arithmetic cases as substitutes.

Conjugate that bounded functor by (RH.2), and extend by ind-colimits. Regard the zero-fibre output as supported in a smooth ambient chart by the closed-support equivalence. The actual regular ind-cycle functor is \[ \Phi_g^{\mathrm{reg}}=\operatorname{Ind}(\Phi_{g,0}^{\mathrm{reg}}). \tag{IAC.26} \] It is t-exact by (IAC.6), retains the bounded unit, cone and monodromy maps, and satisfies \[ H^m\Phi_g^{\mathrm{reg}}F =\Phi_g^{\mathrm{reg}}H^mF. \tag{IAC.27} \] It is the cycle functor in this chartwise ind-regular theory. This construction does not identify it with a functor on all unbounded classical sheaves.

Suppose that for each coherent heart subobject \(A\subset H^mF\), its actual bounded cycle has the isolated-point carrier property in (IAC.19). Exactness on hearts makes the cycle of the filtered union a filtered union of those bounded cycles. The object \(E=\Phi_g^{\mathrm{reg}}F\) therefore satisfies §3.296, giving \[ \Phi_g^{\mathrm{reg}}F\simeq i_*i^!\Phi_g^{\mathrm{reg}}F\oplus Q(F). \tag{IAC.28} \] If one bounded test has nonzero point coefficient, it remains nonzero in this retract. Indeed its injection into the corresponding cycle heart object remains injective after degree-zero \(i^!\): \(H^0i^!\) is Hom from the point module and is left exact on the operator heart. Equations (IAC.21) and (IAC.27) then detect a nonzero cohomology of the point coefficient: \[ i^!\Phi_{g,0}^{\mathrm{reg}}A\ne0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad i^!\Phi_g^{\mathrm{reg}}F\ne0. \tag{IAC.29} \] This supplies the full unbounded splitting and detection deductions of IS.7–IS.8 at this algebraic cycle scope. The bounded support identity AIC.8 and §§3.499–3.502 give the characteristic-to-cycle implication for every ind-regular input satisfying componentwise isolation. Sections 3.517–3.523 give nonvanishing from any finite actual characteristic witness, including zero covectors and degenerate Hessians, without a critical-point condition on invisible strata. The neighbourhood may depend on the finite cohomology subobject. Sections 3.527–3.533 prove the actual proper-cycle and point-image comparison over complex smooth separated finite-type schemes. Sections 3.537–3.543 give original-complex proper detection through universal quadratic parameters under componentwise isolation of the selected compatible point. HRI and RHC give its regular-input Hecke application. GFP.55 makes that input condition available throughout the full original-complex Hecke-lisse category. GZR.33 supplies chartwise ind-regularity for every independently nilpotent-supported object over the complex numbers in every genus.

3.298. Smooth normalization and the scope of descent

For a smooth map of relative complex dimension \(r\), the left-module inverse transfer and (RH.6) give the t-exact normalized pullback \[ f^![-r]=f^\natural. \tag{IAC.30} \] Flatness makes the right side exact on modules, and (IAC.6) extends that assertion to ind-regular inputs. Relative dimensions add, so the normalization composes with its actual transfer maps. Local line Morita equivalences for the half twist in §3.57 are exact and retain these conclusions on their charts.

A limit of categories satisfying (IAC.12) inherits that recovery property whenever its evaluation functors preserve the relevant limits and identify its truncations with the component truncations: evaluate the natural recovery map and use joint conservativity. This deduction uses both hypotheses. The full chart diagram (RH.7) also has nonsmooth refinement arrows; a normalized face calculation alone does not establish their pointwise-truncation and limit properties. In particular, bounded regular stack objects cannot all be declared compact, as the \(B\mathbf G_m\) example (SPT.25) shows. The local cycle retract above is constructed on the scheme presentations used in the bounded proper Hecke test and needs no such global compactness assertion.

Figure 3.45. The affine filtered syzygy remains projective in (IAC.1)–(IAC.3). Its mapping bound gives the actual inverse-limit recovery (IAC.7)–(IAC.12). The point comparison and adjunction maps give the projector, including its identity composite, in (IAC.17)–(IAC.24). The cycle application (IAC.26)–(IAC.29) retains the bounded carrier and nonzero-test hypotheses. The examples distinguish projectivity from freeness, the truncation tower from arbitrary products, and a filtered isolated-point decomposition from a uniform support neighbourhood. Free further reading on the isolated-cycle construction is Arinkin–Gaitsgory–Kazhdan–Raskin–Rozenblyum–Varshavsky, Appendix H.

3.299. Exercise and solution: a projective term that is not globally free

Exercise 3.EH. Let \(R=\mathbf C\times\mathbf C\), \(e=(1,0)\), and \(P=Re\). Compute its dual, mapping functor and projective dimension. Explain which part of the affine proof would fail if its final projective term were called globally free.

Solution 3.EH. The splitting \(R=Re\oplus R(1-e)\) makes \(P\) finite projective of dimension zero. Restriction and evaluation give \[ P^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}_R(P,R)=eR, \qquad R\operatorname{Hom}_R(P,Z)=eZ. \tag{IAC.31} \] This is an identity of full complexes, since the projector \(e\) is exact. The rank on the first component is one and on the second is zero, whereas a free module has equal ranks on both components. Thus \(P\) is not free. It is already an operator example on the two-point smooth affine scheme, whose differential operators are \(R\). It verifies (IAC.7) with \(r=0\) and the zero-dimensional case of (IAC.3). The proof needs the split-projective last term, not an unjustified choice of a global basis.

3.300. Exercise and solution: the specified tower is not an arbitrary limit

Exercise 3.EI. On complexes of vector spaces let \(T(V)=W\otimes V\), where \(W=\bigoplus_{j\ge0}\mathbf C e_j\). Show that this functor is continuous and t-exact and obeys the truncation-tower comparison, but does not preserve countable products.

Solution 3.EI. Tensor over a field is exact and preserves colimits. For the product of copies of \(\mathbf C\) in degree zero, the canonical comparison is \[ \bigoplus_j\prod_n\mathbf C \longrightarrow\prod_n\bigoplus_j\mathbf C. \tag{IAC.32} \] The left side has a single finite set of nonzero \(j\)-coordinates for the entire family. The right side only requires finite \(j\)-support in each row \(n\). The diagonal family with its \(n\)-th row equal to \(e_n\) belongs to the right side and not to the left. Thus the comparison is not surjective.

For \(V=\bigoplus_{a\ge0}\mathbf C[a]\), each degree contains one coefficient copy. Its lower truncations are finite sums, and \[ \lim_nT(\tau^{\ge-n}V) =\bigoplus_{a\ge0}W[a]=T(V). \tag{IAC.33} \] The equality is degreewise, with the actual projection transitions; their fixed-degree systems stabilize. For a general complex, the same stabilized-degree argument is (IAC.13)–(IAC.14). The failure in (IAC.32) is a different inverse limit and supplies no counterexample to that statement.

3.301. Exercise and solution: infinitely many away components

Exercise 3.EJ. On the affine line let \(i\) be the point zero and \(\delta_a\) the regular closed-point delta. In the actual regular ind-category form \[ E=\bigoplus_{j\ge0} \bigl(\delta_0\oplus\delta_{1/(j+1)}\bigr)[j]. \tag{IAC.34} \] Compute the two point adjoints and the projector. Decide whether a single Zariski neighbourhood of zero separates all the away supports.

Solution 3.EJ. Each summand is a shifted bounded regular object, so the finite partial sums define this ind-object. Both point functors are continuous. On the point summand they are the coefficient, and on each distinct closed point they vanish in every degree by disjoint-support restriction. Hence \[ i^!E\xrightarrow{\theta_E,\ \sim}i^*E =\bigoplus_{j\ge0}\mathbf C[j]. \tag{IAC.35} \] The comparison is the identity on every coefficient summand. The maps in (IAC.23) are respectively inclusion of, and projection onto, the \(\delta_0\)-summands. Their composite on that point object is the identity; the complementary object is the displayed sum of the away deltas. These are actual morphisms in the ind-category, including every negative cohomological degree.

Every Zariski neighbourhood of zero in the affine line omits only finitely many closed points: its complement is a proper closed subset, cut out by a nonzero one-variable polynomial, which has finitely many roots by successive polynomial division. The distinct points \(1/(j+1)\) are infinite. Thus no such neighbourhood separates all away supports. Each finite coherent heart piece nevertheless has its isolated point decomposition, which is exactly the hypothesis used in §3.296. This computation concerns the actual ind-regular operations specified in (IAC.16) and makes no identification with all unbounded classical sheaves.

3.302. A smooth conic Lagrangian germ is a conormal at constant rank

Let \(X\) be a complex manifold of dimension \(n\), let \(F\) be a bounded weakly complex constructible complex of complex vector spaces, and fix a nonzero covector \(p=(x,\xi)\in\operatorname{SS}(F)\). Suppose that on a cotangent neighbourhood of \(p\) its microsupport is contained in a smooth complex-conic Lagrangian \(C\), and that the restriction of the projection to \(C\) has constant rank \(d\). The complex constant-rank theorem gives a local image submanifold \(Y\subset X\) of dimension \(d\). The fibre Euler vector \((0,\xi)\) is tangent to \(C\). With the convention \(\omega=d\xi\wedge dx\), isotropy gives \[ 0=\omega\bigl((0,\xi),(v,\alpha)\bigr)=\xi(v), \qquad(v,\alpha)\in T_{(x,\xi)}C. \tag{MCM.1} \] Every vector of \(T_xY\) lifts through this tangent projection. The same calculation at nearby points puts the germ of \(C\) in \(T_Y^*X\). Both are smooth of dimension \(n\); the inclusion has invertible differential and is open near \(p\). Hence \[ C=T_Y^*X\quad\text{as germs at }p. \tag{MCM.2} \] The supported coefficient proof in Local forms and inverse image, formulas LFI9–LFI10, now supplies a bounded coefficient complex \(M\) and an isomorphism \[ F\simeq M_Y\quad\text{in }D^b(\mathbf C_X;p). \tag{MCM.3} \] Here \(M_Y\) is the constant complex on the local submanifold, extended by zero. The assertion concerns the category localized at the covector. It does not assert an isomorphism on an ordinary neighbourhood of its base point.

For an actual weakly complex constructible complex, its microsupport is a closed complex analytic conic Lagrangian, by Complex microlocal stratifications and constructibility, the four-test theorem. On each component one can remove the other components, the singular locus and the rank-drop locus of the projection. The connected regular-locus and maximal-minor proof GC6–GC9 in Weierstrass parametrization and connected regular loci proves that the remaining constant-rank region is dense. Thus the geometric premise above applies at the nonzero generic points of each component.

3.303. A test that inverts arbitrary denominators

Choose a holomorphic \(h\) with \(h(x)=0\) and \(dh_x=\xi\). Its zero fibre \(T\) is smooth after shrinking. On all bounded sheaf complexes define the exact functor \[ \mathcal T_h(A)=(\mu_TA)_p. \tag{MCM.4} \] The arbitrary bounded support theorem MO15 in Microsupport operations gives \(\mathcal T_h(A)=0\) whenever \(p\notin\operatorname{SS}(A)\). Consequently a map whose cone avoids \(p\) becomes an isomorphism under this test, including when the cone is not complex constructible.

Here is the quotient criterion used for (MCM.3). Let \(\mathcal N_p\) be the full subcategory of bounded complexes whose microsupport avoids \(p\). Triangle estimates and the equality for finite direct sums make it thick. Cones in this subcategory define the denominators. For a map \(u:A\to B\) and a denominator \(s:A\to A'\), the homotopy pushout \(B'=B\sqcup_A A'\) gives a denominator \(B\to B'\) with the same cone. Homotopy pullback gives the reversed construction. These supply the common-square rule for both fraction constructions. For cancellation, if a difference of two maps vanishes after precomposition with a denominator, the exact Hom sequence of its triangle factors the difference through its cone \(N\in\mathcal N_p\). Postcomposing with the map to the cofiber of \(N\to B\) kills the difference, and that map is again a denominator. The reversed argument proves the other cancellation rule. The octahedral triangle for a composite retains its cone in the thick subcategory. Fractions modulo these common refinements therefore have the zero criterion that a further denominator kills the numerator. In particular, if the identity of \(A\) is zero in the quotient, a denominator \(s:A'\to A\) satisfies \(s=0\). Its cone is then \(A\oplus A'[1]\); thickness gives \(A\in\mathcal N_p\). Conversely the denominator \(0\to A\) makes every object of \(\mathcal N_p\) zero. Thus \[ A=0\text{ in }D^b(\mathbf C_X;p) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p\notin\operatorname{SS}(A). \tag{MCM.5} \] These are the fraction and null-object constructions of Microlocal categories, MC.1–MC.2. Since \(\mathcal T_h\) sends every denominator to an isomorphism, composing a numerator with the inverse image of its denominator defines its value on a fraction. Common refinements prove independence. The model isomorphism therefore gives \[ \mathcal T_h(F)\simeq\mathcal T_h(M_Y). \tag{MCM.6} \] Only the two endpoints need to be weakly complex constructible in the next comparison. Intermediate objects in the fractions can be arbitrary bounded sheaf complexes.

3.304. The coefficient detected by a transverse function

Suppose also that \(\operatorname{graph}(dh)\) is transverse to \(C\) at \(p\). In coordinates adapted to \(Y\), equality (MCM.2) says exactly that \(h|_Y\) has a nondegenerate critical point at \(x\). The actual normal and conormal comparison in Complex nearby cycles as normal and conormal sections, formula (20), gives \[ \Phi_h(F)_x\simeq\mathcal T_h(F), \qquad \mathcal T_h(M_Y)\simeq\Phi_h(M_Y)_x. \tag{MCM.7} \] The normalization is \(\Phi_h=\operatorname{Cone}(i^*\to\psi_h)[-1]\), as in (RTM.20). The real covector is \(\operatorname{Re}(dh)\); the complex normal-line pairing has no conjugation. The closed-ray Fourier comparison supplies (MCM.7) without an extra rank-two or orientation shift.

The quadratic calculation applies to this holomorphic Morse function. Explicitly, after subtracting its critical value, write \(h|_Y=z^tA(z)z\), where \(A\) is symmetric holomorphic and \(2A(0)\) is the invertible Hessian. One may take its entries from the Taylor integral of the second derivatives along \(tz\), \(0\le t\le1\). A constant change of basis gives successive unit pivots; finite Gram–Schmidt diagonalizes the form holomorphically. Each nonzero diagonal unit has a holomorphic square root on a smaller neighbourhood, using the convergent binomial series after dividing by its value at zero. The resulting coordinates have invertible differential, so the holomorphic inverse-function theorem gives an actual local change of coordinates to \(\sum_{j=1}^d w_j^2\).

The covered-ball retraction and constant-section unit of (RTM.16)–(RTM.20), equivalently Quadratic cycles and the holomorphic microsupport test, its covered quadratic calculation, now give the isomorphism of coefficient complexes \[ \Phi_h(F)_x\simeq M\otimes o_h[-d]. \tag{MCM.8} \] The Morse orientation line \(o_h\) is one-dimensional in degree zero. At \(d=0\), the nearby fibre on \(Y\) is empty, and the same formula reads \(M\). If \(M=0\), (MCM.3) and (MCM.5) would contradict \(p\in\operatorname{SS}(F)\). Tensoring with a line and shifting are invertible, so \[ p\in\operatorname{SS}(F) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \Phi_h(F)_x\ne0. \tag{MCM.9} \] This comparison detects the full coefficient complex. A localized coefficient isomorphism at one covector has not been asserted to intertwine the cycle monodromy; Solution 3.EK distinguishes those assertions.

3.305. The closed carrier of the bounded cycle near the test point

The closed support bound (24) proved in the normal/conormal lesson is \[ \operatorname{supp}\Phi_h(F) \subset\{y:h(y)=0,\ (y,dh_y)\in\operatorname{SS}(F)\}. \tag{MCM.10} \] Shrink so that \(\operatorname{graph}(dh)\) lies in the cotangent neighbourhood used above. Two transverse smooth \(n\)-dimensional germs in a \(2n\)-manifold have an isolated intersection: their defining normal coordinates have invertible combined differential, so the inverse-function theorem makes the intersection the single reduced point. Therefore a neighbourhood \(W\) of \(x\) satisfies \[ \operatorname{supp}\Phi_h(F)\cap W\subset\{x\}. \tag{MCM.11} \] Closed support, rather than just a statement about separate stalks, is used here. Localization for its complement identifies the restricted cycle with the closed point extension of its coefficient. Together with (MCM.8)–(MCM.9), this yields \[ \Phi_h(F)|_{W\cap h^{-1}(0)} \simeq i_*(M\otimes o_h[-d])\ne0. \tag{MCM.12} \] If the bounded input and cycle are perverse, closed point extension is t-exact. Hence \(M\otimes o_h[-d]\) is in degree zero. In the algebraic finite-coefficient setting the cycle t-exactness is Theorem 5.1 of Nearby and vanishing cycles, at the scope specified in §3.297. Its finite-dimensional point coefficient is then an actual nonzero heart object.

3.306. Analytic isolation gives an isolated algebraic carrier

First let \(B\) be a coherent regular holonomic module on a smooth complex algebraic variety \(U\). Its finite composition series is supplied by Holonomic D-modules and duality, Theorem 2.2. By the definition and Serre argument of Regular singularities, §5, its simple factors have presentations \(j_{a,!*}E_a\) on smooth locally closed algebraic strata \(S_a\), with \(E_a\) a nonzero regular connection. Remove any zero-rank open-and-closed components from the chosen stratum. The remaining bundle has positive rank at every point of \(S_a\), and its horizontal coefficient system has that rank by the flat-frame calculation.

The full four-map and t-exact comparison (RH.2) takes this minimal extension to the perverse intermediate extension of that coefficient system. It restricts to the given nonzero system on \(S_a\) and vanishes off \(\overline{S_a}\). Its closed analytic carrier is therefore the analytic closure of \(S_a\). The density statement following Theorem 4.1 of Complex analytic spaces and analytification identifies this with \(\overline{S_a}^{\,\mathrm{an}}\): a dense algebraic open remains analytically dense. That proof uses the radical-ideal comparison and faithful flatness of the analytic local ring, and includes singular closures.

Restriction to an analytic open is perverse t-exact, since the stalk and costalk tests are local. Consequently in a short exact sequence of perverse objects the middle term vanishes on an open exactly when both end terms do. Its closed carrier is the union of their closed carriers. The finite composition series thus gives the actual reduced algebraic closed carrier \[ Z_B=\bigcup_a\overline{S_a}, \qquad \operatorname{supp}\operatorname{DR}(B)=Z_B^{\mathrm{an}}. \tag{MCM.13} \] This assertion concerns closed carriers, and makes no equality of cotangent supports. For a bounded regular operator complex, take the finite union of the carriers of its cohomology modules. Boundedness and exact open restriction give the same assertion without identifying a category with the derived category of its heart.

Suppose now that the analytic closed carrier is contained in \(\{x\}\) on an analytic neighbourhood of \(x\). If \(x\) is absent from \(Z_B\), its algebraic open complement already avoids the carrier. Otherwise write \(A=\mathcal O_{U,x}\), \(H=\mathcal O_{U^{\mathrm{an}},x}\), and let \(I\subset A\) be the ideal of the reduced carrier. Lemma 3.1 of the analytification lesson identifies the extended radical ideal with the actual analytic vanishing ideal. Its zero germ is the single point. Theorem 4.1 gives faithful flatness and contraction of ideals. Hence \[ IH=\mathfrak m_AH, \qquad IH\cap A=I, \qquad I=\mathfrak m_A. \tag{MCM.14} \] Thus the reduced carrier's algebraic local ring is \(\mathbf C\). To see the open component explicitly, take an affine neighbourhood in the reduced carrier with coordinate ring \(D\), and let \(\mathfrak m\) be the maximal ideal of \(x\). It is finitely generated. Each generator vanishes in \(D_{\mathfrak m}=\mathbf C\), so a denominator outside \(\mathfrak m\) kills it. The product \(s\) of those finitely many denominators satisfies \[ s\notin\mathfrak m, \qquad \mathfrak mD_s=0, \qquad D_s=\mathbf C. \tag{MCM.15} \] The principal open \(D(s)\) in the carrier is exactly \(\{x\}\). Since \(x\) is also closed, the global reduced carrier decomposes as \[ Z_B=\{x\}\amalg Z'_B, \qquad x\notin Z'_B, \qquad Z'_B\text{ closed}. \tag{MCM.16} \] This is precisely the isolated closed-carrier premise in (IAC.19). The argument is on the reduced carrier. It does not remove nilpotents from a cotangent-fibre scheme or prove its tangent zero; Solution 3.EM makes that distinction explicit.

3.307. A common microsupport bound for a family

Let \(\{F_\lambda\}\) be any family of bounded weakly complex constructible complexes. Suppose their microsupports are all contained, on one fixed cotangent neighbourhood \(V\), in the same smooth conic Lagrangian \(C\). Assume that the projection of \(C\) has constant rank there and \(\operatorname{graph}(dh)\) meets it transversely at \(p\). The neighbourhood in (MCM.11) depends on \(C,V,h\), rather than on a member of the family. The same support argument gives \[ \operatorname{supp}\Phi_h(F_\lambda)\cap W \subset\{x\}\quad\text{for every }\lambda. \tag{MCM.17} \] Some members may have zero cycles. If \(p\) belongs to the microsupport of one member, its nonzero coefficient is detected by (MCM.9).

For a smooth affine complex algebraic \(U\), a regular function \(h\) and \(E\in\mathscr R_\infty(U)\), take the family \(F_A=\operatorname{DR}(A)\) over every coherent regular heart subobject \(A\subset H^mE\) and every integer \(m\). Assume the common microsupport bound just stated for this family. Its actual bounded algebraic cycles are regular operator heart objects by §3.297. Their closed carriers satisfy (MCM.17), so §3.306 makes each carrier either avoid \(x\) or have \(x\) as an isolated algebraic component. Thus every cycle heart is admissible as in (IAC.19). For one such subobject the nonzero-test implication is \[ p\in\operatorname{SS}(F_A),\quad \operatorname{graph}(dh)\pitchfork C \quad\Longrightarrow\quad H^0i^!\Phi_{h,0}^{\mathrm{reg}}A\ne0. \tag{MCM.18} \] The point heart injection and (IAC.21), (IAC.27) then give \[ i^!\Phi_h^{\mathrm{reg}}E\ne0. \tag{MCM.19} \] This gives the actual unbounded point retract and detection under the stated common microsupport bound. The algebraic neighbourhoods supplied by §3.306 may depend on the coherent object. The natural point comparison in §3.295 and the finite-amplitude argument in §3.296 do not require one common algebraic neighbourhood, and no comparison with all unbounded classical sheaves is used.

3.308. The quadratic test and the operator support comparison

At a point of the reduced bounded Hecke cotangent fibre, (RTM.1)–(RTM.12) construct \(h=g\circ f\) with its exact first derivative and a transverse Hessian graph. If the source covector lies in the actual microsupport of a bounded coefficient complex and in its generic smooth constant-rank region, (MCM.8)–(MCM.12) supply the nonzero isolated cycle coefficient for that test. In particular the source-to-model comparison takes place in the covector-localized category, and the test is transferred by (MCM.4)–(MCM.7).

The differential-operator characteristic support is a further input. The equality that would identify the two notions is \[ \operatorname{SS}(\operatorname{DR}A) =\operatorname{Char}(A). \tag{MCM.20} \] The equality MCM.20 is proved by the analytic density/duality calculation SDR.22–SDR.24 and the algebraic comparison AIC.8. Sections 3.499–3.502 use membership in \(\operatorname{Char}(A)\) to give the nonzero full unbounded cycle retract for actual ind-regular inputs under componentwise isolation, allowing different neighbourhoods for different finite pieces. Sections 3.517–3.523 require only actual characteristic isolation for that finite witness; zero covectors, singular conormals, degenerate Hessians and nonisolated invisible critical loci are included. Sections 3.503–3.504 prove the actual characteristic-support and full unbounded cohomological-support comparison under arbitrary characteristic-zero field extension. Sections 3.527–3.533 prove the actual proper regular Ind-cycle comparison over complex smooth separated finite-type schemes. Regular cycles over new geometric fields, full nilpotent regularity and enhanced geometric-field generation retain their separate requirements. Sections 3.537–3.543 give original-complex proper detection with componentwise isolation of the selected compatible point by an actual universal quadratic family.

Figure 3.46. In the displayed real slice of \(T^*\mathbf C^2\), \(Y=\{z_1=0\}\), \(h=z_1+t^2\), \(z_1=0\) and \(\xi_1=1\); the remaining coordinates are \((t,\xi_t)\). The conormal has \(\xi_t=0\), and the function graph has \(\xi_t=2t\), giving the single transverse point. Equations (MCM.1)–(MCM.12) transfer this test through the covector-localized coefficient model with its exact degree and orientation line. Equations (MCM.13)–(MCM.19) give the algebraic closed carrier and the actual ind-regular point retract under the common microsupport hypothesis. The three solutions retain the distinctions between coefficient complexes and monodromy, arbitrary real denominator cones and weak complex endpoints, and reduced closed carriers and nonreduced fibre schemes. The characteristic-support equality is AIC.8; the common-cone unbounded cycle consequence is proved in §§3.487–3.493.

3.309. Exercise and solution: a coefficient isomorphism need not preserve monodromy

Exercise 3.EK. On a disc let \(j:\Delta^*\hookrightarrow\Delta\), and let \(L\) be the rank-one complex local system with monodromy \(-1\). Put \(F=j_!L[1]\) and \(h(z)=z\). Compute its normalized vanishing coefficient and monodromy. Compare the point coefficient model at a nonzero cotangent vector over zero.

Solution 3.EK. The local system is the sign coefficient of the explicit double cover \(w\mapsto w^2\). On the universal cover the nearby coefficient of \(L\) is \(\mathbf C\), with deck action \(-1\). The stalk of \(j_!L\) at zero is zero. Therefore \[ \Phi_h(F)_0 =\operatorname{Cone}(0\to\mathbf C[1])[-1] =\mathbf C, \qquad T=-\operatorname{Id}. \tag{MCM.21} \] Off zero the complex is locally constant. Its microsupport there is the zero section. At zero it cannot have only zero covectors, since the zero-section local constancy theorem would contradict its zero stalk and nonzero neighbouring stalks. Complex conicity makes the nonzero fibre over zero a single orbit. Thus every nonzero covector there is in its microsupport, and the conormal component is the vertical fibre, of projection rank zero.

Its coefficient model is \(\delta_0\mathbf C\). For that model, \(h\) is zero on its point support, the nearby coefficient is empty, and \[ \Phi_h(\delta_0\mathbf C)_0=\mathbf C, \qquad T=\operatorname{Id}. \tag{MCM.22} \] The coefficient complexes agree. An equivariant isomorphism would have to intertwine \(-1\) and \(1\), and hence would be zero over \(\mathbf C\). Thus their monodromy objects are not isomorphic. The original sheaves also do not agree on an ordinary neighbourhood: one has nonzero punctured stalks and the point model has none.

3.310. Exercise and solution: a denominator cone outside complex constructibility

Exercise 3.EL. Write \(z=a+ib\) on \(\mathbf C\), let \(N=\mathbf C_{\{a\ge0\}}\), and set \(p=(0,db)=\operatorname{Re}(-i\,dz)\), \(h=-iz\). Show that \(N\) is invisible to the test (MCM.4), but its actual holomorphic vanishing coefficient is nonzero. Explain the consequence for fractions through arbitrary bounded objects.

Solution 3.EL. Write \(q(a,b)=a\). The sheaf is the actual pullback \(N=q^{-1}\mathbf C_{[0,\infty)}\). The submersion formula MO10 in Microsupport operations puts its microsupport in the horizontal bundle: every covector has zero \(db\)-component. Thus \(p\notin\operatorname{SS}(N)\) and \[ \mathcal T_h(N)=0. \tag{MCM.23} \] This sheaf is real constructible and not weakly complex constructible near zero. In complex dimension one, proper analytic strata are discrete. A locally finite such stratification cannot make the stalk jump across a whole real line locally constant on its open stratum.

For the actual nearby coefficient, a punctured disc lifted to its logarithmic cover meets the closed right halfplane in disjoint closed angular strips indexed by \(\mathbf Z\). Each strip is a product of a radial logarithmic half-line with a closed interval. It is convex and contractible. Closed-support restriction identifies the section complex on each strip with \(\mathbf C\) in degree zero, and the whole section complex is their product. Shrinking the disc changes only the radial bound and induces the identity on these coefficients. The stalk \(N_0=\mathbf C\) maps to those sections by the diagonal constant-section unit. Since products of vector spaces are exact, the normalized cone gives \[ \psi_h(N)_0=\prod_{m\in\mathbf Z}\mathbf C, \qquad \Phi_h(N)_0= \left(\left(\prod_{m\in\mathbf Z}\mathbf C\right) /\mathbf C_{\mathrm{diag}}\right)[-1]\ne0. \tag{MCM.24} \] The quotient is nonzero, for instance by a family equal to one on one strip and zero on the others. Its only cohomology lies in degree one. For any bounded \(B\), the inclusion \(B\to B\oplus N\) has cone \(N\) and is a denominator at \(p\). The functor \(\mathcal T_h\) inverts it. Applying the ordinary cycle functor to the two terms instead adds the nonzero coefficient (MCM.24). This proves why the endpoint comparison (MCM.7) is used only for weakly complex constructible endpoints, while the functor through arbitrary fractions is (MCM.4).

3.311. Exercise and solution: an isolated carrier does not remove a doubled point

Exercise 3.EM. At zero in the affine line compare the closed scheme \(Z=\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbf C[t]/(t^2))\) with its reduced carrier. Compute their analytic local rings and tangent spaces. Explain why (MCM.14) applies to the carrier and cannot replace the actual fibre-tangent hypothesis of (RTM.2).

Solution 3.EM. Polynomial and convergent division by \(t^2\) leave exactly a constant and a linear coefficient, so \[ \mathcal O_{Z^{\mathrm{an}},0} =\mathbf C\{t\}/(t^2) =\mathbf C\oplus\mathbf C\epsilon, \qquad\epsilon^2=0. \tag{MCM.25} \] The maximal ideal is \(\mathbf C\epsilon\), and its square is zero. Its cotangent space has dimension one, hence so does the tangent space. The reduced carrier instead has \[ I_{Z_{\mathrm{red}}}=(t),\qquad \mathcal O_{Z_{\mathrm{red}},0}=\mathbf C,\qquad T_0Z_{\mathrm{red}}=0,\qquad T_0Z\simeq\mathbf C. \tag{MCM.26} \] The analytic zero set is a single point in both cases. The analytic vanishing ideal is the radical \((t)\), while the full analytic scheme ideal remains \((t^2)\). Lemma 3.1 is applied only to the reduced carrier in (MCM.14). Analytification itself retains the full ideal by Theorem 3.2 of the analytification lesson. Thus the closed-carrier decomposition used for the retract gives no permission to discard the nilpotents or the nonzero tangent of an actual cotangent fibre. Reduced-fibre transversality still needs its precise hypothesis.

3.312. Holomorphic germs on a compact convex set

Work over \(\mathbf C\). If \(K\subset\mathbf C^n\) is compact and convex, write \(\mathcal O(K)\) for germs of holomorphic functions on neighbourhoods of \(K\). This notation retains normal germs when \(K\) is contained in a proper real or complex affine subspace.

There are cofinally many bounded open real polyhedra containing \(K\), inside any prescribed neighbourhood. To prove this, first choose a small \(\eta>0\) with \(K+B_\eta\) in that neighbourhood, and a bounded box containing its closure. For each point \(y\) of the box outside \(K+B_\eta\), minimize distance to \(K\), obtaining \(q\in K\). Differentiating squared distance along \(q+t(z-q)\), \(z\in K\), gives \(\langle y-q,z-q\rangle\le0\). The unit normal \(\nu=(y-q)/|y-q|\) therefore has support value \(h_K(\nu)=\langle\nu,q\rangle\), while \(\langle\nu,y\rangle-h_K(\nu)\ge\eta\). The open condition \(\langle\nu,z\rangle>h_K(\nu)+\eta/2\) excludes a neighbourhood of \(y\). Finitely many such exclusions cover that compact part of the box. Their complementary strict halfspaces, together with the box inequalities, give the desired polyhedron.

Write its inequalities as \(u_j(z)=\operatorname{Re}\ell_j(z)<c_j\), with \(\ell_j\) complex linear. It has the smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion \[ \rho(z)=|z|^2+\sum_j\frac1{c_j-u_j(z)}, \qquad H_\rho\ge H_{|z|^2}. \tag{SCP.1} \] Each \(u_j\) is pluriharmonic and \((c_j-t)^{-1}\) is convex increasing, so the Hessian assertion follows by the chain rule. Approaching a boundary face makes its summand diverge; boundedness of the polyhedron proves exhaustion. The proof of holomorphic acyclicity on such a Stein domain is Stein domains in complex space, Theorems 2.1–2.2: the finite locally square-integrable Dolbeault resolution and its global positive-degree solution give \(H^q(\mathcal O)=0\), \(q>0\). These are the actual domain sheaves and distributional equations of that proof.

Compact-neighbourhood continuity, including its restriction map, is proved in Noncharacteristic deformation, N3–N4. Applying it to the cofinal polyhedra, and using exactness of filtered vector-space colimits, gives \[ R\Gamma(K;\mathcal O)=\mathcal O(K)[0]. \tag{SCP.2} \] This includes a compact ball in a complex hyperplane and the empty set. It is a statement about the restricted sheaf, not a closed-fibre formula for an arbitrary direct image.

3.313. A uniform bound for the actual analytic support tests

Let \(D=\mathcal D^{\mathrm{an}}_{X,x}\) at a point of a complex \(n\)-manifold. In holomorphic coordinates its coefficient ring \(H=\mathbf C\{z_1,\ldots,z_n\}\) is Noetherian regular of dimension \(n\), by Complex analytic spaces and analytification, Lemma 2.1 and Theorem 4.1. The order symbols give \[ \operatorname{gr}D=H[\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n]. \tag{SCP.3} \] This ring is Noetherian regular of dimension \(2n\). The regular-local projective-dimension and polynomial proofs are Regular local rings, Theorem 2.2 and Proposition 3.3.

The strict filtered syzygy proof of (IAC.1)–(IAC.3) works over this coefficient ring as well. Here are the relevant points. Take \(2n\) strict finite filtered free presentations of a finite \(D\)-module and their kernels. Their symbols remain finite, and the last symbol syzygy is graded projective by the regular-ring bound and the chosen-syzygy Ext criterion. A graded splitting shows that it is induced from its finite graded quotient by the positive symbol ideal. Each graded part of that quotient is projective over the local ring \(H\), hence free. Lift its finite homogeneous basis into the filtered last kernel. The induced free operator map has symbol isomorphism; lowering order proves surjectivity, and a leading symbol rules out a nonzero kernel. Thus every coherent analytic module has, locally, a finite free operator resolution of length at most \(2n\). Its finitely many matrices and exactness extend from the stalk to one smaller neighbourhood, by coherence. Internal Hom from that bounded locally free resolution computes the actual solution complex: \[ \mathrm{Sol}(N)=R\mathcal Hom_{\mathcal D^{\mathrm{an}}}(N,\mathcal O) \simeq[\mathcal O^{r_0}\to\cdots\to\mathcal O^{r_{2n}}]. \tag{SCP.4} \] The degrees on the right are \(0,\ldots,2n\). No perverse shift is included in \(\mathrm{Sol}\).

The same finite Dolbeault resolution used above gives \(H^q(V;\mathcal O)=0\) for \(q>n\) on every open \(V\), without a Stein assumption: its terms are smooth-module sheaves acyclic on every open. For an open inclusion \(j\), the exact stalk colimit therefore puts \(Rj_*(\mathcal O|_{\operatorname{dom}j})\) in degrees \([0,n]\). Localization and left exactness of sections with support imply, for every closed local support \(Z\), \[ (R\Gamma_Z\mathcal O)_y\in D(\mathbf C)^{[0,n+1]}. \tag{SCP.5} \] Apply this to the finitely many terms of (SCP.4). The finite filtration of that complex retains all attaching maps, and places every local support test in the fixed interval \[ (R\Gamma_Z\mathrm{Sol}(N))_y\in D(\mathbf C)^{[0,B]}, \qquad B=3n+1. \tag{SCP.6} \] The bound is independent of \(N\) and \(Z\). A resolution neighbourhood may depend on \(N\); finitely many such neighbourhoods can be intersected. No infinite truncation or derived-heart realization is used.

3.314. One symbol cone and a family of compact caps

Let \(P\) be a scalar holomorphic differential operator, of order \(m\ge1\), and suppose its principal symbol is nonzero at a nonzero real covector. Identify a complex covector with its real part, translate the base point to zero, and choose complex linear coordinates \(z=(z',t)\) so that this covector is \(d\operatorname{Re}t\). Homogeneity and compactness of a small ball in the normalized covector variables give a coordinate neighbourhood \(U\) and \(\epsilon>0\) such that \[ \sigma_m(P)(z;\zeta',\zeta_t)\ne0 \quad\text{if }z\in U,\quad |\zeta'|\le\epsilon|\zeta_t|,\quad(\zeta',\zeta_t)\ne0. \tag{SCP.7} \] Indeed normalize \(\zeta_t=1\); at \((0;0,1)\) the symbol is nonzero, so it stays nonzero on a closed small covector ball and a smaller base neighbourhood. Multiplying by any nonzero complex \(\zeta_t\) restores the assertion, with all phases retained.

Fix \(0<\delta<\epsilon\) and use the closed pointed real cone \[ C_\delta=\{(v',v_t):\operatorname{Im}v_t=0, \ \operatorname{Re}v_t\le-\delta|v'|\}. \tag{SCP.8} \] It may have empty interior in the ambient real space. Its unit directions satisfy \[ \langle v,d\operatorname{Re}t\rangle \le-\frac{\delta}{\sqrt{1+\delta^2}}|v|\quad(v\in C_\delta), \qquad H=\{\operatorname{Re}t\ge-h\},\quad L=\{\operatorname{Re}t=-h\}. \tag{SCP.9} \] Choose \(h>0\) and a base neighbourhood \(V\) of zero so small that \(H\cap(V+C_\delta)\subset U\) and \(\operatorname{Re}a_t>-h\) for \(a\in V\). This is possible since \(|z'-a'|\le(\operatorname{Re}a_t+h)/\delta\), while \(\operatorname{Im}t=\operatorname{Im}a_t\); taking \(h/\delta\) and then the radius of \(V\) small puts all the caps in the fixed coordinate neighbourhood.

For \(a\in V\), put \(K_a=(a+C_\delta)\cap H\) and \(L_a=(a+C_\delta)\cap L\). Translate to \(w'=z'-a'\), \(w_t=t+h-i\operatorname{Im}a_t\), and set \(T=\operatorname{Re}a_t+h>0\). These are the exact compact convex sets \[ K_a=\{w_t=s\in[0,T],\ |w'|\le(T-s)/\delta\}, \qquad L_a=\{w_t=0,\ |w'|\le T/\delta\}. \tag{SCP.10} \] The bottom face is a complex tangential ball; its sheaf germs still retain the normal coordinate.

3.315. An actual Cauchy neighbourhood of the whole cap

Let a forcing germ \(f\in\mathcal O(K_a)\) be given. Choose \(\eta>0\) with \(K_a+B_\eta\) contained in its domain and in the fixed coefficient neighbourhood. Set \(R_0=T/\delta\), and choose \(R_0<R<R_0+\eta\). The cap lies strictly in the complex diamond \[ D_R=\{|w_t|/\epsilon+|w'|<R\},\qquad \frac{s}{\epsilon}+|w'| \le\frac T\delta+s\left(\frac1\epsilon-\frac1\delta\right) \le R_0<R\quad(w\in K_a). \tag{SCP.11} \] Thus \[ Z=(K_a+B_\eta)\cap D_R \tag{SCP.12} \] is open and convex, contains \(K_a\), and contains every \((w',0)\) with \(|w'|<R\). For the last assertion, the distance to the bottom ball of radius \(R_0\) is less than \(R-R_0<\eta\). Its containment in \(D_R\) is immediate. This also covers \(n=1\), when the tangential ball is a point.

The full convex Cauchy proof in Continuing analytic Cauchy solutions through convex domains, Theorem 5 and its nonzero-data conclusion, applies on this actual \(Z\), with the symbol cone (SCP.7). It gives the unique holomorphic solution with the specified normal data: \[ Pu=f\text{ on }Z,\qquad \partial_{w_t}^j u(w',0)=g_j(w')\quad(0\le j<m). \tag{SCP.13} \] The data must be holomorphic on the indicated tangential ball. For zero data no extra choice is needed. For data given only as germs on \(L_a\), choose \(R\) still closer to \(R_0\), so their finitely many coefficient germs are defined on that ball. The proof uses the quantitative polydisc Cauchy estimates, continuation through a real noncharacteristic boundary, and the canonical-path gluing of that lesson. The domain is chosen before solving the equation; a pointwise existence assertion alone would not give (SCP.13) on a neighbourhood of the whole cap.

3.316. The actual cap restriction is a quasi-isomorphism

The filtered operator ring is a domain locally, since its symbols form the domain \(H[\xi]\). Right multiplication by the nonzero \(P\) is injective. Hence \(\mathcal D/\mathcal DP\) has its actual two-term free resolution, and its solution complex is \([\mathcal O\xrightarrow P\mathcal O]\) in degrees \([0,1]\). By (SCP.2), its sections over each cap and bottom face are these actual two-term germ complexes.

Zero-data existence in (SCP.13) makes \(P:\mathcal O(K_a)\to\mathcal O(K_a)\) surjective.
