The Cauchy germ theorem along a hypersurface, Theorem 2 of the same continuation lesson, gives surjectivity on \(\mathcal O(L_a)\): a forcing germ is defined on a product neighbourhood of its compact bottom ball, and the unique zero-data germs glue along that ball to one neighbourhood representative. Thus \[ \operatorname{coker}(P:\mathcal O(K_a)\to\mathcal O(K_a))=0, \qquad \operatorname{coker}(P:\mathcal O(L_a)\to\mathcal O(L_a))=0. \tag{SCP.14} \] A homogeneous solution germ at \(L_a\) supplies its first \(m\) normal jets. Formula (SCP.13) with \(f=0\) extends those jets over a neighbourhood of the cap, and local Cauchy uniqueness makes its restriction the original solution germ. Conversely, if a homogeneous solution near \(K_a\) vanishes as a germ at \(L_a\), restrict it to a sufficiently small connected convex thickening of the cap. It vanishes on a nonempty open subset and hence everywhere by the holomorphic identity principle. Therefore the actual restriction map is an isomorphism \[ \ker(P:\mathcal O(K_a)\to\mathcal O(K_a)) \xrightarrow{\sim} \ker(P:\mathcal O(L_a)\to\mathcal O(L_a)). \tag{SCP.15} \] It follows on both cohomological degrees that the natural derived restriction is \[ R\Gamma(K_a;\mathrm{Sol}(\mathcal D/\mathcal DP)) \xrightarrow{\sim} R\Gamma(L_a;\mathrm{Sol}(\mathcal D/\mathcal DP)) \qquad(a\in V). \tag{SCP.16} \] The compact-cap criterion T4–T6, including cap-to-cone and cone-to-test, is proved for arbitrary bounded complexes and arbitrary pointed cones in Detecting and removing directional obstructions. Its hypotheses are exactly (SCP.9), the common base neighbourhood and the actual restriction (SCP.16). It therefore gives every real \(C^1\) support test on a cotangent neighbourhood, not just a test on one linear function. We have proved \[ \operatorname{SS}(\mathrm{Sol}(\mathcal D/\mathcal DP)) \subset\{\sigma_m(P)=0\}. \tag{SCP.17} \] An order-zero operator nonzero at the base point is an invertible function, so its quotient and its solution complex vanish locally. This covers that boundary case separately.

3.317. A finite scalar reduction for every coherent analytic system

Let \(N\) be coherent and \(p\notin\operatorname{Char}(N)\). Choose finite local generators \(u_a\). Each cyclic submodule \(\mathcal D u_a\) is coherent and has characteristic support contained in that of \(N\), by its good induced filtration. The initial ideal of its annihilator is generated by actual leading symbols. Since \(p\) is not in their common zero set, some annihilating \(P_a\) has \(\sigma(P_a)(p)\ne0\).

These operators give a scalar quotient cover. Repeat on its kernel, a total of \(r=3n+2\) times: \[ 0\to K_{j+1}\to L_j\to K_j\to0, \qquad K_0=N,\qquad L_j=\bigoplus_a\mathcal D/\mathcal DP_{j,a},\qquad 0\le j<r. \tag{SCP.18} \] Noetherianity makes every kernel coherent. Its induced filtration makes its characteristic support contained in that of \(L_j\), so it still avoids \(p\). There are finitely many modules and scalar operators in this construction. Intersect their resolution and exactness neighbourhoods and the scalar test neighbourhoods supplied by (SCP.17).

For any defining support test \(T\) in this one common neighbourhood, the contravariant solution triangle and scalar vanishing give \[ T\mathrm{Sol}(N)\simeq T\mathrm{Sol}(K_r)[-r], \qquad [0,B]\cap[r,B+r]=\varnothing, \quad B=3n+1,\ r=B+1. \tag{SCP.19} \] Both ends have their respective degree bounds by (SCP.6); hence they are zero. This is a finite argument with one neighbourhood. At a zero covector outside the characteristic support, the chosen nonzero leading symbols must have order zero, so they are unit functions and already force \(N=0\) near its base. Thus, for every coherent analytic operator module, \[ \operatorname{SS}(\mathrm{Sol}(N)) \subset\operatorname{Char}(N). \tag{SCP.20} \] Holonomicity and regularity were not required for this inclusion.

3.318. Analytification retains the good symbol support

Let \(M\) now be coherent algebraic on a smooth complex variety. The operator normal forms identify \(\mathcal D^{\mathrm{an}}\), as a right algebraic operator module, with \(\mathcal O^{\mathrm{an}}\otimes_{\mathcal O}\mathcal D\). Its right action is the original operator multiplication, with the analytic coefficient on the left. Consequently the underlying analytic extension is \(\mathcal O^{\mathrm{an}}\otimes_{\mathcal O}M\), with the actual Leibniz action.

Faithful local flatness in Complex analytic spaces and analytification, Theorem 4.1, preserves every exact filtered step and its quotient. For a good order filtration, \[ \operatorname{gr}(M^{\mathrm{an}}) =\mathcal O^{\mathrm{an}}\otimes_{\mathcal O}\operatorname{gr}M. \tag{SCP.21} \] The finite symbol module has the analytified support of the algebraic symbol module. Indeed its support is the zero set of the maximal minors defining its zeroth Fitting ideal. Extending the finite presentation extends those minors, and the full analytic ideal construction gives exactly the corresponding analytic zero set. Faithful flatness detects zero. Thus \[ \operatorname{Char}(M^{\mathrm{an}}) =\operatorname{Char}(M)^{\mathrm{an}}. \tag{SCP.22} \] These statements concern actual analytic extension, rather than replacement by a formal completion.

3.319. The reverse inclusion and the solution-evaluation map

The inclusion (SCP.20) does not by itself give equality. On nonzero cotangent points, write \(E,B,C\) for the actual finite-order, full infinite-order and real kernel rings of Regular singularities, §§5.45–5.69. The injective holonomic comparison GM.1 has target \(C\otimes_E N_E\). To use that nonzero operator module as a sheaf-microlocal test, one still needs an actual balanced solution-evaluation map and its required injectivity, with the exact density convention: \[ C\otimes_E N_E\longrightarrow H^0\mu\operatorname{hom}(\mathrm{Sol}(N),\mathcal O). \tag{SCP.23} \] If finite-to-infinite microlocal extension detects \(N_E\ne0\), GM.1 and an injective (SCP.23) would give \[ p\in\operatorname{Char}(N) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad H^0\mu\operatorname{hom}(\mathrm{Sol}(N),\mathcal O)_p\ne0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p\in\operatorname{SS}(\mathrm{Sol}(N)), \tag{SCP.24} \] where the last implication is the arbitrary bounded microlocal Hom support theorem MO15. Construction and injectivity of (SCP.23) are separate from the operator-module injection GM.1. Neither a derived comparison nor a solution-evaluation isomorphism is inferred from it.

There is an independent zero-section calibration for a coherent regular algebraic \(M\). Every graded piece of a good filtration is finite over the local coefficient ring. If its symbol fibre were zero in every degree, Nakayama would make every localized graded piece zero; boundedness below would then make \(M\) zero locally. A nonzero homogeneous symbol fibre has a support point over the base, and its closed conic support contains the zero covector over that same base. Thus the intersection with the zero section is the module's closed base carrier. The finite regular composition-factor argument (MCM.13) identifies its analytification with the closed carrier of \(\operatorname{DR}M\), and the zero-covector support test records exactly that closed carrier. Hence \[ \operatorname{Char}(M^{\mathrm{an}})\cap X^{\mathrm{an}} =\operatorname{SS}(\operatorname{DR}M)\cap X^{\mathrm{an}}. \tag{SCP.25} \] For the full de Rham target (MCM.20), the off-zero solution statement must also be transported through the actual signed solution/de Rham duality and its microsupport convention. The reverse evaluation comparison, that transport and the common support hypothesis in the actual Hecke application remain explicit requirements. A free overview of the scalar-to-system strategy is Pierre Schapira, A short review on microlocal sheaf theory, §6.2; the actual cap, restriction and finite degree argument is given above.

3.320. Exercise and solution: a cap strictly inside its Cauchy diamond

Exercise 3.EN. In the real \((x,s)\)-slice with all imaginary coordinates zero, take \[ \begin{gathered} T=1,\quad\delta=\tfrac12,\quad\epsilon=1, \quad R_0=2,\quad R=\tfrac94,\quad\eta=\tfrac12,\\ K=\{0\le s\le1,\ |x|\le2(1-s)\}. \end{gathered} \tag{SCP.26} \] Verify every strict containment used to construct \(Z\), and give a scalar operator whose symbol satisfies the required complex covector cone condition.

Solution 3.EN. On the cap, \(s+|x|\le2-s\le2<9/4\). Its bottom radius is two, and \(0<R-R_0=1/4<\eta\). Thus the whole cap is inside the diamond and the bottom open ball of radius \(9/4\) is inside \(K+B_{1/2}\). In complex coordinates the same inequalities use \(|w'|\) and \(|w_t|\), so they prove the actual domain statements, not only their real slice. For \[ P=\partial_t+\tfrac12\partial_x, \qquad |\zeta_t+\tfrac12\zeta_x| \ge\tfrac12|\zeta_t|>0 \quad\text{if }|\zeta_x|\le|\zeta_t|,\ \zeta_t\ne0, \tag{SCP.27} \] the complete complex cone condition holds, with all phases allowed. The origin of this translated bottom coordinate system is not the cap vertex; the vertex is \((0,1)\).

3.321. Exercise and solution: the actual first-order extension map

Exercise 3.EO. Put \(P_c=\partial_t+c\partial_x\), \(c=1/2\). On the convex domain \(Z\) above, solve \(P_cu=f\) with \(u(x,0)=g(x)\), and explain why the characteristic integration paths stay in the given domain.

Solution 3.EO. The point \((x-ct,0)\) belongs to the initial ball: on the diamond, \[ |x-ct|\le|x|+|c|\,|t| \le |x|+|t|/\epsilon<R. \tag{SCP.28} \] It and \((x,t)\) are in \(Z\), so their straight complex-parametrized segment, with real segment parameter, stays in \(Z\) by convexity. Writing \(y=x-ct\), integration of \(\partial_t u(y+ct,t)=f(y+ct,t)\) gives \[ u(x,t)=g(x-ct)+\int_0^t f(x-c(t-s),s)\,ds, \qquad P_cu=f,\quad u(x,0)=g(x). \tag{SCP.29} \] The integral is along the straight segment \(s=\lambda t\), \(0\le\lambda\le1\). On compact subsets its integrand and derivatives are bounded; the parameter Cauchy formula proves holomorphy and differentiation under this finite integral. The formula is linear in the actual forcing and data and restricts to their given germs on the bottom face. For example, \[ f=1,\quad g=x^2, \qquad u(x,t)=(x-ct)^2+t. \tag{SCP.30} \] Direct differentiation gives \(P_cu=1\). For zero forcing, the same characteristic coordinate makes any difference with zero initial data zero; this verifies the homogeneous restriction inverse in this example.

3.322. Exercise and solution: a characteristic bottom direction

Exercise 3.EP. On \(\mathbf C_x\times\mathbf C_t\), take \(P=\partial_x\) and the normal covector \(d\operatorname{Re}t\). Show directly why scalar propagation in this direction fails, and exhibit a homogeneous bottom germ which does not extend to the cap vertex.

Solution 3.EP. The symbol is \(\zeta_x\), so the selected covector is characteristic. Local solutions are holomorphic functions of \(t\), constant in \(x\); termwise integration in \(x\) makes the cokernel sheaf zero. At \(a=(0,1)\), the function \((t-1)^{-1}\) is a homogeneous solution on the side \(\operatorname{Re}(t-1)<0\), and it does not extend across \(t=1\). In the localization triangle for this side its class is not in the image of the central solution stalk. The exact degree-zero-to-degree-one boundary therefore gives \[ H^1\bigl(R\Gamma_{\{\operatorname{Re}(t-1)\ge0\}} \mathrm{Sol}(\mathcal D/\mathcal D\partial_x)\bigr)_a\ne0. \tag{SCP.31} \] The nonextendability follows already from the nonzero Laurent coefficient of \((t-1)^{-1}\), or by multiplying a purported holomorphic extension by \(t-1\) and evaluating at one. Thus the very support test at the selected covector is nonzero.

For the cap in Solution 3.EN, the same function is a holomorphic homogeneous germ on the whole compact bottom face \(t=0\). If it were the restriction of a homogeneous germ on a neighbourhood of the cap, its restriction to the normal segment would agree with \((t-1)^{-1}\) by the identity principle and would be holomorphic at its endpoint. This is impossible. Hence \[ \ker\bigl(\partial_x:\mathcal O(K)\to\mathcal O(K)\bigr) \longrightarrow \ker\bigl(\partial_x:\mathcal O(L)\to\mathcal O(L)\bigr) \quad\text{is not surjective}. \tag{SCP.32} \] The failed map is the actual bottom restriction. The missing noncharacteristic hypothesis cannot be repaired by forgetting the normal germs on that face.

Figure 3.47. The real slice has \(T=1\), \(\delta=1/2\), \(\epsilon=1\), \(R=9/4\), and \(\eta=1/2\), as in Solution 3.EN. Its triangle is the closed cap, its bottom segment is the Cauchy face, and the shaded open neighbourhood is the slice of \(Z=(K+B_{1/2})\cap D_{9/4}\). The normal covector points up at the vertex. The full domain is complex; the picture fixes both imaginary coordinates to zero. The displayed restriction and degree arguments are (SCP.16)–(SCP.20), and the characteristic comparison is Solution 3.EP. The drawing uses the exact Euclidean half-unit thickening and rational diamond intercepts.

3.323. The full kernel complex and finite operator cells

Work on a complex coordinate neighbourhood \(U\), and put \(D=\mathcal D_U^{\mathrm{an}}\), \(L=\mathcal O_U\), and \(\pi:T^*U\to U\). The full complex \[ K=\mu\operatorname{hom}(L,L),\qquad F(P)=\mu\operatorname{hom}(R\mathcal Hom_D(P,L),L) \tag{MEC.1} \] uses the ordinary derived microlocal Hom of Local morphisms in cotangent directions, SH02-MH-HOM. In particular \(K\) is a complex, and is not being replaced by its degree-zero cohomology.

Right multiplication by \(a\) is an endomorphism of the free left module \(D\). Applying \(\mathcal Hom_D(-,L)\) makes it left action by \(a\) on \(L\); applying microlocal Hom in its first variable makes it precomposition by that action on \(K\). Thus \(K\) has a right \(\pi^{-1}D\)-action. Its associativity is already the identity \((k\circ a)\circ b=k\circ(ab)\) before taking any normal limit. The output action is postcomposition and commutes with this input action.

These are actions on the derived complexes. One can retain them by resolving \(L\) in left operator modules, and taking the internal Hom complex before normal specialization and Fourier transformation. An injective operator-module sheaf is injective after forgetting to vector sheaves: induction \(D\otimes_{\mathbf C}-\) is exact on stalks. Resolving the output preserves the commuting input and output actions. In the normal deformation the two base maps extend to the diagonal at parameter zero. Their operator-ring actions therefore pass through the inverse and direct images, support cones and Fourier kernel to the indicated pullback ring. The functorial module resolutions and finite totalizations retain the homotopies as well as the degree-zero maps.

For every bounded finite locally free operator complex \(P\), there is a natural equivalence \[ K\otimes^L_{\pi^{-1}D}\pi^{-1}P\simeq F(P). \tag{MEC.2} \] Here is the finite-cell proof. On one free term both sides are the corresponding finite sum of \(K\), and a matrix is sent to its written Hom transpose with the input precomposition action just specified. Before normal specialization the evaluation on homogeneous entries has the sign \[ \Theta(k\otimes p)(f) =(-1)^{|p||f|}\,k(f(p)). \tag{MEC.3} \] The internal Hom differential is \(d(g)=d g-(-1)^{|g|}g d\). Substituting this expression on the two sides of (MEC.3) gives the tensor differential \(d k\otimes p+(-1)^{|k|}k\otimes d p\). Since operator entries have degree zero and \(f\) is operator linear, \(\Theta((k a)\otimes p)=\Theta(k\otimes a p)\). Thus evaluation is balanced and is a cochain map. The normal and Fourier functors preserve this map on each finite sum. Filtering \(P\) by its finitely many free cells, their exact triangles prove (MEC.2) by induction. This also proves naturality for their attaching maps and homotopies. A bounded acyclic projective comparison complex is locally contractible, by splitting successively from its last nonzero term. Consequently different finite resolutions give the same derived comparison. The finite analytic resolution in (SCP.3)–(SCP.4) applies this result to every coherent \(N\).

3.324. The input needed from an actual real kernel

Suppose the actual real-kernel construction provides a density-normalized morphism with the prescribed input action, \[ \kappa:C[0]\longrightarrow K \quad\text{in }D((\pi^{-1}D)^{\mathrm{op}}). \tag{MEC.4} \] This is an analytic hypothesis. Tensor it with a finite resolution of \(N\), then use (MEC.2). The resulting degree-zero map is \[ C\otimes_{\pi^{-1}D}\pi^{-1}N \longrightarrow H^0\mu\operatorname{hom}(\operatorname{Sol}N,\mathcal O). \tag{MEC.5} \] A free resolution of the module \(N\) has degrees at most zero. Hence degree-zero cohomology of \(C\otimes^L N\) is its ordinary right-exact tensor product; no flatness of \(C\) is needed for this identity. For compatible actual ring maps \(D\to E\to C\), tensor associativity identifies its source with \(C\otimes_E(E\otimes_D N)\).

Injectivity of (MEC.5) requires injectivity after this derived tensor operation. An identification of \(H^0K\) alone does not supply it. A quasi-isomorphism (MEC.4) would be a sufficient stronger hypothesis, but is not assumed. In a concrete kernel formula, input differentiation also carries its density transpose; the abstract input action in §3.323 specifies the action which that formula must reproduce.

3.325. A degree-zero kernel map over a regular ring

The failure of a degree-zero shortcut occurs even over \(B=\mathbf C[x,y]\). Set \(k=B/(x,y)\), and use the finite free complexes \[ Q=[B^2\xrightarrow{(x,y)}B],\quad\deg Q=(0,1),\qquad j:B[0]\longrightarrow Q,\quad j(1)=(-y,x). \tag{MEC.6} \] If \(xa+yb=0\), reduction modulo \(x\) gives \(yb=0\) in \(\mathbf C[y]\), so \(b=xc\) and then \(a=-yc\). Conversely each such vector is in the kernel. Thus \[ H^0(Q)=B(-y,x),\qquad H^0(j)\text{ is an isomorphism}. \tag{MEC.7} \] Both complexes in \(j\) are bounded free, so their actual derived tensor with \(k\) is obtained term by term. It gives \[ H^0(B\otimes^L_B k)=k,\qquad H^0(Q\otimes^L_B k)=k^2,\qquad H^0(j\otimes^L_B k)=0. \tag{MEC.8} \] The last map is the literal vector \((-y,x)\) modulo \((x,y)\). The module \(k\) has a length-two free Koszul resolution: the middle kernel is precisely the vector just calculated, and the first map is injective because \(B\) is a domain. Thus neither infinite projective dimension nor a nonflat source is responsible. Positive cohomology of the full kernel complex cannot be discarded when forming (MEC.5).

3.326. A nonreduced coefficient countercheck

There is also a one-parameter example. Let \(B_0=\mathbf C[e]/(e^2)\), \(k_0=B_0/(e)\), and \[ Q_0=[B_0\xrightarrow e B_0],\quad\deg Q_0=(0,1),\qquad j_0:k_0[0]\longrightarrow Q_0,\quad j_0(1)=e. \tag{MEC.9} \] Since \(\ker(e)=eB_0\), the map \(H^0(j_0)\) is an isomorphism. Resolve its source by the complex with a copy of \(B_0\) in every nonpositive degree and differential multiplication by \(e\). It is exact in negative degrees because image and kernel are both \(eB_0\). A lift of \(j_0\) is multiplication by \(e\) in degree zero and zero in negative degrees. It is a chain map because \(e^2=0\). After tensoring with \(k_0\), \[ H^0(k_0\otimes^L_{B_0}k_0)=k_0,\qquad H^0(Q_0\otimes^L_{B_0}k_0)=k_0,\qquad H^0(j_0\otimes^L_{B_0}k_0)=0. \tag{MEC.10} \] The finite complex \(Q_0\) is already free, and the displayed lift computes the actual map. Equality of the two degree-zero vector spaces does not identify that map with an isomorphism.

3.327. The actual matrix Euler module

Now take coordinates \((x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1},t)\), \(n\ge1\), a constant \(r\)-by-\(r\) complex matrix \(A\), and \(r\ge1\). Let \(N_A\) have generators \(u_j\) and relations \[ \partial_{x_i}u_j=0,\qquad (t\partial_t)u_j=\sum_k A_{jk}u_k. \tag{MEC.11} \] This row convention means that a solution column \(f_j\) obeys \(t f'=Af\). No transpose of \(A\) is suppressed in the presentation.

The right-multiplication Koszul complex of the commuting \(\partial_{x_i}\) resolves their quotient. Its symbols are the coordinate sequence \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_{n-1}\) in \(\mathcal O[\xi,\tau]\). For one polynomial variable, division into its constant term and the variable times a polynomial contracts its two-term Koszul complex onto the constant coefficient ring. Iterating this contraction in the finitely many independent variables proves exactness of the symbol complex. Lift a symbol boundary and subtract its operator boundary; finite lowering of order proves exactness of the operator complex. The quotient has normal forms \(\mathcal O\langle\partial_t\rangle\). Right multiplication by the normal relation matrix is injective there, since its leading matrix is \(t\tau I_r\), a nonzero divisor. It commutes with the tangential resolution. Its two-term cone therefore gives a finite free resolution of \(N_A\), and the induced good symbols are \[ \operatorname{gr}N_A =\bigl(\mathcal O[\xi,\tau]/(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_{n-1},t\tau)\bigr)^r. \tag{MEC.12} \] The same order argument proves strictness: a highest nonzero input symbol is multiplied by \(t\tau I_r\) and cannot disappear. Thus \[ \operatorname{Char}(N_A) =T_U^*U\ \cup\ T^*_{\{t=0\}}U. \tag{MEC.13} \] Applying Hom to this actual resolution gives the tangential holomorphic derivative complex with the normal two-term map \(P_A=t\partial_t-A\).

3.328. Central solution germs, including every resonance

Tangential derivatives contract on a product ball by radial integration in \(x\). On a holomorphic \(q\)-form the coefficient formula is \(\int_0^1s^{q-1}\iota_x\omega(sx,t)\,ds\); differentiation gives \(d_xH+Hd_x=1-\operatorname{ev}_{x=0}\). The formula is holomorphic with parameters by the compact-parameter Cauchy formula, and commutes with \(P_A\). In the total complex the two mixed terms cancel with its usual \((-1)^q\) sign. Thus the solution complex is, locally, constant in \(x\) with normal complex \([\mathcal O_t^r\xrightarrow{P_A}\mathcal O_t^r]\) in degrees \([0,1]\).

For \(f(t)=\sum_{m\ge0}f_mt^m\), the normal equation has coefficient equations \[ (mI-A)u_m=f_m. \tag{MEC.14} \] Let \(R_A=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\cap\mathbf Z_{\ge0}\), a finite set. If \(m>2\|A\|\), the Neumann series for \((I-A/m)^{-1}\) gives \(\|(mI-A)^{-1}\|\le2/m\). On all remaining nonresonant degrees there are only finitely many inverse matrices. At resonant degrees choose an inverse from the image to a fixed complementary subspace of the kernel. These estimates preserve the convergence radius of every holomorphic power series. They prove the actual stalk calculations \[ S_A=H^0(\operatorname{Sol}N_A)_0 =\bigoplus_{m\in R_A}t^m\ker(mI-A), \tag{MEC.15} \] \[ T_A=H^1(\operatorname{Sol}N_A)_0 =\bigoplus_{m\in R_A}\operatorname{coker}(mI-A). \tag{MEC.16} \] All other stalk degrees vanish. The cokernel identification records the resonant Taylor coefficients modulo their images. Since each \(mI-A\) is square, rank-nullity gives \(\dim S_A=\dim T_A\), with no diagonalizability assumption.

3.329. Solutions on a negative halfdisc

Let \(W=\{0<|t|<\rho,\ \operatorname{Re}t<0\}\). It is convex, simply connected and avoids zero; choose a holomorphic logarithm there. The matrix \[ Y(t)=\exp(A\log t),\qquad Y^{-1}(t)=\exp(-A\log t),\qquad tY'=AY \tag{MEC.17} \] is holomorphic and invertible. For every holomorphic forcing \(f\) on \(W\), \[ u(t)=Y(t)\left(c+\int_{t_0}^t Y(s)^{-1}f(s)\,\frac{ds}{s}\right) \tag{MEC.18} \] solves \(P_Au=f\). One may use the straight segment, which lies in \(W\) by convexity. For any holomorphic integrand \(g\), its integral is \((t-t_0)\int_0^1g(t_0+s(t-t_0))\,ds\). Differentiating gives the integral of \(g+s(t-t_0)g'\), which is the endpoint difference of \(s g(t_0+s(t-t_0))\) and hence is \(g(t)\). Compactness of the segment inside the open domain justifies holomorphic differentiation under this finite integral by the local Cauchy formula. Applying this construction to \(1/t\) also constructs the logarithm used in (MEC.17): choose its value at \(t_0\), and differentiating \(e^{\log t}/t\) shows that this quotient is the constant one. Formula (MEC.18) now follows by differentiation. For zero forcing it says that \(Y^{-1}u\) is constant. Thus the homogeneous solution space is \(\mathbf C^r\), and the map \(P_A\) on this open set is surjective.

These statements compute derived sections as well. A product ball in \(x\) times \(W\) has the strict plurisubharmonic exhaustion obtained by adding \(|x|^2+|t|^2\), the terms \(-\log(\rho_x^2-|x|^2)\), \(-\log(\rho^2-|t|^2)\), and \(-\log(-\operatorname{Re}t)\). Its holomorphic acyclicity is the finite Dolbeault argument used in §3.312. The finite free solution complex therefore computes derived sections, and its tangential radial contraction commutes with the normal map. Under restriction to smaller product balls and halfdiscs, the constant \(c\) in a fixed branch frame identifies the kernels compatibly. Consequently the actual open-direct-image stalk from \(\operatorname{Re}t<0\) is \[ (Rj_*j^{-1}\operatorname{Sol}N_A)_0=\mathbf C^r[0]. \tag{MEC.19} \] For \(n=1\) the tangential ball and its contraction are omitted.

3.330. An exact defining support test for every matrix

Put \(Z=\{\operatorname{Re}t\ge0\}\), and let \(V_A=(R\Gamma_Z\operatorname{Sol}N_A)_0\). Localization gives the actual fibre sequence \[ V_A\longrightarrow(\operatorname{Sol}N_A)_0 \longrightarrow\mathbf C^r[0]. \tag{MEC.20} \] The map on degree zero is restriction of the actual solution germ. In the frame (MEC.17) it takes \(t^m v\), \(Av=mv\), to \(v\). Distinct eigenspaces are independent, so its image is \[ E_A^+=\bigoplus_{m\in R_A}\ker(mI-A)\subset\mathbf C^r, \tag{MEC.21} \] and it is injective. Independence of the distinct eigenspaces follows by applying \(\prod_{j\in R_A\setminus\{m\}}(A-jI)\) to a relation between them: it kills all terms except the \(m\)-eigenvector, multiplied by the nonzero scalar \(\prod_{j\in R_A\setminus\{m\}}(m-j)\). The long exact sequence, with (MEC.15)–(MEC.19), gives \[ \begin{gathered} H^q(V_A)=0\quad(q\ne1),\\ 0\longrightarrow\mathbf C^r/E_A^+ \longrightarrow H^1(V_A)\longrightarrow T_A\longrightarrow0. \end{gathered} \tag{MEC.22} \] It follows that \[ \dim_{\mathbf C}H^1(V_A)=r. \tag{MEC.23} \] This is nonzero for every positive rank, even when all central solution stalks vanish or when all local monodromy eigenvalues are one.

For any nonzero complex \(\lambda\), repeat the calculation in \(w=\lambda t\); the operator \(t\partial_t-A=w\partial_w-A\) is unchanged. The defining support test with function \(\operatorname{Re}(\lambda t)\) is therefore nonzero. Translating the tangential centre proves that every nonzero conormal to \(\{t=0\}\) belongs to microsupport. Away from that hypersurface the local solution system has rank \(r\), so the constant-function test puts every zero covector there in microsupport. Closedness includes the zero covectors over the hypersurface too. Combining this with the general forward inclusion (SCP.20) proves \[ \operatorname{SS}(\operatorname{Sol}N_A) =\operatorname{Char}(N_A) =T_U^*U\cup T^*_{\{t=0\}}U. \tag{MEC.24} \] If \(r=0\), the module, its solutions and both supports are empty instead. No assertion about arbitrary coherent systems is inferred from the matrix Euler calculation.

3.331. A finite criterion for transporting the model

The following criterion states precisely the additional data needed to use a kernel-module normal form. Fix a nonzero normal covector \(p\) to \(\{t=0\}\), and retain \(r\ge1\). Represent the matrices of finite free resolutions \(P_N,P_A\) on one common neighbourhood \(U\). Let \(D_0\subset\Gamma(U,D)\) be the unital algebra generated by their finitely many operator entries, and let \(P_N^0,P_A^0\) be the finite free matrix complexes over \(D_0\). Their extensions to the sheaf \(D\) are the given resolutions; they need not be resolutions as \(D_0\)-modules. Let \(R\) be an actual unital \(D_0\)-algebra. Suppose a complex \(G\), bounded as a complex of vector sheaves, has a genuine derived \(R\)-module structure and a \(D_0\)-linear equivalence \[ G\simeq\mathcal O \quad\text{in the category localized at }p. \tag{MEC.25} \] Here an algebra acts as its constant sheaf, and linearity means a fraction of \(D_0\)-linear maps with denominator cones of underlying vector sheaves whose microsupport misses \(p\), retaining the full coherent action. This accommodates a ring of actual kernels defined on one fixed coefficient domain. An isomorphism of underlying vector objects without its action is insufficient.

Assume also an actual finite homotopy equivalence of complexes \[ R\otimes_{D_0} P_N^0\simeq R\otimes_{D_0} P_A^0. \tag{MEC.26} \] Applying Hom over \(R\) into \(G\) preserves this homotopy equivalence. Finite free base extension gives literal adjunction \(\mathcal Hom_R(R\otimes_{D_0}P^0,G)=\mathcal Hom_{D_0}(P^0,G)\). With output \(\mathcal O\), the latter is exactly the finite matrix solution complex for the given \(D\)-resolution. Lastly (MEC.25) can be applied to this finite complex: a denominator cone gives a complex with a finite filtration by finite sums of that same cone. The subcategory whose microsupport misses \(p\) is thick by §§3.303–3.304, so the resulting cone still misses \(p\). Thus \[ \operatorname{Sol}N\simeq\operatorname{Sol}N_A \quad\text{in }D^b(\mathbf C_U;p). \tag{MEC.27} \] The nonzero defining test in (MEC.23) makes the model nonzero in this category; hence the same is true for \(\operatorname{Sol}N\). This proves the criterion at its stated hypotheses. It uses the complexes in (MEC.26), and does not substitute an isomorphism of ordinary scalar-extended modules for their homotopy equivalence. The actual cutoff action, any required flatness and contact transport must supply these hypotheses when the criterion is applied. The real-kernel evaluation (SCP.23) is a second possible route to the general reverse inclusion, with its own density and injectivity hypotheses. Neither route is completed by the Euler model alone. Signed de Rham transport remains a further comparison.

3.332. Exercise and solution: two classes at a resonant Jordan block

Exercise 3.EQ. Take \(r=2\) and \(A e_1=0\), \(A e_2=e_1\). Compute the central groups and exhibit two independent degree-one support classes for the negative halfdisc.

Solution 3.EQ. The only resonant degree is zero, and \[ S_A=\mathbf C e_1,\qquad T_A=\mathbf C[e_2],\qquad E_A^+=\mathbf C e_1. \tag{MEC.28} \] Fix a logarithm on that halfdisc. Direct differentiation gives \[ \begin{gathered} v=e_2+(\log t)e_1,\qquad P_Av=0,\\ w=(\log t)e_2+\tfrac12(\log t)^2e_1, \qquad P_Aw=e_2. \end{gathered} \tag{MEC.29} \] Use the localization fibre complex in the order \((a,b)\), with differential \(d(a,b)=(d a,\operatorname{res}a-d b)\); it squares to zero because restriction is a cochain map. Its degree-one entries are central forcing germs and side solution germs. The two cocycles are \[ (0,v),\qquad(e_2,w). \tag{MEC.30} \] The first is not a boundary: a central homogeneous solution restricts only to a multiple of \(e_1\), whereas \(v\) contains the logarithmic branch. The second maps to the nonzero central cokernel class \([e_2]\). They are independent, since any linear relation first maps to that cokernel and then to the nonzero class of \(v\) modulo central homogeneous solutions. Formula (MEC.23) says that the whole space has dimension two, so these classes are a basis. The logarithmic forcing primitive is essential for the second class; a homogeneous solution alone cannot represent its nonzero image in \(T_A\).

3.333. Exercise and solution: no central stalk but a full support test

Exercise 3.ER. Take \(A=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1/2)\). Compute the solution stalk at zero and the defining support test, and explain the zero covector over zero.

Solution 3.ER. Neither eigenvalue is a nonnegative integer. Every matrix \(mI-A\), \(m\ge0\), is invertible, with the large-degree bound already used in (MEC.14). Consequently \[ (\operatorname{Sol}N_A)_0=0,\qquad (R\Gamma_Z\operatorname{Sol}N_A)_0=\mathbf C^2[-1]. \tag{MEC.31} \] The second equality denotes a complex with its sole cohomology in degree one. A branch frame on the negative halfdisc has columns \[ t^{-1}e_1,\qquad t^{1/2}e_2. \tag{MEC.32} \] Both give nonzero boundary classes, since there is no central homogeneous solution. The first column has a pole although its monodromy is one; the second is ramified. On every punctured neighbourhood the solution system has rank two. Its closed carrier therefore contains zero, so closedness of microsupport includes the zero covector there, despite the zero ordinary solution stalk. Confusing closed carrier with the set of nonzero stalks would lose this point.

3.334. Exercise and solution: the actual integer Euler gauge

Exercise 3.ES. Compare the solution complexes for \(A\) and \(A-I\) by differentiation. Compute its cone and explain why it is an equivalence at every nonzero normal covector even when the central stalks differ.

Solution 3.ES. The identity \(\partial_t(t\partial_t)=(t\partial_t+1)\partial_t\) gives \[ \begin{gathered} \partial_t P_A=P_{A-I}\partial_t,\\ \partial_t:[\mathcal O^r\xrightarrow{P_A}\mathcal O^r] \longrightarrow[\mathcal O^r\xrightarrow{P_{A-I}}\mathcal O^r]. \end{gathered} \tag{MEC.33} \] Differentiation is surjective on holomorphic sheaves, by termwise primitives. Its kernel in each degree is constant in \(t\). The induced normal map on these constants is \(-A\). After the tangential contraction this gives an actual short exact sequence of complexes \[ 0\longrightarrow[\mathbf C^r\xrightarrow{-A}\mathbf C^r] \longrightarrow\operatorname{Sol}N_A \xrightarrow{\partial_t}\operatorname{Sol}N_{A-I} \longrightarrow0. \tag{MEC.34} \] One can first form this sequence for the normal two-term complexes and then take their exterior constant tangential factor; the earlier contraction gives the displayed derived identification. The cone of differentiation is \([\mathbf C^r\xrightarrow{-A}\mathbf C^r][1]\), so its microsupport is in the zero section. It follows that differentiation, and hence every positive integer iterate, gives \[ \operatorname{Sol}N_A\simeq\operatorname{Sol}N_{A-mI} \quad\text{at every nonzero normal covector},\qquad m\ge1. \tag{MEC.35} \] This is a statement about the actual chain map and its cone. For example, in rank one when \(A=0\), the central normal complex has one copy of \(\mathbf C\) in each of degrees zero and one, whereas for \(A-I=-1\) its central stalk is zero. They are not isomorphic on an ordinary neighbourhood. Choosing \(m\) larger than the real parts of all eigenvalues removes every nonnegative-integer resonance in the shifted model, while (MEC.35) preserves its nonzero microlocal object. The real halfspace test kills the constant cone directly, so it also preserves that exact test. This provides an alternative reduction of (MEC.23) to the nonresonant case, without discarding the central cokernel in the original model.

Figure 3.48. Equations (MEC.20)–(MEC.23) give the exact degree-one support sequence, including its resonant cokernel. For the Jordan matrix in Solution 3.EQ, the two classes are represented by \((0,v)\) and \((e_2,w)\). On the real path \(t=-e^{-u}\), \(0\le u\le3\), choose \(\log t=-u+i\pi\). The plotted first real coordinates are \(\operatorname{Re}v_1=-u\) and \(\operatorname{Re}w_1=(u^2-\pi^2)/2\). This is a path in the negative halfdisc of radius two, rather than the whole complex solution domain; the formulas retain both imaginary parts. The line and quadratic curve use their exact parametric formulas. Equations (MEC.1)–(MEC.10) explain the full kernel complex, and (MEC.25)–(MEC.27) state the additional data required for a general gauge transport. Solution 3.ES supplies an actual integer gauge with its constant cone.

3.335. Finite-order microlocalization at a nonzero covector

Let \(X\) be a complex \(n\)-manifold, \(x\in X\), and \(p\in T_x^*X\setminus\{0\}\). Write \(D=\mathcal D^{\mathrm{an}}_{X,x}\) and \(E=\mathcal E_{X,p}\). Here \(E\) is the actual finite-order analytic microlocal ring: its homogeneous coefficients have a finite upper degree, one common holomorphic coefficient domain, and a factorial bound for their negative degrees. Its products retain all the spatial derivatives in the ordered Leibniz formula. The coefficient class, actual product and coordinate normalization are proved in Regular singularities, §§5.19–5.22.1 and §5.24.1.

We prove that \(E\) is right \(D\)-flat on arbitrary modules and that, for every coherent analytic \(\mathcal D_X\)-module \(N\), \[ \operatorname{supp}(\mathcal E_X\otimes_{\pi^{-1}\mathcal D_X}\pi^{-1}N) =\operatorname{Char}(N) \qquad\text{on }T^*X\setminus X. \tag{MFL.1} \] The support on the left is the set of nonzero actual module stalks. This is an equality of underlying conic sets. At a fixed nonzero covector the flat extension need not be faithful on all \(D\)-modules.

Choose coordinates \((z_1,\ldots,z_n)\), with last covariable \(\tau\ne0\), and put \(w_i=\xi_i/\tau\). A linear coordinate change makes the central \(w\)-value zero. The order filtration gives \[ \operatorname{gr}D=\mathbf C\{z\}[\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_{n-1},\tau], \qquad \operatorname{gr}E=\mathbf C\{z,w\}[\tau,\tau^{-1}]. \tag{MFL.2} \] The second ring is the conic germ with its integer grading. Every holomorphic coefficient in \((z,w)\) is realized by a single degree-zero symbol with zero lower tail. The kernel of taking its principal coefficient is exactly the part of strictly smaller order. No operator completion is used in (MFL.2).

3.336. The mixed holomorphic coefficient extension

Put \[ A=\bigl(\mathbf C\{z\}[w]\bigr)_{(z,w)},\qquad H=\mathbf C\{z,w\},\qquad \widehat A=\mathbf C[[z,w]]=\widehat H. \tag{MFL.3} \] Both local rings are Noetherian. The convergent-series assertion follows from the Weierstrass proof in Complex analytic spaces and analytification, Lemma 2.1; polynomial extension and localization are proved in Noetherian and Artinian rings, §§1–2. To check the completions in (MFL.3), work modulo each power of the maximal ideal. Taylor truncation gives precisely the finite polynomials in all variables, and a denominator with nonzero constant term has its finite geometric inverse modulo that power. The identifications commute with all quotient maps.

The exact completion theorem in Completion, §§1–3, proves that completion of a Noetherian local ring is faithfully flat. Its hypotheses apply to both rings in (MFL.3). More explicitly, Artin–Rees makes the induced and intrinsic filtrations on every finite submodule cofinal. The surjective quotient transitions then give exact completion, and a finite presentation identifies completion with tensoring by the completed ring. This preserves finite-module injections. An arbitrary tensor and a witness to its vanishing use only finitely many module elements and balancing relations; putting them in finite submodules proves flatness on arbitrary modules. Finally, a nonzero module contains a cyclic submodule \(R/J\), with \(J\) proper; its completed tensor has the nonzero residue field as a quotient. Flatness preserves the cyclic injection, proving faithfulness.

For any injection of \(A\)-modules, tensor with \(H\), then with \(\widehat H\). The composite is tensor with the flat \(\widehat A\). Since \(\widehat H\) is faithfully flat over \(H\), it detects the kernel of the first tensor map. The same composite detects a module whose \(H\)-tensor is zero. Therefore \[ A\longrightarrow H\text{ is faithfully flat},\qquad \operatorname{gr}D\longrightarrow\operatorname{gr}E \text{ is flat}. \tag{MFL.4} \] For the second assertion, first invert \(\tau\), write \(\xi_i=\tau w_i\), localize the degree-zero coefficient ring at the chosen point, and extend scalars by \(A\to H\). Laurent extension in \(\tau\) preserves the exactness just proved. The faithfulness statement concerns this localized coefficient map; the whole map from \(\operatorname{gr}D\) also contains a localization.

3.337. Actual lifts of principal relations

Use left free modules written as rows, so their linear maps are right-multiplication matrices. Suppose \(W:E^a\to E^b\) and \(V:E^c\to E^a\) have order at most zero and \[ VW=0,\qquad \operatorname{im}V_0=\ker W_0 \quad\text{over }H. \tag{MFL.5} \] We will prove \(\ker W=\operatorname{im}V\). The subscript zero means principal degree zero; a strictly negative entry has zero principal coefficient.

Let \(\mu=\ker W_0\). The complete holomorphic coefficient-division proof Regular singularities, MFA.1–MFA.3 supplies finitely many holomorphic standard divisors \(g_\nu\) of \(\mu\). Their initial Taylor orthants cover the initial diagram, and their coefficient division is bounded on one fixed interval of polyradii. Choose holomorphic rows \(a_\nu\) with \(g_\nu=a_\nu V_0\), possible by (MFL.5). Realize these finitely many coefficients as order-zero actual symbols and set \[ R_\nu=a_\nu\circ V,\qquad RW=0,\qquad R_0=(g_\nu)_\nu. \tag{MFL.6} \] All rows have one common coefficient domain. This constructs every needed principal relation lift directly in the image of \(V\).

For the coefficient map \(T_0c=cR_0\), the same division proof gives a support-normalized quotient space \(\mathcal V\), a division map \(\Lambda\), a projection \(q\), and a map \(k\), with \[ \Lambda T_0|_{\mathcal V}=1,\quad q=1-T_0\Lambda,\quad \Lambda q=0,\quad k(bW_0)=qb. \tag{MFL.7} \] These are complex-linear coefficient operators; no \(H\)-linear splitting is asserted. Their bounds hold uniformly on the same radius interval. Define \(Tc=c\circ R\), \(L=T-T_0\), and \(W_-b=b\circ W-bW_0\). Each of \(L\) and \(W_-\) lowers homogeneous order by at least one, including all Leibniz derivative terms.

3.338. The finite upper order and the factorial tail

For an actual relation \(b\circ W=0\), define coefficientwise \[ c=\sum_{j\ge0}(-\Lambda L)^j\Lambda b, \qquad s=b-Tc. \tag{MFL.8} \] We must show that this expression belongs to the actual finite-order ring. The all-index word estimate Regular singularities, MFB.1–MFB.4 has exactly these hypotheses: finitely many right matrices of order zero with factorial negative tails, coefficient divisions bounded on one radius interval, and at least one unit of order loss per correction. It includes derivatives between successive coefficient divisions. For input degree \(m\) and total loss \(K\), the sum of the norms of all words is at most \[ C_0 C_1^K\frac{(|m|+K)!}{|m|!}\,|b_m|_{\mathrm{out}}. \tag{MFL.9} \] The outer and inner domains are fixed independently of \(K\). In that proof, if \(K=Q+J\), the right-tail factorials cost at most \(Q!\), and the \(J\) derivatives share a fixed total radius margin. The inequality \((|m|+K)^JQ!\le e^K(|m|+K)!/|m|!\) absorbs their cost. There are at most exponentially many words of loss \(K\), so they fit in \(C_1^K\). Bounded division at each intermediate radius requires no commutation with differentiation.

Let \(M\) be an upper order of \(b\). Every correction lowers degree, so \(c\) has no coefficient above \(M\). At each output degree, only finitely many input degrees and total losses occur. For output \(-n\) from input \(-a\), with \(1\le a\le n\), (MFL.9) and \(|b_{-a}|\le B D^a a!\) give \[ C_0 B n!\,C_1^{n-a}D^a, \qquad \sum_{a=1}^{n} C_1^{n-a}D^a\le(C_1+D)^n. \tag{MFL.10} \] For each of the finitely many nonnegative input degrees \(0\le m\le M\), the loss is \(n+m\). The binomial bound \[ \frac{(n+2m)!}{m!} \le n!\,2^{n+2m}\frac{(2m)!}{m!} \tag{MFL.11} \] puts its contribution under one constant times \(n!(2C_1)^n\). Thus \(c\) has one factorial negative bound on one domain. Every coefficient is holomorphic there, and a further fixed Cauchy margin controls every fixed derivative. Consequently \(c,s\in E\). This also matches the finite-upper-order clause MF.4 of the same proof. Finite upper order alone would not imply the required factorial estimate.

The coefficient identities in (MFL.7) and the geometric identity for (MFL.8) give \(\Lambda s=0\). Associativity and \(RW=0\) give \(s\circ W=0\). Hence \(qs=s\), and \[ s=-k(W_-s). \tag{MFL.12} \] A nonzero finite-order symbol has a largest nonzero homogeneous degree. The right side of (MFL.12) has strictly smaller order than \(s\), a contradiction. Thus \(s=0\), \(b=cR\), and (MFL.6) proves \(\ker W=\operatorname{im}V\). If the principal kernel is zero, the same largest-degree argument gives injectivity immediately. Empty matrix sizes are included.

3.339. Exact analytic tensoring and the basis shifts

Take a strict finite filtered free \(D\)-resolution of a finite module \(N\), supplied by (SCP.3)–(SCP.4). Its graded complex is exact in negative degrees. Flatness in (MFL.4) preserves that exactness. To retain the precise shifts, declare a source basis vector \(e_i\) to have filtration degree \(s_i\) and a target basis vector \(f_j\) degree \(t_j\). Then \[ \begin{gathered} \operatorname{ord}W_{ij}\le s_i-t_j,\qquad h=\tau^{-1},\\ e_i'=h^{s_i}e_i,\qquad f_j'=h^{t_j}f_j,\\ W'_{ij}=h^{s_i}W_{ij}h^{-t_j}. \end{gathered} \tag{MFL.13} \] These are invertible actual changes of basis over \(E\), and each normalized entry has order at most zero. The leading complex over \(H\) is the degree-zero dehomogenization of the exact graded complex. Adjacent actual differentials still have product zero. Applying (MFL.5)–(MFL.12) at each negative term therefore gives \[ \operatorname{Tor}^D_i(E,N)=0\qquad(i>0). \tag{MFL.14} \] Only finitely many free terms, coefficients, relations and domains are used.

For completeness this implies right flatness on all modules. An injection of finite modules has finite cokernel, so (MFL.14) and the tensor long exact sequence preserve that injection. Given an arbitrary injection, an element of its tensor kernel has finitely many tensor summands. A witness to its zero image is a finite sum of additivity and balancing relations. Choose finite submodules containing these entries and witnesses. Their injection is covered by the finite case and kills the original element. Tensor is right exact, so it is exact. Sheaf exactness follows stalkwise.

3.340. Strictness of the extended presentation

Suppose an input row of order \(a\) has image of order strictly below \(a\) under a normalized differential \(W\). Its leading coefficient lies in \(\ker W_0\), so it is a holomorphic combination of the standard divisors \(g_\nu\). Multiply their actual kernel lifts \(R_\nu\) by coefficients of order \(a\), using \(\tau^a\) to realize the homogeneous degree. Subtracting this row lowers the input order without changing its image. For an image whose order is at most a specified integer \(b\), finitely many such subtractions lower any initial input order to at most \(b\). This proves strictness of the extended differential, with the shifted version obtained by (MFL.13).

Give \(N_E=E\otimes_DN\) the quotient filtration from the extended finite presentation. Strictness identifies its associated graded module: \[ \operatorname{gr}N_E \cong\operatorname{gr}E \otimes_{\operatorname{gr}D}\operatorname{gr}N. \tag{MFL.15} \] Indeed the degree-\(b\) relations in the quotient are exactly the principal degree-\(b\) images of the preceding free term: strictness gives a preimage in that degree, and the reverse inclusion follows from filteredness. These are algebraic stalk tensors of actual operators.

3.341. Zero detection without an assumed separated quotient

Let \(E_0=F_0E\), and use the normalized finite target basis to put \(M_0=F_0N_E\). It is a finite left \(E_0\)-module. Since left multiplication by \(\tau\) sends order at most \(-1\) into order at most zero, \[ F_{-1}E=hE_0,\qquad F_{-1}N_E=hM_0. \tag{MFL.16} \] If \(\operatorname{gr}N_E=0\), then \(M_0=hM_0\). On a finite column of generators this gives \[ m=hA m,\qquad (I-hA)m=0 \quad(A\text{ over }E_0). \tag{MFL.17} \] The matrix \(hA\) has strictly negative order. Its geometric series is an actual order-zero inverse of \(I-hA\): (MFL.9)–(MFL.11), applied to a finite input of order zero, give its one-domain factorial bounds, while telescoping leaves no coefficient in the remainder once the number of factors exceeds that coefficient's loss. Multiplication on either side gives the identity. Thus \(m=0\), \(M_0=0\), and \(N_E=EM_0=0\). Conversely a zero module has zero associated graded module.

Finally, the Laurent graded module in (MFL.15) is determined by its degree-zero part: multiplication by \(\tau\) identifies adjacent degrees, and the finite shifts have been normalized. Localizing the characteristic module in the chosen cotangent chart, then dehomogenizing, gives a finite \(A\)-module. It is nonzero at the chosen point precisely when that point lies in \(\operatorname{Char}(N)\). The faithfully flat map \(A\to H\) detects exactly this nonvanishing. The preceding paragraph detects zero in the actual module, proving (MFL.1).

Figure 3.49. The upper square compares the two local coefficient rings through their common commutative completion; each map to that completion is faithfully flat. Actual principal relation lifts and the one-domain factorial estimate give the middle analytic statement. The lower two examples on a complex line distinguish the zero section from the conormal to \(t=0\). The horizontal and vertical axes are \(t\) and \(\tau\); the drawing shows their real coordinate slice, while the equations describe the full complex conic sets. The marked covector is \((0,1)\). No faithful extension from every \(D\)-module at that fixed covector is asserted.

3.342. Scope of microlocal scalar extension

For coherent \(N\), the ordinary tensor in (MFL.1) also computes the derived tensor, by right flatness. Its characteristic support is now detected by the actual finite-order ring. The argument applies to singular characteristic sets and does not require holonomicity. In dimension zero there are no nonzero cotangent covectors, and the scalar assertion is the identity over \(\mathbf C\).

The comparison of a general solution complex with an Euler model still requires the actual module action, localized denominator and finite chain homotopies in (MEC.25)–(MEC.27), or a complete alternative comparison. Flatness by itself does not provide these maps. In particular, it does not give the reverse solution-microsupport inclusion for arbitrary coherent systems or a nilpotent regularity theorem.

3.343. Exercises on actual flat microlocalization

Exercise 3.ET. In the one-dimensional constant-coefficient chart \(\tau\ne0\), put \(h=\tau^{-1}\). Show that \(\sum_{j\ge0}h^j\) is an actual finite-order symbol and is the inverse of \(1-h\). Explain why its conclusion cannot be inferred merely from the formal existence of an inverse, using \(\sum_{j\ge0}(j!)^2h^j\).

Exercise 3.EU. On a complex line compare the coherent left modules \(D/D\partial_t\) and \(D/Dt\). Compute their characteristic sets directly from their strict one-step presentations. At \(p=(0,1)\), determine which actual \(E\)-tensors vanish. Explain why faithful flatness of \(A\to H\) in (MFL.4) does not imply faithfulness of \(D\to E_p\).

Exercise 3.EV. Over \(E\), let \(W=(t h,1)^{\mathsf T}\) and \(V=(1,-t h)\). Verify (MFL.5), construct the maps in (MFL.7), and solve every relation \(b\circ W=0\) explicitly. Keep the order of every operator product.

3.344. Solutions to the microlocalization exercises

Solution 3.ET. There are no coefficients above degree zero. The coefficient of degree \(-j\) is the constant one, so it is holomorphic on any common coefficient product and satisfies \(1\le j!\) for \(j\ge1\). All spatial derivatives vanish. Since these are constant coefficients, the ordered product is the ordinary coefficient convolution, and \[ (1-h)\sum_{j\ge0}h^j=1 =\left(\sum_{j\ge0}h^j\right)(1-h). \tag{MFL.18} \] Each coefficient identity uses finitely many terms. The second proposed series is formal but violates every factorial bound \((j!)^2\le B C^j j!\). Indeed, for even \(j\), \(j!\ge(j/2)^{j/2}\), so \(j!/C^j\) is unbounded for every fixed \(C\). Its coefficients therefore do not define an actual symbol. Also, substituting a nonzero numerical value for \(h\) into a general factorial negative tail need not give a convergent scalar series; that substitution is not the definition of an analytic microlocal symbol.

Solution 3.EU. Right multiplication by \(\partial_t\) or by \(t\) gives an injective map \(D\to D\). The principal products are multiplication by \(\tau\) or \(t\) in the domain \(\mathbf C\{t\}[\tau]\); nonzero leading coefficients cannot cancel. The same calculation proves strictness, with source shift one for \(\partial_t\) and zero for \(t\). Hence \[ \operatorname{gr}(D/D\partial_t)=\mathbf C\{t\}[\tau]/(\tau), \qquad \operatorname{gr}(D/Dt)=\mathbf C\{t\}[\tau]/(t). \tag{MFL.19} \] The first is the zero section; the second is the conormal line to \(t=0\). At \(p=(0,1)\), \(\partial_t\) has the actual inverse \(h\), so the first tensor is zero. The second tensor is nonzero by (MFL.1). The first original module is nonzero: acting on the constant function one identifies it with \(\mathbf C\{t\}\) by the ordinary ordered operator normal form. Thus the flat map to this fixed microlocal stalk is not faithful. In (MFL.4), faithful coefficient extension comes after inversion of \(\tau\) and localization at the chosen characteristic point; that prior localization can already kill a nonzero module.

Solution 3.EV. Associativity gives \(VW=t h-t h=0\). The principal matrices are \(W_0=(0,1)^{\mathsf T}\) and \(V_0=(1,0)\), so their image and kernel agree. There is one principal divisor \(g=(1,0)\), with actual lift \(R=V\). Set \(T_0c=(c,0)\), \(Tc=(c,-c\circ t h)\), \(\Lambda(b_1,b_2)=b_1\), \(q(b_1,b_2)=(0,b_2)\), and \(k(a)=(0,a)\). These satisfy all four identities in (MFL.7). Since \(\Lambda(T-T_0)=0\), (MFL.8) reduces to \(c=b_1\). The original relation says exactly \(b_2=-b_1\circ t h\), so \(b=cV\). This verifies the relation lemma on an actual matrix with a negative-order entry. No interchange of \(t\) and \(h\) occurs.

3.345. A directional topology inside a coefficient domain

Work over \(\mathbf C\). A finite collection of analytic operators is defined on a common neighbourhood, which may be bounded. The cutoff used in (MEC.25) must respect that actual coefficient domain. We construct it using a relative directional topology and the canonical kernel action.

Let \(D\) be a convex ordinary open set in a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(G\) be a closed convex cone. Give \(D_G\) the subspace topology induced by the global \(G\)-topology, and write \(q:D\to D_G\). A relative directional open \(W\) satisfies \((W+G)\cap D=W\). Its neighbourhood basis is \[ N_{x,\epsilon}=(B_\epsilon(x)+G)\cap D, \qquad \epsilon>0. \tag{RKC.1} \] Balls here are sufficiently small ordinary balls centred in \(D\). If \(x,y\in D\) and \(y-x\in G\), every directional neighbourhood of \(x\) contains \(y\). Thus a directional sheaf \(A\) has a canonical specialization map \(A_x\to A_y\), obtained by taking the germ at \(y\) of a representative near \(x\). Refining the representative proves well-definedness and transitivity. The ordinary inverse-image stalk is \((q^{-1}A)_x=A_x\).

3.346. The exact relative section map

For an ordinary open convex \(U\subset D\), put \(\operatorname{Sat}(U)=(U+G)\cap D\). Pullback and restriction give \[ \Gamma(\operatorname{Sat}(U);A) \xrightarrow{\sim}\Gamma(U;q^{-1}A). \tag{RKC.2} \] Injectivity follows by specialization: every point of the saturation lies above a point of \(U\).

For surjectivity take \(s\in\Gamma(U;q^{-1}A)\) and fix \(y\in\operatorname{Sat}(U)\). For \(x\in U\cap(y-G)\), specialize \(s_x\) to \(A_y\). This value is locally constant as a function of \(x\) in that set. Indeed, near \(x\), represent \(s\) by a directional section \(a\) on a directional neighbourhood \(W\) of \(x\). Shrink an ordinary ball \(B\subset U\cap W\) on which its pullback is \(s\). Since \(y\in x+G\), it belongs to \(W\). For each \(x'\in B\cap(y-G)\), the specialized germ is the same germ \(a_y\). The set \(U\cap(y-G)\) is nonempty and convex, hence connected, so the value is independent of the source point.

These values are germs of a directional section. With the preceding \(B,a\), the directional open \(\operatorname{Sat}(B)\) contains \(y\) and is contained in \(W\). For each point of \(\operatorname{Sat}(B)\), using a source in \(B\) identifies its assigned germ with the germ of \(a\). Thus these representatives glue on the saturation. Its pullback has the prescribed germs on \(U\), proving (RKC.2). All segments used here stay in \(U\cap(y-G)\subset D\); no coefficient is continued outside \(D\).

3.347. Flabby coefficients and the derived unit

Suppose \(A\) is flabby on \(D_G\). Any section of \(q^{-1}A\) on a compact convex \(K\subset D\) extends to \(D\). Compact-neighbourhood continuity first represents it on an ordinary neighbourhood of \(K\). A small Minkowski thickening gives a convex open \(U\) containing \(K\) within that neighbourhood and within \(D\). Formula (RKC.2) represents the section on \(\operatorname{Sat}(U)\), and directional flabbiness extends it to \(D_G\). Pullback supplies the required extension.

Consequently, for every ordinary locally closed convex \(C\subset D\), restriction of \(q^{-1}A\) has the compact-convex extension property and \[ H^j(C;q^{-1}A)=0\qquad(j>0). \tag{RKC.3} \] The precise ordinary extension theorem is Extending sections on convex sets, SH02-OR-CONVEX-COMPACT and SH02-OR-CONVEX-EXHAUSTION. Its proof first projects a compact convex set properly to an interval, using the interval closed-cover argument and the canonical compact-fibre restriction. A compact convex exhaustion with interiors in \(C\) covering \(C\) then permits compatible lifts in an injective resolution. These are the ordinary subspace topology and the full compact-convex extension hypothesis. The compact-fibre proof is Open prerequisite proofs, “Compact proper fibres and the section-restriction map”; its compact lifting input is Duality maps for constructible inverse and direct images, C1–C4. None requires finite rank or constructibility.

Resolve a directional sheaf by directional injectives, which are flabby. Every basic directional open in (RKC.1) is ordinary open convex. Formula (RKC.3) makes each pulled-back injective acyclic for sections there. Its saturation is itself, so (RKC.2) identifies its sections, by the actual unit, with the sections before pullback. Computing the direct image on this basis proves \[ A\xrightarrow{\sim}Rq_*q^{-1}A. \tag{RKC.4} \] Finite truncation triangles give the same result for bounded complexes. Every map is natural for a given constant coefficient-algebra action. For a possibly noncommutative \(\mathbf C\)-algebra, forget the action to apply the ordinary vanishing theorem; injective module sheaves remain vector-injective because induction from vector sheaves is exact on stalks. Thus the same unit holds in that module-derived category. No unbounded assertion is needed below.

3.348. The relative counit passes the real support tests

Let \(F\in D^b(\mathbf C_D)\), and suppose \(Rq_*F\) is bounded. Put \(P_GF=q^{-1}Rq_*F\) and let \(B\) be the cone of its counit. The adjunction identities and (RKC.4) give \[ P_GF\longrightarrow F\longrightarrow B, \qquad Rq_*B=0. \tag{RKC.5} \] For \(G=\{0\}\), the topology map is the identity and \(B=0\). Otherwise, if a covector is strictly negative on every nonzero direction in \(G\), the same remains true in a covector neighbourhood, by compactness of the unit directions. For a real \(C^1\) test function with such differential at \(x\), choose a small convex ball where its derivative along every unit cone direction is at most \(-c<0\). Saturate a smaller negative-sublevel patch by \(G\), intersecting with \(D\), and call the resulting relative directional open \(O\). Near \(x\) it agrees with the negative sublevel: the segment from a source in the patch to a sufficiently nearby target stays in the convex ball, so the function strictly decreases along that segment.

There is a fixed \(K\) such that \(N_{x,\epsilon}\setminus O\subset B_{K\epsilon}(x)\) for small \(\epsilon\). At a source in \(B_\epsilon(x)\), the function differs from its value at \(x\) by at most \(M\epsilon\). Advancing \((M/c+1)\epsilon\) along a unit cone direction enters the negative patch. Every later point still in \(D\) belongs to its saturation. Points reached before that distance are within \((M/c+2)\epsilon\) of \(x\). The relevant short segments lie inside the chosen ball; convexity of \(D\) retains every intermediate point between a source and a target in \(D\).

The differences therefore form a neighbourhood basis at \(x\) in the ordinary closed complement of \(O\). The localization triangles on \(N_{x,\epsilon}\), followed by their exact stalk colimit, identify the support-test stalk with that of \(q^{-1}R\Gamma_{D_G\setminus O}Rq_*B\), which is zero. This is the map calculation of Microsupport tests, SH02-MST-CONE-TO-TEST, with every saturation intersected with \(D\). The shrinking differences lie inside \(D\), so no exterior boundary term is added. Thus \[ \operatorname{SS}(B)\cap \bigl(D\times\operatorname{Int}G^{\circ a}\bigr)=\varnothing. \tag{RKC.6} \] Here \(G^{\circ a}\) is the antipodal polar. The conclusion uses the actual real support tests for arbitrary bounded vector-sheaf complexes.

3.349. An admitted round diamond and a compact cap

Use complex coordinates \((t,x_1,\ldots,x_d)\), put \(n=d+1\), and centre the covector at \(p=d\operatorname{Re}t\). Choose positive constants \(\epsilon,A_j\) and the full thick cone \[ \begin{gathered} G=\left\{\begin{gathered} \operatorname{Re}t=-l\le0,\\ |\operatorname{Im}t|\le\epsilon l,\\ |x_j|\le A_jl \end{gathered}\right\},\\ K_G=(1+\epsilon^2+\sum_jA_j^2)^{1/2}. \end{gathered} \tag{RKC.7} \] This cone is closed, convex and pointed, has ordinary interior, and satisfies \(|v|\le K_Gl\) and \(p(v)=-l<0\) for \(v\ne0\).

Take the round coefficient domain \[ D_R=(R e_t+\operatorname{Int}G) \cap(-R e_t-\operatorname{Int}G),\qquad R>0. \tag{RKC.8} \] Its explicit inequalities are \(|\operatorname{Re}t|<R\), \(|\operatorname{Im}t|<\epsilon(R-|\operatorname{Re}t|)\), and \(|x_j|<A_j(R-|\operatorname{Re}t|)\). Hence it is bounded, convex and contains zero. If endpoints lie in \(D_R\) and consecutive differences lie in \(G\), every intermediate point stays in \(D_R\): addition preserves the first open cone and subtraction of the remaining difference preserves the second. Compact endpoints retain strictly positive margins in these inequalities. This is the roundness used by the actual canonical kernel product, proved in Regular singularities, DL.4 and ID.2. Choose \(R\) so small that \(\overline{D_R}\) lies in the common coefficient neighbourhood and all endpoint differences fit in the finitely many normal coefficient radii. The bounds \(2R\sqrt{1+\epsilon^2}\) in time and \(2A_jR\) in space verify those margins.

Choose \(a,h,h_*\) with \(0<h<h_*\), \(a>0\), \(a+2h_*<R\), and put \[ \begin{gathered} \Omega=(a e_t+\operatorname{Int}G)\cap D_R,\\ \Omega_0=\Omega\cap\{\operatorname{Re}t<-h\},\qquad S=\Omega\setminus\Omega_0,\\ S_*=\Omega\cap\{\operatorname{Re}t\ge-h_*\}. \end{gathered} \tag{RKC.9} \] Both opens are directional relative to \(D_R\), and zero is in the ordinary interior of \(S\). The closures of both truncated caps lie compactly inside \(D_R\). Indeed, if \(u=\operatorname{Re}t\in[-h_*,a]\), their transverse bounds are \(\epsilon(a-u)\), \(A_j(a-u)\). For \(u\ge0\), they are strictly below the diamond bounds because \(a<R\); for \(u\le0\), the required inequality is \(a-2u<R\), supplied by \(a+2h_*<R\). Also \[ |z-a e_t|\le K_G(a+h_*) \quad(z\in\overline{S_*}). \tag{RKC.10} \] Thus these are actual bounded coefficient domains and compact cap margins, with no continuation of coefficients to an infinite cone.

3.350. The single degree-one holomorphic quotient

Now let \(q:\Omega\to\Omega_G\) be the relative topology map. A cofinal basis at \(z\in\Omega\) consists of \(V_{z,b}=(z+b e_t+\operatorname{Int}G)\cap D_R\), for sufficiently small \(b>0\) making it lie in \(\Omega\). Each is a bounded convex Stein domain; so is its nonempty intersection with the strict halfspace defining \(\Omega_0\). Here is an explicit exhaustion. For every translated cone inequality put \(L=\pm\operatorname{Re}t+c>0\), with transverse coordinates \(Y_0=\operatorname{Im}t-c_0\), \(Y_j=x_j-c_j\), and constants \(a_0=\epsilon,a_j=A_j\). Sum the barriers \[ |z|^2+\sum_{\text{cone faces}}\left( -\log L-\sum_{j=0}^d\log(a_j^2L^2-|Y_j|^2)\right), \tag{RKC.11} \] adding \(( -h-\operatorname{Re}t)^{-1}\) for the strict halfspace. The real Hessian of each negative Lorentz logarithm is nonnegative on its cone: scale to \(L^2-|Y|^2\) and use the linear hyperbolic rotation of DL.5, whose Hessian at \((L,0)\) is positive. Its Levi form is nonnegative, and \(|z|^2\) makes the sum strictly plurisubharmonic. Every boundary face makes a barrier diverge. Boundedness makes this a genuine exhaustion. Holomorphic acyclicity follows from the full Dolbeault and positive-weight proof in Stein domains in complex space, Theorems 2.1–2.2. Consequently \[ Rq_*\mathcal O_\Omega =q_*\mathcal O_\Omega[0]. \tag{RKC.12} \] For \(z\in S\), the basis intersection with \(\Omega_0\) is nonempty: a negative vertical segment crosses the bottom before leaving the longer cap \(S_*\Subset D_R\). It is open convex and connected, so holomorphic restriction is injective by the identity principle. The localization sequence and the vanishing just proved show \[ \begin{gathered} R\Gamma_S Rq_*\mathcal O_\Omega\simeq\mathcal F[-1],\\ \mathcal F_z=\underset{b}{\operatorname{colim}} \frac{\mathcal O(V_{z,b}\cap\Omega_0)}{\mathcal O(V_{z,b})} \qquad(z\in S). \end{gathered} \tag{RKC.13} \] Outside \(S\) the relative object is zero. This proves concentration for the actual sheaf, not just a chosen stalk. All quotients and their transition maps are ordinary holomorphic restrictions.

3.351. The whole canonical ring acts on this quotient

Let \(\mathcal R=E(G;D_R)\) be the canonical degree-\(n\) kernel cohomology ring with its input holomorphic top-form line, product and positive diagonal unit from Regular singularities, DL.1–DLG.7. We verify the domain conditions for that construction in the present relative topology.

For compact outputs \(K\Subset\Omega\), relevant inputs in the cap are in \[ (K+G)\cap\{\operatorname{Re}t\ge-h\}. \tag{RKC.14} \] Their cone lengths are bounded by the output time and \(h\), so this set is bounded and closed. It lies inside the global cone \(a e_t+\operatorname{Int}G\), by cone addition from an output there, and inside \(D_R\), by the compact cap margins. Hence it is compact inside the actual input open \(\Omega\). The longer cap supplies a strict margin for collars. Relative directional invariance also gives \[ \begin{gathered} z\in W,\quad u-z\in G,\quad z,u\in D_R \quad\Longrightarrow\quad u\in W,\\ p_1(A_G\cap p_2^{-1}S)\subset S, \end{gathered} \tag{RKC.15} \] where \(W\) is any relative directional output open, \(A_G\) is the kernel relation inside \(\Omega^2\), and \(p_1,p_2\) are output and input. For the second inclusion, an output in \(\Omega_0\) could only have inputs in \(\Omega_0\). The same facts hold for \(S_*\). These are precisely the properness and support-to-image conditions.

To make clear which canonical operation is used, take a full smooth kernel representative \(k=(\alpha,\beta)\) of degree \(n\), and an input relative cochain \(e=(c,f)\). On the two-support complement cube their cup has all four entries \[ \left(\begin{gathered} \alpha\wedge c,\quad\beta\wedge c,\\ (-1)^n\alpha\wedge f,\quad(-1)^{n-1}\beta\wedge f \end{gathered}\right). \tag{RKC.16} \] Apply the finite cube-to-full-cone map \(\Phi_\rho\), with its derivative-of-partition term, then the proper collar \(L_\eta\) equal to one near the intersection, and the normalized input trace \(Q_n\). The complete formulas and homotopies are DLG.1–DLG.5. They give \[ \begin{gathered} \mathcal A_k=Q_nL_\eta\Phi_\rho F(k,-),\\ [\mathcal A_k][\mathcal A_l]=[\mathcal A_{k*l}],\qquad [\mathcal A_1]=1. \end{gathered} \tag{RKC.17} \] Every map is defined on the same actual ordinary complement opens in \(\Omega^2\). The collar exists by (RKC.14); its derivative is away from the intersection, so the complement coefficients extend by zero exactly where the formula permits. No general complement coefficient is extended across its excluded support. A smaller relative directional output retains the input by (RKC.15). The finite-cover comparison DLG.14 therefore commutes with output restriction; its collar comparison remains proper on the common intersection. Consecutive inputs remain in \(D_R\) by roundness and in \(\Omega\) by relative cone invariance. Thus the full eight-entry triple cube and its normalized successive traces prove (RKC.17) here with the same signs and input density.

This supplies endomorphisms of the single cohomology sheaf \(\mathcal F\). Boundary, partition and collar homotopies give equality of these sheaf maps. Formula (RKC.17) is consequently a strict module identity on \(\mathcal F\): it is a genuine sheaf of left \(\mathcal R\)-modules. The construction applies to the whole canonical ring, including classes that have no supported-current representative.

3.352. The finite differential action is the ordinary one

Let \(D_0\) be any unital algebra of finite analytic differential operators with coefficients on \(D_R\). Its diagonal kernel map to \(\mathcal R\) is unital. For \(P=b(z)\partial_z^\nu\), its normalized positive product-Cauchy action is \[ \frac{b(z)}{(2\pi i)^n} \int_{|u_j-z_j|=r_j} \frac{\nu!\,f(u)\,du_1\cdots du_n}{(u-z)^{\nu+1}} =b(z)\partial_z^\nu f(z). \tag{RKC.18} \] Each circle is positively oriented, and their order is the input top-form order. U.2, especially (U.6)–(U.8), proves this normalization from the positive Cauchy point mass and its derivatives. In the full Dolbeault convention the ordered factor \((-1)^{n(n-1)/2}\) and the trace signs are exactly those of DLG.4–DLG.5. Thus the action of \(P\) on each holomorphic side of (RKC.13) is its usual local differential action; it respects restrictions and induces that same action on the quotient sheaf.

It follows that restricting the strict \(\mathcal R\)-module \(\mathcal F\) along \(D_0\to\mathcal R\) gives exactly this strict ordinary \(D_0\)-action. In particular all operator relations agree on the sheaf before choosing derived lifts. Let \[ \mathcal G=q^{-1}\mathcal F[-1]. \tag{RKC.19} \] This is a genuine \(\mathcal R\)-module object with underlying vector cohomology in degree one only. The concentration roof is \(D_0\)-linear: resolve \(\mathcal O_\Omega\) by the common exact vector-injective functor of DL.6, natural in all vector-sheaf maps, retain its strict \(D_0\)-action, and take the good truncation and degree-one projection. Its cohomology is the just-identified \(D_0\)-module \(\mathcal F\). This does not prescribe an action of arbitrary microlocal kernels on \(\mathcal O\) itself.

3.353. An actual localized denominator to holomorphic functions

Closed support commutes with directional direct image in this relative setting: \[ Rq_*R\Gamma_S\mathcal O_\Omega \simeq R\Gamma_S Rq_*\mathcal O_\Omega. \tag{RKC.20} \] Indeed \(S\) is closed in \(\Omega_G\), and its complement \(\Omega_0\) is open in both topologies. Compare the two localization triangles using open restriction and the literal composite direct-image identity. A vector-injective resolution is preserved by these direct images, which are right adjoints to exact inverse images. This proves (RKC.20) with its original maps. Each arrow is \(D_0\)-linear because support, restriction and the resolutions commute with the specified local differential action.

Combining (RKC.13), (RKC.19) and (RKC.20) gives the \(D_0\)-linear roof \[ \mathcal G\simeq q^{-1}Rq_*R\Gamma_S\mathcal O_\Omega =P_G R\Gamma_S\mathcal O_\Omega. \tag{RKC.21} \] The ordinary supported object is bounded: the finite Dolbeault resolution and localization give degrees \([0,n+1]\), as in (SCP.5). Its directional image is the degree-one object (RKC.13). Thus the boundedness premises of (RKC.5) hold in this actual instance. Its counit is a denominator at \(p\) by (RKC.6), and \(R\Gamma_S\mathcal O_\Omega\to\mathcal O_\Omega\) is an ordinary isomorphism near zero, which is in \(\operatorname{Int}S\). On a common small neighbourhood \(U\) this gives \[ \mathcal G|_U\simeq\mathcal O_U \quad\text{in }D^b(D_0\text{-Mod};p). \tag{RKC.22} \] This notation means that the specified \(D_0\)-linear roof has underlying vector-sheaf cones microsupport-null at \(p\). It does not require an ordinary neighbourhood quasi-isomorphism.

3.354. Finite comparison data and their mathematical scope

The construction supplies the genuine bounded cutoff and denominator required in (MEC.25) for the actual canonical ring \(E(G;D_R)\). For any specified finite operator diagram that is realized in this ring on the chosen domain and cone, the same \(\mathcal G\) supplies its coefficient action. Only finitely many domain and normal-radius margins were imposed. The finite realization theorem in Regular singularities, ID.2 and DL.7, retains the actual common ring and witnesses; a new infinite family of germ representatives would need its own common-domain assertion.

In particular, if the finite resolution complexes in (MEC.26) have an actual chain-homotopy equivalence after extension to this \(\mathcal R\), finite free adjunction and (RKC.22) give \[ \operatorname{Sol}(N)\simeq\operatorname{Sol}(N_A) \quad\text{in }D^b(\mathbf C_U;p). \tag{RKC.23} \] The finite Hom construction retains the specified homotopies, and its \(D_0\)-linear denominator cones remain null by their finite cell filtration, exactly as proved in (MEC.25)–(MEC.27). The cutoff now provides that criterion's coefficient object. Applying the criterion to the generic whole-module normal form still requires the actual base-extended resolution homotopies, faithful infinite-order extension and any contact-coordinate comparisons. The reverse solution-microsupport inclusion for arbitrary systems, signed de Rham comparison and nilpotent regularity are not consequences of the cutoff alone.

Figure 3.50. The planar panel is the exact complex \(t\)-plane case \(R=\epsilon=1\), \(a=1/4\), \(h=1/8\), \(h_*=1/4\). The outer diamond is \(D_1\); the inner triangular cap is \(S\), and the longer outlined cap is \(S_*\). Dashed cone faces are excluded; the solid bottom segments are included. All boundary coordinates and the inequality \(a+2h_*<R\) are retained. The maps below refer to the full kernel cup, complement cube, proper collar and normalized trace, then to the \(D_0\)-linear concentration and counit roof. Higher-dimensional transverse inequalities remain those of (RKC.7)–(RKC.10).

3.355. Exercises on the actual cutoff

Exercise 3.EW. Compute the open antipodal polar of (RKC.7). Verify the exact compact containment of both caps for the parameters in Figure 3.50, giving their three vertices in the complex \(t\)-plane.

Exercise 3.EX. In the same one-dimensional setting choose a holomorphic branch of \(\log t\) on the negative halfplane. Show that \([\log t]\) and \([1/t]\) give nonzero quotient germs in \(\mathcal F_0\). Compute their finite differential actions and verify the ordinary commutator on \([1/t]\).

Exercise 3.EY. For every cofinal convex basis domain \(V\) used at zero, prove that differentiation induces an isomorphism on \(\mathcal O(V\cap\Omega_0)/\mathcal O(V)\). Identify its inverse by primitive classes. Explain why the corresponding inverse cannot act on the ordinary holomorphic sheaf with its usual differential action.

3.356. Solutions to the cutoff exercises

Solution 3.EW. Write a real covector as \(\alpha\,d\operatorname{Re}t+\beta\,d\operatorname{Im}t+\sum_j\eta_j\cdot dx_j\), using the real Euclidean pairing in each complex spatial coordinate. For a fixed cone length \(l\), its maximum is \(l(-\alpha+\epsilon|\beta|+\sum_jA_j|\eta_j|)\), since the independent transverse balls attain their respective dual norm bounds. Thus \[ \operatorname{Int}G^{\circ a} =\{\alpha>\epsilon|\beta|+\sum_jA_j|\eta_j|\}. \tag{RKC.24} \] In the planar example this is \(\alpha>|\beta|\), containing \(p\). The cap closures have vertices \[ \begin{gathered} \overline S:\quad(1/4,0),\ (-1/8,3/8),\ (-1/8,-3/8),\\ \overline{S_*}:\quad(1/4,0),\ (-1/4,1/2),\ (-1/4,-1/2). \end{gathered} \tag{RKC.25} \] The outer diamond has vertices \((1,0),(0,1),(-1,0),(0,-1)\). Each cap vertex has \(|\operatorname{Re}t|+|\operatorname{Im}t|\le3/4<1\), so convexity puts the whole compact triangular closure strictly inside \(D_1\). The equal bound \(a+2h_*=3/4\) is precisely the general strict margin.

Solution 3.EX. The negative halfplane is convex, so a branch of \(\log t\) exists there by integrating \(1/t\), as in §3.329 and (MEC.17)–(MEC.18). It restricts to each \(V\cap\Omega_0\). If this restriction extended holomorphically to the connected \(V\), its extension \(g\) would satisfy \(tg'=1\) on the nonempty side open. The identity principle would give that equation on all of \(V\), contradicting its value at zero. Likewise an extension of \(1/t\) would satisfy \(tg=1\) at zero. These arguments work at every sufficiently small cofinal basis domain, so the colimit classes are nonzero. Ordinary differential action gives \[ \partial_t[\log t]=[1/t],\qquad t\partial_t[\log t]=[1]=0,\qquad t[1/t]=0. \tag{RKC.26} \] The constant function extends to \(V\), hence has zero quotient class. Since \(\partial_t[1/t]=[-1/t^2]\), \[ (\partial_t t-t\partial_t)[1/t] =0-t[-1/t^2]=[1/t]. \tag{RKC.27} \] Thus the commutator is the literal finite differential relation on the actual nonzero quotient germ.

Solution 3.EY. Both \(V\) and its nonempty negative-side intersection are convex one-dimensional domains. Every holomorphic function on either has a holomorphic primitive, obtained by integrating on straight segments and differentiating that integral. For a side function \(f\), the class of any side primitive \(F\) is independent of its additive constant. Replacing \(f\) by the restriction of a function on \(V\) changes that primitive by a function extending to \(V\), again up to a constant. This gives a well-defined inverse on the quotient. If \(f'\) extends to \(V\), subtract a primitive there; the remainder is constant on the connected side, so \(f\) also extends. Hence \[ \partial_t:\frac{\mathcal O(V\cap\Omega_0)}{\mathcal O(V)} \xrightarrow{\sim} \frac{\mathcal O(V\cap\Omega_0)}{\mathcal O(V)}. \tag{RKC.28} \] The derivative maps commute with restriction, and their uniquely determined inverse maps therefore commute as well. Passing to the stalk colimit gives the inverse differential action on \(\mathcal F_0\). On the ordinary sheaf, however, \[ \ker(\partial_t:\mathcal O_U\to\mathcal O_U) =\mathbf C_U\ne0. \tag{RKC.29} \] Thus an algebra containing an inverse of \(\partial_t\) cannot act on \(\mathcal O_U\) while restricting to its usual derivative. The bounded cutoff can carry that action. Its equivalence to \(\mathcal O_U\) is the localized denominator (RKC.22), with its stated covector and strict module structure.

3.357. Actual full coefficients and a finite solution comparison

Fix a complex manifold \(X\), a nonzero covector \(p\in T_x^*X\), and the actual rings \[ D=\mathcal D^{\mathrm{an}}_{X,x},\qquad E=\mathcal E_{X,p},\qquad B=\mathcal E^\infty_{X,p}. \tag{HGT.1} \] The last ring has one common holomorphic coefficient domain, the every-\(\varepsilon\) positive-head bounds and the factorial negative-tail bounds of Regular singularities, §§5.44–5.45.
