Its products retain the full ordered derivatives. In particular, it is not the unrestricted ring of formal series or arbitrary entire functions of a covariable.

Let \(N,N'\) be coherent analytic \(\mathcal D_X\)-modules near \(x\). We prove that an actual module isomorphism \[ \alpha:B\otimes_DN_x\xrightarrow{\sim}B\otimes_DN'_x \tag{HGT.2} \] in these same base coordinates gives an equivalence \[ \operatorname{Sol}(N)\simeq\operatorname{Sol}(N') \quad\text{in }D^b(\mathbf C_U;p) \tag{HGT.3} \] on a common neighbourhood \(U\) of \(x\). The solution complexes use the unshifted convention of (SCP.4). The proof constructs the finite resolution maps and homotopies needed by (MEC.25)–(MEC.27), then applies the actual cutoff (RKC.19)–(RKC.22). Neither module is required to be holonomic for this comparison. A change of base coordinates is treated in §3.364; a general contact change needs its own solution transport.

3.358. Faithful extension from finite to full microlocal operators

We use the complete right-flatness and proper-left-ideal proofs of Regular singularities, MF.1–MF.7 and FEP.1–FEP.9. Their exact consequences are right \(E\)-flatness of \(B\) on arbitrary left modules and \[ I\subsetneq E\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 1\notin BI, \qquad B/BI\ne0. \tag{HGT.4} \] Here \(BI\) means finite sums of actual products, with no closure. The analytic quotient in that proof is complex linear, with coefficient projection \(q\), division \(d\), and order-lowering correction \(L\): \[ \mathcal P=q(1+Ld)^{-1},\qquad \mathcal P1=1,\qquad \mathcal P(BI)=0. \tag{HGT.5} \] Its annihilation of the whole ideal includes the second source correction by actual lifted principal relations. Restricting to one coefficient complement would not suffice. FEA.1–FEA.4 gives uniformly bounded complex-linear coefficient divisions; FEB.1–FEB.5 gives the whole word estimates, with one domain chosen before every homogeneous, spatial and iteration index. These prove the actual inverses and both identities in (HGT.5). This is the earlier proved analytic input; the algebraic consequences below retain its full module quantifiers.

For a left ideal \(I\), balancing gives inverse maps \[ \begin{gathered} B\otimes_E(E/I)\longleftrightarrow B/BI,\\ b\otimes(a+I)\longmapsto ba+BI,\qquad b+BI\longmapsto b\otimes(1+I). \end{gathered} \tag{HGT.6} \] If \(0\ne m\in M\), its annihilator \(I\) is proper and \(E/I\to M\), \(a+I\mapsto am\), is injective. Flatness preserves that injection. The class of one in (HGT.6) is nonzero by (HGT.4), and maps to \(1\otimes m\). Hence \[ M\longrightarrow B\otimes_EM, \qquad m\longmapsto1\otimes m \quad\text{is injective for every }M. \tag{HGT.7} \] This also detects nonzero objects. If a morphism becomes zero after tensoring, applying (HGT.7) to each of its values makes it zero. Exactness and detection applied to the kernel and cokernel reflect isomorphisms. None of this asserts fullness or injectivity on higher extension groups.

3.359. Analytic resolutions over the full coefficient ring

The finite-order flatness theorem (MFL.1)–(MFL.19) and ordinary balancing give \[ B\otimes_DM\simeq B\otimes_E(E\otimes_DM). \tag{HGT.8} \] The forward inverse pair sends \(b\otimes m\) to \(b\otimes(1\otimes m)\) and \(b\otimes(e\otimes m)\) to \(be\otimes m\). Both component tensor functors are exact, so \(B\) is right \(D\)-flat. Tensoring the exact sequences defining cycles and boundaries also gives \[ H^i(B\otimes_DC^\bullet) =B\otimes_DH^i(C^\bullet) \tag{HGT.9} \] for every cochain complex; this is a degreewise argument, without a totalization or completion.

Choose the actual finite locally free analytic resolutions of (SCP.3)–(SCP.4), then restrict to stalks. Pad with zero terms to write them in the same interval \([-m,0]\): \[ P^\bullet\longrightarrow N_x,\qquad Q^\bullet\longrightarrow N'_x. \tag{HGT.10} \] Their \(B\)-extensions are bounded finite free resolutions by (HGT.9). Their matrices remain the images of the original finite analytic operator matrices. The smaller algebra generated by these entries is not assumed to have an exact resolution.

3.360. Constructing the two finite comparison maps

For brevity write \(P_B=B\otimes_DP\), \(Q_B=B\otimes_DQ\). Lift \(\alpha\) through the augmentation \(Q_B^0\to B\otimes_DN'_x\), choosing a preimage for each image of a finite basis of \(P_B^0\). This gives \(f^0\). At degree minus one, \(f^0d_P^{-1}\) has zero augmentation because \(f^0\) lifts \(\alpha\). It therefore lies in \(\ker\epsilon_Q=\operatorname{im}d_Q^{-1}\). Lift each finite basis image through that surjection to obtain \(f^{-1}\).

For \(i<-1\), suppose the higher components have been constructed. The chain equation one degree above and \(d_P^2=0\) show that \(f^{i+1}d_P^i\) takes values in \(\ker d_Q^{i+1}=\operatorname{im}d_Q^i\). Again lift the finitely many basis images. Thus \[ d_Q^if^i=f^{i+1}d_P^i \qquad(-m\le i<0). \tag{HGT.11} \] If there is no preceding nonzero term of \(Q_B\), exactness makes the cycle to be lifted zero, so the zero map supplies that component. The finite recursion gives a cochain map \(f:P_B\to Q_B\) lifting \(\alpha\). Applying the same construction to \(\alpha^{-1}\) gives \(g:Q_B\to P_B\). All entries and equations lie in the actual ring \(B\).

3.361. Both homotopies, with their matrix sides

Set \(k=gf-1\) on \(P_B\). Its degree-zero augmentation is zero, so choose \(H^0:P_B^0\to P_B^{-1}\) with \(d_P^{-1}H^0=k^0\). Inductively, if the higher homotopy terms have been chosen, put \[ r^i=k^i-H^{i+1}d_P^i. \tag{HGT.12} \] The chain equation for \(k\) and the homotopy equation in degree \(i+1\) give \(d_P^ir^i=0\). Exactness and the finite free source permit a lift \(H^i\) through \(d_P^{i-1}\). At the bottom, that cycle is zero because the first nonzero differential is injective. Therefore \[ gf-1=d_PH+Hd_P. \tag{HGT.13} \] The same recursion on \(Q_B\) supplies \(K\) with \[ fg-1=d_QK+Kd_Q. \tag{HGT.14} \] The proof used finite free lifting through actual surjections. It does not require \(B\) to be Noetherian, \(\alpha\) to preserve filtrations, or arbitrary modules to have split resolutions.

To fix the noncommutative conventions, write left free modules as rows. Denote the matrices of \(d_P^i,d_Q^i,f^i,g^i,H^i\) by \(D_i,E_i,F_i,G_i,H_i\). Then the equations are \[ \begin{gathered} D_iF_{i+1}=F_iE_i,\qquad E_iG_{i+1}=G_iD_i,\\ F_iG_i-I=H_iD_{i-1}+D_iH_{i+1}. \end{gathered} \tag{HGT.15} \] The corresponding equation for \(G_iF_i-I\) uses \(K_iE_{i-1}+E_iK_{i+1}\). No matrix factors have been interchanged.

3.362. One actual canonical ring for the whole finite diagram

Choose linear base coordinates so that the real covector is \(p=d\operatorname{Re}t\). Include all entries of \(P,Q,f,g,H,K\), their finite products, and all the zero witnesses in (HGT.11)–(HGT.15). The complete finite realization proof in Regular singularities, ID.1–ID.2 and DL.7 represents this finite list in one canonical ring \[ \mathcal R=E(G;D_R). \tag{HGT.16} \] Its final support is the full thick cone (RKC.7), with \(p\in\operatorname{Int}G^{\circ a}\), and its coefficient domain is the admitted round diamond (RKC.8). All actual coefficient products, normal radii, support enlargements and finite boundary witnesses are placed at one common later index before restricting to that diamond. The diagonal finite differential classes retain their ordinary action and input holomorphic top-form normalization. Only finitely many such data occur; no universal map from every \(B\)-germ to a preassigned ring is asserted.

Let \(D_0\) be the unital algebra of the finitely many analytic differential entries of \(P,Q\) on this common domain, and let \(P^\bullet_{\mathrm{alg}},Q^\bullet_{\mathrm{alg}}\) denote the finite free \(D_0\)-matrix complexes they define. Their extensions to the analytic operator sheaf recover the resolutions in (HGT.10). Their extensions to \(\mathcal R\) retain the realized maps and both homotopies: \[ \mathcal R\otimes_{D_0}P^\bullet_{\mathrm{alg}} \simeq_h\mathcal R\otimes_{D_0}Q^\bullet_{\mathrm{alg}}. \tag{HGT.17} \] The symbol \(\simeq_h\) means the actual finite chain-homotopy equivalence (HGT.11)–(HGT.14). The \(D_0\)-complexes need not resolve their \(D_0\)-cokernels. Equation (HGT.17) follows from the realized ring identities, without flatness of \(\mathcal R\) over \(D_0\).

3.363. Apply the strict cutoff and retain the derived maps

The construction (RKC.19)–(RKC.22) supplies a genuine bounded \(\mathcal R\)-module object \(\mathcal G\) and an actual \(D_0\)-linear localized denominator \(\mathcal G\simeq\mathcal O\) at \(p\). Apply \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal R}(-,\mathcal G)\) to (HGT.17). For a homogeneous Hom cochain \(\phi\) of degree \(q\), precomposition with a degree-minus-one homotopy has the sign \[ S_H(\phi)=(-1)^q\phi H. \tag{HGT.18} \] Using \(d\phi=d_{\mathcal G}\phi-(-1)^q\phi d_P\), expansion gives \(dS_H+S_Hd=\phi(d_PH+Hd_P)\); the two terms containing \(d_{\mathcal G}\phi\) cancel. The same formula applies to \(K\). Thus both inverse identities and their homotopies survive in the finite Hom complexes.

Finite free adjunction identifies these with the corresponding \(D_0\)-matrix Hom complexes with coefficients in \(\mathcal G\). Its \(D_0\)-linear denominator then replaces \(\mathcal G\) by \(\mathcal O\): the cone of the induced map has a finite filtration whose pieces are finite sums of shifts of the same null cone. The microsupport-null subcategory is thick, by the full fraction and cone proof in (MCM.3)–(MCM.6). Consequently the denominator stays invertible after each finite Hom construction. The resulting complexes are exactly the finite analytic solution complexes of (SCP.4). This proves (HGT.3).

Two lifts of the same augmented module map differ by a chain map with zero augmentation. The recursion (HGT.12)–(HGT.13) constructs a homotopy for their difference. Thus the resulting localized map is independent of the finite resolution lift, after a common finite realization. Composing two augmented maps and comparing their finite lifts uses that same homotopy argument. This retains the actual comparison data rather than choosing unrelated endomorphisms in a vector-derived category.

3.364. Ordinary coordinate changes preserve the support tests

Let \(\varphi:U\to U'\) be a biholomorphism and let its differential-operator map be the chain-rule map. Pullback gives a literal coefficient isomorphism \(\varphi^{-1}\mathcal O_{U'}\to\mathcal O_U\); applying it to a finite free analytic resolution identifies the solution matrix complexes. In the induced left-module convention, \[ \operatorname{Sol}(\varphi_D^*N') \simeq\varphi^{-1}\operatorname{Sol}(N'). \tag{HGT.19} \] The identification is obtained on the actual analytic Hom complex, so it respects its cochain differential and attaching maps.

This change preserves the real definition of microsupport. A real test \(f'\) on \(U'\) pulls back to \(f'\circ\varphi\); its closed test side pulls back to the same closed side on \(U\), with differential \((d\varphi)^Tdf'\). The inverse homeomorphism identifies sections with those supports, and its exact pullback carries injective resolutions to injective resolutions because it is an equivalence of sheaf categories. Thus the support-test stalks agree in all degrees. Applying the same argument to \(\varphi^{-1}\) gives \[ \operatorname{SS}(\varphi^{-1}F') =\{(x,(d\varphi_x)^T\eta): (\varphi(x),\eta)\in\operatorname{SS}(F')\}. \tag{HGT.20} \] Therefore a holomorphic time shift \(t'=t-\psi(x)\), \(x'=x\), may be included in (HGT.2) with the actual solution transport just proved. A transformation mixing base and cotangent variables has no such inverse-image argument.

3.365. Euler detection in the stated ordinary coordinates

Suppose (HGT.2) has \(N'=N_A\), the actual constant-matrix Euler model of §§3.327–3.330, and \(p\) is a nonzero normal covector to \(t=0\). If \(p\in\operatorname{Char}(N)\), then (MFL.1) gives \(E\otimes_DN_x\ne0\). Formula (HGT.7) implies \(B\otimes_DN_x\ne0\), so the isomorphic model has positive rank. For that rank the complete real support calculation (MEC.20)–(MEC.24) gives \[ \begin{gathered} p\in\operatorname{Char}(N),\quad B\otimes_DN_x\simeq B\otimes_D(N_A)_x\\ \Longrightarrow\quad p\in\operatorname{SS}(\operatorname{Sol}N). \end{gathered} \tag{HGT.21} \] Indeed (HGT.3) identifies the objects in the category localized at \(p\), and the model is nonzero there. Conversely, (SCP.20) gives the forward support inclusion for all coherent analytic \(N\).

There is an exact source match for the standard-coordinate generic normal form. In Regular singularities, GM.A–GM.B, let \(M=E\otimes_DN_x\) be holonomic and let its actual lattice \(M_0\subset M\), with \(EM_0=M\), be free over the commutative factorial coefficient ring \(R_0\) of DP.2. The lattice is the whole \(R_0^r\), not just its reduction or completion. Its coefficient-column actions are \(t=h^2\partial_h+T\), \(z_i=h\partial_i+Z_i\), where \(h=\tau^{-1}\), \(z_i=\xi_i/\tau\). The matrices \(T,Z_i\in M_r(R_0)\) satisfy \(T(0,x)^k=0\) for some \(k\ge1\), \(h^2\partial_hZ_i-h\partial_iT+[T,Z_i]=hZ_i\), and \(h(\partial_iZ_j-\partial_jZ_i)+[Z_i,Z_j]=0\), precisely FG.1. Under these stated hypotheses the complete gauge FG.A–FG.D gives actual inverse matrices \(V,W\) and one constant \(H\), with \[ \begin{gathered} VW=WV=I,\qquad \partial_\tau V=TV-\tau^{-1}VH,\\ \partial_iV+\tau Z_iV=0. \end{gathered} \tag{HGT.22} \] The whole finite presentation GM.8 and the commutators \([t,V]=-\partial_\tau V\), \([D_{x_i},V]=\partial_iV\) give, for \(e_j=\sum_kV_{kj}u_k\), \[ D_{x_i}e_j=0,\qquad tD_te_j=\sum_k(H-I)_{kj}e_k. \tag{HGT.23} \] The inverse frame \(W\) satisfies the original relations by differentiating \(WV=I\). Thus these are inverse maps of the entire \(B\)-module, and the matrix in our row-generator Euler convention is exactly \[ A=(H-I)^{\mathsf T}. \tag{HGT.24} \] Equations (HGT.21)–(HGT.24) prove detection at every positive-rank point of this standard-coordinate parameter open. They use the ordinary Euler model in those coordinates, with no fractional power of \(\tau\) adjoined and no numerical evaluation of a divergent Gevrey series.

3.366. The contact premise for a general characteristic branch

The generic geometry in Regular singularities, DP.6 first applies a finite quadratic contact shear, then an ordinary holomorphic time shift to put a general smooth homogeneous Lagrangian branch into \(t=\xi'=0\). The time shift has the exact solution transport (HGT.19)–(HGT.20). The contact shear also requires a comparison of solution objects or cutoff kernels, with the correct input density and support maps. Ring isomorphisms and their balanced module maps alone do not provide it.

Equations HGT.21–HGT.24 give detection in the stated standard coordinates. The canonical pure coefficient comparison of §§3.440–3.442 carries it through the required finite contact chain without intermediate differential modules. Sections 3.439–3.446 gives holonomic analytic solution support; §§3.451–3.459 gives the density-normalized de Rham identity and bounded holonomic support. Arbitrary nonholonomic systems, the common Hecke-support premise and nilpotent regularity retain their separate hypotheses.

Figure 3.51. Both comparison maps and homotopies are finite matrices in the actual full coefficient ring; one common canonical kernel ring realizes all their equations. The lower panel is the exact normalized contact example of Solution 3.FB, with \(c=1\): the point conormal has \((x,t)=(0,0)\), while its sheared front is \((x',t')=(z,-z^2/2)\). The plotted interval is the real slice \(-1\le z\le1\); its parabola is exact. The contact equation is preserved, but the shear does not arise from a map of the base. All complex coordinates and the precise solution-transport boundary are retained in the text.

3.367. Exercises on actual finite comparison data

Exercise 3.EZ. Let \(a,b\) be arbitrary elements of a unital, possibly noncommutative ring. Prove that \(U=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&a\\b&1+ba\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) is invertible. Contract the two-term row complex with differential \(U\), then construct both homotopies comparing \(P\) with its direct sum with that complex. Retain the order of \(a,b\).

Exercise 3.FA. In the one-dimensional ordered symbol ring, use \(b\circ x=xb+\partial_\tau b\). The entire expression \((1-e^{-x\tau})/x\) would be a left inverse of \(x\). Prove that it fails the every-\(\varepsilon\) positive-head bounds on every common base neighbourhood. For its degree-\(L\) truncation compute the residual and its quotient normal form using \(\mathcal P=\operatorname{ev}_{x=0}\sum_{a\ge0}(-\partial_\tau d)^a\), where \(d\) deletes the constant Taylor term and divides by \(x\).

Exercise 3.FB. On the normalized cotangent chart of a complex surface with contact form \(dt+z\,dx\), verify that \(x'=x+cz\), \(z'=z\), \(t'=t-cz^2/2\) is a contact transformation. Apply it to \(\{x=t=0\}\). For \(c\ne0\), show that it cannot be induced by any local biholomorphism of the base, and identify the ordinary time shift that makes the transformed branch standard.

3.368. Solutions to the finite comparison exercises

Solution 3.EZ. Multiply the two triangular matrices in the stated order: \[ \begin{gathered} U=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\b&1\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}1&a\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\\ U^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-a\\0&1\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-b&1\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}1+ab&-a\\-b&1\end{pmatrix}. \end{gathered} \tag{HGT.25} \] The triangular inverse products are identities by direct multiplication. Thus the two-term complex \(C^{-1}\xrightarrow{U}C^0\) has contraction \(J^0=U^{-1}\): the degree-minus-one equation is \(UJ^0=I\), and the degree-zero equation is \(J^0U=I\), using row maps. Include \(P\) into \(Q=P\oplus C\) and project back. Their composite on \(P\) is the identity. The other composite minus the identity is zero on \(P\) and minus the identity on \(C\), so its homotopy is \(0\oplus(-J)\). These are precisely (HGT.13)–(HGT.15); both compositions and the minus sign are explicit. The two entries \(ab\) and \(ba\) occur in their required different positions.

Solution 3.FA. Its homogeneous coefficient of degree \(j\ge1\) is \((-1)^{j+1}x^{j-1}/j!\). On any fixed base disc \(|x|\le r\), \(r>0\), its norm is \(r^{j-1}/j!\). The every-\(\varepsilon\) bound would imply \[ r^{-1}(r/\varepsilon)^j\le M_\varepsilon \qquad(j\ge1), \tag{HGT.26} \] which is impossible for \(0<\varepsilon<r\). Holomorphy of the entire expression at \(x=0\) therefore does not put it in the actual ring \(B\). Its finite truncation is actual, and cancellation of consecutive terms gives \[ \begin{gathered} b_L\circ x=1+r_L,\qquad r_L=(-1)^{L+1}x^L\tau^L/L!,\\ \mathcal P r_L=-1. \end{gathered} \tag{HGT.27} \] For the last equality only the term \(a=L\) contributes: after \(L\) Taylor divisions, applying \((-1)^L\partial_\tau^L\) to \((-1)^{L+1}\tau^L/L!\) gives \(-1\). At \(r=1/2\) and \(\varepsilon=1/4\), the required weighted degree-\(L\) residual norm is exactly \(2^L\), even though its numerical value at \((x,\tau)=(1/2,1)\) has magnitude \(2^{-L}/L!\). The actual quotient remains nonzero. These are the exact common-domain and coefficient bounds in the proper-ideal theorem, not a completed-ideal argument.

Solution 3.FB. Direct differentiation gives \[ dt'+z'\,dx'=dt-cz\,dz+z(dx+c\,dz)=dt+z\,dx. \tag{HGT.28} \] On \(x=t=0\), the transformed branch has \(x'=cz\), \(t'=-cz^2/2\), \(z'=z\). For \(c\ne0\) it is the front \[ t'=-(x')^2/(2c),\qquad z'=x'/c. \tag{HGT.29} \] An ordinary base biholomorphism sends a cotangent fibre over one point to a cotangent fibre over one point. Its base projection on this branch would have rank zero. The displayed transformed projection has rank one, so this contact map cannot be such a lift. Finally set \[ t''=t'+(x')^2/(2c),\qquad x''=x',\qquad z''=z'-x'/c. \tag{HGT.30} \] Its contact form is again \(dt'+z'\,dx'\), and the branch becomes \(t''=z''=0\). This last step is an ordinary base change. The preceding shear is the part for which a separate solution or cutoff-kernel transport is still required.

3.369. Projective incidence and the two coefficient kernels

Let \(V\) be a complex vector space of dimension \(N+1\), with \(N\geq1\). Put \(X=\mathbf P(V)\), \(Y=\mathbf P(V^*)\), and let \(S\subset X\times Y\) be incidence: a line lies in a hyperplane. Its complement has open embedding \(j:\Omega\hookrightarrow X\times Y\). Transposition of the two factors is denoted by \(\mathrm t\). Define

\[ \begin{gathered} A=j_!\mathbf C_\Omega,\qquad B=Rj_*\mathbf C_\Omega,\\ K=A[N],\qquad L=\mathrm tB[N],\\ \Phi F=Rq_{X!}(K\otimes q_Y^{-1}F),\\ \mathcal TF=Rq_{Y!}(L\otimes q_X^{-1}F). \end{gathered} \tag{LIT.1} \]

In the second formula for a transform the projections belong to \(Y\times X\). Tensor products of complex-vector sheaves are derived tensor products, computed by ordinary stalkwise tensor. Inputs are globally bounded; they need not be constructible or have finite-dimensional stalks. The sheaves \(A\) and \(B\) are different kernels. In particular, the second is a derived open direct image.

The exact earlier proof is GL-DMOD, §5.57, LI.8.1–LI.8.3. Its compact-fibre comparison, punctured-disc boundary map and gluing of the oriented diagonal give

\[ K\circ L\simeq\mathbf C_{\Delta_X},\qquad L\circ K\simeq\mathbf C_{\Delta_Y}. \tag{LIT.2} \]

Here composition integrates the middle projective factor with proper support. The two shifts \([N]\) add to the real affine-fibre shift \([2N]\) in that proof. Thus neither a complex dimension nor a cohomological shift is suppressed in LIT.2.

3.370. The fibre calculation and its diagonal map

For \(x,z\in X\), write \(H_x,H_z\subset Y\) for their incidence hyperplanes and normalize a representative covector to have value one on a representative of \(x\). Then \(Y\setminus H_x\simeq\mathbf C^N\). If \(x=z\), the remaining coefficient is constant. If \(x\ne z\), the second removed hyperplane is one nonempty affine hyperplane \(H\). Proper base change in LI.8.1 gives the actual derived stalk

\[ (K\circ L)_{(x,z)}\simeq \begin{cases} R\Gamma_c(\mathbf C^N;\mathbf C)[2N],&x=z,\\ R\Gamma_c(\mathbf C^N;Rj_{H*}\mathbf C_{\mathbf C^N\setminus H})[2N],&x\ne z. \end{cases} \tag{LIT.3} \]

The first complex is \(\mathbf C[0]\); integration of the positive complex orientation gives its map to \(\mathbf C\). For completeness, the decisive normal calculation for the second is the triangle

\[ \begin{gathered} \mathbf C_{\mathbf C}\longrightarrow Rj_{0*}\mathbf C_{\mathbf C^*} \longrightarrow\mathbf C_{\{0\}}[-1]\xrightarrow{+1},\\ R\Gamma_c(\mathbf C;Rj_{0*}\mathbf C_{\mathbf C^*})=0. \end{gathered} \tag{LIT.4} \]

The compact connecting map is an isomorphism: with \(\eta=d\theta/(2\pi)\) and a radial cutoff \(\rho\) equal to one near zero and zero outside a disc, its representative \(-d\rho\wedge\eta\) has integral one. Compact coordinate contractions in the other \(2N-2\) real directions, explicitly given in LI.36, reduce the second line of LIT.3 to LIT.4. Local projective frames trivialize the diagonal family. Their holomorphic transition maps have positive real Jacobian \(|\det J|^2\), so the integration maps glue to the constant diagonal sheaf. The zero off-diagonal stalks and the single diagonal cohomology sheaf prove the first map in LIT.2. Exchanging \(X\) and \(Y\) proves the second.

3.371. Bounded operators and coherent inverse maps

The transforms in LIT.1 preserve boundedness. One explicit sufficient construction is to represent the bounded tensor input by its tensor with the finite smooth real de Rham resolution on the product. The resolution is exact on stalks by the radial homotopy, and its terms are smooth-function modules, hence acyclic on opens by the partition proof in LI.8.1. The middle projection is proper. This finite resolution computes its derived direct image and gives a finite cohomological bound. For \(B\), the punctured-normal-disc resolution has cohomology only in degrees zero and one, so a bounded truncation can be used first. These constructions permit arbitrary coefficient vector spaces.

Proper-support composition, base change and the tensor projection formula identify the two composite operators with convolution by the kernels in LIT.2. They apply to every attaching map of a bounded input. Consequently

\[ \Phi\mathcal T\simeq\operatorname{Id}_{D^b(\mathbf C_X)},\qquad \mathcal T\Phi\simeq\operatorname{Id}_{D^b(\mathbf C_Y)}. \tag{LIT.5} \]

These inverse maps can be made coherent without guessing a relative scalar. Fix one diagonal isomorphism \(\epsilon_X:K\circ L\to\mathbf C_{\Delta_X}\). Left convolution by \(K\) is fully faithful because LIT.2 supplies an inverse functor. There is therefore a unique isomorphism \(\epsilon_Y:L\circ K\to\mathbf C_{\Delta_Y}\) such that

\[ K\circ\epsilon_Y=\epsilon_X\circ K. \tag{LIT.6} \]

Indeed full faithfulness lifts the isomorphism on the right to \(\epsilon_Y\), and reflects its invertibility. With unit \(\epsilon_Y^{-1}\), LIT.6 is one triangle identity; conjugating it by the inverse equivalence gives the other. The associator is the actual proper-support base-change associator. This is the construction of GL-DMOD, §5.67, IN.1.

3.372. The full nonzero conormal is a graph

Write \(\dot T^*X=T^*X\setminus0_X\), and similarly for \(Y\). Use the underlying real cotangent bundles, identified with holomorphic cotangent bundles by taking real parts of complex-linear forms. The twisted incidence relation is

\[ \begin{gathered} \Lambda=\{(p,q):(x,y;\xi,-\eta)\in\dot T_S^*(X\times Y)\},\\ p=(x;\xi),\qquad q=(y;\eta). \end{gathered} \tag{LIT.7} \]

Both projections of \(\Lambda\) are diffeomorphisms onto the corresponding punctured cotangent bundles. Here is the global linear-algebra check. A nonzero cotangent vector at a line \(\ell\subset V\) is a nonzero map \(V/\ell\to\ell\). Its kernel determines one hyperplane \(H\supset\ell\). It is exactly the first component of one nonzero normal to incidence at \((\ell,H)\). The second normal component is nonzero because varying \(H\) can move it off \(\ell\). The dual argument recovers \(\ell\) from that component. In projective frames these assignments and their inverses are smooth, and the conormal is closed away from its zero section. The projections are thus proper homeomorphisms as well as diffeomorphisms. No unbounded forgotten covector lies above a compact set of endpoints.

In coordinates \(X=(t,x)\), \(Y=(s,y)\), with \(x,y\in\mathbf C^{N-1}\), the incidence equation and its twisted graph are

\[ \begin{gathered} f=s-t-x^{\mathsf T}y=0,\\ \chi(t,x;\tau,\xi) =(t+x^{\mathsf T}\xi/\tau,\ \xi/\tau;\ \tau,-\tau x),\\ \chi^{-1}(s,y;\sigma,\eta) =(s+y^{\mathsf T}\eta/\sigma,\ -\eta/\sigma;\ \sigma,\sigma y). \end{gathered} \tag{LIT.8} \]

These displayed charts require \(\tau=\sigma\ne0\). The global graph does not require that particular chart. Setting \(y=\xi/\tau\) gives the exact identity

\[ \chi^*(\sigma\,ds+\eta^{\mathsf T}dy) =\tau\,d(t+x^{\mathsf T}y)-\tau x^{\mathsf T}dy =\tau\,dt+\xi^{\mathsf T}dx. \tag{LIT.9} \]

All complex normal phases occur. The minus sign in the input covector of LIT.7 is essential for LIT.8–LIT.9.

3.373. Constructibility and the identity section

The two-stratum pair \((\Omega,S)\) gives cohomological constructibility of \(A\), \(B\) and their shifts in precisely the formal-local sense of SH03, Dual kernels. Near \(S\), holomorphic coordinates identify the pair with a tangential ball times a normal disc and its puncture. Radial contractions in nested tangential balls and discs, and the oriented normal circle, identify the ordinary and compact-support formal systems with fixed finite complexes. These contractions commute with further shrinking; this proves representability of the systems, rather than just finiteness of their limits. Away from \(S\) the constant or zero coefficient model suffices.

The local product model and the smooth-submanifold microsupport formula give

\[ \operatorname{SS}(A),\operatorname{SS}(B) \subset 0_{X\times Y}\cup T_S^*(X\times Y). \tag{LIT.10} \]

For \(A\), this also follows from the exact localization triangle \(A\to\mathbf C_{X\times Y}\to\mathbf C_S\xrightarrow{+1}\). The same bound for \(B\) follows by the normal-disc calculation or constructible duality. The off-zero relation in either selected endpoint region is therefore contained in the same graph LIT.7, and has no component with only one endpoint covector zero.

The rotated localization triangle supplies an actual morphism

\[ \mathbf C_S[-1]\xrightarrow{\delta}A\longrightarrow \mathbf C_{X\times Y}\xrightarrow{+1}. \tag{LIT.11} \]

Its cone has only zero microsupport. Thus \(\delta\) is invertible in the localization at every nonzero incidence normal. The SH02 submanifold formula gives \(\mu\operatorname{hom}(\mathbf C_S,\mathbf C_S)|_{\dot T_S^*}=\mathbf C_{\dot T_S^*}\): normal specialization is supported on the zero normal section and its Fourier transform is the constant dual-normal coefficient. This has no codimension shift. The formula takes the identity to the constant section one. Conjugation by \(\delta[N]\), retaining its inverse, consequently proves the identity-induced isomorphism

\[ \mathbf C_{\dot T_S^*}\xrightarrow[\operatorname{id}_K]{\ \sim\ } \mu\operatorname{hom}(K,K)|_{\dot T_S^*}. \tag{LIT.12} \]

Conjugating an identity gives an identity, so the possible sign of a chosen representative of \(\delta\) cancels. An abstract rank calculation is unnecessary.

3.374. Localized equivalence for arbitrary bounded coefficients

For an open \(U\subset\dot T^*X\), put \(U'=\chi(U)\). All hypotheses of SH03, When a kernel quantizes a contact transformation, Theorem 1 now hold: the coefficient field is \(\mathbf C\); the manifolds are finite-dimensional and compact; the kernel is bounded and cohomologically constructible; LIT.7 gives the two proper graph projections; LIT.10 gives both selected-region containments; and LIT.12 is the required identity-induced map. Hence

\[ \begin{gathered} \Phi:D^b(\mathbf C_Y;U')\xrightarrow{\sim}D^b(\mathbf C_X;U),\\ \mathcal T:D^b(\mathbf C_X;U)\xrightarrow{\sim}D^b(\mathbf C_Y;U'). \end{gathered} \tag{LIT.13} \]

Here localization kills exactly the bounded complexes whose microsupport misses the indicated open. The inverse kernel has exactly the shift in LIT.1: with the complex orientations,

\[ \mathrm tR\mathcal Hom(K,q_Y^{-1}\omega_Y) =\mathrm tR\mathcal Hom(A[N],\mathbf C[2N]) \simeq\mathrm tB[N]=L. \tag{LIT.14} \]

To compute it, Verdier duality on \(X\times Y\) gives \(D(A)=B[4N]\). The input shift subtracts \(N\), and the relative orientation subtracts \(2N\) from the product dual, leaving \([N]\). This is precisely the right relative dual, not an unshifted transposed kernel.

The cited theorem proves invertibility of the actual adjunction unit and counit by applying the parameterized kernel construction to the diagonal and detecting their cones with the supported conormal coefficient model. Its dual-kernel proof retains the orientation factors and excludes escaping ambient covectors by graph properness. Its directional-morphism proof uses the actual fourfold Hom kernel, the repeated-variable exceptional restrictions, clean proper projections and compact replacement. Those are applicable here with the graph just verified; no constructibility hypothesis has been imposed on the input of LIT.13.

3.375. Microsupport, morphisms and the unchanged parameter

For every bounded \(F\) on \(X\) and every bounded \(G\) on \(Y\),

\[ \begin{gathered} \operatorname{SS}(\mathcal TF)\cap\dot T^*Y =\chi(\operatorname{SS}(F)\cap\dot T^*X),\\ \operatorname{SS}(\Phi G)\cap\dot T^*X =\chi^{-1}(\operatorname{SS}(G)\cap\dot T^*Y). \end{gathered} \tag{LIT.15} \]

Indeed, for every sufficiently small matched open pair, the transform and its inverse descend and are inverse by LIT.13. An object is zero in the localization at a covector exactly when that covector is absent from its microsupport, by the thick null-object criterion of §3.302–3.303. Apply both functors to this criterion. This proves both implications point by point. No assertion concerning zero covectors is part of LIT.15.

The same theorem gives the natural comparison, for arbitrary bounded \(G_1,G_2\),

\[ \chi^{-1}\bigl(\mu\operatorname{hom}_Y(G_2,G_1)|_{U'}\bigr) \simeq\mu\operatorname{hom}_X(\Phi G_2,\Phi G_1)|_U. \tag{LIT.16} \]

The inverse image is by a homeomorphism. Evaluation and the proper projection counits define this comparison. It respects identities and directional composition: before specialization, both parenthesizations are mates of the same successive evaluation; transitivity of the two projection counits gives the same trace. The full proof with its graded symmetry is SH02, Directional composition. In particular, the endomorphism object in LIT.16 is transported with its product and identity, not just with its cohomology dimensions.

For a smooth parameter manifold \(Z\), the kernel

\[ \Theta_ZK=\operatorname{pr}_{XY}^{-1}K\otimes\mathbf C_{\{z=z'\}} \tag{LIT.17} \]

has twisted relation \((p,z;\zeta)\leftrightarrow(\chi(p),z;\zeta)\). The unchanged-parameter proof identifies its operator with the original convolution with \(Z\) retained. Above a compact set of endpoint covectors its relation is a closed subset of the product of two compact sets, so properness persists even for noncompact \(Z\). The input kernel covector in the second parameter is \(-\zeta\), exactly as required by the twisted relation.

3.376. A strict action of a constant algebra

Let \(R\) be any unital associative complex algebra, with no commutativity, Noetherian or finite global dimension assumption. Write \(R_X\) and \(R_Y\) for the constant sheaves of algebras. Define \(\Phi_R\) and \(\mathcal T_R\) by the same coefficient kernels, tensoring over \(\mathbf C\) and retaining the left \(R\)-action of the input. Then

\[ \begin{gathered} \Phi_R:D^b(R_Y)\xrightarrow{\sim}D^b(R_X),\\ \mathcal T_R:D^b(R_X)\xrightarrow{\sim}D^b(R_Y),\\ \operatorname{For}\Phi_R\simeq\Phi\operatorname{For},\qquad \operatorname{For}\mathcal T_R\simeq\mathcal T\operatorname{For}. \end{gathered} \tag{LIT.18} \]

Here \(\operatorname{For}\) forgets the action. A direct construction proves all assertions. Tensor the bounded input and fixed bounded coefficient kernel, then use the finite smooth resolution from §3.371. Each term has its actual left \(R\)-action, commuting with the differential, restriction and projection. The resolution is functorial for complex-linear maps and homotopies; it neither replaces the action by cohomology endomorphisms nor chooses separate lifts of its generators. Acyclicity on opens holds after forgetting, and the same complexes compute the underlying derived image. Alternatively, forgetting preserves injectives because its left adjoint \(R\otimes_{\mathbf C}-\) is exact. The two diagonal comparisons LIT.2 tensor with the identity of each coefficient module. Their associativity and unit maps are therefore \(R\)-linear, proving both inverse equivalences in LIT.18.

Let \(D^b(R_X;U)\) denote the quotient by objects whose underlying vector complex has microsupport disjoint from \(U\). The vector support theorem and the \(R\)-linear inverse maps prove

\[ \Phi_R:D^b(R_Y;U')\xrightarrow{\sim}D^b(R_X;U). \tag{LIT.19} \]

The coefficient algebra in this assertion is constant on the relevant base neighborhoods. No inverse to a differential operator on ordinary holomorphic functions is inferred.

3.377. Finite free Hom commutes with this transport

Let \(P\) be a bounded complex of finite free left \(R\)-modules and \(G\) a bounded complex of left \(R_Y\)-module sheaves. Denote its constant sheaf complex by \(P_Y\). There is a natural isomorphism of vector complexes

\[ \Phi\,R\mathcal Hom_{R_Y}(P_Y,G) \simeq R\mathcal Hom_{R_X}(P_X,\Phi_R G). \tag{LIT.20} \]

Finite freeness makes internal Hom the actual finite total Hom complex. Its degree \(k\) differential is

\[ d(\varphi)=d_G\varphi-(-1)^k\varphi d_P. \tag{LIT.21} \]

Use the functorial resolution in §3.376. It commutes with finite direct sums, shifts and total complexes, with the tensor symmetry for each shift. Every coefficient of \(d_P\) acts through the retained strict action on \(G\); its image is the same coefficient acting on \(\Phi_R G\). These identifications give LIT.20 at the total-complex level, including LIT.21. They commute with chain maps, their compositions and chain homotopies. Bounded finite free complexes also preserve quasi-isomorphisms by their finite cell filtration, so the construction is independent of the chosen representative of \(G\).

The Hom output in LIT.20 is a vector complex. For noncommutative \(R\) it does not carry an automatic left \(R\)-action: multiplication by a coefficient need not commute with a matrix entry of \(d_P\). The functor on that output is consequently \(\Phi\), not \(\Phi_R\).

If \(\rho:R\xrightarrow{\sim}R'\) is an actual algebra isomorphism and \(\rho(P)\) denotes the same finite complex with transported coefficients, the same result is

\[ \Phi\,R\mathcal Hom_R(P,G) \simeq R\mathcal Hom_{R'}(\rho(P),\rho_*\Phi_R G). \tag{LIT.22} \]

Here \(\rho_*\) means transport of the action by \(\rho^{-1}\). This statement remains valid after the matched microsupport localizations in LIT.19.

3.378. The coefficient comparison needed for holomorphic solutions

Apply the preceding construction to a fixed finite coefficient algebra acting strictly on a source cutoff object \(G_Y\). Write

\[ \widehat G_X=\rho_*\Phi_R G_Y. \tag{LIT.23} \]

This is an actual transported module object. Its finite Hom complexes are those of LIT.22. If a target cutoff object \(G_X\) is equipped with an actual module-derived isomorphism

\[ \eta:\widehat G_X\xrightarrow{\sim}G_X \quad\text{in }D^b(R'_X;U), \tag{LIT.24} \]

then finite cell filtration shows that applying Hom from \(\rho(P)\) preserves this isomorphism: each cell contributes a shift of the underlying denominator cone, and a finite extension of null cones remains null. Combining with LIT.22 gives the comparison with the target coefficient object. The strict cutoff denominators of §§3.354–3.355 can then identify the appropriate finite differential-operator Hom complexes with actual holomorphic solutions, when their exact coefficient subalgebras and denominator maps match.

LIT.24 is an additional mathematical hypothesis. The ring isomorphism defined by the normalized incidence pole classes in GL-DMOD, WT.1–WT.2, does not alone supply it. Nor does a vector-derived isomorphism with no compatible module action. The pole evaluations and their inverse products involve the specified holomorphic input densities and proper traces; identifying them with a comparison of the actual cutoff objects requires those same maps. Thus LIT.13–LIT.22 prove contact transport for bounded sheaves and their transported strict coefficients; they do not assert an identification of \(\Phi\mathcal O_Y\) with \(\mathcal O_X\), or the full reverse characteristic-support theorem for holomorphic solutions.

Figure 3.52. In the displayed \(N=2\) chart, a point \((t_0,x_0)=(1/4,1/2)\) has conormal slice \(\tau=1\), \(\xi=y\). Its image lies on \(s=1/4+y/2\), with \(\sigma=1\), \(\eta=-1/2\). The real parameter slice \(-1\leq y\leq1\) illustrates the exact complex contact map LIT.8. The lower diagram is LIT.20–LIT.24: the transported coefficient object is specified before any comparison with a target cutoff.

3.379. Exercises on the inverse, its shift and point support

Exercise 3.FC. For \(N=1\), compute the off-diagonal convolution fibre when both incidence kernels are replaced by extension by zero and both are shifted by \([1]\). Explain why it cannot be an inverse. Compute the correct derived-open-image fibre and its oriented boundary map.

Solution 3.FC. Fix distinct projective points. The first affine fibre is \(\mathbf C\), and the second deleted hyperplane is a point. Two extensions by zero give \(\mathbf C_{\mathbf C^*}\) on that affine fibre. The triangle \(\mathbf C_{\mathbf C^*}\to\mathbf C_{\mathbf C}\to\mathbf C_{\{0\}}\xrightarrow{+1}\), together with the compact plane calculation, gives

\[ H^qR\Gamma_c(\mathbf C^*;\mathbf C)= \begin{cases}\mathbf C,&q=1,2,\\0,&\text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \tag{LIT.25} \]

The two nonzero degree identifications are explicit: the degree-zero point group maps isomorphically to compact degree one of the puncture, and compact degree two maps isomorphically to the oriented plane group. After the convolution shift \([2]\), the wrong off-diagonal fibre has nonzero cohomology in degrees \(-1\) and \(0\). It is not a diagonal kernel. With the correct second kernel \(Rj_{0*}\mathbf C_{\mathbf C^*}\), LIT.4 instead gives zero. Its compact connecting map takes the normalized circle class to \(-d\rho\wedge d\theta/(2\pi)\), whose integral is one. On the diagonal the affine fibre gives

\[ R\Gamma_c(\mathbf C;\mathbf C)[2]=\mathbf C[0]. \tag{LIT.26} \]

Thus the choice of open image and the total real shift are both necessary.

Exercise 3.FD. Let \(a=(t_0,x_0)\) be a point in the chart LIT.8. Compute \(\mathcal T\mathbf C_{\{a\}}\) and its nonzero microsupport, including the \(\tau\ne0\) chart. Determine the exact real slice in Figure 3.52.

Solution 3.FD. Let \(H_a\subset Y\) be the incidence hyperplane and \(j_a:Y\setminus H_a\hookrightarrow Y\). Restricting \(B\) to \(Y\times\{a\}\) gives \(Rj_{a*}\mathbf C\). To verify this restriction, trivialize the incidence pair near \(a\) by a projective frame sending a fixed representative to the variable representative. The normal punctured-disc resolution and its circle generator then restrict to the identical resolution on the fibre, as in LI.8.3. Tensoring with the point sheaf and projecting gives

\[ \begin{gathered} \mathcal T\mathbf C_{\{a\}}\simeq Rj_{a*}\mathbf C_{Y\setminus H_a}[N],\\ \operatorname{SS}(\mathcal T\mathbf C_{\{a\}})\cap\dot T^*Y =\dot T_{H_a}^*Y. \end{gathered} \tag{LIT.27} \]

The support equality follows either from LIT.15 and the point conormal, or directly from the punctured-normal-disc model. On the selected chart it is

\[ s=t_0+x_0^{\mathsf T}y,\qquad (\sigma,\eta)=(\tau,-\tau x_0),\quad\tau\ne0. \tag{LIT.28} \]

For \(N=2\), \(t_0=1/4\), \(x_0=1/2\), \(\tau=1\) and real \(y\in[-1,1]\), this is the line segment from \((y,s)=(-1,-1/4)\) to \((1,3/4)\), with constant \(\eta=-1/2\). The original base projection has rank zero; the target hyperplane projection has complex rank \(N-1\). No ordinary base biholomorphism carries these two germs when \(N>1\).

3.380. A finite Hom calculation with a noncommutative action

Exercise 3.FE. Let \(R=\mathbf C\langle a,b\rangle\), let \(G\) be a bounded complex of left \(R_Y\)-module sheaves, and take \(P^{-1}=R^2\), \(P^0=R\), with \(d(e_1)=a e_0\), \(d(e_2)=b e_0\). Compute its total Hom differential and prove the comparison LIT.20 for this complex. Check why the Hom output need not be an \(R\)-module.

Solution 3.FE. In degree \(k\), identify a Hom element with \((u,v_1,v_2)\), where \(u\in G^k\), \(v_i\in G^{k-1}\). Left linearity gives \(\varphi(ae_0)=a\varphi(e_0)\); it never interchanges \(a\) and \(b\). Formula LIT.21 becomes

\[ d(u,v_1,v_2)= \bigl(d_Gu,\ d_Gv_1-(-1)^k au,\ d_Gv_2-(-1)^k bu\bigr). \tag{LIT.29} \]

Applying the differential again gives zero: in each last component the two terms involving the action cancel because \(d_Ga=ad_G\), \(d_Gb=bd_G\), and \((-1)^{k+1}=-(-1)^k\). The functorial kernel resolution carries these very actions and differential maps to \(\Phi_R G\). It commutes with this three-term finite-sum description and its totalization; the tensor shift signs are exactly LIT.29 on both sides. This proves the comparison as an actual map of total complexes in the example, with no independently selected lifts of \(a\) and \(b\).

For the last assertion, specialize to a sheaf with coefficient module \(\mathbf C^2\), where \(a=E_{12}\), \(b=E_{21}\). These matrices define a representation of the free algebra. In degree zero, the Hom differential is \(u\mapsto(-au,-bu)\). Componentwise multiplication by \(a\) commutes with this differential only if \(ab=ba\) on \(G\), whereas

\[ \begin{gathered} ab=E_{11},\qquad ba=E_{22},\\ (d\,a-a\,d)(u)=(0,(ab-ba)u). \end{gathered} \tag{LIT.30} \]

For \(u=(1,0)^{\mathsf T}\) the second component is nonzero. This is why the finite Hom comparison is a comparison of vector complexes, while the coefficient object itself retains the strict algebra action.

3.381. Holomorphic density kernels and their coefficient maps

Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be complex manifolds, with \(Y\) compact of complex dimension \(N\). Write \(p_X,p_Y\) for the projections and put

\[ \mathcal H_{XY}=\mathcal O_{X\times Y}\otimes_{p_Y^{-1}\mathcal O_Y}p_Y^{-1}\Omega_Y^N. \tag{HIC.1} \]

This is a holomorphic coefficient line in degree zero. A density kernel map is an ordinary derived morphism \(u:K\to\mathcal H_{XY}[N]\), where \(K\) is a bounded vector sheaf complex on the product. No constructibility of \(K\) is required in this definition. The kernel operator is \(\Phi_KF=Rp_{X!}(K\otimes p_Y^{-1}F)\). We shall construct a natural vector-derived morphism

\[ \vartheta_u:\Phi_K\mathcal O_Y\longrightarrow\mathcal O_X. \tag{HIC.2} \]

The input density, its shift and its trace are part of this construction. The trace used below is the operator-normalized trace of GL-DMOD, §5.67, PE.2, whose complete current, support and sign proofs are §5.34–§5.35. An ordinary map HIC.2 is not by itself a comparison of modules over the target microdifferential coefficient algebra.

3.382. The proper trace on the full Dolbeault complexes

Resolve \(\mathcal H_{XY}\) by smooth \((0,q)\)-forms with that coefficient line, in all product coordinates, with differential \(\delta=\bar\partial\). Resolve \(\mathcal O_X\) by its full Dolbeault complex as well. The exact local contraction and the comparison with currents are R.2–R.4 of the cited §5.34. The injective-resolution and partition argument R.5–R.6 proves that each smooth or current term is \(p_{X!}\)-acyclic and that these complexes compute the actual derived image. Compactness of \(Y\) makes the projection proper; the same source proof also retains proper supports on local coefficient domains.

In a holomorphic input frame \(\eta_Y\), realize a coefficient form by \(J(\alpha\otimes\eta_Y)=\alpha\wedge\eta_Y\). Integrating the full form in the positive complex orientation and returning to coefficient notation gives \(I_q\), of antiholomorphic degree \(q-N\). Define

\[ \begin{gathered} q_N=(2\pi i)^{-N},\\ T_Y^q=q_N(-1)^{N(q-N)}I_q,\quad q\geq N,\\ T_Y^q=0,\quad q<N. \end{gathered} \tag{HIC.3} \]

The source is shifted by \([N]\), so its differential is \((-1)^N\delta\). Fibre integration commutes with the full-form \(\bar\partial\): base differentiation passes under a compact integral, and vertical derivatives integrate to zero. Therefore

\[ T_Y^{q+1}(-1)^N\delta=\delta T_Y^q, \qquad N(q+1-N)+N\equiv N(q-N)\pmod2. \tag{HIC.4} \]

At \(q=N-1\), the only possible term is a vertical derivative of top fibre degree, whose integral is zero by integration by parts. This verifies the chain map in every degree, including that boundary. Its derived map is

\[ T_Y:Rp_{X!}\mathcal H_{XY}[N]\longrightarrow\mathcal O_X. \tag{HIC.5} \]

3.383. Coordinate invariance and an actual derived construction

A holomorphic input coordinate change contributes \(\det J\) to its top holomorphic block and \(\overline{\det J}\) to its top antiholomorphic block. The real change of variables has determinant \(|\det J|^2>0\); thus HIC.3 is unchanged. For a change depending holomorphically on the output, the additional terms in a full-form lift contain an output holomorphic differential. They have fewer than \(N\) vertical holomorphic factors and therefore integrate to zero. The trace is consequently defined on the relative density line without a chosen full-form lift. These statements also follow directly for currents by transposition on compact tests, as proved in V.4.

Multiplication of holomorphic coefficients is the ordinary sheaf morphism

\[ m:\mathcal H_{XY}\otimes p_Y^{-1}\mathcal O_Y\longrightarrow\mathcal H_{XY}. \tag{HIC.6} \]

Tensor over \(\mathbf C\) is exact on stalks. Apply the derived proper image to \(u\otimes1\), then multiplication and HIC.5:

\[ \begin{gathered} \vartheta_u=T_Y\,Rp_{X!}(m[N])\,Rp_{X!}(u\otimes1),\\ Rp_{X!}(K\otimes p_Y^{-1}\mathcal O_Y) \longrightarrow\mathcal O_X. \end{gathered} \tag{HIC.7} \]

All three arrows are actual derived morphisms. The acyclic-resolution comparison in R.6 uses natural germ embeddings, their cokernels and a finite total complex; it identifies the smooth and current models with the injective definition of \(Rp_!\). Thus changing those models or a representative roof of \(u\) does not change HIC.7. The construction is complex-linear and natural in the source kernel. A cochain homotopy between two common-roof evaluations is sent to the corresponding cochain homotopy after tensor, multiplication and trace. It is not inferred from equality on their cohomology groups.

3.384. Consecutive kernels and the ordered density product

Let \(Z\) be compact of complex dimension \(M\). Take \(K\) on \(X\times Y\), \(H\) on \(Y\times Z\), and density kernel maps \(u:K\to\mathcal H_{XY}[N]\), \(v:H\to\mathcal H_{YZ}[M]\). On the triple product, multiply the joint holomorphic coefficients, retaining the ordered holomorphic blocks \(\Omega_Y^N\) before \(\Omega_Z^M\). Apply \(T_Y\), with the \(Z\)-block retained, to define

\[ u\star v:K\circ H\longrightarrow\mathcal H_{XZ}[M]. \tag{HIC.8} \]

The tensor shifts use the specified suspension identification

\[ A[N]\otimes B[M]\longrightarrow(A\otimes B)[N+M], \qquad a\otimes b\longmapsto(-1)^{M|a|}a\otimes b, \tag{HIC.9} \]

where \(|a|\) is its degree before suspension. This follows by checking the differentials in each factor: increasing \(|a|\) contributes the missing \((-1)^M\), and the second-factor differential already has the required total sign. The trace on HIC.8 is then the first-block trace, with the induced tensor regrouping; it is not an additional unsigned trace on a doubly suspended coefficient.

To form the ordinary cup, represent the two derived evaluations on bounded common roofs into their smooth Dolbeault complexes. Their products in the shared middle variables are products of smooth coefficients. The current model is used for the separate diagonal residue below and compared to the smooth model through R.6. No product of arbitrary currents with a shared singular parameter is used here.

3.385. Composition is preserved before cohomology

The maps just constructed satisfy

\[ \begin{gathered} \vartheta_{u\star v} =\vartheta_u\circ\Phi_K(\vartheta_v),\\ \Phi_{K\circ H}\mathcal O_Z\longrightarrow\mathcal O_X, \end{gathered} \tag{HIC.10} \]

using the proper convolution associator. Here is the sign and map check. Before integration, both sides evaluate the same two kernel maps on the pulled-back holomorphic input and multiply the same joint coefficient on \(X\times Y\times Z\). All projections are proper in their forgotten factors. Fubini for smooth coefficients on compact sets identifies the two repeated integrations. For original antiholomorphic degree \(q\), the raw trace signs obey

\[ \begin{gathered} (-1)^{N(q-N)}(-1)^{M(q-N-M)}\\ =(-1)^{NM}(-1)^{(N+M)(q-N-M)},\\ q_Nq_M=q_{N+M}. \end{gathered} \tag{HIC.11} \]

The extra \((-1)^{NM}\) is exactly the tensor regrouping of the two shifted holomorphic blocks in HIC.9. The ungraded coefficient cup has the full-form conversion sign \((-1)^{Nq'}\) when its first holomorphic block crosses a second antiholomorphic block of degree \(q'\). These are V.8 and V.12–V.14, with their full degree computations. They identify the two trace presentations, rather than counting their suspension sign twice. The normalized scalars multiply as in HIC.11, so no new scalar remains.

This calculation takes place on the smooth common-roof evaluation complexes and their proper-image comparisons. Naturality of the actual trace and the tensor–Hom evaluation identifies the resulting derived maps with HIC.7 on both sides. It proves HIC.10 for the whole bounded complexes and their attaching maps. Repeated application gives associativity for every finite sequence of such ordinary density kernel maps.

3.386. The diagonal Cauchy class acts as the identity

Take \(Y=X\), of complex dimension \(N\), locally near the diagonal; only the support on the diagonal is needed to make the projection proper. Put \(w_i=y_i-x_i\). The one-coordinate current identity, proved by the deleted-disc Green calculation R.3, gives

\[ \int_{\mathbf C}\bar\partial(1/w)\wedge dw\ h(w)=2\pi i\,h(0) \tag{HIC.12} \]

for a holomorphic test near zero, with a cutoff equal to one near the current support. The integral means the supported current applied to that test; no extension of the holomorphic test outside its domain is required. Define

\[ \begin{gathered} r_N=(-1)^{N(N-1)/2},\\ C_\Delta^{\rm raw} =r_N\,\bar\partial(1/w_1)\wedge\cdots\wedge\bar\partial(1/w_N)\\ \otimes dy_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dy_N. \end{gathered} \tag{HIC.13} \]

Its ungraded antiholomorphic-first realization is the ordered product of the \(N\) full one-coordinate blocks: moving each \(dy_i\) past later antiholomorphic factors contributes \(r_N\), which cancels the displayed \(r_N\). The current is closed and supported on the diagonal. It defines a map \(u_\Delta:\mathbf C_\Delta\to\mathcal H_{XX}[N]\). The current is multiplied only by locally constant sections of \(\mathbf C_\Delta\) for this map. Coordinate invariance can be checked in the holomorphic normal coordinates: the inverse normal determinant of the residue and the determinant of the input top form cancel on the diagonal. The base-dependent lower vertical-degree terms integrate to zero as in §3.383.

Iterating HIC.12 in the fixed coordinate order and using the top-degree sign \(T_Y^N=q_NI_N\) proves

\[ \vartheta_{u_\Delta}(h)=q_N(2\pi i)^Nh=h, \qquad \vartheta_{u_\Delta}=\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal O_X}. \tag{HIC.14} \]

Indeed \(\Phi_{\mathbf C_\Delta}\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O_X\) in degree zero, so equality on all holomorphic germs proves equality of these ordinary derived degree-zero maps. This is the Cauchy class with the explicit convention HIC.13 and the trace HIC.3. Comparing another diagonal evaluation with this class requires its actual coefficient and source map.

3.387. The two open–closed source maps have opposite directions

Return to the projective incidence of §3.369, with \(\dim X=\dim Y=N\), closed hypersurface \(S\), complement \(j\), and \(A=j_!\mathbf C\), \(B=Rj_*\mathbf C\). There are actual triangles

\[ \begin{gathered} \mathbf C_S[-1]\xrightarrow{\delta}A\longrightarrow\mathbf C_{X\times Y}\xrightarrow{+1},\\ \mathbf C_{X\times Y}\longrightarrow B\xrightarrow{\beta}\mathbf C_S[-1]\xrightarrow{+1}. \end{gathered} \tag{HIC.15} \]

The first is the rotated open–closed triangle. For the second, the normal complex line has its complex orientation and \(i^!\mathbf C_{X\times Y}=\mathbf C_S[-2]\). The disc relative-cohomology calculation gives this purity isomorphism with positive normal orientation; tensoring the normal disc with tangential balls gives the formula locally and the complex orientation glues it. The closed-support triangle \(i_*i^!\mathbf C\to\mathbf C\to Rj_*\mathbf C\xrightarrow{+1}\), rotated once, gives the second line of HIC.15. Thus the derived-open-image map points from \(B\) to the shifted closed source.

For any bounded vector complex \(F\) on the compact input \(Y\), proper product base change, as proved in LI.8.1, gives

\[ Rp_{X!}(\mathbf C_{X\times Y}\otimes p_Y^{-1}F) \simeq\mathbf C_X\otimes R\Gamma(Y;F). \tag{HIC.16} \]

One can test this canonical base-change map on each fibre: the compact-fibre comparison identifies it with the identity of \(R\Gamma(Y;F)\). The complex on the right is bounded by the finite compact-fibre resolution and is locally constant. Its microsupport lies in the zero section. Therefore, after shifting HIC.15 by \([N]\), tensoring with the input and projecting, both resulting maps are denominators at every nonzero output covector. This uses the projected constant product complex; the tensor cone on the whole product need not itself have zero microsupport.

3.388. Forward and reverse holomorphic incidence maps

Restrict the output to the affine chart of LIT.8 and keep the entire projective input. Let \(J_+=\mathbf C_{S_+}[N-1]\), \(J_-=\mathbf C_{S_-}[N-1]\) on the forward and transposed pair spaces. The shifted maps HIC.15 induce

\[ \begin{gathered} c_+:\Phi_{J_+}\mathcal O_Y\longrightarrow\Phi_K\mathcal O_Y,\\ c_-:\Phi_L\mathcal O_X\longrightarrow\Phi_{J_-}\mathcal O_X. \end{gathered} \tag{HIC.17} \]

Each is invertible at the selected nonzero output covector by HIC.16. The ordinary global sections GP.5 and GP.15 of the cited GL-DMOD proof have evaluations

\[ \begin{gathered} u_{+,N}:J_+\longrightarrow\mathcal H_{XY}[N],\\ m_{+,N}=N![\Omega_{\rm hom}/F_h^{N+1}],\\ u_{-,1}:J_-\longrightarrow\mathcal H_{YX}[N],\\ m_{-,1}=N[\Omega'_{\rm hom}/A_h^{N+1}]. \end{gathered} \tag{HIC.18} \]

These are evaluations of closed incidence sections, using the positive connecting convention \((0,-\text{pole})\) of HI.25 in the same source proof. They are not assumed ordinary maps from an open kernel. The homogeneous top forms have weight \(N+1\); division by the indicated powers is invariant under homogeneous scaling, including a base-dependent scaling because Euler contraction of the numerator vanishes. In the ordered affine frames,

\[ \begin{gathered} f=s-t-x^{\mathsf T}y,\qquad g=t-s+y^{\mathsf T}x,\\ D_t^N(\eta_Y/f)=N!\eta_Y/f^{N+1},\\ D_s(\eta_X/g^N)=N\eta_X/g^{N+1}. \end{gathered} \tag{HIC.19} \]

Both signs are positive since the respective output-time derivative of the denominator is \(-1\). The ordered reverse spatial reflection and density are the ones in GP.4; no reflection is absorbed into a newly chosen scalar.

3.389. Actual inverse derivatives and the two vector roofs

Let \(D_t\) act on \(\mathcal O_X\). For any positive integer \(r\), the finite free resolution of \(\mathcal D_X/\mathcal D_XD_t^r\) has one differential given by right multiplication by \(D_t^r\). It is injective since its principal symbol \(\tau^r\) is a nonzero divisor. Its solution complex is the two-term Hom complex with differential \(-D_t^r\). In the cone convention of §§3.323–3.334,

\[ \begin{gathered} \operatorname{Cone}(D_t^r:\mathcal O_X\to\mathcal O_X) \\{}\simeq\operatorname{Sol}(\mathcal D_X/\mathcal D_XD_t^r)[1]. \end{gathered} \tag{HIC.20} \]

The proved SCP upper characteristic-support inclusion puts this cone in \(\{\tau=0\}\). Thus \(D_t^r\) is an actual denominator at every covector with \(\tau\ne0\). Its inverse in that localization is unique. The identical argument applies to \(D_s\) on the other side. It does not give an ordinary inverse of differentiation on a neighborhood.

With HIC.7 applied to HIC.18, define the actual vector-derived maps

\[ \begin{gathered} \vartheta_+=(D_t^N)^{-1}\,\vartheta_{u_{+,N}}\,c_+^{-1},\\ \vartheta_+:\Phi_K\mathcal O_Y\longrightarrow\mathcal O_X,\\ \vartheta_-=(D_s)^{-1}\,\vartheta_{u_{-,1}}\,c_-,\\ \vartheta_-:\Phi_L\mathcal O_X\longrightarrow\mathcal O_Y. \end{gathered} \tag{HIC.21} \]

All arrows are now specified ordinary derived maps or actual selected-covector denominators. The forward source comparison is inverted; the reverse comparison is used in its original direction. Their normalization is HIC.3, with the factorials, ordered frames and derivative powers of HIC.18–HIC.19.

3.390. The exact scope of these coefficient maps

For ordinary proper density kernel maps, HIC.10 proves compatibility with composition and HIC.14 fixes the diagonal normalization. The exact source-counit comparison for HIC.21 is proved in §§3.397–3.400. Without normalizing the reverse map, the unit equations would read

\[ \begin{gathered} \vartheta_+\circ\Phi_K(\vartheta_-)=\epsilon_X(\mathcal O_X),\\ \vartheta_-\circ\Phi_L(\vartheta_+)=\epsilon_Y(\mathcal O_Y) \end{gathered} \tag{HIC.22} \]

These equations require the single reverse-map normalization of §3.401. Its scalar is determined by the actual composed evaluations with the same density and trace convention.

For the holomorphic solution comparison of §3.378, one must also retain the coefficient action: either an actual module-derived roof \(\rho_*\Phi_R G_Y\simeq G_X\), or the corresponding coherent finite diagram for the chosen resolution, maps and homotopies. HIC.21 constructs the underlying vector maps but does not supply that action comparison. Thus no general contact solution equivalence, reverse characteristic-support inclusion or nilpotent regularity conclusion follows yet from HIC.21 alone.

Figure 3.53. The first panel is the actual trace formula HIC.3–HIC.7. The second records the ordered normal-class factor \(r_N\), which makes the full Cauchy block integrate to \((2\pi i)^N\); HIC.14 then gives the identity. The last panel retains the different source arrows of HIC.17 and the derivative denominators of HIC.21. The inverse-pair and module-action comparisons are the additional hypotheses stated in §3.390.

3.391. Exercises on the normal sign and consecutive traces

Exercise 3.FF. In complex dimension two, compute the full-form sign of the unsigned antiholomorphic-first normal coefficient \(\bar\partial(1/w_1)\wedge\bar\partial(1/w_2)\otimes dy_1\wedge dy_2\). Compare its normalized trace with that of HIC.13.

Solution 3.FF. Moving \(dy_1\) to its position immediately after the first antiholomorphic factor crosses exactly one antiholomorphic factor. Hence the full form without \(r_2\) is minus the ordered product of the two positive one-coordinate blocks. Since \(r_2=-1\),

\[ \begin{gathered} I_2(C_{\rm unsigned})=-(2\pi i)^2,\qquad I_2(C_\Delta^{\rm raw})=(2\pi i)^2,\\ T_Y(C_{\rm unsigned})=-1,\qquad T_Y(C_\Delta^{\rm raw})=1. \end{gathered} \tag{HIC.23} \]

At antiholomorphic degree two the trace sign in HIC.3 is positive, so it cannot cancel an omitted normal-class factor. The suspension sign belongs to the definition of that single normal class, before any between-kernel product.

Exercise 3.FG. Take two consecutive one-dimensional complex fibres. Compute the two raw trace signs in original antiholomorphic degree \(q\geq2\), and compare them with the single two-dimensional trace. Account for the tensor regrouping and normalization.

Solution 3.FG. The first trace uses degree \(q\), the second degree \(q-1\). Therefore

\[ (-1)^{q-1}(-1)^{q-2}=-1,\qquad (-1)^{2(q-2)}=1. \tag{HIC.24} \]

The relative sign is \((-1)^{1\cdot1}\). Regrouping the two shifted holomorphic blocks contributes that same sign, by HIC.9 and its first-block suspension convention. Thus the two presentations agree; adding another suspension sign would change the operation. Finally

\[ q_1^2=(2\pi i)^{-2}=q_2. \tag{HIC.25} \]

The equality includes the scalar as well as the parity. It is the \(N=M=1\) instance of the full composition calculation, not an unsigned Fubini assertion.

3.392. The one-dimensional incidence calibration

Exercise 3.FH. Let \(N=1\) and use affine coordinates \(t,s\). Identify the two closed incidence source operators, compute the maps from the globalizing double poles, and simplify the vector roofs HIC.21. Explain what this calculation does and does not establish in general dimension.

Solution 3.FH. Incidence is the diagonal \(s=t\). Both shifted closed kernels are \(\mathbf C_\Delta[0]\), so each closed-source coefficient operator is \(\mathcal O\) in degree zero. The input densities are \(ds\) forward and \(dt\) reverse. The source maps remain

\[ c_+:\mathcal O_X\longrightarrow\Phi_K\mathcal O_Y,\qquad c_-:\Phi_L\mathcal O_X\longrightarrow\mathcal O_Y. \tag{HIC.26} \]

For a holomorphic germ \(h\), the positive one-variable Cauchy formula and its derivative give

\[ \begin{gathered} \frac1{2\pi i}\oint\frac{h(s)}{s-t}\,ds=h(t),\\ \frac1{2\pi i}\oint\frac{h(s)}{(s-t)^2}\,ds=h'(t). \end{gathered} \tag{HIC.27} \]

For example, expand \(h\) in its convergent Taylor series on a smaller circle. Uniform convergence permits termwise integration, and the only nonzero period has exponent \(-1\). This proves both formulas and their positive normalization. The double pole is a relative class or a finite derivative of the simple-pole distribution; it is not asserted locally integrable. The positive connecting representative \((0,-h/(s-t))\) becomes the current \(\bar\partial(h/(s-t))\) by V.2, so the source evaluation has exactly the sign used in HIC.27. The reverse formulas use \(h(t)/(t-s)\) and \(h(t)/(t-s)^2\) with the positive input \(dt\) orientation. The globalizing factors in HIC.18 are both one when \(N=1\). Consequently

\[ \vartheta_{u_{+,1}}=D_t,\qquad \vartheta_{u_{-,1}}=D_s. \tag{HIC.28} \]

At a nonzero time covector these derivatives are denominators by HIC.20, so HIC.21 simplifies to

\[ \vartheta_+=c_+^{-1},\qquad \vartheta_-=c_-. \tag{HIC.29} \]

Each is therefore a vector-derived isomorphism in this one-dimensional case. Ordinary differentiation still has nonzero kernel: on a disc,

\[ 0\longrightarrow\mathbf C\longrightarrow\mathcal O \xrightarrow{D_t}\mathcal O\longrightarrow0. \tag{HIC.30} \]

Surjectivity follows by integrating a convergent Taylor series on a smaller disc, and the kernel consists of constants. Localization removes the constant cone, rather than choosing an ordinary inverse on \(\mathcal O\). This calculation fixes the displayed vector maps for the diagonal incidence. The source-counit normalization is given in §3.401; the compatible cutoff module action is the additional condition of §3.402.

3.393. A local vector inverse pair for holomorphic coefficients

Use the projective incidence kernels \(K,L\), the contact map \(\chi\), and the two vector maps \(\vartheta_+,\vartheta_-\) of LIT.1–LIT.16 and HIC.21. Fix a covector \(p\) with \(\tau\ne0\), and \(q=\chi(p)\). All statements in this section concern sufficiently small matched cotangent neighborhoods of \(p,q\). Put

\[ \begin{gathered} a=\vartheta_+:\Phi_K\mathcal O_Y\longrightarrow\mathcal O_X,\\ b=\vartheta_-:\Phi_L\mathcal O_X\longrightarrow\mathcal O_Y. \end{gathered} \tag{VIT.1} \]

Theorem. There is a nonzero constant \(\lambda\) such that \(a\) and \(\widetilde b=\lambda^{-1}b\) are inverse coefficient maps relative to the coherent source counits of LIT.6. In particular \(a\) and \(b\) are vector-derived isomorphisms in the matched localizations. The proof retains the actual ordinary density evaluations and their normalized trace.

The object \(\mathcal O_X\) is nonzero in this localization. Choose a complex linear coordinate \(t\) whose real differential represents \(p\). The holomorphic function \(1/t\) on a negative real half-ball cannot extend across zero, by the identity theorem. The support long exact sequence therefore injects its nonzero quotient class into the degree-one support test at \(p\). The class stays nonzero on every smaller ball. This is an actual defining support test, so \(p\in\operatorname{SS}(\mathcal O_X)\).

A cone invisible only at the matched product conormal cannot be discarded without further information. For example, let the output be an affine line, the input be \(\mathbf P^1\), and take the kernel \(C=\mathbf C_{\{t=0\}}\boxtimes\mathbf C_Y\). Then

\[ \Phi_C\mathcal O_Y =\mathbf C_{\{0\}}\otimes R\Gamma(Y;\mathcal O_Y)\ne0. \tag{VIT.2} \]

Its degree-zero coefficient contains the nonzero global section \(1\), so it has the point conormal. On the affine endpoint pair, \(u=t,w=t'-t\), its kernel is constant in \(w\) and misses every nonzero diagonal conormal. The shifted algebraic solution source is \(\delta_u\boxtimes\mathcal O_w\), whose global \(D_w\)-action is locally nilpotent. Polynomial derivative torsion alone therefore does not justify the coefficient-transform descent. The proof below uses an additional actual trivial connection factor.

3.394. Removing a trivial polynomial connection from all morphisms

Let \(B\) be a polynomial Weyl algebra and let \(A_u\) be the Weyl algebra of one variable \(u\). The exact functor

\[ \begin{gathered} \mathsf F(M)=\mathbf C[u]\otimes_{\mathbf C}M,\\ D_u=\partial_u,\qquad A=A_u\otimes_{\mathbf C}B. \end{gathered} \tag{VIT.3} \]

is fully faithful on bounded coherent derived categories, including every shifted morphism. Here is a direct proof. Resolve \(\mathbf C[u]\) by \([A_u\xrightarrow{\cdot D_u}A_u]\) in degrees \(-1,0\), and use bounded finite projective \(B\)-resolutions for the other input. Such resolutions and polynomial Weyl Noetherianity are the filtered operator results used in SCP and GL-DMOD, AS.0–AS.5. Finite projectivity identifies the resulting mapping complex with the total tensor of the reduced mapping complex and

\[ [\mathbf C[u]\xrightarrow{-\partial_u}\mathbf C[u]] \quad\text{in degrees }0,1. \tag{VIT.4} \]

This last complex contracts to its constant coefficient. If \(i\) includes constants and \(\epsilon\) is evaluation at zero, the degree-minus-one homotopy is

\[ h^1(f)=-\int_0^u f(v)\,dv,\qquad dh+hd=1-i\epsilon. \tag{VIT.5} \]

The integral is a finite polynomial primitive. The identities follow by differentiation and the fundamental theorem of calculus; the negative sign matches VIT.4. Tensoring this contraction with the reduced mapping complex, with the total differential signs, proves the claimed mapping quasi-isomorphism. The inclusion is induced by the actual exterior-product functor, so it preserves compositions and identities. Iterate for several \(u\)-coordinates.

Consequently the maps and equalities in a finite source-roof diagram can be represented in the reduced derived category. The displayed mapping contraction retains their finite homotopy comparisons on common projective models. When clearing \(D_w\)-denominators, the finite coherent-lattice construction of OD.2 can be performed in the reduced algebra \(B\), before restoring the connection factor. No lattice chosen in an unrestricted ambient algebra is presumed to retain that factor.

3.395. The entire incidence convolution has that factor

Use affine endpoint coordinates \(u=(t,x)\), \(w=t'-t\), \(z=x'-x\), with \(d=N-1\). On the projective middle space make the homogeneous change

\[ \begin{gathered} v_h=s_h-t\lambda-x^{\mathsf T}y_h,\\ F_h=v_h,\qquad G_h=w\lambda-v_h+z^{\mathsf T}y_h. \end{gathered} \tag{VIT.6} \]

The change is unipotent with determinant one. It is an algebraic automorphism over the endpoint base, and the transformed equations and the middle infinity divisor are independent of every \(u\)-coordinate. In its affine chart the normal sum is \(F=w+z^{\mathsf T}y\). The exact affine Spencer model AS.6–AS.10 is

\[ \begin{gathered} Q=\mathbf C[u]\otimes Q_{\mathrm{red}},\\ Q_{\mathrm{red}} =\bigl(\mathbf C[z,y,\tau]e\otimes\Lambda^\bullet(dy),\\ \ \sum_jdy_j\wedge(\partial_{y_j}+z_j\tau)\bigr)[d],\\ D_{u_i}=\partial_{u_i},\qquad \tau=D_w,\\ D_{z_j}=\partial_{z_j}+y_j\tau,\qquad w=-z^{\mathsf T}y-\partial_\tau. \end{gathered} \tag{VIT.7} \]

The normal residue map and its explicit homotopy in AS.1 do not involve \(u\). Every relative degree, the top section and the endpoint actions retain this factor. The raw Spencer terms need not be finite modules over the endpoint algebra. Their bounded coherent derived object is supplied by the actual proper algebraic realization AS.5; take finite projective models of that object when using VIT.3.

The same conclusion holds for the closed projective convolution \(\overline Q\), its affine-boundary comparison and the diagonal module:

\[ \begin{gathered} \overline Q=\mathcal O_{\mathbf A^N_u}\boxtimes\overline Q_{\mathrm{red}},\\ Q=\mathcal O_{\mathbf A^N_u}\boxtimes Q_{\mathrm{red}},\\ \Delta_{\mathrm{alg}}=\mathcal O_{\mathbf A^N_u}\boxtimes\Delta_{\mathrm{red}}. \end{gathered} \tag{VIT.8} \]

To see this on whole complexes, use the fixed finite standard cover in \((\lambda,v_h,y_h)\). The coordinate localization complexes for the two incidence modules, their tensor and the relative Spencer differentials are independent of \(u\). The cover and all its intersections are fixed in these coordinates; their finite Čech totalization tensors with \(\mathbf C[u]\). This proves VIT.8 for the proper and open-direct models and their comparison maps. On the sheaf side the same coordinate change makes the constant incidence pairs independent of \(u\), and proper product base change retains the factor. The full algebraic RH equivalence and its actual exterior comparison identify these with the displayed operator factors. Those exact maps, including ordinary inverse, exterior products and proper trace, are proved in RH Theorems 1.12, 1.19, 1.22–1.23. VIT.3 then reduces every map of the source roofs as well.

3.396. Derivative torsion with the factor is invisible to coefficient realization

In the reduced polynomial Weyl algebra \(B\), powers of \(\tau=D_w\) form the Ore set of AS.11–AS.12; its localization is right flat. For a finite module \(T\) with zero localization, the finite Taylor calculation FD.11–FD.14 gives

\[ \begin{gathered} \Pi(m)=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(-w)^k}{k!}\tau^km,\qquad T=\mathbf C[w]\otimes\ker\tau,\\ m=\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{w^j}{j!}\Pi(\tau^jm). \end{gathered} \tag{VIT.9} \]

Each sum is finite on each vector. The Weyl commutator makes \(\tau\Pi=0\), and the binomial coefficient sum proves the last identity. Applying \(\Pi\tau^r\) to the highest power of a polynomial relation proves injectivity. Taylor coefficients of finitely many generators give finite generation of \(\ker\tau\) over the spatial algebra. This is a polynomial calculation; no nilpotence after arbitrary analytic multiplication is asserted.

The finite connection resolution and a holomorphic primitive in \(w\) give the actual unshifted solution comparison OD.2. Restoring the \(u\)-factor gives

\[ \operatorname{Sol}(\mathcal O_u\boxtimes T) =\mathbf C_u\boxtimes\mathbf C_w\boxtimes\operatorname{Sol}(\ker\tau). \tag{VIT.10} \]

In the original endpoint times this is constant in both \(t\) and \(t'\). Its spatial variables may still be coupled by \(z=x'-x\). Tensoring with any bounded input, including \(\mathcal O_{X'}\), leaves a constant output \(t\)-factor. Product base change for proper-support image therefore makes its kernel output pulled back from the spatial output. Its microsupport has \(\tau_t=0\).

For a bounded reduced coherent complex whose cohomology is \(\tau\)-torsion, use its finite cohomological truncation triangles. Solution and kernel realization are exact on these triangles, so every output cone is null at \(\tau_t\ne0\). Thus the contravariant functor

\[ \mathcal V(T)= \Phi_{\operatorname{Sol}(\mathcal O_u\boxtimes T)[N]}\mathcal O_{X'} \quad\text{in }D^b(\mathbf C_X;p) \tag{VIT.11} \]

kills the reduced localization kernel. OD.2's finite coherent lattices and its actual cleared homotopies consequently make it descend on the image of bounded coherent \(B\)-complexes in the localized derived category. This controls all forgotten input covectors, including zero. It is the property missing in VIT.2.

3.397. The exact ordinary source roofs

Let \(J_+=\mathbf C_{S_+}[N-1]\), \(J_-=\mathbf C_{S_-}[N-1]\), and use the actual \(\delta,\beta\) of HIC.15. With the coherent counits \(\epsilon_X,\epsilon_Y\), the two source roofs are

\[ \begin{gathered} K\circ L\ \longleftarrow\ J_+\circ L\ \longrightarrow\ J_+\circ J_-,\\ L\circ K\ \longleftarrow\ L\circ J_+\ \longrightarrow\ J_-\circ J_+. \end{gathered} \tag{VIT.12} \]

The left arrows use \(\delta\), and the right arrows use \(\beta\). They are precisely the shifted ordinary roofs SN.5–SN.6: both factors are shifted by \(N\). Each comparison cone has locally constant finite cohomology on the entire affine endpoint pair. The cone from \(\delta\) integrates the derived open direct image on the compact middle space, hence the ordinary cohomology of an affine \(N\)-space. The cone from \(\beta\) integrates the incidence hyperplane \(\mathbf P^{N-1}\). The finite de Rham–Čech calculation in SN.1 proves finiteness, and projective frames trivialize the families, with the positive circle boundary of SN.0. On affine endpoint pairs these local systems are constant. These are actual cone and map computations, not a matched-conormal rank argument.

The closed convolution is \(Rp_!\mathbf C_{\overline W}[2N-2]\). PE.1's proper solution comparison and its shift give

\[ \begin{gathered} J_+\circ J_-\simeq\operatorname{Sol}(\overline Q)[N],\\ \mathbf C_\Delta=\operatorname{Sol}(\Delta_{\mathrm{alg}})[N]. \end{gathered} \tag{VIT.13} \]

The source roof therefore corresponds under the full algebraic RH equivalence to a coherent operator roof between \(\overline Q\) and \(\Delta_{\mathrm{alg}}\). Its constant cones become derivative torsion. The closed-to-affine boundary has both times free, exactly as OD.4 proves. All these objects have VIT.8's factor, and VIT.3 reduces the maps. Consequently their source comparisons become isomorphisms after reduced \(\tau\)-localization and may be used in VIT.11.

Endpoint coefficients may first be restricted to affine neighborhoods and extended by zero. These are input denominators in the matched localization, so LIT's actual graph equivalence permits the replacements. The middle projective space is retained, as in GP.1–GP.4. Affine time derivatives extend as the holomorphic projective translation vector fields, so differentiating the stated global sections preserves their global middle representatives. All subsequent affine-input integrations use proper-support representatives, not restriction of a proper-support section to an arbitrary source open. R.5–R.7 and HIC's trace proof give the same ordinary composition on these supports.

3.398. The two globalizers contribute N + 1 derivatives

Let \(\mathfrak a,\mathfrak b\) denote the forward and opposite raw pole sections, so \(m_{+,N}=D_t^N\mathfrak a\) and \(m_{-,1}=D_s\mathfrak b\). Write \(U=\vartheta_{u_{+,N}}\), \(V=\vartheta_{u_{-,1}}\) for the ordinary closed-source coefficient maps. The exact time intertwining is

\[ U\,\Phi_{J_+}(D_s)=D_tU,\qquad V\,\Phi_{J_-}(D_t)=D_sV. \tag{VIT.14} \]

Here the derivative on the right acts on the target holomorphic sheaf; no ordinary derivative action on an unspecified transformed coefficient object is being assumed. To check the maps, use the unipotent coordinates of VIT.6 and the corresponding reverse coordinates. The global meromorphic density sections and the fixed finite localization/current cover are independent of the common time. Differentiating a pulled-back input coefficient \(h(s,y)\), with \(s=t+x^{\mathsf T}y+v\), gives exactly \(D_sh\). The relative density's full-form lift adds only lower vertical holomorphic-degree terms, whose trace is zero by HIC.3–HIC.5. Differentiation commutes with the proper trace; the vertical total derivative integrates to zero in every cochain degree. The positive relative-pole representatives and the full Dolbeault/Spencer comparison therefore give VIT.14 on the actual evaluation complexes, including their complement terms. The global translation vector extends to the projective middle space, and its action on the homogeneous density is the same determinant-one change.

At the operator section level this is the relative Spencer boundary

\[ [m_{+,N}\otimes D_s\mathfrak b] =-[D_sm_{+,N}\otimes\mathfrak b] =D_t[m_{+,N}\otimes\mathfrak b]. \tag{VIT.15} \]

Indeed the differential of the next-to-top middle Spencer term inserts the total middle derivative.
