\[ \operatorname{DR}^{\mathrm{ind}}_U(Q_+) =\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\mathbf C_{\{0\}}[-n],\qquad \operatorname{DR}^{\mathrm{ind}}_U(Q_-) =\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\mathbf C_{\{0\}}[n]. \tag{AIC.30} \]

These are coproducts in \(\mathscr B_{\Lambda,\infty}(U)\). Their maps, shifts and colimit presentations are part of AIC.15; no inverse tower or infinite ordinary-sheaf test was substituted for them.

3.475. Common charts force noncharacteristic arrows

Let \(Y\) be a smooth locally finite-type complex algebraic stack with affine diagonal, and let \(a:U\to Y\) and \(b:V\to Y\) be smooth finite-type affine charts. Work componentwise when dimensions vary. A chart arrow includes a map \(f:U\to V\) and its specified isomorphism \(bf\simeq a\). Form its actual common chart and section:

\[ W=U\times_Y V,\qquad p:W\to U,\quad q:W\to V, \qquad \sigma:U\to W,\quad p\sigma=1_U,\quad q\sigma=f. \tag{NCS.1} \]

Both \(p,q\) are smooth, by base change of the chart maps. The affine diagonal makes \(W\) affine and of finite type; it is smooth over \(\mathbf C\). The section and these equalities include the given stack isomorphism.

Suppose a family of closed algebraic conic sets \(\Lambda_U\subset T^*U\) has, on every such common chart, the compatibility

\[ \Lambda_W=p^\sharp\Lambda_U=q^\sharp\Lambda_V,\qquad h^\sharp C=\{(z,dh_z^t\eta):(h(z),\eta)\in C\}. \tag{NCS.2} \]

Smoothness makes \(dp^t,dq^t\) injective. For \(u\in U\), put \(w=\sigma(u)\). If \(\eta\in(\Lambda_V)_{f(u)}\), compatibility supplies \(\xi\in(\Lambda_U)_u\) with

\[ dq_w^t\eta=dp_w^t\xi,\qquad \xi=d\sigma_u^tdq_w^t\eta=df_u^t\eta . \tag{NCS.3} \]

Conversely, starting with any \(\xi\in(\Lambda_U)_u\), the other equality in NCS.2 supplies such an \(\eta\). If \(df_u^t\eta=0\), then \(\xi=0\) and injectivity of \(dq_w^t\) gives \(\eta=0\). We have proved

\[ (U\times_V\Lambda_V)\cap\ker(df^t) \subseteq U\times_V 0_V,\qquad f^\sharp\Lambda_V=\Lambda_U. \tag{NCS.4} \]

The first assertion is precisely noncharacteristicity on this cone. The arrow \(f\) need not be smooth. This proof uses the actual common-chart section, not a claim that every arrow between smooth charts is smooth.

3.476. The nilpotent Higgs cones have this compatibility

Take \(Y=\operatorname{Bun}_G(X)\), with \(X\) a smooth projective connected complex curve and \(G\) any connected reductive complex group. Every genus and bundle component is allowed. The family description of cotangent vectors is proved in The moduli stack of bundles, §5, using the deformation complex of its Proposition 2.1 and relative Serre duality. It gives

\[ \Lambda_U= (U\times_Y\operatorname{Nilp}_G)_{\mathrm{red}} \hookrightarrow T^*U,\qquad \langle\lambda_U,v\rangle =\langle\phi,da(v)\rangle . \tag{NCS.5} \]

Here \(\phi\) is a nilpotent coadjoint-valued Higgs field on the bundle classified by \(u\). The pairing is the Serre-duality pairing with its first-order deformation. Smoothness of the chart makes the tangent map onto the deformation space: the dual-number deformation lifts through the smooth chart with its chosen special point. Thus the transpose embeds the cotangent cone in \(T^*U\). Nilpotence is imposed by the invariant-polynomial zero fiber, independently of a chosen adjoint/coadjoint pairing.

On \(W\), the two pulled-back bundles are identified by its specified isomorphism. This identifies their Higgs fields and the invariant-polynomial equations. Functoriality of the deformation pairing gives

\[ \langle dp^t\lambda_U,v\rangle =\langle\phi,d(ap)(v)\rangle =\langle\phi,d(bq)(v)\rangle =\langle dq^t\lambda_V,v\rangle . \tag{NCS.6} \]

Every nilpotent field on this common bundle occurs on both sides. Consequently NCS.2 holds. These identifications are induced by bundle isomorphisms and by pullback of the same family; they compose with every further chart map. Passing to reductions gives exactly the support cones of NC.1. Equality at complex points suffices for these reduced algebraic closed sets by the Nullstellensatz. The Higgs zero-fiber equations themselves are retained in the family description.

The chartwise upper bound NC.1 is \(\dim\Lambda_U\le\dim U\). It is unnecessary for the noncharacteristic argument, but implies holonomicity of every coherent module supported there. If \(n_U=\dim U\), \(n_V=\dim V\), and \(r_a,r_b\) are the chart relative dimensions, then

\[ r_f:=n_U-n_V=r_a-r_b,\qquad f^!=Lf^*[r_f]. \tag{NCS.7} \]

This is the left-module normalization of Inverse images, equation 0.1. The relative dimension difference may be negative; it does not assert smoothness of \(f\).

3.477. Bounded inverse transfer on the prescribed support

Let \(f:U\to V\) be any algebraic map of smooth varieties satisfying the first condition of NCS.4 for \(\Lambda_V\), and assume \(f^\sharp\Lambda_V\subseteq\Lambda_U\). Both conditions hold for the actual chart arrows just proved. Let \(M\) be coherent with \(\operatorname{Char}(M)\subseteq\Lambda_V\). The complete algebraic noncharacteristic theorem is Inverse images, Proposition 6.3 and Theorem 6.5. Its conclusion is

\[ Lf^*M=f^*M\text{ in degree }0,\qquad \operatorname{Char}(f^*M) =f^\sharp\operatorname{Char}(M)\subseteq\Lambda_U . \tag{NCS.8} \]

We recall the mechanisms used in that theorem. For a normal coordinate \(t\), a monic normal-symbol annihilator lifts to an actual annihilating operator. Repeated commutation with \(t\) makes \(t:M\to M\) injective. The monic relation makes the good symbol module finite over the tangent-symbol ring, giving coherence after restriction. Its image filtration need not be strict for multiplication by \(t\). The Rees argument instead removes the finite homogenizing torsion and compares its kernel and cokernel lengths at every minimal component. Involutivity excludes vertical components, so the difference of these lengths is positive. This gives equality of supports, including embedded and nonreduced symbol modules at the level of their support. Successive normal coordinates and the actual graph factorization prove NCS.8 for every \(f\).

For \(M\) regular holonomic, its pullback is regular holonomic by the bounded four-map theorem used in RH.2–RH.4. Therefore, with the full mapping complexes,

\[ f^!:\mathscr R_{\Lambda_V}(V) \longrightarrow\mathscr R_{\Lambda_U}(U),\qquad H^j(f^!M)= \begin{cases}f^*M,&j=-r_f,\\0,&j\ne-r_f.\end{cases} \tag{NCS.9} \]

The same statement for a bounded complex follows by finite truncations. The characteristic support condition is not replaced by regularity: NCS.8 itself applies to every coherent differential module with the stated noncharacteristic support.

3.478. Arbitrary supported heart modules

For the full unbounded quasicoherent differential-module category on an affine chart \(V\), use the independent condition

\[ \begin{gathered} Q\in\mathcal D_{\Lambda_V}(V)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\\ \operatorname{Char}(M)\subseteq\Lambda_V \text{ for every }i\\ \text{and every finite }\mathcal D_V\text{-submodule }M\subset H^iQ . \end{gathered} \tag{NCS.10} \]

Finite generation here is in the actual affine operator-module category of IAC.1–IAC.4. Its operator ring is Noetherian. Thus every heart module \(L\) satisfying this support condition is the filtered union of its coherent submodules:

\[ L=\operatorname*{colim}_\alpha M_\alpha,\qquad \operatorname{Char}(M_\alpha)\subseteq\Lambda_V. \tag{NCS.11} \]

The finite sums supply the directed system. Exact-sequence characteristic support makes the same class closed under subobjects, quotients and extensions. Each quotient \(M_\beta/M_\alpha\) is again coherent with this support. NCS.8 and its higher-Tor vanishing therefore make \(f^*M_\alpha\to f^*M_\beta\) injective.

Derived inverse transfer commutes with filtered colimits; it is inverse image followed by the transfer tensor. Alternatively the finite graph model below proves this directly. Applying NCS.8 at every stage yields

\[ Lf^*L=f^*L=\operatorname*{colim}_\alpha f^*M_\alpha \text{ in degree }0,\qquad \operatorname{Char}(N)\subseteq\Lambda_U \quad\text{for every finite }N\subset f^*L . \tag{NCS.12} \]

Indeed the colimit is a union of the coherent supported pullbacks. Finite generators of \(N\) lie in one of them; Noetherianity and exact-sequence characteristic support give the last inclusion. This argument requires no regularity or finite rank of \(L\).

3.479. A finite graph calculation for every unbounded complex

The underlying inverse transfer is \( \mathcal O_U\otimes^L_{f^{-1}\mathcal O_V}f^{-1}Q\), by the PBW comparison in Inverse images, §2. Its all-degree calculation is finite in the graph direction. Locally choose étale coordinates \(z_i\) on \(U\), \(y_j\) on \(V\). In the graph factorization \(U\to U\times V\to V\), the graph ideal near its chosen point has the regular generators

\[ g_j=y_j-f^*y_j(z),\qquad 1\le j\le n_V. \tag{NCS.13} \]

Their independent \(y\)-derivatives give regular graph coordinates; in an étale neighborhood the coordinate-equality locus containing the graph is this graph itself. The projection to \(V\) is smooth and its coefficient extension is flat. Its pullback \(p_V^*Q\) is an actual unbounded complex. The finite Koszul complex represents

\[ \begin{gathered} Lf^*Q\simeq K(g_1,\ldots,g_{n_V};p_V^*Q)\big|_{\mathrm{graph}}, \\ K^{-k,\bullet}=\bigwedge^k\mathbf C^{n_V}\otimes p_V^*Q^\bullet. \end{gathered} \tag{NCS.14} \]

The notation means the underlying graph-supported derived coefficient complex, with its actual transfer action; individual Koszul terms need not be annihilated by the graph ideal. The index \(-k\) is its graph degree and the bullet retains every internal degree of \(Q\). Exactness of the graph Koszul resolution follows by induction on its regular sequence, as in Proposition 4.1 of the inverse-image lesson. The terms of that coefficient resolution are flat over the target coefficient ring. It is K-flat: tensoring an acyclic complex with each flat term remains acyclic, and its finite graph filtration makes the total complex acyclic as well. Thus it computes the derived tensor against arbitrary unbounded \(Q\).

The calculation retains the differential-operator action. On the smooth product pullback use the tangent lifts

\[ \widetilde\partial_{z_i} =\partial_{z_i} +\sum_j\partial_{z_i}(f^*y_j)\partial_{y_j}, \qquad \widetilde\partial_{z_i}(g_j)=0 . \tag{NCS.15} \]

Here \(\partial_{y_j}\) acts on the whole product pullback by its coefficient derivative and its action on \(Q\). Thus the tensor balancing is exactly the chain rule. The lifts commute because mixed second derivatives of \(f^*y_j\) agree. They commute with Koszul multiplication by every \(g_j\), act trivially on its exterior basis, and commute with the internal differential of \(Q\). On a free differential resolution these are precisely the tangent operators of the transfer construction. The K-flat coefficient model sends the acyclic cone of that resolution to zero, so the comparison gives the same differential-linear derived model for every unbounded input. This gives the actual \(\mathcal D_U\)-linear action on the filtered calculation and on its edge maps.

Filter by the finite Koszul degree. Flatness of the product coefficient extension first computes the internal cohomology of \(Q\). The next differential is the Koszul differential on that cohomology, giving

\[ E_2^{-k,j} =\operatorname{Tor}^{\,f^{-1}\mathcal O_V}_k (\mathcal O_U,f^{-1}H^jQ) \ \Longrightarrow\ H^{j-k}(Lf^*Q), \qquad 0\le k\le n_V . \tag{NCS.16} \]

This spectral sequence converges for every unbounded \(Q\): each total degree has only \(n_V+1\) graph positions, and the filtration has that fixed finite length. Its usual successive kernel/image construction therefore reaches the total cohomology after finitely many pages in each degree. No infinite diagonal totalization or Postnikov-limit exchange occurs.

If \(Q\) satisfies NCS.10, NCS.12 makes every \(k>0\) term zero. The sole column gives the canonical differential-linear identities

\[ H^j(Lf^*Q)\simeq f^*H^jQ,\qquad H^j(f^!Q)\simeq f^*H^{j+r_f}Q \quad(j\in\mathbf Z). \tag{NCS.17} \]

By NCS.12 each module on the right has the required support on \(U\). Thus \(f^!\) preserves the independently defined full unbounded support condition, with no ind-regularity assumption on \(Q\).

3.480. The full independent support diagram

Apply NCS.17 to the compatible nilpotent cones of §3.476. Every arrow, stack isomorphism and higher composition in the actual smooth-chart diagram restricts to

\[ f^!:\mathcal D_{\Lambda_V}(V) \longrightarrow\mathcal D_{\Lambda_U}(U). \tag{NCS.18} \]

The transfer composition maps are the actual tensor multiplication and chain-rule maps. Derived associativity gives their coherent compositions, as proved in the inverse-image lesson's Theorem 2.1 and the full diagram construction of RH.4. Since the supported subcategories are full and every transition preserves them, all these same transformations and homotopies restrict. No new comparison maps are chosen from cohomology alone.

The full stack differential-module category is the chart limit constructed in §§1.10–1.12. A limit of full inclusions is fully faithful: mapping complexes are the same homotopy-coherent chart ends, and a Cartesian family belongs to the sublimit exactly when all its components belong to the indicated subcategories. Therefore

\[ \lim_{\mathcal I_Y}\mathcal D_{\Lambda_U}(U) =\{M\in\operatorname{Dmod}(Y): a^!M\in\mathcal D_{\Lambda_U}(U) \text{ for every smooth affine chart }a\}. \tag{NCS.19} \]

For \(\Lambda_U=(U\times_Y\operatorname{Nilp}_G)_{\mathrm{red}}\), this is the untwisted form of the cohomological nilpotent support condition of (3.1), with its full unbounded scope. Its actual half twist is transported in §3.483. Neither bounded generation nor regularity was inserted into its definition or its chart transitions.

3.481. The normalized chart complexes

The chart normalization used in NC.3 is compatible with these arrows. If \(Q_U=a^!M\), \(Q_V=b^!M\), put \(L_U=Q_U[-r_a]\), \(L_V=Q_V[-r_b]\). Actual transfer composition and NCS.7 give

\[ f^!L_V\simeq L_U[r_f],\qquad Lf^*L_V\simeq L_U,\qquad H^jL_U\simeq f^*H^jL_V . \tag{NCS.20} \]

The last assertion uses NCS.17 for the supported input. These comparisons include the chosen bundle isomorphism in the chart arrow. The shift differences add along every composable string, while the chain-rule maps compose by transfer multiplication. Thus the normalized cohomology identities agree with the full Cartesian data. A varying stabilizer dimension does not replace \(r_a\): it is the relative dimension of the smooth chart, and \(\dim Y=(g-1)\dim G\) is the stack dimension.

3.482. Supported regular ind-transitions

The bounded regular statement NCS.9 restricts the actual Riemann–Hilbert comparison on every arrow:

\[ \operatorname{DR}_U f^! \xrightarrow{\ \beta_f\ } f^{\mathrm{an},!}\operatorname{DR}_V \quad\text{on }\mathscr R_{\Lambda_V}(V). \tag{NCS.21} \]

Here AIC.13 identifies the two bounded supported categories. Its full faithfulness and the actual \(\beta_f\) imply that the Betti transition preserves \(\mathscr B_{\Lambda_V}(V)\) as well. The coefficient, density, unit and counit normalizations of RH.4 are retained. In particular a non-smooth chart arrow is not assigned the raw flat-frame identity.

Ind-extension then gives the whole supported regular diagram comparison

\[ \operatorname{DR}^{\mathrm{ind}}_U: \mathscr R_{\Lambda_U,\infty}(U) \xrightarrow{\sim}\mathscr B_{\Lambda_U,\infty}(U), \qquad \beta_f^{\mathrm{ind}}\text{ on every chart arrow}. \tag{NCS.22} \]

The source transitions are restrictions of the actual continuous affine inverse transfer, as in RH.4. Their values on supported compact inputs are the bounded functors just proved to preserve support. Hence their ind-extensions land in the supported ind-subcategories. Applying the full ind mapping formula AIC.16 extends every specified transformation and homotopy. This argument covers every unbounded object of these ind-categories.

3.483. Supported descent and its exact relation to regularity

Taking the actual diagram limit in NCS.22 gives

\[ \operatorname{DR}^{\mathrm{ind}}_Y: \lim_{\mathcal I_Y}\mathscr R_{\Lambda_U,\infty}(U) \xrightarrow{\sim} \lim_{\mathcal I_Y}\mathscr B_{\Lambda_U,\infty}(U). \tag{NCS.23} \]

Indeed the inverse chart equivalences and their unit and counit transport every simplex of the descent data, exactly as in RH.9. On mapping ends, the componentwise equivalences give an equivalence of their derived totalizations. This proves full faithfulness and essential surjectivity of NCS.23 without interchanging a chart limit with ind-completion.

By AIC.24 the source embeds fully faithfully into the independent full nilpotent category NCS.19. Its components are supported ind-regular objects; every such component satisfies the cohomological support condition. Equality with NCS.19 would additionally require regularity of all its objects and the full unbounded supported factorization criterion AIC.17 on every chart. Those assertions are not consequences of preservation of the chart diagrams.

The half twist changes none of these support statements. The line-module Morita maps of §§3.57–3.58 are exact, have exact inverses, and conjugate the actual transfer functors. A local line frame changes a vector-field operator only by a term of order zero, so its good symbol support is unchanged. The specified line and inverse line cancel in the full transfer comparisons. Finally, along a string \(U\xrightarrow fV\xrightarrow gT\),

\[ r_f+r_g=n_U-n_T,\qquad (gf)^!\simeq f^!g^!,\qquad \beta_{gf}\text{ is the specified composite of }\beta_f,\beta_g . \tag{NCS.24} \]

Thus NCS.19 and NCS.23 apply to the actual twisted or untwisted chart diagrams with their original normalizations. Nilpotent regularity, equality with the full Hecke-lisse projector image and original-field extensions retain their separate geometric hypotheses.

Figure 3.61. The upper diagram is NCS.1–NCS.4: \(p\sigma=1\), \(q\sigma=f\), and \(dq^t\eta=dp^t\xi\) force \(\xi=df^t\eta\) and exclude a nonzero kernel covector. The lower finite strip is NCS.14–NCS.17. Its graph degrees are \(-n_V,\ldots,0\); noncharacteristicity leaves only its zero Tor column, even when cohomology is unbounded in both directions.

3.484. A chart section and its degree shift

Exercise 3.GD. Regard \(V=\mathbb A^1_y\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf C\) and \(U=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf C\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf C\) as smooth charts. Let \(f:U\to V\) be the zero section. For the zero-section cotangent cones, compute \(Lf^*\mathcal O_V\) and \(f^!\mathcal O_V\). Compare with the characteristic point module \(\delta=\mathcal D_V/\mathcal D_Vy\).

Solution 3.GD. The arrow \(f\) is not smooth, but its cone on \(V\) is the zero section, so it is noncharacteristic for \(\mathcal O_V\). The graph Koszul complex is

\[ \bigl[\,\mathcal O_V\xrightarrow{\,y\,}\mathcal O_V\,\bigr] \text{ in degrees }-1,0,\qquad Lf^*\mathcal O_V=\mathbf C,\qquad f^!\mathcal O_V=\mathbf C[-1]. \tag{NCS.25} \]

Thus the exclamation pullback has its nonzero cohomology in degree one, because \(r_f=-1\). Under Riemann–Hilbert, \(\operatorname{DR}_V\mathcal O_V=\mathbf C_V[1]\), whose extraordinary restriction to the point is \(\mathbf C[-1]\), in agreement with NCS.21 and the actual positive normal orientation.

For \(\delta\), the basis is \(e,\partial_y e,\partial_y^2e,\ldots\) with \(ye=0\). Commuting \(y\) past the derivatives gives \(y\partial_y^ne=-n\partial_y^{n-1}e\). Multiplication by \(y\) is surjective and has kernel \(\mathbf C e\). Therefore

\[ Lf^*\delta=\mathbf C[1],\qquad f^!\delta=\mathbf C, \qquad \operatorname{Char}(\delta)=T^*_{\{0\}}V. \tag{NCS.26} \]

Its nonzero conormal covectors are killed by \(df^t\). Thus it violates the noncharacteristic support hypothesis, exactly as its extra degree in the unshifted pullback shows.

3.485. A ramified arrow between smooth charts

Exercise 3.GE. Let \(Y=\mathbb A^1_z\), \(U=\mathbb A^2_{z,x}\), \(V=\mathbb A^2_{z,y}\), with chart maps forgetting \(x\) and \(y\). Take \(f(z,x)=(z,x^2)\) and let the cone on \(Y\) be \(T^*_{\{0\}}Y\). Compute its chart cones, noncharacteristicity and the pullback of \(M=\delta_z\boxtimes\mathcal O_y\).

Solution 3.GE. The chart cones and covector map are

\[ \Lambda_V=\{z=0,\eta_y=0\},\quad \Lambda_U=\{z=0,\xi_x=0\},\qquad df^t(\zeta,\eta_y)=(\zeta,2x\eta_y). \tag{NCS.27} \]

On \(\Lambda_V\) the second input covector is zero. A kernel covector then has \(\zeta=0\) as well, including at \(x=0\). Thus the map is noncharacteristic on this cone, although the coordinate map is ramified and not smooth there. Its relative dimension difference is zero.

The normal \(z\)-module is unchanged, and the generator of \(\mathcal O_y\) is killed by \(\partial_y\). The chain rule on its pullback is \(\partial_x(b\otimes m)=\partial_x b\otimes m+2xb\otimes\partial_y m\). It follows that

\[ f^!M=f^*M=\delta_z\boxtimes\mathcal O_x,\qquad \operatorname{Char}(f^*M)=\Lambda_U. \tag{NCS.28} \]

All higher Tor groups vanish by NCS.8. The coefficient \(2x\) is retained in the actual action; its vanishing at the ramification point does not erase the normal \(z\)-covector or the pulled-back module.

3.486. A doubly unbounded supported complex

Exercise 3.GF. Keep \(Y=\mathbb A^1_z\) and \(V=\mathbb A^2_{z,y}\), but let \(U=\mathbb A^1_z\) and \(f(z)=(z,0)\). Put \(M=\delta_z\boxtimes\mathcal O_y\) and

\[ Q=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}M[2n],\qquad f^!Q=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}\delta_z[2n-1]. \tag{NCS.29} \]

Prove the second formula and compute its cohomology and de Rham ind-image.

Solution 3.GF. The same horizontal cones make this section noncharacteristic. Now \(r_f=-1\). The finite graph model gives \(Lf^*M=\delta_z\) in degree zero, so \(f^!M=\delta_z[-1]\). Continuity of actual inverse transfer proves the second formula in NCS.29. Every finite partial sum is a bounded regular supported compact; these coproducts therefore also have explicit presentations in the supported ind-categories.

The only source cohomology degrees are even, with module \(M\). NCS.17 reads \(H^j(f^!Q)=f^*H^{j-1}Q\), hence the only output degrees are odd. Since \(\operatorname{DR}_U\delta_z=\mathbf C_{\{0\}}\), we obtain

\[ H^j(f^!Q)= \begin{cases}\delta_z,&j\text{ odd},\\0,&j\text{ even},\end{cases} \qquad \operatorname{DR}^{\mathrm{ind}}_U(f^!Q) =\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}\mathbf C_{\{0\}}[2n-1]. \tag{NCS.30} \]

The calculation uses the finite graph strip for all degrees and the actual coproduct functor. It does not replace the negative tail by a colimit of lower truncation quotients. The same finite-strip argument NCS.16 applies to every independently supported unbounded complex, even without such an explicit compact presentation.

3.487. A fixed characteristic cone and an unbounded cycle

Let \(U\) be smooth affine over \(\mathbf C\), of dimension \(d\), and let \(\Lambda\subset T^*U\) be reduced, closed and algebraically conic, with \(\dim\Lambda\le d\). Use the actual affine embedding IAC.4–IAC.6. Suppose

\[ \begin{gathered} E\in\mathscr R_\infty(U),\\ \operatorname{Char}(A)\subset\Lambda \quad\text{for every }m\in\mathbf Z\\ \text{and every finite }\mathcal D_U\text{-submodule }A\subset H^mE. \end{gathered} \tag{FCR.1} \]

There is no cohomological bound on \(E\). Fix \(p=(x,\xi)\), with \(\xi\ne0\), and a cotangent analytic neighbourhood \(\mathcal V\) on which \(\Lambda^{\mathrm{an}}\) is a smooth complex-conic Lagrangian \(C\). Assume that \(C\to U^{\mathrm{an}}\) has constant rank there. Let \(h\) be regular on \(U\), with

\[ h(x)=0,\qquad dh_x=\xi,\qquad T_pC\cap T_p\operatorname{graph}(dh)=0. \tag{FCR.2} \]

Suppose that \(p\in\operatorname{Char}(A_0)^{\mathrm{an}}\) for some finite \(A_0\subset H^{m_0}E\). Let \(\Phi_h^{\mathrm{reg}}\) be the actual continuous ind-extension of the bounded, perverse-normalized algebraic cycle functor IAC.26, followed by closed transfer of its zero-fibre output to \(U\). Put \(i:\{x\}\hookrightarrow U\), \(B=\Phi_h^{\mathrm{reg}}E\) and \(V=i^!B\). Then

\[ i_*V\xrightarrow{u_E}B\xrightarrow{r_E}i_*V,\qquad r_Eu_E=1_{i_*V},\qquad H^{m_0}V\ne0. \tag{FCR.3} \]

The maps are natural on the full subcategory satisfying the common-cone conditions. The witness \(A_0\) is needed only for nonvanishing. The proof below takes place in the actual ind-regular category and its full affine embedding.

3.488. One microsupport bound for all coherent heart pieces

The affine operator ring is Noetherian. By IAC.6, every \(H^mE\) is the filtered union of its coherent regular holonomic subobjects. A finite set of generators lies in one coherent regular image in an ind-presentation. Its submodule is coherent by Noetherianity and regular by the regular-holonomic Serre property. Thus

\[ H^mE=\operatorname*{colim}_{A\subset H^mE,\ A\ \mathrm{finite}}A, \qquad A\text{ regular holonomic}. \tag{FCR.4} \]

The algebraic support identity AIC.8 gives

\[ \operatorname{SS}\bigl(\operatorname{DR}_d(A^{\mathrm{an}})\bigr) =\operatorname{Char}(A)^{\mathrm{an}} \subset\Lambda^{\mathrm{an}}. \tag{FCR.5} \]

These are bounded constructible Riemann–Hilbert images with the density shift \(d\). All of them, across every cohomological degree and every finite subobject, satisfy the same bound \(C\) on the same \(\mathcal V\). The equality uses the actual analytification and support comparison, including its differential and density normalizations.

3.489. The transverse test and its nonzero coefficient

The constant-rank calculation MCM.1–MCM.2 identifies the germ of \(C\) with the conormal of a smooth local submanifold \(S\). Indeed the nonzero fibre Euler vector is tangent to \(C\). Its symplectic pairing with a tangent vector shows that the covector annihilates every projected tangent vector. Both \(C\) and the conormal have dimension \(d\), so

\[ C=T_S^*U^{\mathrm{an}}\quad\text{as germs at }p. \tag{FCR.6} \]

Transversality in FCR.2 and the inverse-function theorem give an analytic base neighbourhood \(W\) of \(x\) on which the graph of \(dh\) lies in \(\mathcal V\) and meets \(C\) only at \(p\). Choose \(W\) from \(C,h,\mathcal V\), independently of \(A\). The bounded cycle support bound MCM.10 therefore gives

\[ \operatorname{supp} \Phi_h\bigl(\operatorname{DR}_d(A^{\mathrm{an}})\bigr)\cap W \subset\{x\}\quad\text{for every }A. \tag{FCR.7} \]

For \(A_0\), MCM.3–MCM.9 give a nonzero coefficient. The covector-localized coefficient model has a nonzero bounded complex \(M\) on \(S\). Its transverse quadratic test is \(M\otimes o_h[-\dim S]\), where \(o_h\) is a nonzero line. The test inverts every microsupport-null denominator; the ordinary cycle functor is used only on the actual weakly complex constructible endpoints. The normal/conormal comparison identifies the two endpoint coefficients. Bounded algebraic cycle t-exactness then gives

\[ \begin{gathered} \Phi_h\bigl(\operatorname{DR}_d(A_0^{\mathrm{an}})\bigr)_x \simeq M\otimes o_h[-\dim S]\ne0,\\ H^0i^!\Phi_{h,0}^{\mathrm{reg}}A_0\ne0. \end{gathered} \tag{FCR.8} \]

The second coefficient is in degree zero because \(A_0\), its Riemann–Hilbert image and its normalized algebraic cycle are heart objects, and the cycle is locally point-supported.

3.490. Analytic isolation and the algebraic closed carrier

Each bounded cycle \(B_A=\Phi_{h,0}^{\mathrm{reg}}A\), with closed transfer understood, is coherent regular holonomic. Its analytic closed carrier is the analytification of its reduced algebraic closed carrier \(Z_A\), by MCM.13. To see this, use a finite regular composition series. Each minimal-extension factor has the closure of its positive-rank open stratum as carrier. Exact open restriction makes carriers form unions in short exact sequences.

By FCR.7, either \(Z_A\) avoids \(x\), or its analytic germ is the point \(x\). In the latter case write \(R=\mathcal O_{U,x}\), \(H=\mathcal O_{U^{\mathrm{an}},x}\), and let \(I\subset R\) define the reduced carrier. Analytic radical-ideal comparison and faithful flatness, as in MCM.14, give

\[ IH=\mathfrak m_xH,\qquad IH\cap R=I,\qquad I=\mathfrak m_x. \tag{FCR.9} \]

In an affine neighbourhood in the reduced carrier, a finite generating set of the maximal ideal vanishes after localization at \(x\). One denominator outside that ideal kills every generator. Its principal open is exactly \(\{x\}\). Since \(x\) is also closed,

\[ Z_A=\{x\}\amalg Z'_A,\qquad Z'_A\text{ closed},\quad x\notin Z'_A. \tag{FCR.10} \]

Closed-support restriction and its adjunctions give

\[ B_A=i_*V_A\oplus B'_A,\qquad V_A\in\operatorname{Vect}^{\heartsuit},\qquad x\notin\operatorname{supp}B'_A. \tag{FCR.11} \]

If the carrier avoids \(x\), take \(V_A=0\). Mapping complexes between a point object and an away object vanish in both directions. The point projector is therefore natural in all maps between these pieces. The away carriers may depend on \(A\); no common algebraic neighbourhood avoiding every one of them is required.

3.491. The cycle heart and both point functors

The actual cycle functor is t-exact and continuous by IAC.26–IAC.27. It takes inclusions of finite heart subobjects to inclusions. Hence

\[ H^mB=\Phi_h^{\mathrm{reg}}H^mE =\operatorname*{colim}_{A\subset H^mE}B_A. \tag{FCR.12} \]

This is a filtered union of the admissible pieces FCR.11. Both actual point functors are continuous on the regular ind-category by IAC.16. On a bounded point summand their canonical comparison is the identity; on a bounded away summand both vanish. Passing to the filtered union gives

\[ i^!H^mB\xrightarrow{\sim}i^*H^mB =\operatorname*{colim}_{A\subset H^mE}V_A \quad\text{in degree zero}. \tag{FCR.13} \]

This proves purity for the cycle hearts, with their actual transition maps. It makes no assertion that an arbitrary heart object has an isolated point part.

3.492. A finite window for every output degree

The point functors have the uniform safe amplitudes IAC.18:

\[ \begin{aligned} i^!(D^{[a,b]})&\subset D^{[a,b+2d]},\\ i^*(D^{[a,b]})&\subset D^{[a-3d,b+d]}. \end{aligned} \tag{FCR.14} \]

Fix an output degree \(m\). Choose integers

\[ L\le m-2d-2,\qquad H\ge m+3d+2,\qquad B_{[L,H]}=\tau^{\le H}\tau^{\ge L}B. \tag{FCR.15} \]

For either functor, the low tail has no output cohomology in degrees \(m-1,m,m+1\), by its upper amplitude bound. The high tail has none in those degrees, by its lower bound. Thus the degree-\(m\) comparison is computed from the finite Postnikov window \(B_{[L,H]}\). On that window FCR.13 makes each heart contribution pure in its own degree. Its finite filtration collapses and proves, naturally,

\[ H^m(TB)=H^0\bigl(T(H^mB)\bigr), \qquad T=i^!,i^*,\quad m\in\mathbf Z. \tag{FCR.16} \]

The comparisons are the functors' actual truncation maps. This finite-window proof handles both infinite cohomological tails and uses no interchange of an ambient product with the regular embedding.

3.493. The actual inclusion, retraction and idempotent

Let \(\varepsilon_B:i_*i^!B\to B\) be the right-adjunction counit, and \(\eta_B:B\to i_*i^*B\) the left-adjunction unit. Define

\[ \theta_B: i^!B\simeq i^*i_*i^!B\xrightarrow{i^*\varepsilon_B}i^*B. \tag{FCR.17} \]

Equations FCR.13 and FCR.16 identify every cohomology map of \(\theta_B\) with an isomorphism. Thus it is an equivalence. Put

\[ u_E=\varepsilon_B,\qquad r_E=i_*(\theta_B^{-1})\eta_B,\qquad r_Eu_E=1. \tag{FCR.18} \]

Naturality of the left unit identifies \(\eta_B\varepsilon_B\) with \(i_*\theta_B\), because that unit is the identity on the fully faithful image of \(i_*\). This proves the last identity as an identity of actual maps. Consequently

\[ e_E=u_Er_E,\qquad e_E^2=e_E,\qquad B\simeq i_*V\oplus\operatorname{cofib}(u_E). \tag{FCR.19} \]

The monomorphism \(A_0\hookrightarrow H^{m_0}E\) remains a monomorphism after the heart-exact cycle functor. The functor \(H^0i^!\), being Hom from the point delta module on the operator heart, is left exact. Therefore the nonzero coefficient in FCR.8 injects into \(H^0i^!H^{m_0}B\). By FCR.16 this is \(H^{m_0}V\), proving FCR.3.

3.494. Algebraic transverse tests at generic nonzero covectors

At a smooth point \(p=(x,\xi)\), \(\xi\ne0\), the symmetric-graph construction IS.1–IS.4 gives a regular \(h\) satisfying FCR.2 after shrinking to an affine coordinate neighbourhood. In étale coordinates \(z\) centred at \(x\), it gives a symmetric \(Q\) with

\[ \begin{gathered} T_pC\cap\operatorname{graph}(Q)=0,\\ h(z)=\langle\xi,z\rangle+\tfrac12 z^{\mathsf t}Qz,\qquad dh_z=\xi+Qz. \end{gathered} \tag{FCR.20} \]

For completeness, the linear construction includes every projection rank. For a \(d\)-dimensional tangent plane \(W\subset V_0\oplus V_0^*\), let \(P\) be its projection and \(K=W\cap V_0^*\). Then \(\dim P=\dim\operatorname{Ann}(K)\), and \(W\) induces \(A:P\to\operatorname{Ann}(K)^*\). The symmetric form constructed by pairing the common intersection with itself and the two complementary bases with one another restricts to an invertible map \(B_P\). Hence

\[ \det(tB_P-A)\ne0\quad\text{for all but finitely many }t, \qquad Q=tB. \tag{FCR.21} \]

The leading coefficient is \(\det B_P\ne0\). For zero-dimensional \(P\), the determinant is one and every graph is transverse. Symmetry makes \(Qz\) the derivative of the quadratic term.

If a nonzero characteristic component of \(A_0\) is contained in \(\Lambda\), holonomicity and \(\dim\Lambda\le d\) make it a whole \(d\)-dimensional component of \(\Lambda\). Remove the other components, its singular locus, the zero section and the projection rank-drop locus. Involutivity makes the smooth locus Lagrangian; the generic-rank argument gives a dense constant-rank region. A complex point in this nonempty region supplies FCR.1–FCR.2 and the nonzero witness. This assertion concerns components containing nonzero covectors.

3.495. Exact images of the point retract

Let \(T\) be any exact functor on the cycle category. Applying it to FCR.18 gives

\[ T(i_*V)\xrightarrow{T(u_E)}T(B) \xrightarrow{T(r_E)}T(i_*V),\qquad T(r_E)T(u_E)=1. \tag{FCR.22} \]

Thus the image cannot vanish when \(T(i_*V)\ne0\). In a proper-image application, this is used with a specified actual cycle comparison. For a proper \(f:U\to Z\), \(h=g\circ f\), \(x\mapsto z\), and the induced zero-fibre map \(f_0\), the relevant formulas are

\[ \begin{gathered} \Phi_g^{\mathrm{reg}}f_*^{\mathrm{reg}}E \simeq f_{0,*}^{\mathrm{reg}}\Phi_h^{\mathrm{reg}}E,\\ f_{0,*}^{\mathrm{reg}}i_*V=j_*V,\quad j:\{z\}\hookrightarrow g^{-1}(0). \end{gathered} \tag{FCR.23} \]

Whenever the bounded proper-cycle comparison and the indicated continuous functors are established in the chosen theory, the first comparison extends to their ind-extensions on every unbounded input: evaluate it on a filtered presentation by bounded objects, and retain its natural transformation and inverse. The second equality is composition of closed point transfer and proper direct image, and retains the coefficient \(V\). Formulas FCR.22–FCR.23 then exhibit the nonzero target cycle retract.

The fixed-cone result proves this step for full unbounded ind-regular inputs. Regularity of every independently nilpotent operator complex, its supported compact factorization, the full projector image and the applicable general proper-cycle and field-extension statements retain their own hypotheses.

Figure 3.62. The first panel is FCR.4–FCR.8: every finite heart subobject has the same local characteristic bound, and a transverse graph gives isolated cycles, with a nonzero witness. The second panel is FCR.14–FCR.16: a fixed output degree uses a finite input window despite both infinite tails. The final panel displays the actual unit, counit and inverse comparison in FCR.17–FCR.19. The arrows are maps of coefficient complexes; no geometric scale is implied.

3.496. A thick point module in every even degree

Exercise 3.GG. On \(U=\mathbf A^1_t\), put \(M_\ell=D/Dt^\ell\), \(\ell\ge1\), and \(E=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}M_\ell[2n]\). Use \(h=t\). Compute its point coefficient, retaining the multiplicity \(\ell\) and both infinite tails.

Solution 3.GG. AIC.25–AIC.27 prove regularity and the good symbol quotient \(\mathbf C[t,\zeta]/(t^\ell)\). Its reduced characteristic set is \(T^*_{\{0\}}U\). Finite partial sums give the actual regular ind-presentation of \(E\). At \(p=(0,dt)\), the graph of \(dt\) meets this fibre transversely.

Right PBW identifies the vector space and its coordinate action as

\[ \begin{gathered} M_\ell=\mathbf C[u,t]/(t^\ell),\qquad t\cdot P=(t-\partial_u)P,\\ \ker(t\cdot)=e^{ut}\bigl(\mathbf C[t]/(t^\ell)\bigr). \end{gathered} \tag{FCR.24} \]

Here \(u\) represents the ordered derivative vectors. Both \(e^{ut}\) and \(e^{-ut}\) are finite polynomials modulo \(t^\ell\). The equation \((t-\partial_u)P=R\) is solved by multiplying by \(e^{-ut}\), taking the negative polynomial primitive in \(u\), and multiplying by \(e^{ut}\). Thus coordinate multiplication is surjective and its kernel has dimension \(\ell\). The finite point Hom resolution gives

\[ i^!M_\ell=\mathbf C^\ell\quad\text{in degree zero},\qquad \Phi_t^{\mathrm{reg}}M_\ell=M_\ell. \tag{FCR.25} \]

For the second assertion, the module is supported on the zero fibre, so its nearby restriction is zero. The normalization \(\Phi_t=\operatorname{Cone}(i^*\to\psi_t)[-1]\) is the identity on this supported object. Continuity now gives

\[ B=E,\qquad V=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}\mathbf C^\ell[2n],\qquad H^mV= \begin{cases}\mathbf C^\ell,&m\text{ even},\\0,&m\text{ odd}.\end{cases} \tag{FCR.26} \]

Both retract maps identify with the supported-point equivalence and its inverse. The multiplicity survives although the reduced conic set suffices to choose the transverse test.

3.497. A cone bound without a nonzero witness

Exercise 3.GH. Keep \(U=\mathbf A^1_t\), \(p=(0,dt)\), \(h=t\), and take \(\Lambda=T_U^*U\cup T^*_{\{0\}}U\). Let \(E=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}\mathcal O_U[2n]\). Verify the fixed bound and transversality, and compute the cycle. Identify the missing nonvanishing hypothesis.

Solution 3.GH. Each coherent submodule of a heart module has characteristic contained in the zero section, by exact-sequence support and the flat-connection symbol calculation. Near \(p\), the cone \(\Lambda\) is the smooth vertical fibre, and the graph of \(dt\) is transverse to it. But

\[ \operatorname{Char}(\mathcal O_U)=T_U^*U,\qquad p\notin\operatorname{Char}(A) \quad\text{for every finite }A\subset H^mE. \tag{FCR.27} \]

The flat-frame de Rham complex is \(\mathbf C_U[1]\). For the coordinate \(t\), its nearby coefficient and central restriction are both \(\mathbf C[1]\), and specialization is the identity, represented by the same constant section on the covered disc. Therefore

\[ \Phi_t^{\mathrm{reg}}\mathcal O_U=0,\qquad \Phi_t^{\mathrm{reg}}E=0,\qquad V=0. \tag{FCR.28} \]

All common-cone hypotheses for the natural projector hold. The witness \(A_0\) in FCR.3 is absent, so the point retract is zero. Membership in an upper support bound alone does not assert membership at every point of that bound.

3.498. A ramified proper image with two infinite tails

Exercise 3.GI. Let \(f:\mathbf A^1_z\to\mathbf A^1_t\) be \(t=z^a\), \(a\ge2\), and let \(C_f=f_*^{\mathrm{reg}}\mathcal O_{\mathbf A^1_z}\) be its actual bounded regular direct image. In the target regular ind-category put \(Q=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}C_f[2n]\). Compute \(\Phi_t^{\mathrm{reg}}Q\), with its coefficient and monodromy.

Solution 3.GI. The map is finite and proper. The bounded actual Riemann–Hilbert comparison gives \(\operatorname{DR}(C_f)=Rf_*\mathbf C[1]\). The direct covered-fibre calculation IS.12 takes the normalized cycle to the quotient of the diagonal map

\[ \mathbf C\longrightarrow\mathbf C^a,\qquad v\longmapsto(v,\ldots,v),\qquad W_a=\mathbf C^a/\mathbf C(1,\ldots,1). \tag{FCR.29} \]

The specialization map is that diagonal because the source disc is connected and its punctured fibre has \(a\) points. After the shift in the normalization the quotient is in degree zero. It has dimension \(a-1\); monodromy cyclically permutes the \(a\) coordinates, preserving the diagonal. Continuity of the actual ind-cycle functor gives

\[ \begin{gathered} \Phi_t^{\mathrm{reg}}Q =i_*\left(\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}W_a[2n]\right),\\ H^m i^!\Phi_t^{\mathrm{reg}}Q= \begin{cases}W_a,&m\text{ even},\\0,&m\text{ odd}.\end{cases} \end{gathered} \tag{FCR.30} \]

Outside zero the cover is étale, so the bounded coefficient is lisse and its characteristic set is zero-section there. AIC.8 bounds its full characteristic set by the zero section together with the vertical fibre at zero. The fixed cone is therefore valid for every finite submodule in every degree of \(Q\). The nonzero cycle coefficient supplies the nonzero point part. The actual cotangent-fibre equation is \(az^{a-1}\eta=0\); at \(\eta\ne0\) its local length is \(a-1\), as in IS.13. That multiplicity agrees with \(\dim W_a\). Both infinite tails and the cyclic monodromy survive the calculation.

3.499. Isolation separately for each coherent piece

Let \(U\) be smooth affine of dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbf C\), \(E\in\mathscr R_\infty(U)\), \(x\in U(\mathbf C)\), and \(h\in\mathcal O(U)\), with \(h(x)=0\) and \(dh_x\ne0\). Put \(p=(x,dh_x)\). Impose the following condition:

\[ \begin{gathered} \text{For every }m\in\mathbf Z\text{ and finite }A\subset H^mE,\\ \operatorname{graph}(dh)\cap\operatorname{Char}(A)^{\mathrm{an}} \text{ lies over }\{x\}\\ \text{on some analytic neighbourhood }W_A\text{ of }x. \end{gathered} \tag{CIC.1} \]

The neighbourhood may depend on \(A\) and \(m\). There need be no common closed holonomic cone or common analytic neighbourhood. Let \(B=\Phi_h^{\mathrm{reg}}E\), with closed transfer of its zero-fibre output to \(U\) understood, and \(i:\{x\}\hookrightarrow U\). Then the actual point comparison is an equivalence, and there are natural maps

\[ \begin{gathered} \theta_B:i^!B\xrightarrow{\sim}i^*B,\\ i_*i^!B\xrightarrow{u_E}B\xrightarrow{r_E}i_*i^!B, \qquad r_Eu_E=1. \end{gathered} \tag{CIC.2} \]

No cohomological boundedness is imposed. A smooth transverse characteristic witness will give nonvanishing in §3.502. The componentwise isolation framework also appears in Arinkin–Gaitsgory–Kazhdan–Raskin–Rozenblyum–Varshavsky, Appendix H.3; the actual ind-regular functors and their proof here use the adjunctions and finite-amplitude bounds IAC.16–IAC.29.

3.500. The isolation class in the operator heart

By IAC.6, the affine embedding of the regular ind-category is fully faithful and t-exact. Its heart modules are filtered unions of coherent regular holonomic subobjects. The operator ring is Noetherian, and regular holonomicity is a Serre property. Thus

\[ H^mE=\operatorname*{colim}_{A\subset H^mE,\ A\ \mathrm{finite}}A. \tag{CIC.3} \]

The finite pieces are directed by finite sums. The isolation property for their characteristic sets is preserved under subobjects, quotients and finite extensions, by the exact-sequence characteristic-support identity. For a quotient of a possibly infinite heart module, lift finitely many generators of a finite submodule. They lie in a finite submodule upstairs, and its image contains the proposed finite quotient piece. Explicitly,

\[ L\twoheadrightarrow L'',\quad C\subset L''\text{ finite} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad C\subset\operatorname{im}(A\to L'')\text{ for some finite }A\subset L. \tag{CIC.4} \]

For an extension, a finite submodule in the middle intersects the first module in a finite submodule and has finite image in the last, by Noetherianity. The union of their characteristic sets is its characteristic set; intersect the two isolation neighbourhoods. This proves that the heart modules satisfying CIC.1 form a Serre class. It follows from the cohomology exact sequence that

\[ \mathscr I_{h,x}:= \{E\in\mathscr R_\infty(U):\text{all }H^mE\text{ satisfy CIC.1}\} \quad\text{is stable and closed under truncations}. \tag{CIC.5} \]

In particular all natural maps in CIC.2 are maps on this full stable subcategory. No compact-generation assertion for this subcategory is required.

3.501. Admissible cycle hearts and the full unbounded retract

Every finite \(A\subset H^mE\) is regular holonomic. The exact support identity AIC.8 and the bounded cycle support bound MCM.10 give

\[ \operatorname{supp} \Phi_h\operatorname{DR}_d(A^{\mathrm{an}})\cap W_A \subset\{x\}. \tag{CIC.6} \]

The bounded cycle \(B_A=\Phi_{h,0}^{\mathrm{reg}}A\), transferred to \(U\), is a regular holonomic heart object. MCM.13 identifies its closed analytic carrier with the analytification of its reduced algebraic carrier. If \(x\) lies in that carrier, the isolated analytic germ and faithful contraction give \(I=\mathfrak m_x\) in the algebraic local ring, exactly as in FCR.9. Killing the finitely many maximal-ideal generators by one denominator makes \(\{x\}\) an open and closed component of this carrier. Consequently

\[ B_A=i_*V_A\oplus B'_A,\qquad V_A\in\operatorname{Vect}^{\heartsuit},\qquad x\notin\operatorname{supp}B'_A. \tag{CIC.7} \]

When the carrier avoids \(x\), set \(V_A=0\). Point/away mapping complexes vanish in both directions, so these splittings are natural in all maps between finite pieces, even when their neighbourhoods differ.

The actual ind-cycle functor is continuous and t-exact. Hence \(H^mB\) is the filtered union of the \(B_A\), with inclusions. Both regular point adjoints are continuous by IAC.16. Their comparison is the identity on every bounded point part and zero on every away part. Therefore

\[ i^!H^mB\xrightarrow{\sim}i^*H^mB \simeq\operatorname*{colim}_{A\subset H^mE}V_A \quad\text{in degree zero}. \tag{CIC.8} \]

For a fixed output degree \(m\), the uniform amplitudes \(i^!\in[0,2d]\) and \(i^*\in[-3d,d]\) cut the input to the finite window

\[ \begin{gathered} L\le m-2d-2,\qquad H\ge m+3d+2,\\ H^m(TB)=H^0T(H^mB),\quad T=i^!,i^*. \end{gathered} \tag{CIC.9} \]

Indeed the low tail has output in degrees at most \(m-3\), and the high tail in degrees at least \(m+3\). On the intervening finite Postnikov window, CIC.8 makes each heart contribution pure in its own degree, so its finite filtration collapses. These are the actual truncation comparisons, as in FCR.14–FCR.16. Thus \(\theta_B\) is an isomorphism on all cohomologies. With the actual left unit \(\eta_B\) and right counit \(\varepsilon_B\), put

\[ \begin{gathered} u_E=\varepsilon_B,\qquad r_E=i_*(\theta_B^{-1})\eta_B,\\ \eta_B\varepsilon_B=i_*\theta_B,\qquad r_Eu_E=1,\qquad B\simeq i_*i^!B\oplus\operatorname{cofib}(u_E). \end{gathered} \tag{CIC.10} \]

Naturality of the left unit on the fully faithful point image proves the middle identity. This proves CIC.2 on the full unbounded category \(\mathscr I_{h,x}\), with the specified maps. No common neighbourhood for the whole filtered union or ambient inverse-limit comparison has been used.

3.502. A nonzero witness and the precise geometric scope

For nonvanishing, suppose a finite \(A_0\subset H^{m_0}E\) has the following properties:

\[ \begin{gathered} p\in\operatorname{Char}(A_0)^{\mathrm{an}},\\ \operatorname{Char}(A_0)^{\mathrm{an}} \text{ has a smooth conic Lagrangian germ at }p,\\ \text{with constant projection rank, and}\\ T_p\operatorname{Char}(A_0)^{\mathrm{an}} \cap T_p\operatorname{graph}(dh)=0. \end{gathered} \tag{CIC.11} \]

Only this witness needs the smooth transverse coefficient calculation. The conormal endpoint comparison MCM.3–MCM.9 gives a nonzero bounded normalized cycle coefficient in degree zero. The injection \(A_0\hookrightarrow H^{m_0}E\) remains injective after the heart-exact cycle functor, and \(H^0i^!\) is left exact because it is point Hom on the operator heart. Thus

\[ 0\ne H^0i^!B_{A_0}\hookrightarrow H^0i^!H^{m_0}B =H^{m_0}i^!B. \tag{CIC.12} \]

The general direct-image lower-bound argument must construct one actual test for which the isolation condition holds for every finite piece. A generic point of the target characteristic image, viewed as a rational point over an algebraic closure of its function field, is the geometric construction in Appendix H.4 of the free reading above. That construction additionally needs the corresponding regular algebraic cycle and point functors over the new field, their proper-image comparison, and the actual global Hecke presentations. The scalar-support calculation below addresses support and subobjects; it does not supply those cycle functors or nilpotent regularity.

3.503. Characteristic support under an arbitrary field extension

For this and the next section, let \(k\) be any field of characteristic zero, \(K/k\) any extension, and \(U=\operatorname{Spec}R\) smooth affine of finite type over \(k\). Put \(D=\Gamma(U,\mathcal D_{U/k})\), \(R_K=R\otimes_kK\), and \(D_K=\Gamma(U_K,\mathcal D_{U_K/K})\). The actual coefficient-and-derivative map gives

\[ D\otimes_kK\xrightarrow{\sim}D_K,\qquad \operatorname{gr}D_K=(\operatorname{gr}D)\otimes_kK. \tag{CIC.13} \]

Here is the filtered verification, including infinite \(K\). On an étale coordinate chart, the PBW bases have the same derivative monomials, with the coefficients extended from \(R\) to \(R_K\). The chain rule identifies their restrictions and the actual operator map. The map is an isomorphism on every associated graded order, hence on each filtered order by induction in its short exact sequence, and on the union of the orders. These local maps agree on overlaps. The quasi-coherent affine sheaf/module description makes their global sections commute with the field extension. This is the construction FE.9 and its following scalar-extension calculation.

Let \(M\) be any coherent \(D\)-module with a good filtration \(F\), and set \(M_K=M\otimes_kK\). Flatness of the field extension and the PBW comparison give a good filtration

\[ F_jM_K=F_jM\otimes_kK,\qquad \operatorname{gr}_F(M_K)=\operatorname{gr}_F(M)\otimes_kK. \tag{CIC.14} \]

To check the full support equality, put \(S=\operatorname{gr}D\), \(S_K=S\otimes_kK\), and \(N=\operatorname{gr}_F M\). For every \(q\in\operatorname{Spec}S_K\) lying over \(a\in\operatorname{Spec}S\),

\[ (N\otimes_kK)_q=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad N_a=0. \tag{CIC.15} \]

The forward implication follows by finite Nakayama. If \(N_a\ne0\), then \(N_a/aN_a\ne0\), and its extension from the residue field \(\kappa(a)\) to \(\kappa(q)\) is nonzero. It is exactly the residue of \(N_a\otimes_{S_a}(S_K)_q\). The reverse implication is localization of the zero module. Equivalently the map \(S_a\to(S_K)_q\) is flat and local, hence faithfully flat. This verifies the equality at every cotangent prime, not just at base closed points. Consequently

\[ \operatorname{Char}_{K}(M_K) =\operatorname{Char}_{k}(M)\times_{\operatorname{Spec}k} \operatorname{Spec}K \quad\text{as closed support sets}. \tag{CIC.16} \]

The graded module in CIC.14 retains its nonreduced annihilator and every symbol multiplicity. CIC.16 concerns its support set and makes no identification of reduced and nonreduced schemes.

3.504. Every finite subobject after extension and all unbounded degrees

Let \(Q\) be an arbitrary unbounded \(D\)-module complex. Its actual scalar extension is \(Q_K=Q\otimes_kK\). It can also be computed by \(D_K\otimes_D^{\mathbf L}Q\). Indeed \(D_K=D\otimes_kK\) is free as a right \(D\)-module after choosing a \(k\)-basis of \(K\), so ordinary extension already computes the derived functor. Hence

\[ H^m(Q_K)=H^mQ\otimes_kK\quad(m\in\mathbf Z),\qquad Q_K=0\Longleftrightarrow Q=0. \tag{CIC.17} \]

The affine rings \(D,D_K\) are Noetherian over these fields. Their symbol rings are the symmetric algebras of the finite projective tangent modules, hence are Noetherian. Lifting finitely many homogeneous generators of an ideal of leading symbols, and subtracting them to reduce the order, proves the ascending-chain condition for operator ideals. The same good-filtration argument gives coherence for finite modules. Every heart module is the filtered union of its finite \(D\)-submodules, and field extension preserves their inclusions. A finite \(D_K\)-submodule \(C\subset H^m(Q_K)\) has finitely many generators. Each generator uses finitely many tensors from that union. A common finite original submodule \(A\subset H^mQ\) contains them all after extension, so

\[ C\subset A_K\subset H^m(Q_K) \quad\text{for some finite }A\subset H^mQ,\qquad \operatorname{Char}_K(C)\subset\operatorname{Char}_K(A_K). \tag{CIC.18} \]

The last inclusion is exact-sequence characteristic support over the Noetherian ring \(D_K\). It does not assert that every new submodule descends individually to \(k\).

Let \(\Lambda\subset T^*U\) be any closed algebraic conic set and \(\Lambda_K\) its inverse image on \(T^*U_K\). Define \(\mathcal D_\Lambda(U)\) by the independent condition NCS.10 on every finite submodule of every cohomology. Equations CIC.16 and CIC.18 prove preservation of that condition. They also prove reflection. For any finite \(A\subset H^mQ\), flatness gives \(A_K\subset H^m(Q_K)\). If the new condition holds, CIC.16 puts its original characteristic set in \(\Lambda\): every prime outside \(\Lambda\) has a prime above it after the faithfully flat field extension, and CIC.15 detects a nonzero symbol module there. Thus

\[ Q\in\mathcal D_\Lambda(U) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Q_K\in\mathcal D_{\Lambda_K}(U_K). \tag{CIC.19} \]

This is an assertion about the scalar extension of \(Q\), not essential surjectivity onto all supported objects over \(K\). Along \(k\subset K\subset L\), actual tensor associativity gives

\[ (Q_K)_L\simeq Q_L,\qquad (A_K)_L\simeq A_L,\qquad \operatorname{gr}\bigl((A_K)_L\bigr) =(\operatorname{gr}A)\otimes_kL. \tag{CIC.20} \]

These are the specified coefficient and operator maps, so all successive support comparisons agree. No boundedness, regularity, choice of a complex embedding, or interchange of an infinite Postnikov tower is needed.

Figure 3.63. The first panel shows the finite-piece isolation mechanism CIC.1–CIC.10. The middle panel depicts the exact accumulating-point example of Solution 3.GJ: each finite set has an isolation neighbourhood, but the entire sequence has none. The bottom panel records the scalar-support calculation CIC.14–CIC.19, including every new finite submodule in a base-extended original piece. The support arrows are categorical or set-theoretic maps; the point coordinates are the stated exact rational sequence.

3.505. Accumulating point modules with both infinite tails

Exercise 3.GJ. On \(U=\mathbf A^1_t\), write \(\delta_b=D/D(t-b)\), and put

\[ b_j=\frac1{j+1}\ (j\ge1),\qquad L=\delta_0\oplus\bigoplus_{j\ge1}\delta_{b_j},\qquad E=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}L[2n]. \tag{CIC.21} \]

For \(h=t\) and \(x=0\), prove CIC.1, show that neither a common analytic neighbourhood nor a closed characteristic bound of dimension at most one exists, and compute the full cycle.

Solution 3.GJ. Finite sums of point modules and shifts give the actual regular ind-presentation. Every finite submodule in every cohomological degree lies in a finite sum of those deltas. Its characteristic set is contained in finitely many vertical fibres. The graph of \(dt\) meets each fibre over its one base point. A neighbourhood of zero can remove the finitely many nonzero points for each piece. This proves CIC.1, and \(\delta_0\) is the smooth transverse witness.

The sequence \(b_j\) tends to zero, so no one analytic neighbourhood removes every away point. For a common algebraic bound, suppose \(P(t,\zeta)\) vanishes on every vertical fibre at the \(b_j\). Expanding gives

\[ P(t,\zeta)=\sum_{r=0}^N p_r(t)\zeta^r,\qquad p_r(b_j)=0\ \text{for all }j \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p_r=0\ \text{for all }r. \tag{CIC.22} \]

Each coefficient polynomial has infinitely many distinct roots. Thus the vertical fibres have Zariski-dense union in the two-dimensional \(T^*\mathbf A^1\), so no closed cone of dimension at most one contains them.

The normalized cycle of \(\delta_0\) is the identity, since the nearby restriction is zero. For \(b_j\ne0\), the bounded cycle of \(\delta_{b_j}\) at the zero fibre vanishes on a disc avoiding its support. Continuity of the specified ind-cycle gives

\[ \begin{gathered} \Phi_t^{\mathrm{reg}}E =\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}\delta_0[2n],\\ i^!\Phi_t^{\mathrm{reg}}E =\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}\mathbf C[2n]. \end{gathered} \tag{CIC.23} \]

The point retract is the whole cycle, with

\[ H^m i^!\Phi_t^{\mathrm{reg}}E= \begin{cases}\mathbf C,&m\text{ even},\\0,&m\text{ odd}.\end{cases} \tag{CIC.24} \]

This calculation is in the actual regular ind-category; it makes no identification with ordinary cycles on every unbounded classical sheaf at an accumulation point.

3.506. A nonisolated carrier has no such point retraction

Exercise 3.GK. Let \(U=\mathbf A^2_{s,t}\), \(h=t\), \(x=(0,0)\), and \(M=\mathcal O_{\mathbf A^1_s}\boxtimes\delta_{0,t}\), in degree zero. Compute \(B=\Phi_t^{\mathrm{reg}}M\), both point functors, and their comparison. Decide whether the right-adjunction counit \(i_*i^!B\to B\) splits.

Solution 3.GK. The good product filtration gives

\[ \begin{gathered} \operatorname{Char}(M)=\{t=0,\ \eta_s=0\},\\ \operatorname{graph}(dt)\cap\operatorname{Char}(M) =\{(s,0;0,1):s\in\mathbf C\},\qquad B=M. \end{gathered} \tag{CIC.25} \]

The cycle is the identity because \(M\) is supported on the zero fibre. The displayed intersection is a whole line, so CIC.1 fails at \(x\).

The point Hom is computed by the finite cochain Koszul complex for multiplication by \(s,t\). Right PBW writes \(M=\mathbf C[s,u]\), where \(u\) denotes the normal derivative vectors, with \(t=-\partial_u\). Multiplication by \(t\) is surjective and has kernel \(\mathbf C[s]\). The remaining cochain multiplication by \(s\) is injective with cokernel \(\mathbf C\) in degree one. Thus \(i^!M=\mathbf C[-1]\). Bounded regular duality fixes \(M\), since the flat line connection and point delta are self-dual, and the actual ordinary/extraordinary duality comparison gives

\[ i^!B=\mathbf C[-1],\qquad i^*B=\mathbf C[1],\qquad \theta_B=0. \tag{CIC.26} \]

The last equality holds because the degree-zero mapping group from \(\mathbf C[-1]\) to \(\mathbf C[1]\) is zero in complexes of vector spaces. Moreover the left point adjunction gives

\[ \operatorname{Hom}(B,i_*\mathbf C[-1]) =\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbf C[1],\mathbf C[-1])=0. \tag{CIC.27} \]

The right counit is nonzero: its right adjoint is the identity on \(i^!B\). Every possible degree-zero retraction is zero by CIC.27, so this counit cannot split. Holonomicity and regularity alone do not give isolated-cycle purity or the point retract.

3.507. A ramified image of the accumulating family

Exercise 3.GL. Let \(f:\mathbf A^1_s\to\mathbf A^1_t\) be \(t=s^a\), \(a\ge2\), and take the family \(E\) of CIC.21 on the \(s\)-line. Compute its actual regular direct image and the target cycle for \(h=t\). Determine whether ramification multiplies the point coefficient by \(a\).

Solution 3.GL. For each point \(b\), composition of proper point transfer gives, with the coefficient retained,

\[ f_*\delta_b=(f\circ i_b)_*\mathbf C =\delta_{b^a}. \tag{CIC.28} \]

The proper regular ind-functor is the continuous extension of this bounded transfer. Hence

\[ \begin{gathered} f_*^{\mathrm{reg}}E =\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z} \left(\delta_0\oplus\bigoplus_{j\ge1}\delta_{b_j^a}\right)[2n],\\ \Phi_t^{\mathrm{reg}}f_*^{\mathrm{reg}}E =\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}\delta_0[2n]. \end{gathered} \tag{CIC.29} \]

The positive rational numbers \(b_j^a\) are distinct and tend to zero. The target therefore satisfies componentwise isolation with a transverse point witness, while again admitting no common neighbourhood or closed holonomic cone. Its point coefficient is one copy in every even degree. Although

\[ \begin{gathered} f^{-1}(0)=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf C[s]/(s^a), \qquad \operatorname{length}f^{-1}(0)=a,\\ i_0^!\Phi_t^{\mathrm{reg}}f_*\delta_0=\mathbf C. \end{gathered} \tag{CIC.30} \]

the coefficient of a point input is one. Scheme-fibre length alone does not count this direct-image coefficient. For a flat line input the separate cycle calculation FCR.29 gives rank \(a-1\); its input and specialization map are different. The present calculation uses actual point-transfer composition and continuity. It does not apply the nonzero-differential test CIC.1 to the critical source function \(s^a\) at zero.

3.508. The cycle comparison at a critical differential

Let \(U\) be smooth affine of dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbf C\), let \(h\in\mathcal O(U)\), and put \(Y=h^{-1}(0)\). The normalized convention remains

\[ \Phi_hF=\operatorname{Fib}(F|_Y\longrightarrow\psi_hF). \tag{ICR.1} \]

The differential of \(h\) is allowed to vanish. On \(U^{\mathrm{an}}\), write \(H=\{\operatorname{Re}h\geq0\}\) and \(A=\{\operatorname{Re}h<0\}\). For coefficients in a field \(k\), the positive-real-support comparison identifies the actual functors, naturally in every bounded complex-constructible complex:

\[ (\Phi_hF)_y\simeq(R\Gamma_HF)_y,\qquad y\in Y. \tag{ICR.2} \]

Here is the map and the reason it remains valid at a critical point. With the covering \(e^{2\pi iw}\), choose the negative-sector lift \(1/4<\operatorname{Re}w<3/4\). Extension by zero of that sheet gives \(k_A\to L_h\), where \(L_h\) is the proper-support sum of the covering sheets. The trace square gives

\[ [k_A\longrightarrow k_U]\longrightarrow [L_h\longrightarrow k_U], \qquad \Phi_hF\longrightarrow(R\Gamma_HF)|_Y . \tag{ICR.3} \]

Both coefficient complexes have degrees \(-1,0\). On the two fibre triangles the middle map is the identity of \(F|_Y\); the other map restricts the entire lifted punctured neighbourhood to the selected negative strip. The cofinal-ball and restriction proof uses the local curve direct image on arbitrarily small ball–target-disc intersections. Off the central value that image is locally constant. On the contractible covering halfplane and the selected half-strip, whole-complex evaluation commutes with restriction and is invertible. The resulting stalk colimit proves that ICR.3 is invertible. Neither a regular zero fibre nor \(dh_y\ne0\) enters this argument. The chosen strip retains the covering convention and its deck transport.

The defining neighbourhood criterion for microsupport now gives the closed carrier bound

\[ \operatorname{supp}\Phi_hF \subset\{y\in Y:(y,dh_y)\in\operatorname{SS}(F)\}. \tag{ICR.4} \]

Indeed, if \((y,dh_y)\) is outside microsupport, choose a cotangent neighbourhood disjoint from that closed set. Continuity of the section \(dh\) gives a base neighbourhood on which the section stays in the chosen open set. All the corresponding supported tests vanish there by the defining criterion, so ICR.2 vanishes on that whole neighbourhood. This proves the bound for closed support. The same reasoning applies to a zero covector; no limiting argument through nonzero covectors is needed.

3.509. Componentwise isolation without a nonzero first jet

Let \(E\in\mathscr R_\infty(U)\), \(h(x)=0\), and impose CIC.1 on every finite \(A\subset H^mE\), for every \(m\). There is no condition on \(dh_x\). Set \(B=\Phi_h^{\mathrm{reg}}E\), with the closed transfer of the zero-fibre output to \(U\), and \(i:\{x\}\hookrightarrow U\). Then

\[ \begin{gathered} \theta_B:i^!B\xrightarrow{\sim}i^*B,\\ i_*i^!B\xrightarrow{\varepsilon_B}B \xrightarrow{i_*\theta_B^{-1}\eta_B}i_*i^!B, \\ (i_*\theta_B^{-1}\eta_B)\varepsilon_B=1 . \end{gathered} \tag{ICR.5} \]

To prove this, apply AIC.8 and ICR.4 to the finite regular module \(A\). Its bounded cycle has analytic carrier isolated at \(x\) or avoiding \(x\). The reduced algebraic-carrier argument MCM.13 and CIC.7 therefore gives its natural point/away decomposition \(B_A=i_*V_A\oplus B'_A\), with \(V_A\) in degree zero. The Serre argument CIC.3–CIC.5 did not use a nonzero differential: it uses exact characteristic sets, finite lifts through quotients, and finite intersections and images in extensions. It applies unchanged.

The actual algebraic regular cycle is t-exact, including for a critical function, by IAC.26. Its continuous ind-extension and both continuous point adjoints give

\[ i^!H^mB\simeq i^*H^mB \simeq\operatorname*{colim}_{A\subset H^mE}V_A \quad\text{in degree zero}. \tag{ICR.6} \]

Different finite pieces may have different isolation neighbourhoods. Naturality follows from the vanishing of point/away mapping complexes in both directions. The amplitudes \(i^!\in[0,2d]\), \(i^*\in[-3d,d]\) reduce each output degree to the finite Postnikov window CIC.9. All its heart contributions are pure in their corresponding degrees, so the actual comparison is invertible in every degree. Finally \(\eta_B\varepsilon_B=i_*\theta_B\) by the adjunction identities, giving ICR.5. This proves the assertion for both infinite cohomological tails. It does not yet assert that \(i^!B\) is nonzero.

3.510. An isolated stratified critical cluster and its maps

For nonvanishing, first work with a bounded finite-rank perverse \(K\)-sheaf \(P\), for any field \(K\), on a complex manifold \(M\) near \(x\). Fix a locally finite connected complex Whitney \((a,b)\) stratification adapted to \(P\); only finitely many strata occur in a sufficiently small chart. Suppose \(h(x)=0\) and

\[ h|_S\text{ has no critical point in }S\setminus\{x\} \quad\text{for every original local stratum }S. \tag{ICR.7} \]

The stratum through \(x\) can have positive dimension. Both \(dh_x=0\) and a degenerate tangential Hessian are allowed. Condition ICR.7 concerns all the original strata, including those with zero generic normal object.

Retain \(C_S=\overline{T^*_SM}\), \(p=(x,dh_x)\), and \(\Sigma=\bigcup_SC_S\). Whitney \((a)\) implies that a member of a limiting conormal over a stratum annihilates its tangent space. Thus ICR.7 implies that \(\Sigma\cap\operatorname{graph}(dh)\) lies over \(x\) after shrinking. The original-pair proof IH0–IH9 and whole-cluster proof IH10–IH21 give

\[ \begin{aligned} M_h(P)_x &:=(R\Gamma_{\{\operatorname{Re}h\geq0\}}P)_x\\ &\simeq\operatorname{Fib}\bigl( R\Gamma(C;P)\longrightarrow R\Gamma(L;P)\bigr), \end{aligned} \tag{ICR.8} \]

on an original sufficiently small closed ball \(C\) and regular Milnor fibre \(L\). These are comparisons of the actual restriction arrows.

For clarity, retain the entire perturbed cluster, rather than a perturbed stalk at \(x\). A generic small linear perturbation \(h_\alpha=h-\alpha z\) has finitely many stratified Morse points converging to \(x\), with distinct critical values. Choose a regular \(v\) avoiding those values and their finitely many perpendicular bisectors. For \(b=|h_\alpha-v|^2\), let \(B_0\subset\cdots\subset B_N\) cross those critical levels successively. The controlled top restriction \(R\Gamma(C;P)\to R\Gamma(B_N;P)\) and the bottom-fibre comparison are invertible. The reverse exit filtration IH20–IH21 is

\[ \begin{gathered} F_r=\operatorname{Fib}\bigl(R\Gamma(B_N;P) \longrightarrow R\Gamma(B_{N-r};P)\bigr),\\ F_0=0,\quad F_N\simeq M_h(P)_x,\qquad F_{r-1}\longrightarrow F_r\longrightarrow Q_{N-r+1} \xrightarrow{+1}. \end{gathered} \tag{ICR.9} \]

Here \(Q_j=\operatorname{Fib}(R\Gamma(B_j;P)\to R\Gamma(B_{j-1};P))\). The triangle is the fibre-of-composite triangle for the two restriction maps through \(B_{N-r+1}\). It does not reverse cohomology arrows or choose a splitting. At a Morse point on \(S\), the real index of \(b|_S\) is \(\dim_{\mathbf C}S\), giving

\[ Q_j\simeq N_S(P)[-\dim_{\mathbf C}S]=:\mu_S(P). \tag{ICR.10} \]

The normal coefficients, complex orientation lines and continuation paths are those of the actual local pair. Connected generic conormal continuation identifies the isomorphism classes needed here; a global trivialization of their monodromy is not assumed.

3.511. Positive integer multiplicity and visible nonvanishing

The normal-Morse degree proof PD1–PD6 makes every \(\mu_S(P)\) a finite-dimensional vector space in degree zero. Apply the cohomology sequence to ICR.9. Induction begins with zero and gives

\[ F_r\in D^{[0,0]}(K),\qquad 0\longrightarrow H^0F_{r-1}\longrightarrow H^0F_r \longrightarrow H^0Q_{N-r+1}\longrightarrow0. \tag{ICR.11} \]

Let \(n_S\) be the local intersection integer of the original complex conormal cycle \(C_S\) with \(\operatorname{graph}(dh)\) at \(p\), summing its local branches. Set \(n_S=0\) if \(p\notin C_S\). The finite analytic and intersection proof IH10–IH14, IHA1–IHA3 identifies this integer with the number of perturbed Morse points on \(S\). In particular

\[ \begin{gathered} n_S\in\mathbf Z_{\geq0},\qquad p\in C_S \ \Longrightarrow\ n_S>0,\\ \dim_KH^0M_h(P)_x =\sum_S n_S\dim_K\mu_S(P). \end{gathered} \tag{ICR.12} \]

The positivity has a concrete geometric reason. On each pure-\(\dim M\) conormal branch through \(p\), the map \((z,\xi)\mapsto dh_z-\xi\) has isolated zero fibre. A small compact source cut makes it proper; its compact affine analytic fibres are finite. The finite analytic-image dimension theorem makes each retained branch dominate the parameter ball. A generic small parameter therefore has at least one point on each branch. Avoiding the finite-image discriminant puts these points in the smooth transverse conormal locus, where the complex orientation gives sign \(+1\). Homotopy of the original Thom evaluation through the compact cut proves that their count is the original intersection integer. The analytic/Samuel argument applies to non-Cohen–Macaulay conormals; their intersection integer is not in general a raw quotient length.

The visible-conormal theorem NG1–NG9, with the real-part identification of complex cotangents, gives

\[ \begin{gathered} \operatorname{SS}(P)=\bigcup_{\mu_S(P)\ne0}C_S,\\ p\in\operatorname{SS}(P)\Longrightarrow M_h(P)_x\ne0. \end{gathered} \tag{ICR.13} \]

Indeed one visible \(C_S\) contains \(p\); its term in ICR.12 is strictly positive, and all other terms are nonnegative. This includes singular conormal points and zero covectors. The equality is an integer dimension calculation before passing to the field \(K\), so positive characteristic causes no reduction of the intersection integer modulo the characteristic. The free scholarly antecedent is Massey, A Little Microlocal Morse Theory, version 2, Theorem 1.1; the original-pair, cluster and coefficient proofs used above are the programme arguments just linked.

3.512. One isolated witness detects the full ind-object

Return to ICR.5 over \(\mathbf C\). Suppose there exist \(m_0\) and a finite \(A_0\subset H^{m_0}E\) with

\[ p\in\operatorname{Char}(A_0)^{\mathrm{an}}, \qquad P_0=\operatorname{DR}_d(A_0^{\mathrm{an}}) \text{ has an adapted stratification satisfying ICR.7}. \tag{ICR.14} \]

Then \(P_0\) is perverse and AIC.8 identifies its microsupport with that characteristic set. Equations ICR.2 and ICR.13 imply that the point coefficient \(V_{A_0}\) of its bounded regular cycle is nonzero. Heart-exactness of the actual regular cycle sends \(A_0\hookrightarrow H^{m_0}E\) to a monomorphism. The functor \(H^0i^!\), being point Hom on the operator heart, is left exact. Together with ICR.6 and the finite-amplitude comparison, this gives

\[ 0\ne V_{A_0}\hookrightarrow H^0i^!\Phi_h^{\mathrm{reg}}H^{m_0}E =H^{m_0}i^!\Phi_h^{\mathrm{reg}}E . \tag{ICR.15} \]

Thus ICR.5 is a nonzero retract. No smoothness of the characteristic germ, constant projection rank, transverse graph or nondegenerate Hessian is required in ICR.14. The stated isolation on all strata is required for this nonvanishing argument. The other finite cohomology pieces need only their separate characteristic isolation CIC.1.

For a positive-rank flat connection on a smooth carrier \(S\), this test reduces to an isolated critical point of \(h|_S\); the single smooth stratum of \(S\) suffices. Closed transfer retains the actual support test, since its sections are the sections on \(S\) with the pulled-back support. Its local system \(V_S[\dim S]\) has \(\mu_S=V_S\). Therefore

\[ \dim_{\mathbf C}V_{A_0} =\operatorname{rank}(V_S)\, I_{(x,0)}\bigl(T^*_SS,\operatorname{graph}(d(h|_S))\bigr)>0. \tag{ICR.16} \]

Every exact functor preserves the specified retract. Applying this to a proper direct image and then identifying cycles requires the actual proper-cycle comparison for that map, with its coefficient and field hypotheses. Characteristic support under arbitrary field extension in CIC.13–CIC.20 does not alone construct regular cycle functors over that field. These local statements do not establish the global nilpotent regularity or supported-generation assertions.

3.513. A nonreduced cotangent fibre and a zero source covector

Let \(f:\mathbf A^1_z\to\mathbf A^1_t\), \(t=z^a\), \(a\geq2\), and take the source zero section. Over \((t,\eta)=(0,1)\), the compatible-cotangent fibre is

\[ \operatorname{Spec} \frac{\mathbf C[z]}{(z^a,az^{a-1})} =\operatorname{Spec}\frac{\mathbf C[z]}{(z^{a-1})}, \qquad \xi=df_z^t(1)=az^{a-1}. \tag{ICR.17} \]

Its underlying space is a point. Its length is \(a-1\); for \(a\geq3\) its tangent space has dimension one. In particular reduced-point isolation does not imply the zero-tangent hypothesis of RTM.2. A target function \(g(t)=t\) has nonzero differential, while \(h=g\circ f=z^a\) has \(dh_0=0\) and degenerate Hessian for \(a\geq3\).

For constant perverse input \(V[1]\) on a small source disc, a small nonzero fibre consists of \(a\) points. The central unit is the actual diagonal, so

\[ (\Phi_{z^a}V[1])_0 \simeq V\otimes \bigl(\mathbf C^a/\mathbf C(1,\ldots,1)\bigr) \quad\text{in degree zero}. \tag{ICR.18} \]

The contractible-disc and covered-fibre calculation is RTM.20 and FCR.27. Its monodromy is the cyclic permutation on that quotient. This has rank \((a-1)\dim V\), agreeing with ICR.12 and the isolated gradient intersection. Scheme length \(a-1\) is appropriate here because the smooth zero-section gradient equations form the finite complete intersection; it is not a universal identification for singular conormals. The source support condition is isolated despite the zero covector, so ICR.5 also applies to the corresponding ind-regular module with both infinite shift tails.

3.514. An exact quartic cluster

Exercise 3.GM. For \(0\leq s\leq1\), consider

\[ g_s(z)=\frac{z^4}{4}-\frac{s z}{64},\qquad |z|\leq1. \tag{ICR.19} \]

Find every critical point and critical value for \(s>0\). Give a common boundary exclusion for a target disc of radius \(1/5\). At \(s=1\), take \(v=-(1+i)/16\); give explicit increasing regular levels for \(|g_1-v|^2\) crossing all three critical values. Identify the actual filtration and cycle rank for \(V[1]\) at the unperturbed zero-source-covector test.

Solution 3.GM. If \(\zeta_j^3=1\), then

\[ p_j(s)=\frac{s^{1/3}\zeta_j}{4},\qquad c_j(s)=-\frac{3s^{4/3}\zeta_j}{1024},\qquad g_s''(p_j)=3p_j^2\ne0 . \tag{ICR.20} \]

These are all the zeros of \(g_s'=z^3-s/64\). On the boundary,

\[ |g_s(z)|\geq\frac14-\frac1{64} =\frac{15}{64}>\frac15. \tag{ICR.21} \]

All critical values lie in that target disc and all three points converge to zero. At \(s=1\), their squared distances from \(v\), in increasing order, are

\[ \ell_0=\frac{7817}{1048576},\qquad \ell_-=\frac{8393-192\sqrt3}{1048576},\qquad \ell_+=\frac{8393+192\sqrt3}{1048576}. \tag{ICR.22} \]

The middle value is from \(\zeta=(-1+i\sqrt3)/2\), the last from its conjugate. The choices

\[ \begin{gathered} a_0=\frac1{256},\quad a_1=\frac{1975}{262144},\quad a_2=\frac{2075}{262144},\quad a_3=\frac{49}{4096},\\ a_0<\ell_0<a_1<\ell_-<a_2<\ell_+<a_3 \end{gathered} \tag{ICR.23} \]

follow by direct substitution and \(1<\sqrt3<2\). Put \(\eta=1/64\) and \(R=7/64\). One has \(\eta<|v|/4\), \(R>|v|+\eta\), \(R+|v|<1/5\), and \(a_3=R^2\); these follow from \(|v|=\sqrt2/16\), for example by squaring the positive bounds. The bottom disc contains no critical value: \(\sqrt{a_0}=1/16<|v|-3/1024\). Each critical value is at distance at most \(3/1024<\eta\) from zero. Thus these levels enclose the whole cluster in the common boundary-controlled target range.

The endpoints of the pair comparison can also be checked directly here. All bottom and top boundary levels are regular for every \(s\), and their preimages miss \(|z|=1\) by ICR.21. On that circle the outward radial derivative of \(|g_s-v|^2\) is at least \(2[1/4-1/256-(1/64+|v|)(65/64)]>0\). Outside the top sublevel the real gradient has no zero: its only zeros are over \(g_s=v\) or at the three complex critical points, all inside. The decreasing-gradient flow, normalized by its derivative of the level, therefore stays inside the disc and reaches the top sublevel in finite time on every compact band. This gives the top restriction equivalence for constant coefficients. The bottom disc is free of branch values and its preimage is a finite trivial covering, so evaluation on its central fibre is an equivalence. Along \(s\), the same regular compact boundary families admit the controlled time lifts of IH15; they identify the actual whole pair at \(s=0\) and \(s=1\). This verifies the chosen finite perturbation, rather than only an unspecified smaller perturbation.

For the sets \(B_j=\{|z|\leq1,\ |g_1(z)-v|^2\leq a_j\}\), retain the top and bottom pair comparisons of ICR.8–ICR.9. They give

\[ \begin{gathered} F_r=R\Gamma(B_3,B_{3-r};V[1]),\qquad F_0=0,\quad F_3\simeq(\Phi_{z^4/4}V[1])_0,\\ 0\longrightarrow H^0F_{r-1}\longrightarrow H^0F_r \longrightarrow V_r\longrightarrow0,\qquad V_r\simeq V,\quad r=1,2,3 . \end{gathered} \tag{ICR.24} \]

The three copies retain their orientation and continuation data. Hence the cycle rank is \(3\dim V\). No preferred splitting of these sequences or preferred global basis is implied. Independently, the original gradient ideal is \((z^3)\), of length three, and the original four-point fibre gives ICR.18 with \(a=4\). These calculations check the unperturbed object rather than replacing it by one perturbed stalk.

Figure 3.64. The left panel uses \(4p_j=\zeta_j\); the middle uses \(1024c_j=-3\zeta_j\). Both are exact complex-coordinate diagrams at \(s=1\), with different explicitly stated scales. The right panel records the ordered real levels of ICR.22–ICR.23; its heights show order only. The lower panel gives the restriction-fibre filtration ICR.24. Those arrows are maps of complexes, not paths between the drawn critical points. Proofs: ICR.19–ICR.24.

3.515. A nonzero ambient covector with a degenerate tangential test

Exercise 3.GN. In \(U=\mathbf A^2_{s,t}\), let \(j:S=\{t=0\}\hookrightarrow U\), \(A=j_+\mathcal O_S\), and \(h=t+s^a\), \(a\geq3\). Determine the full local conormal intersection, the normalized cycle and the full unbounded point retract for \(E=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}A[2n]\). Explain why nonzero \(dh_0\) does not make the tangential test Morse.

Solution 3.GN. With cotangent coordinates \((\sigma,\tau)\),

\[ \begin{gathered} \operatorname{Char}(A)=\{t=0,\ \sigma=0\},\qquad dh=(a s^{a-1},1),\\ \mathcal O_{\operatorname{Char}(A)\cap\operatorname{graph}(dh),p} =\frac{\mathbf C\{s\}}{(s^{a-1})}. \end{gathered} \tag{ICR.25} \]

Here \(p=(0,0;0,1)\). The graph meets the smooth conormal only at \(p\) locally, but the scheme length is \(a-1\) and the tangential Hessian is zero. The local Riemann–Hilbert image is \(j_*\mathbf C_S[1]\). Sections with the support \(\{\operatorname{Re}h\geq0\}\) are exactly the sections on \(S\) with support \(\{\operatorname{Re}s^a\geq0\}\). ICR.2 and ICR.18 therefore identify

\[ \begin{gathered} \Phi_h^{\mathrm{reg}}A\simeq i_*\bigl(\mathbf C^a/\mathbf C_{\mathrm{diag}}\bigr),\\ i^!\Phi_h^{\mathrm{reg}}E\simeq \bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z} \bigl(\mathbf C^a/\mathbf C_{\mathrm{diag}}\bigr)[2n]. \end{gathered} \tag{ICR.26} \]

The calculation is local at zero; globally the cycle is also supported there. The indicated isomorphism uses the actual diagonal and retains its cyclic monodromy.
