Let \(Z\subset M\) be a closed algebraic subset and \(j:M-Z\hookrightarrow M\). Write \(\mathscr R_0(M)_Z\) for bounded regular objects whose restrictions to the complement are zero. Define the actual localization functor \[ \Gamma_ZK=\operatorname{Fib}(K\longrightarrow j_+j^!K). \tag{HRI.4} \] On an affine chart, finitely many equations \(f_1,\ldots,f_r\) for \(Z\) give the finite alternating localization complex on the opens \(D(f_i)\). Its coefficient localizations have the differentiated operator action. This computes HRI.4 and commutes with colimits on arbitrary module complexes: its Čech direction has fixed finite length. Finite affine covers give the global assertion. The usual localization triangle is therefore the actual triangle \[ \Gamma_ZK\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow j_+j^!K, \qquad j^!\Gamma_ZK=0. \tag{HRI.5} \] These finite localization maps and the closed normal equivalence are proved in Kashiwara's equivalence and singular spaces. On a bounded regular input, HRI.5 and the bounded four-map theorem make \(\Gamma_ZK\) bounded regular and supported on \(Z\). Continuity now gives \[ \operatorname{Ind}\mathscr R_0(M)_Z \ \simeq\ \{K\in\mathscr R_\infty(M):j^!K=0\}. \tag{HRI.6} \] Here the left side has its actual full embedding in \(D_{\mathrm{qc}}(\mathcal D_M)\). To prove essential surjectivity, present \(K\) by bounded regular \(K_i\). Then \(\Gamma_ZK=\operatorname{colim}_i\Gamma_ZK_i\) belongs to that left side, and HRI.5 identifies it with \(K\). The reverse inclusion follows by restriction. Nilpotent thickenings of \(Z\) leave this localization functor unchanged.

Regular Ind membership is local for a finite Zariski cover. Indeed choose a finite affine cover \(M=\bigcup_{i=1}^r U_i\), and suppose \(K|_{U_i}\in\mathscr R_\infty(U_i)\). All finite intersections \(U_I\) are affine because \(M\) is separated. Their inclusions \(j_I:U_I\hookrightarrow M\) are affine: intersection with every affine target open is affine. For these inclusions direct image is the exact quasicoherent open pushforward with its actual operator action. Consequently \[ K\simeq\operatorname{Tot} \left[ \bigoplus_i(j_i)_+K|_{U_i}\longrightarrow \bigoplus_{i<j}(j_{ij})_+K|_{U_i\cap U_j} \longrightarrow\cdots \right]. \tag{HRI.7} \] Locally on a member \(U_i\), inserting its index contracts the augmented restriction complex, with the alternating signs. This proves HRI.7 on module complexes. The Čech direction has length at most \(r-1\), so the same contraction and totalization work for arbitrary positive and negative cohomological tails. Each term is regular Ind by HRI.2 and direct-image continuity; finite totalizations remain in the stable image HRI.1.

This is a statement about unrestricted regular Ind objects and closed base support. Neither open direct image nor \(\Gamma_Z\) is asserted to preserve a prescribed nilpotent cotangent cone. HRI.6 does not replace the microlocal factorization condition AIC.17.

3.549. Inverse image on an embedded singular scheme

Let \(U\hookrightarrow M\) be a closed finite-type scheme, possibly singular or nonreduced, and let \(a:U\to V\), where \(M,V\) are smooth separated finite-type schemes. The graph \[ \Gamma_a\hookrightarrow P=M\times V, \qquad \pi:P\to M,\quad p:P\to V \tag{HRI.8} \] is closed. The projection from \(\Gamma_a\) to \(U\) is an isomorphism. In the supported ambient category the actual extraordinary inverse image is represented on \(M\) by \[ \mathsf T_M(a,K) =\pi_+\Gamma_{\Gamma_a}(p^!K). \tag{HRI.9} \] The closed-support functor is HRI.4. Projection from the graph support is the actual exact supported equivalence given by the projection proof of Kashiwara's equivalence, Theorem 5.1. For this first projection only \(U\to M\) must be closed; its second coordinate may be the arbitrary map \(a\). Local coordinate lifts give the inverse smooth-graph equivalence, as checked below. The projection retains its normal-density evaluation map.

Here is a check of the graph formula and its independence. If \(U\) is smooth, its graph inclusion \(b:U\hookrightarrow P\) is smooth on its source, and closed localization and inverse composition give \[ \Gamma_{\Gamma_a}p^!K \simeq b_+b^!p^!K=b_+a^!K, \qquad \mathsf T_M(a,K)\simeq i_+a^!K . \tag{HRI.10} \] Thus the shifts and normal determinant are those of the actual inverse transfer, not an ordinary tensor on a singular coordinate ring.

For an additional smooth ambient factor \(\mathbf A^s\), lift the coordinates of its embedding of \(U\) locally through \(\mathcal O_M\to\mathcal O_U\). Their graph \(c\) is a section of the added smooth projection \(q\). For an object \(L\) on the old \(M\times V\), nested closed localization and inverse composition give \[ \Gamma_{\Gamma_{\mathrm{joint}}}q^!L =c_+\Gamma_{\Gamma_a}(c^!q^!L) \simeq c_+\Gamma_{\Gamma_a}L, \qquad q_+c_+=\mathrm{id}. \tag{HRI.11} \] The notation identifies the old graph support with its image in this smooth section. This proves compatibility with the projection comparison, including its unit and counit. If the added factor is a general smooth affine scheme, embed it in affine space. Localization on the joint closed support factors through that smooth closed inclusion, and inverse composition gives the same comparison. Shrinking affine neighbourhoods in both factors and using the intrinsic projection functor glue the comparisons; this is the actual gluing argument in Theorem 5.1. Triple products give the composition maps, and fourfold associativity gives their cocycle. Double graphs check inverse-image composition by the same nested-localization and smooth-section calculation. In particular HRI.9 is the extraordinary pullback used in the smooth-chart definition of D-modules, also for singular \(U\).

Every operation in HRI.9 is continuous and preserves bounded regular objects. HRI.2 handles \(p^!\) and \(\pi_+\); HRI.4 handles closed localization. It follows that \(a^!\) carries regular Ind inputs to supported regular Ind objects on \(U\), in every smooth ambient presentation. This proves the statement on the actual unbounded functor by its finite localization and transfer models.

3.550. Zariski lifts of a family to a bundle atlas

Put \(Y=\operatorname{Bun}_G(X)\), with \(X\) a smooth projective connected complex curve and \(G\) connected reductive. Fix the faithful closed representation \(G\hookrightarrow GL_n\) constructed in The moduli stack of bundles, §1.3. For a map \(r:T\to Y\) from a finite-type scheme, let \(E\) be the associated vector bundle on \(X\times T\).

Fix the very ample line \(A\) of that lesson. On the open locus \(T_{d,m}\) where \(E\) has fibre degree \(d\), \(E(m)\) is generated by its sections and its positive fibre cohomology vanishes, the preceding lesson proves \[ W_m=\pi_{T*}E(m)\text{ finite locally free}, \qquad W_m\otimes_{\mathcal O_T}\mathcal O_{T'} \simeq\pi_{T'*}E_{T'}(m). \tag{HRI.12} \] Its proof is BA.1–BA.2: a two-term affine Čech complex has a finite projective replacement, cancellation removes its positive terms, and the cancellation survives every base tensor. Hence no reducedness assumption on \(T'\) is needed.

The framed Quot chart and its reduction scheme give a smooth scheme map \(q_m:\mathscr S_m\to Y\) with \[ \mathscr S_m\times_Y T_{d,m} \simeq\operatorname{Fr}(W_m) \longrightarrow T_{d,m}. \tag{HRI.13} \] These are the full cartesian functors BA.7 and BA.17–BA.18, proved in The moduli stack of bundles, §§1.2–1.5. A basis of sections gives its evaluation quotient, and the original \(G\)-bundle supplies the reduction. An automorphism preserving that quotient is the identity. Thus HRI.13 retains the specified bundle and all arrows.

The right side is the frame torsor of a finite locally free module. On every Zariski open where \(W_m\) has a basis it has a section. The inverse map of HRI.13 therefore gives \[ r|_{T_i}\simeq q_i a_i,\qquad a_i:T_i\to V_i,\quad q_i:V_i\to Y\text{ smooth},\quad V_i\text{ smooth affine}. \tag{HRI.14} \] To obtain \(V_i\), take an affine open of \(\mathscr S_m\) and restrict the inverse image of that open in \(T_i\). The scheme \(\mathscr S_m\) is smooth over \(\mathbf C\), because its map to the smooth stack \(Y\) is smooth; smoothness of \(Y\) is proved in §2.2 of the preceding lesson. Serre generation and vanishing make the loci \(T_{d,m}\) cover \(T\). Quasicompactness then selects a finite collection of affine \(T_i\). Thus \[ T=\bigcup_{i=1}^s T_i \quad\text{has the finite Zariski lifts HRI.14}. \tag{HRI.15} \] No Zariski triviality of a \(G\)-torsor or a finite arc-frame torsor was used. The trivialized torsors in HRI.13 are the ordinary \(GL_{\operatorname{rk}W_m}\) frame torsors.

3.551. Regular Ind inputs on singular Hecke sources

Let \(F\in D(Y)\) satisfy the actual chartwise regular Ind condition: \(q^!F\in\mathscr R_\infty(V)\) on every smooth finite-type affine chart \(q:V\to Y\). Let \(r:T\to Y\) be a finite-type scheme map, and suppose \(T\hookrightarrow M\) is a smooth separated finite-type ambient embedding. On \(T\), the notation \(\mathscr R_\infty(T)\) means the supported ambient regular Ind category of HRI.6, with its canonical graph comparisons. Then its actual inverse image, represented on \(M\), satisfies \[ i_+r^!F\in\mathscr R_\infty(M), \qquad \operatorname{Supp}(i_+r^!F)\subset i(T). \tag{HRI.16} \] Here \(i_+\) denotes the supported ambient realization when \(T\) is singular; the smooth closed-embedding theorem is not applied directly to a singular \(T\).

For the proof take the finite Zariski lifts HRI.14–HRI.15. On \(T_i\), inverse composition identifies \(r^!F\) with \(a_i^!q_i^!F\), with the specified bundle isomorphism of HRI.14. The actual graph model HRI.9 makes this a regular Ind object on an ambient neighbourhood of \(T_i\). Choose ambient opens whose intersections with \(T\) are these \(T_i\), and refine them by finitely many affine opens. Add the complement \(M-T\), where the object is zero. HRI.7 proves global regular Ind membership. The object already has its canonical inverse-image gluing maps; no new infinite Čech descent or boundedness of \(F\) is assumed.

For a bounded regular kernel \(K\) on \(T\) and any integer \(s\), one consequently has \[ \mathcal N_{r,K,s}(F)=r^!F\otimes^!K[s] \in\mathscr R_\infty(T). \tag{HRI.17} \] To check the tensor in ambient terms, for two objects represented on \(M\) use \[ A\otimes^! B=\Delta_M^!(A\boxtimes B) \in D(\mathcal D_M)_{i(T)}. \tag{HRI.18} \] Its support is contained in the intersection of the two base supports. HRI.3 preserves regular Ind membership, and the graph comparisons HRI.11 show independence of the ambient embedding. All determinant lines and shifts are those of the inverse transfer. This is the extraordinary tensor, not a derived tensor over \(\mathcal O_T\).

In particular let \(T\to B\times C\) be a bounded Hecke base change, with its projective finite-frame presentation and smooth projective-bundle ambient, as in Fusion, §2. Write \(i:T\hookrightarrow M\) for this embedding and \(f:M\to B\times C\) for the proper projective-bundle projection. Let \(r\) be the other-bundle map. Its bounded intersection-complex kernel is regular: it is the middle extension of the constant regular connection on the smooth open relative-position stratum. Bounded open images and their subquotients are regular by the four-map theorem and its Serre property. Smooth frame pullback commutes with this middle-extension characterization, so this global intersection complex agrees with the descended Satake kernel, with the prescribed normalization shift. Applying HRI.17 and actual proper direct image gives \[ i_+\mathcal N_{r,K,s}(F)\in\mathscr R_\infty(M), \qquad f_+i_+\mathcal N_{r,K,s}(F) \in\mathscr R_\infty(B\times C). \tag{HRI.19} \] For completeness, the bounded smooth middle-extension comparison just used follows from the strict boundary tests in Intermediate extensions and intersection complexes, §1. On a boundary stratum of dimension \(c\), they are the ordinary stalk bound \(\leq-c-1\) and costalk bound \(\geq-c+1\). A smooth pullback of relative dimension \(d\), normalized as \(q^*[d]\) on sheaves, changes the stratum dimension to \(c+d\) and subtracts \(d\) from both bounds. The actual stalk and costalk comparisons are checked in local smooth product coordinates; extraordinary pullback there is ordinary pullback shifted by \(2d\), with its complex orientation. Both strict bounds and the specified open restriction are consequently preserved. Uniqueness of middle extension gives its actual comparison, and uniqueness also gives the cocycle. The bounded RH comparison transports these maps to the operator modules. Only the bounded kernel is being descended in this argument.

The proper-detection theorem UQD.1–UQD.24 therefore applies to this actual input once its source characteristic witness and the selected-point compatible-set isolation are bound to the same correspondence. This establishes its regular Ind input premise over \(\mathbf C\). It does not establish independent nilpotent regularity, the full supported-generation criterion, or the projector image for arbitrary inputs.

Figure 3.68. HRI.12–HRI.15 provide the frame-atlas lift. HRI.8–HRI.11 identify the actual graph inverse image, and HRI.4–HRI.7 preserve closed base support and both cohomological tails. HRI.17–HRI.19 give the regular kernel-weighted Hecke input. The graph construction retains the nilpotent source scheme while its supported category depends on its closed base support. The bottom row applies closed-support localization, followed by projection.

3.552. Three inverse-image and frame calculations

Exercise 3.GY. For \(i:\{0\}\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1_z\), compute \(i^!\mathcal O_{\mathbf A^1}\), its ambient closed-support realization, and both operations on \(\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}\mathcal O_{\mathbf A^1}[2n]\).

Solution 3.GY. The ordinary derived coefficient pullback of the free connection is \(\mathbf C\). The inverse-image shift is \(0-1=-1\), so \[ i^!\mathcal O_{\mathbf A^1}=\mathbf C[-1], \qquad \Gamma_{\{0\}}\mathcal O_{\mathbf A^1} \simeq\bigl(\mathbf C[z,z^{-1}]/\mathbf C[z]\bigr)[-1] \simeq\delta_0[-1]. \tag{HRI.20} \] The localization inclusion has zero kernel and the displayed quotient, so its fibre has exactly that shift. The quotient is the point module: \(z\) kills \(z^{-1}\), its successive derivatives are \((-1)^r r!z^{-r-1}\), and these span all negative powers. The normal module basis therefore gives the isomorphism with \(\delta_0\). Continuity yields \[ i^!\!\left(\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}\mathcal O[2n]\right) =\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}\mathbf C[2n-1], \qquad \Gamma_{\{0\}}\!\left(\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}\mathcal O[2n]\right) =\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}\delta_0[2n-1]. \tag{HRI.21} \] Both tails occur. No lower-truncation limit was changed into a filtered colimit.

Exercise 3.GZ. Let \(U=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf C[s]/(s^2)\subset\mathbf A^1_s\), and let \(a:U\to\mathbf A^1_t\) send \(t\) to \(s\). Compute HRI.9 for the free connection. Compare it with replacing \(U\) by its reduced point.

Solution 3.GZ. In \(P=\mathbf A^2_{s,t}\) the graph has ideal \[ I_{\Gamma_a}=(s^2,t-s),\qquad \sqrt{I_{\Gamma_a}}=(s,t),\qquad p^!\mathcal O_{\mathbf A^1_t}=\mathcal O_P[1]. \tag{HRI.22} \] The two coordinate localizations compute \(\Gamma_{\{(0,0)\}}\mathcal O_P\) in degree two. Its coefficient quotient has basis \(s^{-r-1}t^{-q-1}\), \(r,q\ge0\), with the normal derivative action. It is \(\delta_{(0,0)}[-2]\). Closed-support localization depends on the radical of the ideal, since the complements and the finite localization refinements are the same. Proper point-image composition, or the normal transfer augmentation, gives \(\pi_+\delta_{(0,0)}=\delta_0\), with coefficient one. Therefore \[ \mathsf T_{\mathbf A^1_s}(a,\mathcal O_{\mathbf A^1_t}) \simeq \pi_+\delta_{(0,0)}[-1] \simeq\delta_0[-1]. \tag{HRI.23} \] The reduced graph gives the same result. This does not identify the classical cotangent of the square-zero scheme, generated by \(ds\) at its point, with the zero cotangent of its reduced point. It identifies their actual supported inverse-image objects. Applying the calculation to all shifts in HRI.21 gives the corresponding two-tail result on \(U\).

Exercise 3.HA. Take \(X=T=\mathbf P^1\), \(G=\mathbf G_m\), and the family \(P=\operatorname{pr}_T^*\mathcal O_T(1)\) on \(X\times T\). Identify HRI.13 with \(m=0\). Explain why local sections suffice despite the absence of a global frame.

Solution 3.HA. The family has degree zero along \(X\). Its section line is \(\pi_{T*}P=\mathcal O_T(1)\), with no positive fibre cohomology; evaluation generates \(P\). The rank-one degree-zero framed quotient of \(\mathcal O_X\) is its identity quotient: on every fibre a surjection between degree-zero line bundles is an isomorphism, and the fibrewise kernel and cokernel vanish by Nakayama. Thus the atlas chart is a point and its pullback is \(\mathcal O_T(1)^\times\). The two usual affine opens of \(\mathbf P^1\) have frames with their usual coordinate transition. There is no global frame: a global section of \(\mathcal O(1)\) is a homogeneous linear form \(aX+bY\), and a nonzero such form vanishes at \([-b:a]\).

For an explicit input let \(F=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}\omega_Y[2n]\), where \(Y=\operatorname{Bun}_{\mathbf G_m}(X)\) and \(\omega_Y\) is the extraordinary tensor unit. Smooth inverse image takes that unit to the unit. Hence \(F\) satisfies the chartwise regular Ind condition. With \(r:T\to Y\) the displayed family, inverse composition gives \[ r^!F=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}\omega_T[2n] =\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^1}[2n+1] \in\mathscr R_\infty(\mathbf P^1). \tag{HRI.24} \] For the structure map \(t:\mathbf P^1\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf C\), HRI.2 gives \(t^!\mathbf C=\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^1}[1]\); this is the extraordinary tensor unit by inverse-image composition. Thus the last shift is exact. The finite two-open Čech complex HRI.7 proves membership from the two local lifts. No compactness of \(\omega_Y\) on the bundle stack, and no global section of its frame pullback, is required.

3.553. The cohomological Hecke criterion for regular Ind inputs

Let \(Y=\operatorname{Bun}_G(X)\), where \(X\) is a smooth projective connected complex curve and \(G\) is connected reductive. An input \(F\) is assumed to satisfy the chartwise regular Ind condition of HRI.16. On a smooth chart \(A\to Y\), use the independent support convention \[ \operatorname{SS}_\infty(F_A) =\bigcup_{\substack{m\in\mathbf Z\\ L\subset H^mF_A\ {\rm coherent}}} \operatorname{Char}(L). \tag{RHC.1} \] There is no closure of this union. Fixed normalization shifts do not change it. Write \(\mathcal N_A\) for the cotangent pullback of the global nilpotent cone, as in NU.4. On an affine bundle chart \(B\) and an affine curve coordinate \(C\), put \[ \Gamma_{\mathrm{rel},B,C}=T^*B\times 0_C,\qquad \Gamma_{\mathrm{nil},B,C}=\mathcal N_B\times 0_C. \tag{RHC.2} \] Here \(0_C\) is the zero section in \(T^*C\).

For the actual one-point functors SH.16, the following are equivalent: \[ \begin{aligned} &\operatorname{SS}_\infty(F_A)\subset\mathcal N_A &&\text{on every smooth affine bundle chart};\\ &\operatorname{SS}_\infty \bigl((\mathrm H_{V_\nu}F)|_{B\times C}\bigr) \subset\Gamma_{\mathrm{rel},B,C} &&\text{for every dominant label }\nu \text{ and every }B,C. \end{aligned} \tag{RHC.3} \] The first condition implies the stronger bound \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{nil},B,C}\) in the second line. The same assertions hold for the RA.2 normalized families and the SH.19 half-twist transport. These are cohomological characteristic conditions on regular Ind inputs. They do not identify a cohomologically supported object with an Ind of bounded supported objects; AIC.17 remains a separate condition.

3.554. Finite witnesses on the identity self-nerve

We first verify that the chart covectors in RHC.1 are genuine stack cotangents. For a smooth map \(u:W\to A\) of relative dimension \(r\), the flat normalized inverse transfer and finite-generator argument of NS.7 and NU.3 give \[ u^\natural=u^![-r],\qquad \operatorname{SS}_\infty(u^\natural K) =du^t\bigl(W\times_A\operatorname{SS}_\infty(K)\bigr). \tag{RHC.4} \] For clarity, a finite coherent submodule of a pulled-back cohomology module has finitely many generators. On affine charts each generator is a finite sum of input sections times coefficient functions. The operator span of the finitely many input sections is coherent and its flat pullback contains those generators. The chain rule makes that pullback stable under every source operator. The induced good filtration gives the upper containment. Pulling a finite input submodule back injectively and applying NS.7 gives the reverse containment. Thus this is equality of actual unions, including both infinite tails.

Let \(q:A\to Y\) be a smooth affine chart, and form \(W=A\times_Y A\), with projections \(p_1,p_2\) and identity section \(\delta:A\to W\). The affine diagonal makes \(W\) affine; it is smooth over \(\mathbf C\). The actual descent comparison identifies \(p_1^\natural F_A\) with \(p_2^\natural F_A\). If \(\alpha\in\operatorname{Char}(L)_a\) is a finite witness, RHC.4 and finite-generator containment provide a finite coherent second witness and a covector \(\beta\) at the same point \(a\), with \[ dp_1^t\alpha=dp_2^t\beta \quad\text{at }\delta(a),\qquad d\delta^t dp_1^t=d\delta^t dp_2^t=\mathrm{id}, \qquad \beta=\alpha. \tag{RHC.5} \] If \(v\in T_aA\) induces the zero bundle deformation, an isomorphism from that deformation to the constant one, reducing to the identity, gives a tangent of \(W\) at \(\delta(a)\) whose projections are \(v,0\). Evaluating RHC.5 on it gives \(\alpha(v)=0\). Smooth lifting makes \(T_aA\to H^1(X,\operatorname{ad}P)\) surjective. The residue-duality calculation HG.2–HG.3 therefore identifies a unique global Higgs covector: \[ \alpha=dq_a^t\xi,\qquad \xi\in H^1(X,\operatorname{ad}P)^* =H^0(X,\operatorname{ad}^*P\otimes\omega_X). \tag{RHC.6} \] This argument concerns each finite witness; it requires neither a group-stable choice of that witness nor a common finite support cone.

The same common-chart argument proves the smooth-stack version of RHC.4. For a smooth scheme map \(r:H\to Y\), at a point \(h\), \[ \bigl(\operatorname{SS}_\infty(r^!F)\bigr)_h =dr_h^t\bigl(\operatorname{SS}_\infty(F)_{r(h)}\bigr). \tag{RHC.7} \] Indeed \(H\times_Y A\) has two smooth projections. RHC.4 transfers finite witnesses both ways, and RHC.6 identifies the input chart covector with its unique stack covector. Equality after the first smooth projection reflects equality on \(H\). For \(Y\times C\) the argument leaves the curve covector unchanged.

3.555. The exact projective Hecke input

Keep the orientation \(\alpha:P_2|_{X-x}\to P_1|_{X-x}\) of HG.1. For a dominant relative-position label \(\nu\), the source over a fixed output is described by the inverse Schubert bound: \[ \mu=-w_0\nu,\qquad Z_\mu\longrightarrow B\times C,\qquad i:Z_\mu\hookrightarrow M,\quad \pi:M\longrightarrow B\times C\text{ proper and smooth}. \tag{RHC.8} \] Here \(M\) is a smooth projective bundle. The actual endpoint construction and its all-coefficient projectivity are SH.13–SH.14. One can see the finite descent directly. In a faithful representation choose a lattice bound \(u^NO^n\subset L\subset u^{-N}O^n\). For \(m\ge2N\), an element \(1+u^mA(u)\), and its inverse, preserve every such lattice. The congruence kernel consequently fixes the entire bound on all coefficient rings. Its finite Plücker representation descends through the output frame torsor to a projective bundle, in which the associated closed Schubert support is \(Z_\mu\). Beauville–Laszlo gluing identifies this scheme, its arrows and its other-bundle map \(r:Z_\mu\to Y\) with the actual bounded correspondence. The open relative-position stratum is smooth.

Let \(d=\dim Y\), take pure-dimensional bundle charts \(U,B\) of dimensions \(a,b\), and write \(e=b+1=\dim(B\times C)\). The kernel specified by SH.15 has the exact normalizations \[ K_U=IC_{\mathcal H_U}[a],\qquad K_{Z_\mu}=IC_{Z_\mu}[b],\qquad \widehat K_{Z_\mu}=IC_{Z_\mu}[b+1]. \tag{RHC.9} \] In the input frame diagram SH.15 is the pullback of \(\omega_U\boxtimes\mathcal F_{1,D}\). Its open coefficient is the constant orbit connection times the constant curve connection, while \(\omega_U=\mathcal O_U[a]\). The two smooth frame maps have the same relative dimension, so their shifts cancel and give the first identity. On the common input/output chart the two shifts are \[ a+(b-d)=b+(a-d). \tag{RHC.10} \] Smooth middle-extension uniqueness, proved in HRI.19, extends the specified open comparison, including its normal-density evaluation, and gives the second identity. RA.2 gives the third. For the unit label these are precisely \(F_B\boxtimes\mathcal O_C\) and \(F_B\boxtimes\omega_C\), as required by SH.18 and RA.3. There is no orbit-dimension shift left over.

The actual SH.14 base-change and SH.17 tensor maps now identify \[ q_{B,C}^!\mathrm H_{V_\nu}(F) \simeq\pi_+i_+\mathcal E_\nu,\qquad \mathcal E_\nu=r^!F\otimes^!IC_{Z_\mu}[b],\qquad i_+\mathcal E_\nu\in\mathscr R_\infty(M). \tag{RHC.11} \] The last assertion is HRI.16–HRI.19. For the normalized family replace \([b]\) by \([b+1]\). All these functors act on the actual unbounded objects. A smooth nonproper atlas of \(Z_\mu\) is not used as the source of the proper direct image.

3.556. Orbit annihilators for the coefficient kernel

At a finite jet level, the bounded spherical IC is strongly equivariant for the smooth finite jet group \(G_m\). We record why its characteristic covectors annihilate the orbit tangents. On a smooth affine representation space, take finite operator generators of a coherent strong module and enclose them in a finite-dimensional rational subrepresentation \(V\), by the finite coaction argument of NU.7. The good filtration \(F_k=\mathcal D_{\le k}V\) is invariant. The strong infinitesimal identity says that each orbit vector field acts by the rational infinitesimal action, so it preserves \(F_k\). Hence \[ \sigma(\zeta)F_k\subset F_k,\qquad \operatorname{symbol}(\sigma(\zeta))\,\operatorname{gr}F=0 \quad(\zeta\in\operatorname{Lie}G_m). \tag{RHC.12} \] This also proves the assertion on a projective Plücker ambient. Pull to its line-frame open in the affine representation, apply open direct image to that affine representation, and take its finitely many coherent cohomology modules. These retain their rational action and strong identity, by the finite transfer and localization models. Apply the affine filtration argument and restrict back. The smooth formula NS.7 reflects the orbit-annihilator assertion on the projective ambient. Thus every stratum, including a boundary orbit, is included. In a curve coordinate the one-point coefficient is external with \(\mathcal O_C\), so its curve covector is zero.

On the actual input frame diagram the source is the smooth pullback specified in SH.17: \[ p^!\bigl(F_U\boxtimes IC_{\mathrm{bd}}\boxtimes\mathcal O_C\bigr) \quad\text{with its specified fixed shifts}. \tag{RHC.13} \] The finite-generator proof of BK.8–BK.9 works with any coherent kernel: finitely many coefficients in the input module lie in a coherent input submodule. The product good filtration over the field gives exact external characteristic support. Consequently every finite source cohomology submodule, after smooth frame comparison, has \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Char}(A_{\mathrm{fr}}) &\subset d\widetilde p^{\,t} \left(\widetilde T_{\mathrm{fr}} \times_{U\times P\times C}\Xi\right),\\ \Xi&=\operatorname{Char}(L_U)\times \operatorname{Char}(IC_{\mathrm{bd}})\times0_C . \end{aligned} \tag{RHC.14} \] locally, for an actual finite \(L_U\subset H^mF_U\). Here \(P\) is the smooth Plücker ambient and \(\widetilde p\) a local smooth ambient lift of the frame map. The next section verifies the fixed-covector comparison for these lifts. The kernel component in this formula annihilates the tangent of the relative-position orbit at that point. Coherent submodules need not themselves be equivariant: their induced filtrations give containment in the enclosing product module.

3.557. Fixed covector tests through the smooth frame diagrams

We spell out the presentation issue in RHC.14. Let a bounded regular module \(A\) on a possibly singular \(Z\) be represented on a smooth ambient, and let \(f:Z\to B\times C\). Fix \(y,\eta\ne0\). Use the universal family \(g_{y,\eta}\) of UQD.1–UQD.7. On any local smooth ambient extension \(\widetilde f\), its exact carrier is \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Supp} C_{g\circ(\mathrm{id}_Q\times\widetilde f)} (\mathcal O_Q\boxtimes A)&=Q\times Z_A(y,\eta),\\ Z_A(y,\eta)&=\{z:f(z)=y,\ d\widetilde f_z^t\eta\in\operatorname{Char}(A)\}. \end{aligned} \tag{RHC.15} \] The bounded RH comparison and proper closed-extension comparison identify the left side with the vanishing cycles of the intrinsic sheaf on \(Z\), for the restriction of the same function. Thus the point set on the right is independent of that ambient extension. This uses closed supports of cycles, not nonzero stalks at every point.

For a smooth source cover \(v:Z'\to Z\), normalized inverse image commutes with these bounded cycles. Indeed smooth local presentations are étale over a product with affine space; analytically they are local products. On such a product the punctured cover, the central unit and its cone are the external products of the original maps with the constant oriented factor. This proves the comparison with its actual maps. Smooth maps are open, so closure of the nonzero-stalk locus pulls back to the closure of its inverse image. Consequently \[ Z_{v^\natural A}(y,\eta)=v^{-1}Z_A(y,\eta). \tag{RHC.16} \] No arbitrary nonproper nearby-cycle base change is used.

A smooth source map and a map to a smooth target admit the ambient lifts needed to use this observation with RHC.14. Locally present the smooth source map as étale over a projection and lift its finitely many equations to the ambient. For the target, choose étale coordinates, lift their functions, and form the étale fibre product with the target coordinate chart. The given map on the closed source defines the required section there; removing the other closed-source sheets gives an étale ambient neighbourhood on which it extends. NS.7 now applies to the lifted smooth map. The graph comparisons HRI.11 and RHC.15 identify this with the original test. This construction does not identify unequal classical cotangent spaces of singular stages.

Apply it to the common input/output charts and their finite frames. A compatible covector of a finite source piece therefore has, on the tangent of its relative-position stratum, the input component from RHC.14; the kernel and curve components vanish on that stratum. RHC.6 descends the input component to a global Higgs covector. If the target covector is the pullback of \((\xi_2,\xi_x)\), the result is \[ \begin{gathered} p_2^*\xi_2+s^*\xi_x=p_1^*\xi_1 \quad\text{on the moving orbit stratum},\\ A_2=\alpha^*A_1\text{ on }X-x,\qquad \xi_x=\operatorname{Res}_{u=0}B(A_2,g^{-1}g')\,dx . \end{gathered} \tag{RHC.17} \] Here both fields are regular on their bundles. To verify the second line, use the complete fixed-point gluing complex HG.4. The stratum tangent is exactly the kernel of \((a_1,a_2,b)\mapsto b-a_1+a_2\bmod(L_1+L_2)\): the local orbit tangent is the image of \(L_1+L_2\), by the all-ring finite orbit calculation. The map onto \(W/(L_1+L_2)\) is surjective. The difference of the two bundle functionals vanishes on its kernel, so factors through that quotient. Evaluation on \((0,w,0)\) and \((w,0,0)\) identifies the factor with the two Laurent expansions. They coincide and annihilate both lattices. HG.8–HG.9 gives their unique compatible global fields. Evaluating the moving direction is exactly the positive-sign discrepancy HG.13. Added smooth chart directions are annihilated, so the equality descends from the common frame chart to this actual gluing groupoid.

3.558. The moving residue of a nilpotent compatible field

This calculation is at complex geometric points. Suppose \(A_1,A_2\) are compatible regular Higgs fields and \(A_2\) is nilpotent. By the Cartan decomposition proved in Orbits and Schubert varieties, §1, write \[ \begin{gathered} g=k_1u^\lambda k_2,\qquad k_1,k_2\in G[[u]],\\ D=\operatorname{Ad}_{k_2}A_2,\qquad \operatorname{Ad}_{u^\lambda}D =\operatorname{Ad}_{k_1^{-1}}A_1\in\mathfrak g[[u]]. \end{gathered} \tag{RHC.18} \] Differentiating this product, invariance of \(B\) moves the first arc derivative to the regular field on the right. The last arc derivative is paired with the regular \(A_2\). Both residues vanish. The middle term therefore gives \[ \operatorname{Res}B(A_2,g^{-1}g') =\operatorname{Res}B(D,d\lambda/u) =B(D(0),d\lambda). \tag{RHC.19} \] For a root of negative \(\lambda\)-weight, regularity of \(\operatorname{Ad}_{u^\lambda}D\) forces its constant coefficient to vanish. Hence, with \(M_\lambda=C_G(\lambda)\), \[ D(0)\in\mathfrak p_\lambda =\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\mathfrak g_n,\qquad D_0=\lim_{s\to0}\operatorname{Ad}_{\lambda(s)}D(0) \in\mathfrak m_\lambda . \tag{RHC.20} \] The limit remains nilpotent, since the nilpotent cone is closed and conjugation invariant. The compatible Jordan decomposition of §3.23 identifies this Levi element as nilpotent in the Levi, with zero central semisimple part. Thus \(D_0\in[\mathfrak m_\lambda,\mathfrak m_\lambda]\). Weight orthogonality and invariance of \(B\) give \[ B(D(0),d\lambda)=B(D_0,d\lambda)=0: \quad B([a,b],d\lambda)=B(a,[b,d\lambda])=0 . \tag{RHC.21} \] This includes central cocharacters and torus factors. The invariant transport HG.10–HG.11 then proves, for every compatible point in RHC.17, \[ \xi_1\in\mathcal N \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \xi_2\in\mathcal N,\qquad \xi_x=0. \tag{RHC.22} \] The statement concerns the reduced geometric characteristic supports in RHC.1. It is not a residue-vanishing identity on all nonreduced coefficient schemes; Exercise 3.HC exhibits that distinction.

3.559. Proper upper bounds with both cohomological tails

Let \(\pi:M\to B\times C\) be proper with \(M\) smooth, and \(A\) bounded regular. If its compatible set at \(y,\eta\ne0\) is empty, RHC.15 gives zero source family cycles. The actual PIC.19 comparison and the product comparison give \[ C_g(\mathcal O_Q\boxtimes\pi_+A) \simeq(\mathrm{id}_Q\times\pi)_+ C_h(\mathcal O_Q\boxtimes A)=0. \tag{RHC.23} \] Normalized cycles are exact on regular holonomic hearts. Applying cohomology, HC and the target universal-family identity therefore yield \[ Z_A(y,\eta)=\varnothing \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \eta\notin\operatorname{Char}H^j(\pi_+A)_y \quad\text{for every }j. \tag{RHC.24} \] This upper implication does not require isolated source points.

Here is the passage to an arbitrary \(E\in\mathscr R_\infty(M)\). The finite Spencer–Čech model PIC.4–PIC.10 gives an interval \([a,b]\) for the cohomology of \(\pi_+\) on heart objects, independent of the input. For a chosen output degree \(n\), truncation triangles give \[ H^n\pi_+E \simeq H^n\pi_+ \bigl(\tau^{\le n-a+1}\tau^{\ge n-b-1}E\bigr). \tag{RHC.25} \] The lower discarded part maps into degrees at most \(n-2\), and the upper discarded part into degrees at least \(n+2\); this proves the comparison, without taking an infinite truncation limit. Each cohomology module of this finite window is a filtered union of global coherent regular submodules. Continuity and exact filtered colimits give \[ H^j\pi_+H^mE =\operatorname{colim}_{A\subset H^mE\ {\rm coherent}} H^j\pi_+A. \tag{RHC.26} \] The condition that every finite submodule have characteristic support in a fixed closed cone \(\Gamma\) is Serre and survives filtered colimits, by NU.2–NU.4. Apply that rule to RHC.26 and then to the finite Postnikov triangles of the window. Thus an upper target cone valid for every finite source cohomology piece is valid in every degree of \(\pi_+E\). No full supported Ind factorization is used.

We will also use the pointwise version. For a fixed covector \(\eta\), the condition that every finite submodule avoid \(\eta\) is Serre: characteristic support in a finite exact sequence is the union of the subobject and quotient supports. It survives filtered colimits because each finite submodule of the colimit is contained in a finite coherent image from a stage. The same finite window argument therefore excludes \(\eta\) from the full output whenever RHC.24 excludes it for every finite source piece. No common target neighbourhood of \(\eta\) is required.

3.560. Nilpotent regular inputs satisfy the curve bound

Assume the first line of RHC.3. The output of RHC.11 is regular Ind on every target chart by HRI.19, and is the restriction of the actual stack Hecke object. RHC.6, applied to \(Y\times C\), makes every finite target characteristic witness horizontal in the bundle-chart directions. Suppose such a witness lies outside \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{nil},B,C}\). It represents a genuine nonzero target covector \(\eta=(\xi_2,\xi_x)\).

For every finite \(A\subset H^m(i_+\mathcal E_\nu)\), RHC.14–RHC.17 would make a compatible point give an actual input Higgs covector in \(\operatorname{SS}_\infty(F)\). It is nilpotent by hypothesis, so RHC.22 forces \(\xi_2\) nilpotent and \(\xi_x=0\). Therefore \[ \eta\notin\Gamma_{\mathrm{nil},B,C} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad Z_A(y,\eta)=\varnothing \quad\text{for every finite source piece }A . \tag{RHC.27} \] The pointwise form of RHC.24–RHC.26 excludes the chosen finite target witness; the individual finite source pieces need not descend to objects on the target stack. Testing closed finite characteristic supports at complex points is sufficient by the programme Nullstellensatz AIC.9. Consequently \[ \operatorname{SS}_\infty \bigl(q_{B,C}^!\mathrm H_{V_\nu}(F)\bigr) \subset\mathcal N_B\times0_C . \tag{RHC.28} \] The argument includes every boundary orbit of the kernel. The actual curve-normalized family has the same support, since it differs by one cohomological shift.

3.561. A nonnilpotent witness and the selected compatible point

Conversely suppose the first line of RHC.3 fails. A finite coherent characteristic difference from \(\mathcal N_A\) has a complex point. RHC.6 gives its global Higgs field. A nonzero invariant section has a point where it is nonzero, again by the affine Nullstellensatz. Choose such an \(x\). The centralizer construction and formal normalization HG.14–HG.16 provide \[ A_1(0)=C,\qquad g_0=u^\lambda,\qquad B(C,d\lambda)\ne0,\qquad \xi_x=B(C,d\lambda)\,dx . \tag{RHC.29} \] Let \(\nu\) be the dominant representative of \(\lambda\) and \(\mu=-w_0\nu\) that of \(-\lambda\). The actual functor is \(\mathrm H_{V_\nu}\), while its fixed-output source is \(Z_\mu\). HG.8 glues the compatible output field \(\xi_2\). Choose an affine output chart with a lift of that bundle and put \[ y=(b,x),\qquad \eta=(dq_B^t\xi_2,\xi_x)\in T_y^*(B\times C),\qquad \xi_x\ne0 . \tag{RHC.30} \]

On the open relative-position stratum, the kernel is the constant connection with its exact shift RHC.9. RHC.7 and BK.13 give actual membership of the pulled target covector. In an ambient open whose intersection with \(Z_\mu\) is this smooth stratum, NS.8 retains all normal covectors. HRI.6 and finite-generator containment then give a global finite coherent source witness: \[ A_0\subset H^{m_0}(i_+\mathcal E_\nu),\qquad d\pi_{z_0}^t\eta\in\operatorname{Char}(A_0). \tag{RHC.31} \] Indeed the ambient cohomology is the union of global coherent regular images. A finite local set of generators lies in one such image; its characteristic containment transfers the witness. There is no closure of an infinite union in this step.

For any finite \(A\subset H^m(i_+\mathcal E_\nu)\), restrict its compatible set near \(z_0\) to this open stratum. RHC.17 places it in the actual fixed-output compatible-Higgs fibre. HG.9 identifies that fibre, with its specified output identification and no extra automorphisms, with the Springer fibre for \(A_2\) in the inverse bound. In the normalized frames the two disc fields are the same Levi series; HG.16 therefore makes \(u^{-\lambda}\) an open reduced point there. Thus \[ z_0\notin Z_A(y,\eta) \quad\text{or}\quad z_0\text{ is isolated in }Z_A(y,\eta) \quad\text{for every finite }A . \tag{RHC.32} \] Other components may be positive dimensional. The assertion is isolation of the selected point, not finiteness of the entire fibre.

3.562. Detection in the actual Hecke output

All hypotheses of UQD.1–UQD.24 now hold for the actual proper ambient map and input in RHC.11: HRI gives regular Ind membership, RHC.31 is a finite source witness, and RHC.32 gives the selected-point condition. The universal quadratic parameter family and its actual full unbounded section retract therefore give \[ L_0\subset H^{n_0} \bigl(q_{B,C}^!\mathrm H_{V_\nu}(F)\bigr) \text{ coherent},\qquad \eta\in\operatorname{Char}(L_0)_y . \tag{RHC.33} \] This is an actual finite target witness. It has nonzero curve component by RHC.30, so it contradicts the second line of RHC.3. We conclude \[ \left[ \operatorname{SS}_\infty \bigl(q_{B,C}^!\mathrm H_{V_\nu}(F)\bigr) \subset T^*B\times0_C\text{ for all }\nu,B,C \right] \Longrightarrow \operatorname{SS}_\infty(F)\subset\mathcal N . \tag{RHC.34} \] Combined with RHC.28 this proves the promised equivalence, with its stronger upper implication: \[ \begin{gathered} \operatorname{SS}_\infty(F)\subset\mathcal N \quad\Longleftrightarrow\\ \text{all one-point IC Hecke outputs satisfy}\\ \text{the cohomological curve bound}. \end{gathered} \tag{RHC.35} \] All genera and bundle components are included. The nonnilpotent construction is invoked only when such an actual witness exists.

3.563. Categorical Hecke-lissity and half twists

The full Hecke-lisse condition HLA.13 implies the curve bound used above. Its curve category is the image of the ind-connection embedding. On a scheme chart, an external product with a finite connection has zero curve covector by its good filtration. The same holds for its Ind extension and for the full tensor-category image: NU.2–NU.4 make the cohomological curve condition stable under triangles and colimits. Thus a regular Ind object in the actual Hecke-lisse subcategory has nilpotent cohomological singular support.

For the established half root \(L\), SH.19 is the actual conjugation \[ \mathrm H^{\,L}_{V_\nu} =\mathcal T_{Y\times X}^{-1} \mathrm H_{V_\nu}\mathcal T_Y . \tag{RHC.36} \] The two intermediate lines cancel through the specified Morita evaluation maps RH.17. On charts their operator changes have order zero, so principal symbols and the support tests are unchanged. The target line is pulled from \(Y\), leaving the curve direction unchanged. Regular Ind membership is transported with the same Morita equivalence. Therefore RHC.28–RHC.35 hold in that convention with their actual maps and all normalization shifts retained.

For objects with no lower bound on a genus-zero curve, the converse from the cohomological curve condition to full categorical Hecke-lissity requires an additional argument. Nor does this theorem prove independent nilpotent regularity, AIC.17 on both tails, or the nilpotent image of a projector on arbitrary inputs. Those require their own arguments. Free further reading for the geometric Hecke comparison is Arinkin–Gaitsgory–Kazhdan–Raskin–Rozenblyum–Varshavsky, §§14.2 and 20.4–20.8. The arguments above supply the proofs used here.

Figure 3.69. The self-nerve identities are RHC.5–RHC.7. The actual kernel and proper map are RHC.8–RHC.11; selected-point survival is RHC.29–RHC.33. The lower panel is the exact addition model RHC.40–RHC.42, with conormal vector \((1,1)\). The geometric nilpotent residue calculation is RHC.18–RHC.22 and its nonreduced limit is Exercise 3.HC.

3.564. Three characteristic and residue calculations

Exercise 3.HB. Let \(G=GL_4\), use the trace pairing, and set \[ C=\operatorname{diag}(2,2,-2,-2)+E_{12}+E_{34},\qquad \lambda=(1,1,-1,-1). \tag{RHC.37} \] For \(A(u)=Cq(u)\,du\), \(q(0)=1\), compute the complementary adjoint inverse, the tangent equations at \(u^\lambda\), and the moving residue.

Solution 3.HB. Write \(N_+=N_-= \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) on the two blocks. On a cross-block \(2\)-by-\(2\) matrix \(T\), the adjoint block is \(4I+D\), where \(D(T)=N_+T-TN_-\). The commuting left and right nilpotent operations square to zero, so \(D^3=0\). Its exact formal inverse and residue are \[ \begin{aligned} \bigl(q(u)(4I+D)\bigr)^{-1} &=q(u)^{-1}\bigl(\tfrac14 I-\tfrac1{16}D+\tfrac1{64}D^2\bigr),\\ \operatorname{Res}B(A,g^{-1}g') &=\operatorname{tr}(C\,d\lambda)=8 . \end{aligned} \tag{RHC.38} \] There are four cross-block root spaces of weight two. Their eight tangent coefficients are the matrices \(u^{-2}T_2+u^{-1}T_1\). The highest negative coefficient first kills \(T_2\) by the invertible constant block; the next then kills \(T_1\). The finite local-ring argument AS.6 gives the open reduced point. For the inverse orbit the constant block is \(-4I+D'\), with inverse \(-I/4-D'/16-(D')^2/64\), and the reversed moving residue is \(-8\). This local field occurs, for example, for a trivial bundle and \(C\omega\) when a chosen global one-form \(\omega\) is nonzero at the chosen point. The example assumes such a form; it does not assert its existence in genus zero.

Exercise 3.HC. For \(G=GL_2\), let \(g=\operatorname{diag}(u^m,1)\), \(m\ge1\), and let \(A_2=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-a\end{pmatrix}du\) over \(\mathbf C[[u]]\). Suppose \(A_2\) is nilpotent and both \(A_2,\operatorname{Ad}_gA_2\) are regular. Compute the residue. Then repeat over \(\mathbf C[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)\) for \(a=\varepsilon,b=1,c=0\).

Solution 3.HC. Regularity requires \(c\in u^m\mathbf C[[u]]\). Nilpotence is \(a^2+bc=0\), hence \(a(0)^2=0\) and \(a(0)=0\) over the field. Therefore \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Res}\operatorname{tr}(A_2g^{-1}g') &=m\,a(0)=0 &&\text{over }\mathbf C,\\ A_{2,\varepsilon} &=\begin{pmatrix}\varepsilon&1\\0&-\varepsilon\end{pmatrix}du,\\ \operatorname{Res}\operatorname{tr}(A_{2,\varepsilon}g^{-1}g') &=m\varepsilon\ne0 &&\text{over }\mathbf C[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2). \end{aligned} \tag{RHC.39} \] In the second line both the trace and determinant are zero and the conjugate field is regular, with upper-right entry \(u^m\). Thus even the invariant nilpotent equations do not give a scheme-theoretic residue-zero identity here. RHC.22 uses geometric points of characteristic support, for which the first line is exact.

Exercise 3.HD. Consider the affine addition model \(a:\mathbf A^2_{z,t}\to\mathbf A^1_x\), \(a(z,t)=z+t\), with target bundle chart \(\mathbf A^1_z\) and curve coordinate \(t\). Take the proper output map to be the identity and the input \(\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}\delta_0[2n]\). Compute both kernel normalizations and their curve covectors.

Solution 3.HD. Put \(u=z+t,v=t\). Smooth inverse transfer adds \([1]\). For the ordinary normalization \(b=1\), the kernel is \(IC_{\mathbf A^2}[1]=\mathcal O_{\mathbf A^2}[1]\), and extraordinary tensor subtracts \([2]\). Thus \[ \mathcal E=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}\delta_{\{z+t=0\}}[2n], \qquad \widehat{\mathcal E} =\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}\delta_{\{z+t=0\}}[2n+1]. \tag{RHC.40} \] The point-normal presentation in these coordinates is \[ \begin{aligned} \delta_{\{z+t=0\}} &=\mathcal D_{\mathbf A^2}/ \bigl(\mathcal D_{\mathbf A^2}(z+t) +\mathcal D_{\mathbf A^2}(\partial_t-\partial_z)\bigr),\\ \operatorname{Char}&=\{z+t=0,\ \xi_t=\xi_z\}. \end{aligned} \tag{RHC.41} \] Indeed \(\partial_v=\partial_t-\partial_z\) at fixed \(u\), and the associated graded module has the free normal symbol \(\xi_u\). The identity output map retains every coefficient. In every even degree the first object has cohomology this line module, and in every odd degree the second does; the other parities vanish. At each point of the line it contains the actual covector \[ dz+dt,\qquad \operatorname{Supp}(\delta_{\{z+t=0\}})=\{z+t=0\},\qquad \xi_t=1\ne0 . \tag{RHC.42} \] Both objects therefore fail the relative cohomological curve bound. This is an exact scheme model of the characteristic mechanism, not an identification of an affine line with a global bundle stack.

3.565. External connection factors in regular complexes bounded below

Let \(B\) be a smooth affine complex scheme and \(X\) a connected smooth projective complex curve. Write \[ \begin{gathered} \mathscr R_B=\operatorname{Ind}D^b_{\mathrm{rh}}(B),\qquad \mathscr I_X=\operatorname{Ind}\mathscr L_X,\\ J_B:\mathscr R_B\otimes\mathscr I_X \longrightarrow\operatorname{Dmod}(B\times X). \end{gathered} \tag{EFC.1} \] The full bounded connection category \(\mathscr L_X\) and its actual operator embedding are RSC.1–RSC.3. In left-module coordinates \(J_B\) is ordinary exterior product. Density side change and the fixed curve shift give the embedding of HLA.13. Shifting an entire curve coefficient does not change its essential image.

For every \(K\in\mathscr R_\infty(B\times X)\) bounded below, we will prove \[ \operatorname{SS}_\infty(K)\subset T^*B\times0_X \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K\in\operatorname{im}J_B . \tag{EFC.2} \] Bounded below means \(H^mK=0\) for all sufficiently negative \(m\); the remaining cohomology modules may be arbitrary ind-regular modules. A simple coherent regular module satisfying this support bound has the more precise form \[ \begin{gathered} N\simeq M_B\boxtimes E_X,\\ M_B\text{ simple regular holonomic},\qquad E_X\text{ an irreducible finite connection}. \end{gathered} \tag{EFC.3} \] The assertion includes modules on singular closed supports. We first prove their product geometry and the specified comparison maps.

3.566. Conic Lagrangians with no curve covectors

Let \(\Lambda\) be an irreducible component of the characteristic variety of a coherent holonomic module on a smooth variety \(V\). The componentwise involutivity and dimension proof in Good filtrations and the characteristic variety, §7 makes \(\Lambda\) Lagrangian on its smooth locus. Let \(Z\) be its projection to \(V\), with reduced structure. This projection is closed: conicity puts \((v,0)\) in \(\Lambda\) for every point over \(v\), so its image is its intersection with the zero section. It is irreducible.

At a general smooth point of \(\Lambda\), the projection has image \(T_zZ\). Indeed in characteristic zero the differential of a dominant map has generic rank equal to the dimension of its image: take a separating transcendence basis of the image's function field, whose independent differentials remain independent in the source. Remove the closed rank-drop locus and the singular loci. For the radial tangent \(e=\sum\xi_i\partial_{\xi_i}\), conicity and the Lagrangian condition give \[ \theta=\sum_i\xi_i\,dv_i,\qquad \omega=\sum_i dv_i\wedge d\xi_i,\qquad \theta(w)=-\omega(e,w)=0\quad(w\in T\Lambda). \tag{EFC.4} \] Consequently the general covector annihilates \(T_zZ\). Both \(\Lambda\) and the closure of the conormal of \(Z_{\mathrm{sm}}\) are irreducible of dimension \(\dim V\). The containment just proved therefore gives \[ \Lambda=\overline{T^*_{Z_{\mathrm{sm}}}V}. \tag{EFC.5} \]

Now set \(V=B\times X\) and suppose \(\Lambda\subset T^*B\times0_X\). At a general smooth point of \(Z\), EFC.5 says that every conormal annihilates the curve tangent, so that tangent is contained in \(TZ\). The projection \(Z\to B\) thus has a one-dimensional generic tangent kernel. Its fibres have dimension at most one. Generic rank in characteristic zero gives \[ W=\operatorname{pr}_B(Z),\qquad \dim Z=\dim W+1,\qquad Z=W\times X . \tag{EFC.6} \] Here \(W\) is closed because \(X\) is proper. The last equality follows because \(Z\) is closed in the irreducible variety \(W\times X\) and has its dimension. We conclude, for finitely many closed \(W_i\subset B\), \[ \operatorname{Char}(N) =\bigcup_i\left(\overline{T^*_{(W_i)_{\mathrm{sm}}}B}\times0_X\right). \tag{EFC.7} \] Thus the finite bound on the \(B\)-cotangents follows from the module's own components; no fixed stratification for all ind-pieces is assumed.

3.567. Splitting an irreducible coefficient on a product open

Assume \(N\) is simple. The simple-object theorem in Intermediate extensions and intersection complexes, §2 and the actual RH comparison identify its irreducible support as \(W\times X\). Remove from \(W_{\mathrm{sm}}\) the proper \(W_i\)'s of EFC.7. On the resulting smooth connected dense open \(U\), Kashiwara's normal formula NS.8 removes precisely the normal conormal factor. The remaining characteristic variety is the zero section of \(U\times X\). The zero-characteristic calculation of §3.1 makes the restricted module a finite connection \(V\) there.

Its local system is irreducible. A nonzero proper connection subobject on this open would, by the heart adjunction for the open immersion, give a nonzero image in \(N\) whose restriction is that proper subobject. Simplicity of \(N\) forbids it. Fix base points. Paths and their homotopies in a product are pairs of paths and homotopies, so \[ \pi_1(U\times X)=\Gamma_U\times\Gamma_X,\qquad \rho_U(\gamma)\rho_X(\delta)=\rho_X(\delta)\rho_U(\gamma). \tag{EFC.8} \] These actions are on the finite-dimensional fibre of \(V\).

Choose a nonzero irreducible \(\Gamma_X\)-submodule \(L\) of least positive dimension. The \(\Gamma_U\)-translates of \(L\) are isomorphic irreducible \(\Gamma_X\)-modules. Their sum is nonzero and invariant under both groups, hence is the whole fibre. Finitely many translates suffice. A finite sum of simple submodules is semisimple: add one at a time, using that its intersection with the preceding sum is either zero or the entire simple module. Thus the fibre is \(L\)-isotypic. An endomorphism of \(L\) is scalar, since over \(\mathbf C\) it has an eigenvalue and its corresponding nonzero kernel is invariant. Evaluation therefore gives an isomorphism \[ U_0=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Gamma_X}(L,V_{(u,x)}),\qquad U_0\otimes L\xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{ev}\ }V_{(u,x)} . \tag{EFC.9} \] The first group acts on \(U_0\), the second on \(L\); evaluation intertwines both. A proper invariant subspace of \(U_0\) would give a proper product-invariant subspace of \(V_{(u,x)}\), so \(U_0\) is irreducible. The proved finite connection/local-system equivalence now turns this specified evaluation into \[ E_U\boxtimes E_X\xrightarrow{\sim}V . \tag{EFC.10} \] The two connections are regular: they are the restrictions of the regular connection \(V\) to the two smooth slices. \(E_X\) is a connection on all of \(X\), not a connection with a deleted point.

3.568. The actual middle-extension comparison

Let \(j:U\hookrightarrow B\) denote the locally closed inclusion and put \[ M_B=j_{!*}E_U,\qquad j_{!*}E_U=\operatorname{im} \bigl(H^0j_!E_U\longrightarrow H^0j_+E_U\bigr). \tag{EFC.11} \] This is an image in the operator heart. Its regularity and comparison with the sheaf intermediate extension are The Riemann–Hilbert correspondence, equations (1.ui)–(1.uk). They apply to singular \(W\) and retain the chosen identification on \(U\).

We verify that \(M_B\boxtimes E_X\) is the required extension of EFC.10. Use a finite boundary stratification in \(B\) for \(M_B\). On a boundary stratum \(S\) of dimension \(s\), the strict stalk and costalk bounds for its perverse realization \(P_B\) are \[ \begin{aligned} i_S^*P_B&\in D^{\le-s-1},\qquad i_S^!P_B\in D^{\ge-s+1},\\ i_{S\times X}^*(P_B\boxtimes L_X[1]) &\in D^{\le-s-2},\\ i_{S\times X}^!(P_B\boxtimes L_X[1]) &\in D^{\ge-s}. \end{aligned} \tag{EFC.12} \] The second line follows by the exact exterior tensor with the local system \(L_X\) and the indicated shift. These are precisely the strict bounds for a stratum of dimension \(s+1\). They exclude all boundary subobjects and quotients. The same assertion on the open is perversity of a local system shifted by its support dimension.

The RH exterior comparison uses its actual evaluation and transfer maps. Consequently \(M_B\boxtimes E_X\) is a regular operator heart object with the prescribed open restriction and no boundary subquotient. The unique middle-extension comparison extends EFC.10: \[ M_B\boxtimes E_X\xrightarrow{\sim}N . \tag{EFC.13} \] The same no-boundary-subquotient characterization proves uniqueness over the given open map. It retains the coefficient's monodromy and the normal-density comparison; it is not only an isomorphism of characteristic sets. This proves EFC.3.

3.569. Full faithfulness and all finite extensions

The functor \(J_B\) in EFC.1 is fully faithful and continuous. Here is a direct mapping-complex verification. The affine operator identity and rectangular descent used in RN.9 give \[ \operatorname{Dmod}(B)\otimes\operatorname{Dmod}(X) \simeq\operatorname{Dmod}(B\times X). \tag{EFC.14} \] The proof of RN.9 also applies when its first factor is affine: that module category is dualizable, while the proper curve category is compactly generated by RN.4. Tensor therefore passes through the two descent diagrams. On every affine rectangle the two sets of vector fields commute and PBW identifies the full operator rings.

More explicitly, bounded coherent \(M,M'\) on \(B\) and bounded connection complexes \(E,E'\) on \(X\) have \[ \begin{aligned} &\operatorname{RHom}_{B\times X}(M\boxtimes E,M'\boxtimes E')\\ &\hspace{1em}\simeq \operatorname{RHom}_B(M,M') \otimes_{\mathbf C}\operatorname{RHom}_X(E,E'). \end{aligned} \tag{EFC.15} \] Take their finite local projective operator resolutions as in RN.4, and the finite ordered affine Čech mapping diagrams of that proof. On a rectangle the tensor–Hom map is the usual finite-projective evaluation. The two bounded resolution directions and the finite Čech directions totalize to both sides of EFC.15, with the same Koszul signs and composition evaluations. This is the displayed map. It does not require internal operator Hom to be quasi-coherent.

The sources are compact in their ind-categories and their exterior products are bounded coherent, hence compact in the full operator category, again by RN.4's finite local mapping proof. The full multi-object free bar therefore extends EFC.15 to \(J_B\), proving full faithfulness on arbitrary objects. The image is stable, closed under colimits and closed under retracts.

Every coherent regular module with the curve bound has a finite composition series, by Holonomic D-modules and duality, Theorem 2.2. Characteristic support is the union in an exact sequence, so each simple factor satisfies the same bound and has EFC.13's form. Each extension triangle lifts through the full \(J_B\), including its actual extension morphism. Induction on length gives \[ N\text{ coherent regular},\quad \operatorname{Char}(N)\subset T^*B\times0_X \quad\Longrightarrow\quad N\in\operatorname{im}J_B . \tag{EFC.16} \] No semisimplicity of \(N\) or of a finite connection is required.

3.570. Ind-regular objects bounded below and their actual maps

Let \(K\) satisfy the left side of EFC.2. By HRI.6 each \(H^mK\) is a filtered union of global coherent regular submodules. Each has the curve bound and so belongs to the image by EFC.16. Full faithfulness lifts the entire filtered diagram, including its paths and compositions. Continuity then gives \[ H^mK=\operatorname*{colim}_{N\subset H^mK\ \mathrm{coherent}}N \in\operatorname{im}J_B . \tag{EFC.17} \] First suppose \(K\) is bounded in both directions. Its finitely many Postnikov triangles also lift through this full stable image. This constructs a preimage with an actual comparison to \(K\).

For a general \(K\) bounded below, each \(\tau^{\le n}K\) is bounded in both directions and has the same finite support conditions. Its actual truncation maps form the direct system \(\tau^{\le n}K\to\tau^{\le n+1}K\to K\). The colimit of this system is \(K\): in each cohomological degree its modules are eventually constant with value \(H^mK\), and filtered colimits are exact. Cohomology detects zero in the actual operator category, so the resulting colimit comparison is an isomorphism. Full faithfulness lifts all these maps and continuity gives a preimage of \(K\). This proves the forward implication of EFC.2 for objects bounded below.

For the reverse implication, exterior products of bounded regular objects and finite connections have zero curve covectors by the product good filtration. Their source compact generators generate the tensor category by the full free bar. The independent support condition is stable under triangles, retracts and all colimits by NU.2–NU.4. Thus, even without boundedness, \[ \operatorname{im}J_B \subset\{K:\operatorname{SS}_\infty(K)\subset T^*B\times0_X\}. \tag{EFC.18} \] This completes EFC.2. Every morphism between the resulting factors is the unique lift of its ambient operator morphism.

3.571. Relative operator coherence on a curve coordinate

There is a useful additional consequence for each finite witness. Let \(C\subset X\) be affine with an étale coordinate \(t\), and write \[ A=\mathcal O(C),\qquad R=D(B)\otimes A,\qquad S=D(B\times C)=R\langle\partial_t\rangle . \tag{EFC.19} \] The commutation rule is \([\partial_t,a]=\partial_t(a)\); the \(B\)-operators commute with \(\partial_t\). With \(B\)-order on \(R\) and total order on \(S\), PBW gives \[ \operatorname{gr}R=\mathcal O(T^*B)\otimes A,\qquad \operatorname{gr}S=(\operatorname{gr}R)[\xi_t]. \tag{EFC.20} \] Both graded rings are noetherian. The leading-symbol induction also makes \(R\) left noetherian: an ascending chain of left ideals has a stabilizing chain of graded ideals; equality of leading symbols then gives equality of the original ideals by descending order.

For a coherent \(S\)-module \(N\) with zero curve characteristic covectors, a good filtration has \[ (\operatorname{gr}N)_{\xi_t}=0,\qquad \xi_t^k\operatorname{gr}N=0\text{ for some }k,\qquad \operatorname{gr}N\text{ finite over }\operatorname{gr}R . \tag{EFC.21} \] The first statement follows from the support bound. A finite generating set gives a common annihilating power. Adjoin its first \(k\) powers of \(\xi_t\) to a finite homogeneous generating set to prove the last statement. Lift a finite homogeneous \(\operatorname{gr}R\)-generating set. Subtracting a lift of any leading symbol lowers the order and terminates at the filtration's lower bound. These lifts generate \(N\) over \(R\). Noetherianity consequently proves \[ N\text{ coherent over }D(B)\otimes A. \tag{EFC.22} \] This is relative operator coherence. It does not assert finite rank over \(A\), and does not assert that the chosen filtration is preserved by \(\partial_t\).

3.572. The actual curve connection gives flatness

The module in EFC.22 is \(A\)-flat. To prove this, localize at a closed point \(c\) of \(C\). Central localization leaves \(R_c\) noetherian, and \(N_c\) is finite over it. The ring \(A_c\) is a DVR, with uniformizer \(u=t-t(c)\) and \(\partial_tu=1\). The connection extends to this localization by the quotient rule.

The \(u\)-power-torsion part \(T\subset N_c\) is an \(R_c\)-submodule. It is finite. If it is nonzero, let \(h\ge1\) be the least exponent with \(u^hT=0\). Differentiating a torsion equation shows \[ u^j n=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u^{j+1}\partial_t n=-j u^j n=0 , \qquad \partial_tT\subset T. \tag{EFC.23} \] For any \(n\in T\), differentiation now gives \[ 0=\partial_t(u^hn) =h u^{h-1}n+u^h\partial_tn=h u^{h-1}n . \tag{EFC.24} \] Since \(h\) is invertible in characteristic zero, this contradicts minimality. Thus \(N_c\) is torsion free over the DVR \(A_c\). A torsion-free module over a DVR is a filtered union of its finite torsion-free, hence free, submodules. Exactness of filtered colimits and tensor proves their union flat. Flatness is local on \(A\), so \[ \begin{gathered} N\text{ is }A\text{-flat},\\ H^mK\text{ is }A\text{-flat if all its finite pieces have the curve bound}. \end{gathered} \tag{EFC.25} \] The second statement follows by their exact filtered union. It applies to both infinite cohomological tails. Its conclusion is flatness, not membership of an arbitrary unbounded \(K\) in the image of \(J_B\).

3.573. Descent of the bounded factors to bundle stacks

Let \(Y=\operatorname{Bun}_G(X)\), and use the full smooth affine chart diagram defining its operator category. Let \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{reg}}\) be the chartwise regular Ind subcategory of HRI.16. The finite inverse-transfer comparisons there preserve these subcategories and their actual descent maps. Hence \[ \mathcal M_{\mathrm{reg}} =\lim_{A\to Y}\mathscr R_A,\qquad \mathcal M_{\mathrm{reg}}\otimes\mathscr I_X \simeq\lim_{A\to Y}(\mathscr R_A\otimes\mathscr I_X). \tag{EFC.26} \] The second equality uses dualizability of \(\mathscr I_X\), proved by its compact full generator model and HLA.17–HLA.18. Tensor with a dualizable category has both adjoints given by tensor with its dual, so preserves these limits.

Suppose \(K\) on \(Y\times X\) is chartwise regular Ind, every \(K|_{A\times X}\) is bounded below, and every finite characteristic witness has zero \(X\)-covector. EFC.2 supplies preimages on all charts. The functors \(J_A\) are full; all transition comparisons and every higher descent path therefore lift uniquely over the given ambient ones. Their spaces of lifts are contractible. EFC.26 supplies the actual global preimage: \[ \begin{gathered} K\in\operatorname{im}J_Y,\\ J_Y:\mathcal M_{\mathrm{reg}}\otimes\mathscr I_X \longrightarrow\operatorname{Dmod}(Y\times X). \end{gathered} \tag{EFC.27} \] The comparison maps agree with those on each chart, not just on their characteristic sets. The shifts in extraordinary chart inverse images are retained; they do not change either essential image.

Inclusion in the full automorphic category gives in particular \[ K\in\mathcal M\otimes\mathscr I_X. \tag{EFC.28} \] Tensoring the full inclusion by the dualizable \(\mathscr I_X\) preserves full faithfulness, so this uses exactly the curve coefficient category of HLA.13.

3.574. The categorical criterion for regular inputs locally bounded below

Assume \(F\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{reg}}\) and that every smooth affine bundle-chart restriction of \(F\) is cohomologically bounded below. For each fixed label \(\nu\) and output chart \(B\), its actual Hecke output is bounded below on \(B\times X\). Here the finite projective source \(Z_\mu\), \(\mu=-w_0\nu\), matters. HRI.14–HRI.19 gives a finite Zariski cover with lifts into input bundle charts. On each member the graph inverse transfer is computed by finite normal-localization and Spencer directions. The bounded IC tensor has finite amplitude on a smooth ambient: its derived coefficient tensor has finite flat length there. Finally PIC.4–PIC.10 uses finite Spencer and finite Čech directions for proper output. Thus each fixed finite diagram has lower bounds \[ \begin{gathered} H^jF_{U_i}=0\ (j<a_i),\\ H^j\bigl((\mathrm H_{V_\nu}F)|_{B\times X}\bigr)=0 \ (j<c_\nu). \end{gathered} \tag{EFC.29} \] One obtains the second lower bound by adding the finite lower operation bounds on each input-cover member and taking their minimum. A finite affine coordinate cover of \(X\) makes the same conclusion global over \(B\times X\). No uniform bound over all labels or all bundle charts is asserted.

For a nilpotent \(F\), RHC.28 supplies the stronger output bound \(\mathcal N_B\times0_X\). HRI supplies regular Ind membership. EFC.27–EFC.28 and EFC.29 therefore give the full HLA.13 condition. Conversely that condition implies the cohomological curve bound by RHC.36 and hence nilpotent support by RHC.34. We have proved, under the stated local lower boundedness and regular Ind hypotheses, \[ \begin{gathered} F\in\mathcal M^{\mathrm{Hl}} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{SS}_\infty(F)\subset\mathcal N,\\ \operatorname{SS}_\infty\bigl((\mathrm H_{V_\nu}F)|_{B\times X}\bigr) \subset\mathcal N_B\times0_X . \end{gathered} \tag{EFC.30} \] The second line is the upper assertion for a nilpotent input. Every genus, bundle component and connected reductive group is included. Fixed curve normalization and the actual SH.19 Morita conjugation preserve this assertion: \[ \widehat{\mathrm H}_{V_\nu}F=(\mathrm H_{V_\nu}F)[1], \qquad \mathrm H^L_{V_\nu} =\mathcal T_{Y\times X}^{-1}\mathrm H_{V_\nu}\mathcal T_Y . \tag{EFC.31} \] The first shift is RA.2; the second uses RH.17's specified intermediate line evaluations. Their principal symbols leave the curve direction unchanged, and their full functor maps give the same lifted factors.

3.575. The generated class and the remaining unbounded comparison

Let \(\mathcal T\) be the smallest full stable colimit-closed subcategory of \(\mathcal M\) containing all chartwise regular Ind objects locally bounded below, with nilpotent cohomological support. Then \[ \begin{gathered} \mathcal T\subset \mathcal M^{\mathrm{Hl}}\cap\mathcal M_{\mathrm{reg}},\\ \operatorname{SS}_\infty(\mathcal T)\subset\mathcal N . \end{gathered} \tag{EFC.32} \] For the Hecke condition this follows from EFC.30 and the full colimit-closed kernel description HLA.13. Regular Ind membership is closed under colimits and triangles on charts. The nilpotent cohomological support condition has the same property by NU.2–NU.4. Thus EFC.32 includes constructions unbounded in both directions, provided their stated colimit presentation is given.

It is a separate assertion that every cohomologically nilpotent regular Ind object belongs to this generated class: \[ \{F\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{reg}}: \operatorname{SS}_\infty(F)\subset\mathcal N\} \ \subset\ \mathcal T . \tag{EFC.33} \] The proof of EFC.2 uses finite Postnikov towers followed by a direct colimit of truncations bounded in both directions. For an object with no lower bound, those same upper truncations need not be bounded in both directions. This does not prove EFC.33 by passing to an inverse limit. Likewise the coefficient categories \[ \mathscr I_X \longrightarrow\mathscr Q_X =\lim_n\mathscr I_X^{\ge-n} \tag{EFC.34} \] retain their distinction from RSC.1. No equality is substituted for this map. AIC.17's full supported factorization, independent nilpotent regularity and equality with all independently nilpotent-supported objects retain their requirements. GFP.55–GFP.56 give original-field enhanced generation and regular nilpotent landing for arbitrary projector inputs.

Free further reading for external products with characteristic constraints is Arinkin–Gaitsgory–Kazhdan–Raskin–Rozenblyum–Varshavsky, Appendices E.7–E.9 and F.9. The conormal, representation, middle-extension, finite-extension and descent arguments used here are given above.

Figure 3.70. The product components are EFC.4–EFC.7, the evaluation and middle-extension map are EFC.9–EFC.13, and their full mapping comparison is EFC.15. The cross is the real coordinate section of the complex characteristic variety in EFC.40. The coefficient square records the two commuting nilpotent parts of EFC.35–EFC.37. Relative curve flatness is EFC.23–EFC.25. The two-tail example EFC.41 is given by an actual exterior-product object, with no inference of EFC.33.

3.576. Three external-factor calculations

Exercise 3.HE. Let \(B=\mathbf G_m\) and let \(X\) be an elliptic curve. A rank-two coefficient on \(B\) has monodromy \(I+N\), \(N=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\). A coefficient on \(X\) has monodromies \(I+N,I\) on its two generators. Compute the two nontrivial monodromies on their exterior product, in the ordered basis \(e_{11},e_{12},e_{21},e_{22}\), including their mixed coefficient.

Solution 3.HE. The elliptic relation is a commutator, so the indicated matrices define its local system. The finite regular connection exists by the proved finite connection/local-system equivalence. This does not assert that its underlying bundle is trivial. The exterior monodromies are \[ \begin{gathered} A=I+P,\quad P=E_{13}+E_{24},\\ B_1=I+Q,\quad Q=E_{12}+E_{34},\quad B_2=I . \end{gathered} \tag{EFC.35} \] Direct multiplication gives \[ P^2=Q^2=0,\qquad PQ=QP=E_{14},\qquad AB_1=B_1A=I+P+Q+E_{14}. \tag{EFC.36} \] Thus the corner coefficient is nonzero. In particular the product of the two inverse unipotent monodromies is \[ A^{-1}B_1^{-1}=I-P-Q+E_{14}. \tag{EFC.37} \] The common evaluation is the tensor-basis map. Both rank-two factors are nonsplit, and their tensor is not claimed to be irreducible. EFC.16 includes their extensions with these actual mixed coefficients.

Exercise 3.HF. Take \(B=\mathbf A^1_z\) and \(M=D_B/D_B(z\partial_z-\tfrac12)\). Let \(E\) be an irreducible finite connection on \(X\). Compute a basis and the characteristic variety of \(M\boxtimes E\), and check the boundary factor.

Solution 3.HF. The module is the regular Kummer connection extended across zero: \[ M=\mathbf C[z,z^{-1}]e,\qquad v_n=z^ne,\qquad z v_n=v_{n+1},\quad \partial_zv_n=(n+\tfrac12)v_{n-1}\quad(n\in\mathbf Z). \tag{EFC.38} \] These relations give a map from the cyclic presentation. Ordered Weyl monomials reduce to these vectors, while their Laurent realizations are linearly independent, proving the presentation. Every nonzero finite sum yields one weight vector by polynomial interpolation in \(z\partial_z\). The nonzero coefficients \(n+\tfrac12\), together with multiplication by \(z\), reach every \(v_n\). Hence \(M\) is simple and is its own middle extension from \(\mathbf G_m\). The logarithmic connection has residues \(\tfrac12\) and \(-\tfrac12\) at zero and infinity, so it is regular.

For the order filtration, multiplication by the single defining operator is strict, since the symbol ring is a domain and its leading symbol is \(z\xi_z\). Therefore \[ \operatorname{gr}M =\mathbf C[z,\xi_z]/(z\xi_z). \tag{EFC.39} \] The product filtration with the connection gives \[ \operatorname{Char}(M\boxtimes E) =\bigl(\{\,\xi_z=0\,\}\cup\{\,z=0\,\}\bigr)\times0_X . \tag{EFC.40} \] Both the zero section and the boundary conormal occur. The extension is \(J_B(M,E)\), so that boundary component does not obstruct an actual external connection factor.

Exercise 3.HG. On \(B=\mathbf A^1_z\), compute the relative operator generators and the curve rank for \[ \begin{aligned} N&=\delta_{z=0}\boxtimes E,\\ K&=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}N[2n]\\ &=J_B\left(\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}\delta_{z=0}[2n],E\right). \end{aligned} \tag{EFC.41} \] Here \(E\) is any nonzero finite connection on \(X\).

Solution 3.HG. On a curve coordinate \(C\) with a bundle frame for \(E\), the Weyl normal basis gives \[ \begin{aligned} N|_{B\times C}&=\bigoplus_{r\ge0}E_C\,\partial_z^r,\\ \operatorname{Char}(N)&= \{z=0,\ \xi_z\ \mathrm{arbitrary}\}\times0_X . \end{aligned} \tag{EFC.42} \] A finite basis of \(E_C\) generates over \(D(B)\otimes\mathcal O(C)\); all normal derivatives are supplied by \(D(B)\). As a curve module it is free of infinite rank. The fibrewise normal basis proves its independence and agrees with EFC.25's flatness. In every even cohomological degree \(K\) has this module, and in odd degrees it has zero cohomology. Continuity of \(J_B\) proves the actual equality in EFC.41, including both infinite tails. It is this exhibited exterior-product presentation that proves membership in its image.

3.577. Actual operator Postnikov limits on affine charts

Let \(T\) be a smooth separated complex scheme of finite type. All operator complexes have quasi-coherent underlying structure modules. We first prove effectivity of compatible lower-truncation towers: \[ \begin{gathered} K_n\in\operatorname{Dmod}(T)^{\ge-n},\qquad K_n\simeq\tau^{\ge-n}K_{n+1} \quad\Longrightarrow\\ K=\lim_nK_n,\quad \tau^{\ge-n}K\simeq K_n . \end{gathered} \tag{PAC.1} \] The specified transition maps and all their paths are retained. For an affine \(T\), the full category is \(\operatorname{Mod}_{D(T)}\), as in KF.8. Its module products are exact. The actual homotopy limit of a tower is \[ \lim_nK_n= \operatorname{Fib}\left( \prod_nK_n\xrightarrow{\,1-\mathrm{shift}\,}\prod_nK_n\right). \tag{PAC.2} \] An inverse sequence is freely generated by its adjacent arrows. A cone is a family of maps to its terms with paths identifying the adjacent composites; composing those paths supplies the higher compatibilities. Its mapping-space limit is therefore the homotopy equalizer of identity and shift on the product. In a stable category that equalizer is the fibre of their difference, which proves PAC.2 with the original maps. Here shift uses the original transition \(K_{n+1}\to K_n\). Exact products identify the cohomology of either product with the product of the cohomology modules. The long exact sequence gives \[ \begin{gathered} 0\longrightarrow \operatorname{coker}\left(1-\mathrm{shift}: \prod_nH^{q-1}K_n\to\prod_nH^{q-1}K_n\right) \longrightarrow H^q(\lim_nK_n)\\ \longrightarrow \ker\left(1-\mathrm{shift}: \prod_nH^qK_n\to\prod_nH^qK_n\right) \longrightarrow0 . \end{gathered} \tag{PAC.3} \] Each cohomology sequence is eventually a sequence of isomorphisms. For such a sequence \(A_{n+1}\xrightarrow{f_n}A_n\), solve \(a_n-f_na_{n+1}=b_n\) by choosing \(a_N=0\) on an isomorphism tail, recursing forward with \(f_n^{-1}\), and then backward through the finitely many earlier terms. Thus the cokernel in PAC.3 is zero. Its kernel is the stable value. This proves PAC.1 on affines. The same calculation recovers every actual module from its truncations. It proves a natural comparison, without changing the tower to an unrelated sequence of representatives.

3.578. Flat restriction and effective operator descent

For an affine open immersion \(V\hookrightarrow U\), inverse transfer has relative dimension zero. Its underlying module operation is flat coefficient localization and exact affine sections. This is the normalized inverse-transfer calculation of NS.7 and RN.1. Consequently restriction is t-exact on all module complexes. For a tower as in PAC.1 the natural comparison is an isomorphism: \[ (\lim_nK_n)|_V\xrightarrow{\sim}\lim_n(K_n|_V). \tag{PAC.4} \] Indeed PAC.3 computes the cohomology of both limits as their stable cohomology values. Exact restriction takes that stable value to the stable value of the restricted sequence. The comparison induces precisely that identity. This proof does not say that restriction preserves arbitrary products.

Choose a finite affine cover of \(T\). All finite intersections are affine by separatedness. The actual full descent equivalence is D-modules on stacks, ind-schemes and the de Rham prestack, §§1–2, with the same operator and transfer maps as KF.8–KF.9. Take the affine limit of the tower on each intersection. PAC.4 identifies their restrictions; functoriality of limits carries all the original overlap paths and higher compatibilities. These objects glue to an actual \(K\) on \(T\).

For an arbitrary test object \(A\), mapping descent and the universal property of limits give \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Map}_T(A,K) &\simeq\lim_{\check C(U)} \lim_n\operatorname{Map}_{U_H}(A|_{U_H},K_n|_{U_H})\\ &\simeq\lim_n\operatorname{Map}_T(A,K_n). \end{aligned} \tag{PAC.5} \] Limits over two indexing categories commute because both classify the same compatible cones. Thus the glued object is the global limit. Truncations and cohomology are tested on these exact open restrictions, so the affine comparison gives globally \[ \operatorname{Dmod}(T) \xrightarrow{\sim} \lim_n\operatorname{Dmod}(T)^{\ge-n}. \tag{PAC.6} \] This is effectivity and the full mapping-space statement. No interchange of localization with an arbitrary product was used.

3.579. Realizing the completed curve category

Fix the smooth projective connected complex curve \(X\). Retain the full categories \(\mathscr I_X,\mathscr Q_X\) of RSC.1. In this construction use its t-exact left-module embedding \(i_X:\mathscr I_X\to D_X=\operatorname{Dmod}(X)\), which sends a degree-zero connection to that connection in degree zero.
