The final inclusion is into independent nilpotent support; its converse is a separate statement.

3.611. Exercise and solution: a conjugate algebraic connection

Exercise 3.HM. Let \(E\) be the projective curve and differential \[ Y^2Z=X^3-XZ^2,\qquad x=X/Z,\ y=Y/Z,\qquad \omega=\frac{dx}{2y}. \tag{GFP.57} \] Check smoothness and regularity of \(\omega\), including infinity. For transcendental \(\alpha\in\mathbf C\), construct a countable field model of \(d+\alpha\omega\) and compute its conjugate under \(\alpha\mapsto2\alpha\).

Solution 3.HM. In the affine part, the possible branch points have \(y=0\) and \(x=0,1,-1\). There \(3x^2-1\ne0\), and \(\omega=dy/(3x^2-1)\) is regular. Away from them \(y\) is invertible. The same derivatives prove affine smoothness. The unique point at infinity is \([0:1:0]\), where the derivative of the equation with respect to \(Z\) is nonzero.

On \(Y=1\) put \(u=X/Y,v=Z/Y\). Direct differentiation gives \[ v=u^3-uv^2,\qquad (1+2uv)\,dv=(3u^2-v^2)\,du,\qquad \omega=-\frac{du}{1+2uv}. \tag{GFP.58} \] The denominator is a unit at \((0,0)\), so the differential is regular and nonzero there. For the last equality substitute \(x=u/v,y=1/v\) into \(dx/(2y)\) and use \(u^3=v+uv^2\).

Over the countable field \(k_0=\mathbf Q(\alpha)\), the trivial line has the algebraic connection \[ \nabla_\alpha(f e)=(df+\alpha\omega f)e,\qquad \sigma(\alpha)=2\alpha,\qquad \nabla_{\alpha,\sigma}=d+2\alpha\omega . \tag{GFP.59} \] Transcendence makes this field embedding well defined. The curve and differential are defined over \(\mathbf Q\), so they are unchanged. On a smooth curve every two-form is zero; hence the curvature vanishes. The degree-zero good filtration of this finite line bundle has no positive symbol action: \[ \nabla_\alpha^2=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ch}(\mathcal O_E,\nabla_\alpha)=0_E, \qquad \operatorname{Ch}(\mathcal O_E,\nabla_{\alpha,\sigma})=0_E . \tag{GFP.60} \] The conjugation concerns algebraic coefficient matrices. It makes no assertion about applying \(\sigma\) to analytic periods or exponentials of those periods.

3.612. Exercise and solution: a new submodule inside an old finite extension

Exercise 3.HN. On the affine line let \[ \delta=D/Dz,\quad M=\delta\oplus\delta,\quad K=\mathbf C(u),\qquad A=\{(m,um):m\in\delta_K\}\subset M_K . \tag{GFP.61} \] Show that \(A\) is a coherent new-field operator submodule which does not descend as a submodule of \(M\). Compute its characteristic support and relate it to GFP.10.

Solution 3.HN. Both component actions commute with multiplication by \(u\). Thus the graph is an actual submodule isomorphic to \(\delta_K\), and the multiplicity-space projector is \[ e(u)=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\u&0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad e(u)^2=e(u),\qquad \operatorname{im}e(u)=K(1,u). \tag{GFP.62} \] In the normal basis \(z\partial^j\delta=-j\partial^{j-1}\delta\). Every submodule of \(\delta^2\) is \(\mathbf C[\partial]\otimes W\) for a subspace \(W\subset\mathbf C^2\). Indeed the operator \(-\partial z\) acts on the finitely many degrees of any vector by the distinct integers \(j\). Polynomial interpolation extracts each homogeneous component; applying \(z^j\) extracts its constant coefficient. These coefficients lie in \(W=\ker z\) of the submodule, and \(\partial\) recovers all their normal monomials. In particular descent of \(A\) would require \[ W\otimes_{\mathbf C}K=K(1,u),\qquad W=\mathbf C(a,b),\quad a\ne0,\qquad u=b/a\in\mathbf C , \tag{GFP.63} \] contradicting transcendence.

The extended old finite module \(M_K\) nonetheless contains \(A\). Its order filtration restricts to the usual filtration on \(\delta_K\), giving \[ \operatorname{gr}A=K[\xi],\quad z=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ch}(A)=T^*_{\{0\}}\mathbf A^1_K =\operatorname{Ch}(M)_K . \tag{GFP.64} \] Thus support control requires containment in an extended finite old module, as GFP.10 proves. Descent of the new submodule itself is unnecessary. The cone in this example is the indicated cotangent fibre, not a claim about the global nilpotent cone of a bundle stack.

3.613. Holonomic coefficients with no curve covectors

Let \(X/\mathbf C\) be a smooth projective connected curve, of any genus, and let \(B\) be smooth affine of finite type. Use left operator modules and ordinary exterior products. Write \[ \begin{gathered} \mathscr H_B=\operatorname{Ind} \bigl(D^b_{\mathrm{hol}}(\mathcal D_B)\bigr),\\ \mathscr I_X=\operatorname{Ind}(\mathscr L_X),\qquad \mathscr Q_X=\lim_n\mathscr I_X^{\ge-n}. \end{gathered} \tag{HCF.1} \] Here the bounded holonomic category is the full subcategory of bounded operator complexes with holonomic cohomology. This notation does not identify it with an abstract bounded derived category of its heart. The curve categories and the full realization of \(\mathscr Q_X\) are those of RSC.1 and PAC.8–PAC.12.

For a simple holonomic module there is a precise factorization: \[ \begin{gathered} N\text{ simple holonomic},\quad \operatorname{Char}(N)\subset T^*B\times0_X\\ \Longrightarrow\quad N\simeq M_B\boxtimes L,\\ M_B\text{ simple holonomic},\quad L\text{ an irreducible finite connection on all of }X . \end{gathered} \tag{HCF.2} \] Regularity of \(M_B\) is not a premise or a conclusion. We will also prove the actual external-category membership \[ \begin{gathered} K\text{ bounded below},\quad H^mK\text{ ind-holonomic},\quad \operatorname{SS}_\infty(K)\subset T^*B\times0_X\\ \Longrightarrow\quad K\in\operatorname{im}\bigl(\mathscr H_B\otimes\mathscr I_X \longrightarrow\operatorname{Dmod}(B\times X)\bigr). \end{gathered} \tag{HCF.3} \] Ind-holonomic means that every coherent submodule is holonomic. For objects with this cohomological condition and both infinite tails, the corresponding exact criterion is \[ \begin{gathered} \operatorname{SS}_\infty(K)\subset T^*B\times0_X\\ \Longleftrightarrow\quad K\in\operatorname{im}\bigl(\operatorname{Dmod}(B)\otimes\mathscr Q_X \longrightarrow\operatorname{Dmod}(B\times X)\bigr). \end{gathered} \tag{HCF.4} \] The proof will retain the full operator action and all maps, not only the cohomology modules.

3.614. Proper horizontal Hom has a finite connection on the base

Let \(U\) be smooth connected and let \(V\) be a finite connection on \(U\times X\). No condition is imposed at a compactification of \(U\). For a finite connection \(L\) on \(X\), put \[ \begin{gathered} W=p_X^*L^\vee\otimes V,\qquad C_L(V)=Rp_{U,*}\operatorname{DR}_{X}(W),\\ \operatorname{DR}_{X}(W)= [\,W\xrightarrow{\nabla_X}W\otimes p_X^*\Omega_X^1\,], \qquad\text{degrees }0,1 . \end{gathered} \tag{HCF.5} \] This is the ordinary relative de Rham complex. With the direct-image normalization of Direct images and the relative de Rham complex, §6, its degree-zero cohomology is \[ M_L(V)=H^0C_L(V)=H^{-1}p_{U,+}W . \tag{HCF.6} \] In particular it is not degree zero of the shifted operator direct image.

Each term of HCF.5 is coherent over the structure sheaf. Properness of \(p_U\), and Coherence of higher direct images under proper morphisms, Theorem 4.1, make the finitely many terms of its hypercohomology spectral sequence coherent on \(U\). A finite affine cover of \(X\) gives a bounded Čech–de Rham totalization, so there are only finitely many possible total degrees. It follows that every \(H^qC_L(V)\) is coherent.

The product gives a specified horizontal action of base vector fields. For a base field \(\xi\) and a curve field \(\eta\), integrability gives \[ [\nabla_\xi,\nabla_\eta]=0,\qquad \nabla_\xi(a s)=\xi(a)s+a\nabla_\xi(s). \tag{HCF.7} \] Thus the base action commutes with the relative differential and the Čech maps, and induces an integrable connection on every cohomology module. The Taylor and coherent-connection argument of §3.1 makes a coherent module with this connection locally free. Consequently \[ H^qC_L(V)\in\operatorname{Conn}_{\mathrm f}(U) \quad\text{for every }q. \tag{HCF.8} \] This proof uses proper coherent image and the actual connection operators; it uses no regularity assertion for \(V\) along \(U\).

3.615. Fibre comparison and the actual evaluation map

Work on an affine open \(\operatorname{Spec}A\subset U\), and take a finite affine cover of the separated curve \(X\). All finite intersections are affine. Sections of the terms of HCF.5 on these products are flat over \(A\): their coordinate rings are flat over \(A\), and the coefficient bundles are finite projective on each affine product. Therefore the bounded total complex \(C\) is a complex of flat \(A\)-modules and has the termwise comparison \[ C\otimes_A^L A' \simeq C\otimes_A A' \simeq C_L(V)_{A'} \quad\text{for every }A\text{-algebra }A'. \tag{HCF.9} \] The last complex is the actual relative Čech–de Rham complex of the pulled-back bundle. Its relative connection is defined after any such change of base.

After shrinking the base, the finitely many modules \(H^qC\) are finite projective, by HCF.8. Choose cycle lifts of their projective generators. Projectivity lifts the identity of \(H^qC\) to an \(A\)-linear map into the cycles, and hence gives a quasi-isomorphism \[ \bigoplus_q H^qC[-q]\longrightarrow C . \tag{HCF.10} \] Only finitely many terms occur. Both sides are K-flat: the first is a bounded projective complex, the second a bounded flat complex. Tensoring the comparison therefore computes derived tensor. Taking its cohomology proves base change for each \(H^qC\). In particular, for every complex point \(u\), \[ M_L(V)_u \simeq H^0_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,L^\vee\otimes V_u) =\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal D_X}(L,V_u). \tag{HCF.11} \] The final equality follows directly from the degree-zero cocycle condition: it is a global horizontal section of the Hom bundle. The auxiliary \(A\)-linear splitting HCF.10 is used only for base change. No splitting compatible with the base connection is asserted.

A section of \(M_L(V)\) is a relative horizontal map from \(L\). Evaluating such sections gives \[ \mathrm{ev}:p_U^*M_L(V)\otimes p_X^*L \longrightarrow V . \tag{HCF.12} \] The Leibniz connection on Hom makes this map compatible with the base derivatives. Relative horizontality makes it compatible with the curve derivatives. It is thus a map of the actual connections on \(U\times X\). Formula HCF.11 identifies each fibre with the usual evaluation of horizontal maps.

3.616. Splitting a simple algebraic connection

Assume now that \(V\ne0\) is simple as an algebraic connection on \(U\times X\). Choose a complex point \(u_0\). Finite connections on \(X\) form an abelian category: submodules and quotients of a finite bundle are coherent, and the connection theorem makes them locally free. A proper nonzero subquotient has strictly smaller positive rank. Hence \(V_{u_0}\) contains a simple finite connection \(L\).

Its endomorphisms are finite dimensional, since \[ \operatorname{End}_{\mathcal D_X}(L) \subset H^0(X,L^\vee\otimes L), \qquad \dim_{\mathbf C}H^0(X,L^\vee\otimes L)<\infty . \tag{HCF.13} \] Finiteness is proper coherent cohomology. A nonzero endomorphism of a simple object is invertible. Each element of this finite division algebra has a complex eigenvalue under left multiplication; subtracting that scalar cannot be invertible. It must be zero. Thus \[ \operatorname{End}_{\mathcal D_X}(L)=\mathbf C . \tag{HCF.14} \] For any finite connection \(E\) on \(X\), evaluation \[ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal D_X}(L,E)\otimes L\longrightarrow E \quad\text{is injective}. \tag{HCF.15} \] Indeed a finite direct sum of copies of a simple object is semisimple. One elementary proof is induction on the number of summands: a simple subobject has a nonzero projection to one summand, which splits it; quotient by it and continue. If the evaluation from a basis of Hom had nonzero kernel, that kernel would contain a copy of \(L\). Its component maps would be scalars by HCF.14, giving a nonzero linear relation among that basis. This is impossible.

Apply HCF.15 to every \(V_u\). HCF.11 shows that HCF.12 is injective on all fibres. A map of finite vector bundles with injective fibres is locally a split injection: an appropriate maximal minor is a unit near each point. Thus its image is a subbundle with connection. It is nonzero at \(u_0\), so it is a nonzero subconnection of the simple \(V\). Therefore \[ M_L(V)\boxtimes L\xrightarrow{\sim}V . \tag{HCF.16} \] Any nonzero proper subconnection of \(M_L(V)\) would give one of \(V\); hence \(M_L(V)\) is simple. The splitting is the specified evaluation map, rather than an identification obtained from topological monodromy.

3.617. The product open of a simple holonomic module

Let \(N\) satisfy the hypotheses of HCF.2. Componentwise involutivity, generic rank and conic isotropy give EFC.4–EFC.7. Their proof applies to every holonomic module: it uses the Lagrangian property, not regular singularities. Thus \[ \operatorname{Char}(N)= \bigcup_i\bigl(\overline{T^*_{(W_i)_{\mathrm{sm}}}B}\times0_X\bigr). \tag{HCF.17} \] By Preservation of holonomicity and minimal extensions, Theorem 5.1, the support of a simple holonomic module is irreducible. Here it is \(W\times X\), for one closed irreducible \(W\subset B\). Remove the singular locus of \(W\) and its intersections with the proper \(W_i\)'s. On a nonempty smooth connected open \(U\) of \(W\), supported Kashiwara removes the normal conormal factor. The remaining module has zero characteristic variety, so \[ N|_{U\times X}=V,\qquad V\text{ a nonzero finite connection on }U\times X . \tag{HCF.18} \] Restriction here includes Kashiwara's inverse on the smooth support, with its actual normal line and shift.

The connection \(V\) is simple. Restriction of a simple holonomic module to a nonempty open in its support remains simple: a proper nonzero subobject would give, by the heart shriek adjunction, a nonzero map to the original simple module. That map is surjective; restriction would make the proper subobject surject onto the whole restriction. This contradiction, and exact supported Kashiwara, prove the assertion. HCF.16 now gives \[ V\simeq E_U\boxtimes L,\qquad E_U=M_L(V)\text{ simple finite on }U . \tag{HCF.19} \] For \(j:U\hookrightarrow B\) put \[ M_B=j_{!*}E_U . \tag{HCF.20} \] The arbitrary holonomic minimal-extension theorem, not a regular Riemann–Hilbert comparison, defines this module.

3.618. Middle extension commutes with the finite curve factor

Let \(g=j\times\operatorname{id}_X\). The actual comparisons are \[ \begin{aligned} (j_*E_U)\boxtimes L&\simeq g_*(E_U\boxtimes L),\\ (j_!E_U)\boxtimes L&\simeq g_!(E_U\boxtimes L). \end{aligned} \tag{HCF.21} \] To prove the first, factor the locally closed map into a closed embedding and an open immersion. Closed transfer is the finite normal operator formula and commutes with the independent finite connection. Open transfer is the ordinary finite affine Čech localization complex. On each product chart its sections and localizations commute with the exterior factor; these identities respect both sets of derivatives and all Čech maps. This proves the first comparison with its specified restriction.

For the second comparison use \[ \mathbb D_{B\times X}(A\boxtimes L) \simeq\mathbb D_B(A)\boxtimes L^\vee, \qquad A\in D^b_{\mathrm{hol}}(B). \tag{HCF.22} \] Here the finite local operator-projective resolution of \(A\) and the finite Spencer resolution of \(L\) compute the dual. On a product chart their tensor–Hom evaluation is the tensor of the two finite dual evaluations. The Koszul signs are those of the total tensor complex. Side change uses \(\omega_{B\times X}=\omega_B\boxtimes\omega_X\); the dimension shifts add. The connection Spencer calculation cancels the curve dimension shift and gives \(L^\vee\). The finite chart mapping diagrams glue these evaluations. This proves HCF.22 and its compatibility with the actual evaluation maps. Duality applied to the first HCF.21 comparison now proves the second.

Under HCF.21, the extraordinary-to-ordinary map is \[ (j_!E_U\longrightarrow j_*E_U)\boxtimes\operatorname{id}_L . \tag{HCF.23} \] Both are the adjunction map whose restriction is the identity; the transfer evaluation comparisons retain that adjunction. Exterior tensor with a finite locally free connection is exact. It therefore commutes with the heart image defining minimal extension, and gives \[ g_{!*}(E_U\boxtimes L) \simeq (j_{!*}E_U)\boxtimes L \xrightarrow{\sim}N . \tag{HCF.24} \] For the last map, the simple \(N\) has no boundary submodule or quotient relative to its nonzero restriction. The uniqueness part of the same minimal-extension theorem extends HCF.19. This proves HCF.2, including singular closed supports.

3.619. Full external categories and finite extensions

The exterior functor and its actual mapping comparison are \[ \begin{gathered} J^{\mathrm{hol}}_B:\mathscr H_B\otimes\mathscr I_X \longrightarrow\operatorname{Dmod}(B\times X),\\ \operatorname{RHom}(A\boxtimes L,A'\boxtimes L') \simeq\operatorname{RHom}_B(A,A') \otimes\operatorname{RHom}_X(L,L'). \end{gathered} \tag{HCF.25} \] Use bounded coherent holonomic \(A,A'\) and bounded finite connection complexes \(L,L'\) first. The finite local operator resolutions and ordered finite Čech mapping diagrams of EFC.14–EFC.15 give precisely this map; that calculation did not use regularity of its first factor. These objects are compact in their ind-categories. Their products are bounded coherent operator objects, compact in the target by RN.4. The full multi-object free bar extends the mapping comparison to arbitrary objects. Thus \[ \begin{gathered} J^{\mathrm{hol}}_B\text{ is full and continuous};\\ \text{its stable image is closed under retracts}. \end{gathered} \tag{HCF.26} \] Every coherent holonomic \(N\) has finite length. Characteristic support is a Serre condition, so every simple factor of a module with zero curve covectors satisfies HCF.2. Its finite extension triangles, with their actual extension morphisms, lift through the full stable image. Therefore \[ \begin{gathered} N\text{ coherent holonomic},\quad \operatorname{Char}(N)\subset T^*B\times0_X\\ \Longrightarrow N\in\operatorname{im}J^{\mathrm{hol}}_B . \end{gathered} \tag{HCF.27} \] An arbitrary quasi-coherent operator module on \(B\times X\) is the filtered union of its coherent operator submodules. The HRI.6 proof uses coherent structure-sheaf submodules containing finitely many prescribed vectors and their operator spans; local operator Noetherianity makes these spans coherent. That proof imposes no regularity condition. For ind-holonomic cohomology every such finite span is holonomic. Apply HCF.27 to these spans, then continuity to their entire filtered diagram. Finite Postnikov triangles handle bounded complexes. If \(K\) is only bounded below, its upper truncations give the actual comparison \[ \operatorname*{colim}_{n}\tau^{\le n}K \xrightarrow{\sim}K \in\operatorname{im}J^{\mathrm{hol}}_B . \tag{HCF.28} \] It is an equivalence because each cohomology module is eventually constant and filtered colimits are exact. Fullness lifts all truncation maps. This proves HCF.3 in every genus.

3.620. Both infinite tails and the original affine operator action

Let \(K\) now have arbitrary unbounded ind-holonomic cohomology and zero curve covectors. Put \(R=D(B)\) and use the exact coefficient functor of PAC.14: \[ \mathsf U_BK=p_{X,*}\operatorname{oblv}_{B\text{-}\mathcal D}K, \qquad H^m\mathsf U_BK=\mathsf U_BH^mK . \tag{HCF.29} \] These are ordinary affine sections, retaining the commuting curve action; they are not de Rham integration over \(B\). For each finite holonomic submodule \(N\subset H^mK\), HCF.27 supplies a preimage. The continuous bilinear map \((A,L)\mapsto\Gamma(B,\operatorname{oblv}A)\otimes L\) has, after \(i_X\), exactly the functor \(\mathsf U_BJ_B\). The full free bar extends its exterior-generator comparison. Thus \(\mathsf U_BN\) lies in the image of \(i_X\), in degree zero. Its cohomology is an ind-connection by PAC.9. Taking the actual coherent unions gives \[ H^m(\mathsf U_BK)\in\operatorname{Ind}\operatorname{Conn}_{\mathrm f}(X), \qquad j_X(Q)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathsf U_BK,\quad Q\in\mathscr Q_X . \tag{HCF.30} \] No lower bound was used: PAC.9 is precisely the full completed coefficient criterion on both tails.

Retain the entire original left \(R\)-action on \(\mathsf U_BK\). Continuity of \(j_X\) gives \[ j_X(R^{\otimes n}\otimes Q) =R^{\otimes n}\otimes j_X(Q). \tag{HCF.31} \] Its full faithfulness lifts every action face, multiplication, unit and higher homotopy of the free \(R\)-module bar. Unit insertion contracts the augmentation after \(j_X\), hence before this conservative functor as well. PAC.13 identifies the resulting module with an actual exterior-category object: \[ \widetilde K\in\operatorname{Dmod}(B)\otimes\mathscr Q_X,\qquad J_B^{\mathscr Q}\widetilde K\xrightarrow{\sim}K . \tag{HCF.32} \] Both functions and derivatives in \(R\) are retained. This proves the forward implication of HCF.4 with all original maps.

3.621. The reverse implication and chart descent

The functor \(J_B^{\mathscr Q}\) is fully faithful: it is \(R\)-internal modules in the full \(j_X\), by PAC.13 and PAC.21–PAC.22. Its comparison identifies its exact essential image by forgetting only the base operator action: \[ K\in\operatorname{im}J_B^{\mathscr Q} \Longleftrightarrow \mathsf U_BK\in\operatorname{im}j_X . \tag{HCF.33} \] Every ind-connection on \(X\) has zero characteristic covectors. Its restriction to an affine curve chart is flat over the curve ring. Hence the underlying module of every \(H^m(\mathsf U_BK)\) is a union of finite connections. For a coherent submodule \(N\subset H^mK\), finitely many operator generators on a curve chart are contained in such a finite curve connection after applying \(\mathsf U_B\). The original \(R\)-action can produce more vectors, but it commutes with the curve operators. Their \(D_X\)-spans stay finite connections. The good-filtration argument of EFC.19–EFC.24, equivalently its relative finite-generator criterion, gives \[ \operatorname{Char}(N)\subset T^*B\times0_X . \tag{HCF.34} \] Here is also the direct symbol argument. Choose finitely many generators of \(N\) over \(D(B)\otimes D(C)\). Place all of them in one finite \(D(C)\)-connection submodule \(E\) of the underlying curve module. Commutation defines a map from \(D(B)\otimes_{\mathbf C}E\) into \(H^mK|_{B\times C}\). Its image \(P\) is coherent and contains \(N|_{B\times C}\), since it contains the chosen operator generators. The product good filtration on the induced module has support in \(T^*B\times0_C\). Its quotient \(P\) and then the submodule \(N|_{B\times C}\) have that support by the characteristic Serre rule. The finite connection \(E\) need not itself be contained in \(N\). Localization in the \(B\)-coordinates and the finite curve cover give HCF.34. Taking all finite cohomology submodules proves the reverse HCF.4 implication.

For a smooth bundle chart or one of the bounded quotient presentations of §1.15 the same condition can be tested on an affine cover. Smooth inverse transfer retains ind-holonomic cohomology and the zero curve covectors, with its fixed line and shift. The chartwise lifts HCF.32 have unique compatible transition maps by fullness. Since \(\mathscr Q_X\) is dualizable by PAC.12, tensor by it commutes with the actual strong-descent limits. Therefore \[ \begin{gathered} J_Y^{\mathscr Q}:\operatorname{Dmod}(Y)\otimes\mathscr Q_X \hookrightarrow\operatorname{Dmod}(Y\times X) \text{ is full},\\ K\text{ chartwise ind-holonomic},\quad \operatorname{SS}_\infty(K)\subset T^*Y\times0_X \Longleftrightarrow K\in\operatorname{im}J_Y^{\mathscr Q}. \end{gathered} \tag{HCF.35} \] The equivalence is asserted within the indicated ind-holonomic class. It includes \(Y=\operatorname{Bun}_G(X)\) using the same normalized smooth chart convention as PAC.23. On arbitrary coefficient objects there is no assertion that the first factor is holonomic.

Both affine action lifting and descent retain the actual operator object: \[ J_Y^{\mathscr Q}\widetilde K\simeq K,\qquad \operatorname{Map}(\widetilde K,\widetilde K') \simeq\operatorname{Map}(K,K'). \tag{HCF.36} \] The comparison does not tensor an individual infinite product of mapping complexes with a field or with a coefficient category.

3.622. Genus and the remaining Hecke support converse

For positive genus PAC.12 identifies completed coefficients with ind-connections. HCF.4 and HCF.35 therefore give, on both cohomological tails, \[ \begin{gathered} g(X)>0,\quad K\text{ chartwise ind-holonomic}:\\ \operatorname{SS}_\infty(K)\subset T^*Y\times0_X \Longleftrightarrow K\in\operatorname{im} \bigl(\operatorname{Dmod}(Y)\otimes\mathscr I_X \longrightarrow\operatorname{Dmod}(Y\times X)\bigr). \end{gathered} \tag{HCF.37} \] In every genus HCF.3 supplies the ind-connection conclusion for objects bounded below on each relevant chart. For the unrestricted projective-line coefficient, keep the actual loop action: \[ B_{\mathrm{loop}}=T_{\mathbf C}(\mathbf C[1]),\quad |u|=-1, \qquad v=u^2,\quad |v|=-2,\qquad \mathscr Q_{\mathbf P^1}=\operatorname{Mod}_{B_{\mathrm{loop}}}. \tag{HCF.38} \] Its ind-connection subcategory is the \(v\)-torsion subcategory PAC.32, not the whole completed category. Accordingly \[ \begin{gathered} K\in\operatorname{im}J_B^{\mathscr I} \Longleftrightarrow Q\in\operatorname{Loc}_{\mathscr Q_{\mathbf P^1}}(\mathbf C),\\ Q\text{ the actual coefficient of HCF.30}. \end{gathered} \tag{HCF.39} \] To justify the backward implication, the full \(R\)-action lifts through the full continuous inclusion of this subcategory, with the same split bar HCF.31. The forward implication follows by applying ordinary affine sections to the exterior generators and their full bar.

These results remove the regular-input assumption from the holonomic curve-parameter factorization. They do not themselves identify every independently nilpotent-supported bundle object with the Hecke-lisse category: \[ \begin{gathered} \{F:\operatorname{SS}_\infty(F)\subset\operatorname{Nilp}_G\} \ \subset\ \mathcal M^{\mathrm{Hl}} \\ \text{remains a separate assertion}. \end{gathered} \tag{HCF.40} \] Its application requires the actual Hecke kernel support transport on the full input class, and in genus zero the restricted coefficient condition. GFP.55–GFP.56 gives the reverse containment and regularity on the actual image. AIC.17's full supported factorization, the other geometric ground fields and derived tempered Satake retain their separate requirements.

Free further reading for parameter tensor products is Arinkin–Gaitsgory–Kazhdan–Raskin–Rozenblyum–Varshavsky, Appendix E.9. The proper horizontal-Hom evaluation, algebraic middle-extension comparison and full completed action arguments used here are proved above.

Figure 3.74. HCF.5–HCF.16 give the proper horizontal Hom bundle and its actual evaluation for a simple connection. HCF.17–HCF.28 extend it across singular supports and through finite extensions and upper truncations. HCF.29–HCF.36 retain the full affine action on both tails. HCF.37–HCF.39 state the genus-dependent coefficient conclusions.

3.623. Exercise and solution: an irregular base factor

Exercise 3.HO. Let \(X\) and its nonzero regular differential \(\omega\) be the elliptic curve in GFP.57–GFP.58. For \(\alpha\in\mathbf C\), take the finite line connection \(L_\alpha=(\mathcal O_X,d+\alpha\omega)\), and put \[ M=(\mathcal O_{\mathbf A^1_z},d+3z^2\,dz),\qquad V=M\boxtimes L_\alpha . \tag{HCF.41} \] Compute \(M_{L_\alpha}(V)\), its evaluation, and the connection at infinity of the base. Explain why HCF.2 does not assert regular singularities of its base factor.

Solution 3.HO. A rank-one finite connection on a connected smooth variety is simple: a coherent subconnection and its quotient are locally free; their ranks add to one, so a nonzero subconnection is the whole one. The tensor \(L_\alpha^\vee\otimes L_\alpha\) is the specified trivial connection. The curve is proper connected and smooth, so its global regular functions form a finite reduced complex algebra with no nontrivial idempotents. Such an algebra is a finite product of finite field extensions of \(\mathbf C\); connectedness leaves one factor and algebraic closedness makes it \(\mathbf C\). Consequently \[ \begin{gathered} H^0_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,L_\alpha^\vee\otimes L_\alpha)=\mathbf C,\\ M_{L_\alpha}(V)=M,\qquad \mathrm{ev}=\operatorname{id}_{M\boxtimes L_\alpha}. \end{gathered} \tag{HCF.42} \] The equalities use the canonical evaluation pairing of the line with its dual. They commute with the base derivative, including the term \(3z^2\).

In the coordinate \(w=z^{-1}\) at infinity, \[ 3z^2\,dz=-3w^{-4}\,dw . \tag{HCF.43} \] For a meromorphic line gauge \(f=w^m h(w)\), with \(h\) a holomorphic unit, \(d\log f=m\,dw/w+d\log h\) has at most a simple pole. It cannot cancel the order-four term. Thus no logarithmic lattice exists there; the base line has an irregular singularity at infinity. On \(\mathbf A^1\times X\) it is nevertheless a finite connection and has \[ \operatorname{Char}(V)=0_{\mathbf A^1\times X} \subset T^*\mathbf A^1\times0_X . \tag{HCF.44} \] The degree-zero bundle filtration proves this support identity. The example concerns a product chart, not the global nilpotent cone of a bundle stack.

3.624. Exercise and solution: why simplicity matters for evaluation

Exercise 3.HP. On the same elliptic curve set \[ E=\mathcal O_Xe_1\oplus\mathcal O_Xe_2,\qquad \nabla e_1=0,\quad \nabla e_2=\omega e_1,\qquad V=M\boxtimes E , \tag{HCF.45} \] where \(M\) is the line in HCF.41. Take \(L=\mathcal O_X\). Compute its horizontal Hom bundle and evaluation. Determine whether the curve extension splits.

Solution 3.HP. The connection is flat because \(\Omega_X^2=0\). Every global section of \(E\) has constant coefficients. If \(N e_2=e_1\) and \(N e_1=0\), the horizontal equation is \(\omega N(ae_1+be_2)=0\), so \[ N=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad N^2=0,\qquad H^0_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,E)=\ker N=\mathbf C e_1 . \tag{HCF.46} \] The nonzero differential \(\omega\) forces \(b=0\). It follows from the actual relative Hom complex that \[ M_{\mathcal O_X}(V)=M,\qquad \mathrm{ev}:M\boxtimes\mathcal O_X\longrightarrow M\boxtimes E, \quad m\longmapsto m e_1 . \tag{HCF.47} \] This is a nonzero injection with quotient \(M\boxtimes\mathcal O_X\); it is not an isomorphism. A splitting of the curve quotient would send its constant unit to \(e_2+f e_1\), for a global regular \(f\). Such an \(f\) is constant, and \[ \begin{gathered} \nabla(e_2+f e_1)=\omega e_1\ne0,\\ 0\longrightarrow\mathcal O_Xe_1\longrightarrow E \longrightarrow\mathcal O_X\longrightarrow0 \text{ is nonsplit}. \end{gathered} \tag{HCF.48} \] Thus evaluation detects the isotypic subconnection of a general finite connection. Simplicity of \(V\), used in HCF.16, is exactly what makes that subconnection the whole object. The nonsplit extension and its actual connection matrix remain in the finite-extension argument HCF.27.

3.625. Nilpotent inputs and the actual bounded Hecke kernel

Let \(X/\mathbf C\) be a smooth projective connected curve, let \(G\) be connected reductive, and put \(Y=\operatorname{Bun}_G(X)\). Use the normalized half-twisted category of §§1.10–2.8. Define \[ \mathscr S_Y= \{F\in\operatorname{Dmod}_{1/2}(Y): \operatorname{SS}_\infty(F)\subset\mathcal N_Y\}. \tag{NHT.1} \] Here support means the union of the characteristic varieties of actual coherent submodules of every chart cohomology, as in NU.1–NU.4. There is no boundedness or regularity condition in this definition.

We prove the following upper bound for every finite spherical coefficient \(V\), in every genus: \[ F\in\mathscr S_Y \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{SS}_\infty(\mathsf H_VF) \subset\mathcal N_Y\times0_X . \tag{NHT.2} \] The Hecke functor has its normalization SH.15–SH.17, including the curve shift and the density lines. Those fixed shifts do not change characteristic sets. In positive genus, NHT.2 and HCF.35–HCF.40 will identify \(\mathscr S_Y\) with the full Hecke-lisse category and hence with the restricted projector image. The unrestricted genus-zero ind-connection condition retains its separate requirement.

For clarity, use the actual proper presentation of RHC.8–RHC.11. On a smooth finite-type target chart \(B\to Y\), and a curve coordinate open \(C\subset X\), the bounded relative-position source \(Z\) has a closed embedding into a smooth projective-bundle ambient \(M\): \[ Z\xrightarrow{i}M\xrightarrow{\pi}B\times C,\qquad \pi\text{ proper},\qquad (\mathsf H_VF)|_{B\times C}=\pi_+E . \tag{NHT.3} \] The object \(E\) is the supported ambient realization of the actual inverse-image and bounded spherical IC kernel on \(Z\). The inverse bound \(-w_0\nu\), finite-jet Plücker construction and canonical kernel comparisons are those proved in RHC.8–RHC.11 and SH.13–SH.17. Only \(\pi\) is used for proper direct image. A smooth frame cover of \(Z\) will be used to inspect covectors; it is never used as a proper map.

3.626. A characteristic covector under a change of ambient space

We need only a statement about restrictions to tangent vectors, not a cotangent bundle of a singular scheme. Let \(Z\) be closed in two smooth varieties \(M_1,M_2\), with embeddings \(e_1,e_2\). Represent one coherent supported operator module by \(A_1,A_2\). On the joint ambient it is represented by \(A_{12}\). The exact equivalences and their actual comparison maps are proved in Kashiwara's equivalence and singular spaces, §5.

First restrict to affine neighbourhoods in both ambients and embed each smooth affine ambient as a closed subvariety of an affine space. The closed normal formula NS.8 says that pushing to this larger ambient takes the characteristic variety to the full inverse image under cotangent restriction. Thus a given covector lifts to a characteristic covector upstairs; a characteristic covector upstairs restricts to one downstairs. Their values on the tangent to \(Z\) are unchanged. It suffices, therefore, to prove the assertion after these enlargements, and we denote the two affine spaces again by \(M_1,M_2\).

Now extend \(e_2\) to \(f:M_1\to M_2\) and \(e_1\) to \(g:M_2\to M_1\): lift each coordinate function through the surjection from the ambient polynomial ring to the coordinate ring of the closed \(Z\). Both extensions exist on these same affine spaces. No inverse relation between \(f\) and \(g\) on the ambients is required.

Kashiwara equivalence for the smooth graphs, together with its projection inverse, identifies the joint object as \[ A_{12}\simeq(\Gamma_f)_+A_1 \simeq(\Gamma_g)_+A_2 , \tag{NHT.4} \] where the second graph is ordered in \(M_1\times M_2\). This does not apply a smooth-embedding theorem to the possibly singular \(Z\). The closed normal formula NS.8, in graph coordinates, therefore gives both exact characteristic formulas \[ \begin{aligned} (\beta_1,\beta_2)\in\operatorname{Ch}(A_{12}) &\Longleftrightarrow \beta_1+df^t\beta_2\in\operatorname{Ch}(A_1),\\ &\Longleftrightarrow dg^t\beta_1+\beta_2\in\operatorname{Ch}(A_2). \end{aligned} \tag{NHT.5} \] Indeed, the symbol of a tangent operator to the graph is the corresponding displayed sum; every normal symbol is free. This is exactly the local normal-derivative description of graph direct image, with no holonomicity or regularity hypothesis.

In particular, if \(\beta_1\in\operatorname{Ch}(A_1)\) at \(z\), then \((\beta_1,0)\) lies in the joint characteristic variety. Thus \[ \beta_2=dg^t\beta_1\in\operatorname{Ch}(A_2),\qquad \beta_2(de_2v)=\beta_1(de_1v)\quad(v\in T_zS) \tag{NHT.6} \] for every smooth locally closed stratum \(S\subset Z\) through \(z\). The last equality is the derivative of \(g e_2=e_1\) on \(S\). The transferred covector can depend on the extensions; its restriction to this tangent does not. Restricting back from the enlarged affine ambients by NS.8 proves the assertion in the original ambients as well. We do not identify the different ambient conormal directions.

3.627. Smooth frame covers and finite coherent witnesses

Let \(v:Z'\to Z\) be a smooth source cover. Locally it is étale over a projection \(Z\times\mathbb A^r\to Z\). Lift that presentation to the chosen ambient. Normalized smooth inverse image is exact on hearts; NS.7 sends an ambient characteristic covector \(\beta\) to \((\beta,0)\) in this product presentation: \[ \operatorname{Ch}(v^\natural A) =d\widetilde v^{\,t} \bigl(M'\times_M\operatorname{Ch}(A)\bigr). \tag{NHT.7} \] Changing from this ambient to the common Hecke frame ambient uses NHT.4–NHT.6. Hence a given covector survives that change with the same values on the lifted relative-position stratum. The exact equivalence preserves a coherent submodule and its inclusion into the ambient cohomology. This proves the covector comparison needed for upper bounds through the singular source.

In the common frame the actual kernel object is the smooth pullback of \[ F_U\boxtimes IC_{\mathrm{bd}}\boxtimes\mathcal O_C \quad\text{with the fixed SH.17 shifts}. \tag{NHT.8} \] The frame map is smooth over the singular Schubert support, so its normalized inverse image is exact. The bounded IC complex has only finitely many coherent cohomology modules. Over \(\mathbf C\), the cohomology of the external product is the finite direct sum of the corresponding external cohomology modules in each degree. This follows by taking complexes of vector spaces: split their cycles and boundaries as vector spaces, so acyclic summands contract, and tensor the resulting complexes. It asserts the cohomology formula, not a splitting of operator-module complexes.

Consequently a finite coherent submodule of a cohomology module in NHT.8 has all its generators in a finite sum of actual modules \[ L_U\boxtimes H^j(IC_{\mathrm{bd}})\boxtimes\mathcal O_C, \qquad L_U\subset H^iF_U\text{ coherent}. \tag{NHT.9} \] For each generator write finitely many external tensors and collect their input coefficients. Their operator span is a coherent submodule of the actual input cohomology. Taking the sum of these spans handles all generators. The smooth-pullback version follows by expressing finitely many pulled-back sections in finitely many downstairs sections, as in BK.8–BK.9 and NU.3. Thus NHT.9 remains valid after the frame comparison. No regularity of \(L_U\) has been used.

Product good filtrations and the coherent submodule support rule now enclose the covector by an actual input characteristic covector and an IC characteristic covector: \[ \operatorname{Ch}(A_{\mathrm{fr}}) \subset d\widetilde p^{\,t} \left(\bigcup_{i,j} \operatorname{Ch}(L_U)\times \operatorname{Ch}(H^jIC_{\mathrm{bd}})\times0_C\right). \tag{NHT.10} \] The union here is finite locally for the selected coherent witness.

3.628. From stratum tangents to compatible global Higgs fields

Strong finite-jet equivariance of the spherical IC implies that its characteristic covectors annihilate orbit tangents, including the boundary orbits. Here is the symbol argument, RHC.12. Enclose finite generators of a strong equivariant module in a finite-dimensional rational representation \(W\), and filter by \(\mathcal D_{\le k}W\). Each orbit vector field preserves this filtration because its operator action equals its rational infinitesimal action. Its principal symbol therefore kills the associated graded module. On a projective ambient use its line-frame open and the smooth formula to reflect the same annihilator statement. Coherent submodules use containment in this enclosing equivariant module; they need not be equivariant.

Suppose \(\pi^t(\xi_2,\xi_x)\) is a characteristic covector of a coherent \(A\subset H^mE\) in NHT.3. Apply NHT.7 and NHT.6 to move it to the common frame. On the relative-position stratum, NHT.10 and the preceding annihilator argument give \[ p_2^*\xi_2+s^*\xi_x=p_1^*\xi_1 . \tag{NHT.11} \] The input covector is supplied by an actual coherent submodule of input cohomology in NHT.9. The identity self-nerve argument RHC.4–RHC.7 says that such a characteristic covector annihilates the infinitesimal chart-fibre directions. Indeed normalized smooth descent identifies the two pullbacks; varying the identity arrow while holding one endpoint fixed forces annihilation of these directions by NS.7. The smooth chart's tangent surjects onto bundle deformations, so \(\xi_1\) is the pullback of a global Higgs covector. Its nilpotence follows from \(F\in\mathscr S_Y\). This argument is an operator and smooth-descent argument and has no regularity premise.

We recall why NHT.11 gives compatible fields, including at a boundary orbit. In the notation HG.1–HG.5 put \[ W=\mathfrak g((u)),\quad V=\Gamma(X-x,\operatorname{ad}P),\quad L_2=\mathfrak g[[u]],\quad L_1=\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}L_2 . \tag{NHT.12} \] The fixed-point gluing tangent is the quotient of \(W^2\oplus V\) by the arrows HG.4. The tangent to the selected relative-position orbit is the kernel of the surjection \[ (a_1,a_2,b)\longmapsto b-a_1+a_2 \pmod{L_1+L_2}. \tag{NHT.13} \] This is the tangent to that actual orbit, not to the entire singular Schubert closure. A functional vanishing on the kernel factors through this quotient. Evaluation on \((w,0,0)\) and \((0,w,0)\), using the perfect Laurent residue pairing HG.3, identifies that factor with the two Laurent expansions. They coincide and annihilate both lattices. HG.8–HG.9 therefore gives regular global Higgs fields \(A_1,A_2\), compatible away from \(x\). The moving-coordinate computation HG.13 gives the remaining component with its positive sign: \[ A_2=\alpha^*A_1\text{ on }X-x,\qquad \xi_x=\operatorname{Res}_{u=0} B(A_2,g^{-1}g')\,dx . \tag{NHT.14} \] All extra smooth frame directions are annihilated, so these equalities descend to the original correspondence.

3.629. The nilpotent residue and the source characteristic bound

The following is a statement at complex geometric points, as appropriate for reduced characteristic sets. Write a Cartan decomposition and transport the regular field: \[ g=k_1u^\lambda k_2,\qquad D=\operatorname{Ad}_{k_2}A_2,\qquad \operatorname{Ad}_{u^\lambda}D\in\mathfrak g[[u]] . \tag{NHT.15} \] The two arc derivative terms pair with regular fields and have zero residue. Invariance of \(B\) leaves \[ \operatorname{Res}B(A_2,g^{-1}g') =B(D(0),d\lambda). \tag{NHT.16} \] Negative \(\lambda\)-weight coefficients of \(D(0)\) vanish by the regularity in NHT.15. Thus \(D(0)\in\mathfrak p_\lambda\). The weight-zero limit \(D_0\) is nilpotent in the Levi: nilpotence is closed under the cocharacter limit, and compatible Jordan decomposition has zero central semisimple part. Since \(d\lambda\) is central in that Levi, invariance gives \[ B(D(0),d\lambda)=B(D_0,d\lambda)=0 . \tag{NHT.17} \] This is the full reductive argument RHC.18–RHC.22; it includes the central torus. Compatible Higgs fields have the same invariant polynomials by HG.10–HG.11. Hence input nilpotence implies output nilpotence, while NHT.17 makes the moving covector zero.

For every coherent \(A\subset H^mE\) we have therefore proved \[ \{(z,\eta):d\pi_z^t\eta\in\operatorname{Ch}(A)\} \subset \pi^{-1}(\Gamma),\qquad \Gamma=\mathcal N_B\times0_C\subset T^*(B\times C). \tag{NHT.18} \] The zero covector is allowed throughout. In particular this argument is an upper bound; it does not use a nonvanishing cycle detector or an isolated compatible point. Reduced nilpotence in NHT.17 is not a vanishing assertion over arbitrary nonreduced coefficient rings.

3.630. Proper direct image for arbitrary coherent pieces

The proper characteristic theorem NS.1–NS.6 applies to every bounded coherent operator complex on smooth ambient schemes. There is no regularity hypothesis in that theorem. To recall its mechanism, a good input filtration gives the Spencer symbol equations \[ \xi_M-d\pi^t\xi_{B\times C}=0 . \tag{NHT.19} \] Their Koszul complex resolves the transfer symbol relation. The relation projects properly to \(T^*(B\times C)\), being the base change of the proper map \(\pi\). Proper coherent direct image and the finite Spencer–Čech complex give coherent graded output. The Noetherian stabilization and separated filtration argument of NS.2–NS.6 give a genuine good filtration, including filtration torsion. Its support satisfies \[ \operatorname{Ch}H^j(\pi_+A) \subset \{\eta:\exists z,\ d\pi_z^t\eta\in\operatorname{Ch}(A)\} \subset\Gamma . \tag{NHT.20} \] For a bounded coherent complex use its finite cohomological filtration and the characteristic Serre rule. Thus NHT.18 controls proper direct images of all finite coherent pieces, including irregular pieces.

There is an interval \([a,b]\), independent of the input, such that \[ H^j(\pi_+M)=0\quad(j\notin[a,b]) \quad\text{for every heart module }M . \tag{NHT.21} \] The finite Spencer length gives the lower bound and a finite affine Čech cover gives the upper bound. The same complexes compute arbitrary modules and commute with colimits. The full unbounded assertion, including the canonical truncation comparisons, is SH.14 and Adjunctions, base change and the projection formula, Theorem 3.4. These are finite operator models, so NHT.21 applies to the actual functor on both cohomological tails.

3.631. A finite window for each output degree

Fix \(n\), and set \[ l=n-b-1,\qquad u=n-a+1,\qquad E_{[l,u]}=\tau^{\le u}\tau^{\ge l}E . \tag{NHT.22} \] There is a natural zigzag, not an arbitrary choice of a splitting, \[ E\longrightarrow\tau^{\ge l}E \longleftarrow E_{[l,u]} . \tag{NHT.23} \] The discarded lower tail is in degrees at most \(l-1=n-b-2\); its direct image is in degrees at most \(n-2\). The discarded upper tail is in degrees at least \(u+1=n-a+2\); its image is in degrees at least \(n+2\). The two truncation triangles therefore make both arrows in NHT.23 isomorphisms after \(H^n\pi_+\): \[ H^n\pi_+E\simeq H^n\pi_+E_{[l,u]} . \tag{NHT.24} \] There is no interchange of an inverse Postnikov limit with proper direct image in this step.

Each cohomology module in the finite window is a filtered union of actual coherent submodules. The characteristic condition \(\operatorname{SS}\subset\Gamma\) is Serre and stable under filtered colimits, by NU.2. Continuity of \(\pi_+\) and NHT.20 therefore give this condition for its direct image. The finite Postnikov filtration of \(E_{[l,u]}\) gives the same condition for every cohomology of its image. NHT.24, for each \(n\), proves \[ \operatorname{SS}_\infty(\pi_+E)\subset\Gamma . \tag{NHT.25} \] The proof is local on \(B\times X\), and normalized smooth pullback preserves and reflects the characteristic tests NU.3–NU.4. The actual proper-kernel chart comparisons SH.14–SH.17 consequently glue NHT.25 to NHT.2 on \(Y\times X\).

3.632. Completed curve coefficients and all higher action maps

NC.1–NC.3 give \(\dim\mathcal N_B\le\dim B\). Thus the characteristic bound just proved has dimension at most \(\dim B+1\). Bernstein's inequality implies that every nonzero coherent submodule of every output cohomology is holonomic. In symbols, \[ (\mathsf H_VF)|_{B\times X} \text{ has ind-holonomic cohomology and } \operatorname{SS}_\infty\subset T^*B\times0_X . \tag{NHT.26} \] The algebraic factorization HCF.29–HCF.40 therefore applies, with no premise of regularity in \(B\). It gives the actual completed coefficient lift \[ \mathsf H_VF\in \operatorname{Dmod}_{1/2}(Y)\otimes\mathcal Q_X . \tag{NHT.27} \] This notation means membership in the full realized category. On an affine chart the lift carries the full \(\mathcal D(B)\)-action: ordinary affine sections over \(B\), followed by the full completed curve embedding, lift both functions and derivatives and every action-bar face. Full mapping descent then gives the global object with the specified kernel maps, rather than an object with merely isomorphic cohomology groups.

The argument also retains spectator parameters. If a smooth parameter space \(T\) has zero characteristic covectors on the input, the same frame calculation has that extra zero factor. The correspondence is the identity in \(T\); its cotangent equations preserve this factor. Thus \[ \mathcal N_Y\times0_T \longmapsto\mathcal N_Y\times0_T\times0_X . \tag{NHT.28} \] Iterating proves the corresponding estimate for disjoint modifications at every finite set of points. On the factorization diagonals the actual kernel identifications are those of SH.16–SH.17. Because the realized coefficient embeddings are full, every original composition, fusion map, unit and higher homotopy between objects in their image lifts uniquely as a point of the corresponding mapping space. One may apply the completed coefficient criterion successively to the curve coordinates, retaining the other variables and their full operator actions. This gives \[ \mathsf H_{V_1,\ldots,V_r}F\in \operatorname{Dmod}_{1/2}(Y)\otimes\mathcal Q_X^{\otimes r}. \tag{NHT.29} \] Extension from finite coefficients and their finite complexes to the continuous action uses the same compact coefficient generators and action bars as SH.17. This does not assert a new unital monoidal structure on the Ran transpose.

3.633. Positive genus: the full supported projector image

Suppose now that \(g(X)>0\). PAC.19–PAC.28 identify the completed curve category with the actual ind-category of finite connections: \[ \mathcal Q_X=\mathcal I_X . \tag{NHT.30} \] Substitute this equality into NHT.27–NHT.29, with all the action maps just specified. This is the full Hecke-lisse condition, not just a condition on finite cohomology objects. Consequently \[ \mathscr S_Y\subset\mathcal N_{\mathrm{Hl}}(Y). \tag{NHT.31} \] The reverse containment is GFP.55–GFP.56: every object of the full original-complex Hecke-lisse category is chartwise ind-regular and has independent nilpotent support. Combining these actual inclusions gives \[ \mathscr S_Y=\mathcal N_{\mathrm{Hl}}(Y) =\operatorname{EssIm}(\Pi_{\mathrm{res}}),\qquad \mathscr S_Y\subset\mathscr R_\infty(Y) \quad(g(X)>0). \tag{NHT.32} \] Here \(\Pi_{\mathrm{res}}\) is the normalized restricted projector of RSE.37–RSE.38 and NTR.16. Its given natural identity on the full Hecke-lisse image is therefore a natural identity on the independently defined category \(\mathscr S_Y\). This identifies its full image on arbitrary input objects and proves independent nilpotent ind-regularity over \(\mathbf C\) in every positive genus, with both cohomological tails. No finite-rank, compactness or boundedness assumption is imposed.

In genus zero NHT.2 and NHT.27–NHT.29 still hold. But the completed category and the ind-connection category differ: \[ \mathcal Q_{\mathbf P^1}\simeq \operatorname{Mod}_{T_{\mathbf C}(\mathbf C[1])}, \qquad \mathcal I_{\mathbf P^1} =\{u^2\text{-torsion objects}\}\subset\mathcal Q_{\mathbf P^1}, \qquad |u|=-1 . \tag{NHT.33} \] GZR.24–GZR.32 supply the actual torsion and restricted-action argument giving the unrestricted genus-zero inclusion. NHT.2 alone is the characteristic upper bound. The supported compact factorization condition AIC.17 for chartwise supported ind-categories also remains a separate assertion: NHT.32 identifies the full global supported category, not an unproved replacement of each chart by such an ind-completion. Other geometric ground fields and derived tempered Satake retain their stated requirements.

Figure 3.75. NHT.5–NHT.7 transfer a characteristic covector through graphs while preserving its restriction to the actual stratum tangent. NHT.18–NHT.25 apply proper characteristic transport in a finite cohomological window. NHT.27–NHT.33 separate the all-genus completed coefficient bound from the positive-genus full supported-image equality.

3.634. Two explicit ambient and cohomological calculations

Exercise 3.HQ. Let \(Z\) be the cusp \(y^2=x^3\) in \(M_1=\mathbb A^2_{x,y}\). Embed it in \(M_2=\mathbb A^3_{x,y,z}\) by \(z=x^2\). Use the extensions \[ f(x,y)=(x,y,x^2),\qquad g(x,y,z)=(x,y),\qquad df^t(a,b,c)=(a+2xc,b). \tag{NHT.34} \] At \(t\ne0\) on its smooth stratum \((x,y)=(t^2,t^3)\), transfer an arbitrary characteristic covector \((p,q)\) of \(A_1\) by NHT.6, and compute its tangent pairing in both ambients. Describe the full graph relation and explain why the same comparison at the cusp does not identify the ambient cotangent spaces.

Solution 3.HQ. The joint object lies on the graph of \(f\). Its characteristic relation is \[ (\xi_x,\xi_y;\,a,b,c)\in\operatorname{Ch}(A_{12}) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (\xi_x+a+2xc,\xi_y+b)\in\operatorname{Ch}(A_1). \tag{NHT.35} \] Taking the second covector zero and using the opposite graph transfers \((p,q)\) to \((p,q,0)\in\operatorname{Ch}(A_2)\). The stratum tangent and its image are \[ (2t,3t^2),\qquad (2t,3t^2,4t^3). \tag{NHT.36} \] Both pairings are \(2tp+3t^2q\). More generally the graph direct-image formula for \(A_2=f_+A_1\) reads \[ (a,b,c)\in\operatorname{Ch}(A_2) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (a+2xc,b)\in\operatorname{Ch}(A_1). \tag{NHT.37} \] This also shows the different normal directions explicitly: \((-2xc,0,c)\) is conormal to the smooth graph \(f(M_1)\). At the cusp the point stratum has zero tangent, so restriction to that stratum gives no identification between the two- and three-dimensional ambient cotangent spaces. The covector transfer remains a valid characteristic implication.

Exercise 3.HR. A continuous operator functor has heart amplitude \([-3,2]\). Determine a finite input window sufficient for output degree \(5\), including the natural zigzag and the degrees of the discarded output tails. Then test the reduced-point qualification in NHT.17 using \(G=GL_3\), \(B(A,B)=\operatorname{tr}(AB)\), \[ \lambda(s)=\operatorname{diag}(s^4,s,s^{-2}),\qquad D=E_{12}+E_{23}. \tag{NHT.38} \] Finally work over \(R=\mathbf C[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)\) with \(D_\varepsilon=\operatorname{diag}(\varepsilon,0,-\varepsilon)\). Does matrix nilpotence over \(R\) force the same residue vanishing as over complex geometric points?

Solution 3.HR. NHT.22 gives \(l=2,u=9\), so the natural comparison is \[ E\longrightarrow\tau^{\ge2}E \longleftarrow\tau^{\le9}\tau^{\ge2}E,\qquad H^5TE\simeq H^5T(\tau^{\le9}\tau^{\ge2}E). \tag{NHT.39} \] The lower discarded tail has degrees at most \(1\), hence its image has degrees at most \(3\). The upper discarded tail has degrees at least \(10\), hence its image has degrees at least \(7\). Thus neither can affect the adjacent degrees needed for \(H^5\) in the two truncation triangles.

Both roots in \(D\) have weight \(3\), so \[ \operatorname{Ad}_{u^\lambda}D =u^3(E_{12}+E_{23}),\qquad D^3=0,\qquad \operatorname{tr}(D\,d\lambda)=0. \tag{NHT.40} \] This is a nonzero nilpotent example with a regular transported field and zero moving residue. Its Levi limit \(D_0\) is zero. Over the dual numbers, however, the diagonal field commutes with \(u^\lambda\) and has square zero, while \[ D_\varepsilon^2=0,\qquad \operatorname{tr}(D_\varepsilon\,d\lambda) =6\varepsilon\ne0\quad\text{in }R. \tag{NHT.41} \] It specializes to zero at every complex point. Thus the geometric characteristic-set implication proved above is compatible with this nonreduced counterexample. It cannot be promoted to a residue identity on all coefficient schemes.

3.635. The projective-line coefficient problem

Work over \(\mathbf C\), with \(X=\mathbf P^1\), a point \(x\), \(G\) connected reductive, \(H=\check G\), and \(Y=\operatorname{Bun}_G(X)\). Retain the full categories \(\mathcal M=\operatorname{Dmod}_{1/2}(Y)\) and \(\mathscr S_Y=\operatorname{Dmod}_{\mathcal N}(Y)\) of NHT.1. Put \(\mathfrak h=\operatorname{Lie}H\) and \(d=\dim H\). The coefficient algebra and its two distinct categories are \[ \begin{gathered} B_\Omega=T_{\mathbf C}(\mathbf C[1]),\quad |u|=-1,\quad \Delta u=u\otimes1+1\otimes u,\\ v=u^2,\qquad \mathcal Q=\operatorname{Mod}_{B_\Omega},\quad \mathcal I=\{v\text{-torsion modules}\}\subset\mathcal Q . \end{gathered} \tag{GZR.1} \] These are the complete Hopf tensor and localization constructions RSC.19–RSC.27. In particular \(u^2\) is not zero in the algebra. We shall prove the actual ind-connection condition for Hecke outputs without asserting \(\mathcal I=\mathcal Q\).

Use the strong \(!\)-tensor normalization \(j_!(E)=j_X(E)[1]\), so \(j_!(\mathbf1)=\omega_X\), as in PAC.7–PAC.12. The normalized fibre is \[ \varepsilon_x(E)=i_x^!j_!(E),\qquad \varepsilon_x:\mathcal Q\longrightarrow\operatorname{Vect}. \tag{GZR.2} \] It is the forgetful functor for \(B_\Omega\)-modules. For bounded-below objects this is the connection fibre comparison RSC.22 and RSP.2. For arbitrary objects the finite noncharacteristic graph calculation NCS.13–NCS.17 computes each cohomology from the same fibre. The effective lower truncation tower PAC.6–PAC.10 then gives the displayed comparison with all its action maps. Thus it is exact, continuous, conservative and symmetric monoidal. There is no extra curve shift in GZR.2.

The all-genus estimate NHT.2 applies to every \(F\in\mathscr S_Y\). The fibre embedding is noncharacteristic for \(\mathcal N_Y\times0_X\). NCS.8–NCS.17, applied on charts and descended with the fixed half twist, consequently gives \[ \mathsf H_{V,x}F :=(\operatorname{Id}\otimes i_x^!)\mathsf H_VF \in\mathscr S_Y . \tag{GZR.3} \] This statement includes both infinite cohomological tails.

3.636. A presentable envelope for one supported input

Fix one arbitrary \(F\in\mathscr S_Y\). Choose a small skeleton of finite-dimensional \(H\)-representations, including their duals and the unit. Let \(\mathcal W_F\) be the set of finite fixed-point Hecke words \[ \mathcal W_F= \{\mathsf H_{V_r,x}\cdots\mathsf H_{V_1,x}F:r\ge0\}. \tag{GZR.4} \] The empty word is \(F\). The full stable colimit closure inside \(\mathcal M\) is denoted \[ \mathcal C_F=\operatorname{Loc}_{\mathcal M}(\mathcal W_F). \tag{GZR.5} \] It is presentable, with its full continuous inclusion into \(\mathcal M\). Here is the size argument, with no assertion of ordinary compactness. The module model for \(\mathcal M\) from §1.15 and KF.9 permits one to choose an uncountable regular \(\kappa\) such that every word in this set is \(\kappa\)-compact. Close these objects under stable colimits of size less than \(\kappa\) and retracts, obtaining a small full \(\mathcal K_F\subset\mathcal M^\kappa\).

The full \(\operatorname{Ind}_\kappa\) construction in HLA.1–HLA.3 maps fully faithfully to \(\mathcal M\): maps out of an object of \(\mathcal K_F\) commute with the specified filtered colimits, and maps out of their colimits are the corresponding limits of those full mapping complexes. Its image is closed under colimits of size less than \(\kappa\) and under \(\kappa\)-filtered colimits. Every small colimit is a \(\kappa\)-filtered colimit of its subdiagrams with fewer than \(\kappa\) cells, so the image is colimit closed. Conversely all its objects are built from the words by these colimits. Hence \[ \mathcal C_F\simeq\operatorname{Ind}_\kappa(\mathcal K_F). \tag{GZR.6} \] The choice of \(\kappa\) is only a size choice. It does not give a presentation by bounded coherent supported objects, and does not assume AIC.17.

Each fixed-point Hecke functor is continuous. It sends the generating words to words, and therefore \[ \mathsf H_{V,x}(\mathcal C_F)\subset\mathcal C_F, \qquad \mathcal C_F\subset\mathscr S_Y . \tag{GZR.7} \] The second inclusion follows from GZR.3 and the stable colimit closure NU.1–NU.4. The same assertion for derived representation coefficients follows by their full finite-representation bars.

3.637. Lifting the entire loop action into this envelope

For any presentable linear category \(\mathcal C\), the augmented free-action bar gives \[ \mathcal C\otimes\mathcal Q \simeq B_\Omega\text{-}\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal C). \tag{GZR.8} \] An internal module is its object, operator action, unit, all associativity maps and higher homotopies. The extra unit degeneracy contracts the augmented bar. This proves GZR.8 on all objects and full mapping complexes, as in RSC.27 and PAC.13.

If \(\mathcal C\hookrightarrow\mathcal M\) is full and continuous, the induced internal-module inclusion is full and its image is characterized by the underlying object: \[ K\in B_\Omega\text{-}\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal C) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{oblv}K\in\mathcal C . \tag{GZR.9} \] For the reverse implication lift every action-bar map through the full inclusion. The same full mapping spaces lift its equations and higher homotopies. The resulting augmentation realizes in \(\mathcal C\), since the inclusion preserves colimits. This proves the criterion without assuming that \(\mathcal C\) is dualizable.

NHT.27 gives an actual \(\mathcal Q\)-coefficient lift of \(\mathsf H_V\). Shift its t-exact \(j_X\)-lift by \([-1]\) to use the strong \(!\)-tensor realization \(j_!\) of GZR.2; the realized Hecke object is unchanged. For \(r\) parameters use the corresponding total shift \([-r]\). With this normalization its underlying object on \(\mathcal C_F\) is precisely \(\mathsf H_{V,x}\). GZR.7–GZR.9 therefore yield a continuous lift \[ \widehat{\mathsf H}^{\,F}_V: \mathcal C_F\longrightarrow\mathcal C_F\otimes\mathcal Q . \tag{GZR.10} \] For a finite set of points, use internal modules over \(B_\Omega^{\otimes r}\). Evaluation at \((x,\ldots,x)\) is the fixed-point word with the actual collision identifications. The same argument gives \[ \widehat{\mathsf H}^{\,F}_{V_1,\ldots,V_r}: \mathcal C_F\longrightarrow\mathcal C_F\otimes\mathcal Q^{\otimes r}. \tag{GZR.11} \] All the original Hecke comparisons lift through these full inclusions. This includes composition, fusion, empty and unused coordinates, and their higher relations. It does not replace the operator action by its cohomology action.

3.638. The full completed-coefficient Ran action

The category \(\mathcal Q=\operatorname{Mod}_{B_\Omega}\) is dualizable by its free compact generator, PAC.12. Transpose its continuous Hopf tensor multiplication using its actual categorical dual: \[ \delta_{\mathcal Q}=m_{\mathcal Q}^{\vee}: \mathcal Q^\vee\longrightarrow \mathcal Q^\vee\otimes\mathcal Q^\vee . \tag{GZR.12} \] Its counit is the transpose of the tensor unit. No self-duality by ordinary global sections is imposed. Use the full finite-point relations of HLA.23, with coefficient category \(\mathcal Q^\vee\), to form \[ \mathcal R_{\mathcal Q} =\operatorname*{colim}_{\psi:I\to J} \operatorname{Rep}(H)^{\otimes I} \otimes(\mathcal Q^\vee)^{\otimes J}. \tag{GZR.13} \] The transition maps use representation multiplication and the iterated transposed tensor, with the counit at unused coordinates. The small-relations construction HLA.1–HLA.3 retains all stage objects and complete coherent strings; it does not require these transitions to preserve compact objects. Disjoint union gives its continuous symmetric tensor and its unit.

Pair the lifts GZR.11 with the full dual coefficients: \[ (\vec V,P;M)\longmapsto (\operatorname{Id}\otimes\operatorname{ev}) \bigl(\widehat{\mathsf H}^{\,F}_{\psi}(\vec V;M)\otimes P\bigr). \tag{GZR.14} \] Moving a collision through this evaluation is exactly GZR.12. The actual kernel comparison supplies every composition of collisions. Thus the proof of HLA.25–HLA.27 applies to these stages and gives a continuous unital action \[ \mathcal R_{\mathcal Q}\otimes\mathcal C_F \longrightarrow\mathcal C_F . \tag{GZR.15} \] Its coefficients under duality are exactly GZR.10–GZR.11. The empty stage gives the unit; no unital monoidal structure on a tensor transpose is asserted.

3.639. Framing the universal completed coefficient

The same transposition proves the full tensor universal property: for a presentable symmetric monoidal target \(\mathcal T\), continuous strong symmetric monoidal functors from \(\mathcal R_{\mathcal Q}\) are precisely the tensor functors \[ \operatorname{Rep}(H)\longrightarrow\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal Q. \tag{GZR.16} \] Transpose the one-point functor; its tensor and unit maps give the collision and empty-stage relations. Conversely evaluate the full stage diagram. Evaluation–coevaluation cancellation identifies both composites and all transformation spaces. This is the argument of §3.223 with the specified coefficient dual.

Evaluation by \(\varepsilon_x\) defines the base-point functor from \(\operatorname{Rep}(H)\). Let \(S_x\) be its regular frame algebra, the image of \(\mathcal O(H)\). The Hopf-module framing calculation RSE.15–RSE.18 gives \[ \mathcal R_{\mathcal Q}^{\mathrm{fr}} =\operatorname{Mod}_{S_x}(\mathcal R_{\mathcal Q}). \tag{GZR.17} \] A tensor functor from this category is exactly GZR.16 with a chosen trivialization of its underlying fibre as \(V\mapsto\underline V\otimes\mathbf1_{\mathcal T}\). The free regular-module bar proves this on the entire space of frames and their higher maps.

Set \[ D_{\mathcal T}=\operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal T} (\mathbf1_{\mathcal T},\mathbf1_{\mathcal T}), \qquad A_0=\operatorname{Sym}_{\mathbf C}(\mathfrak h^\vee[1]). \tag{GZR.18} \] The first is a commutative DG algebra, with the coherent commutativity of tensoring endomorphisms of the unit. The second has \(d\) odd degree-minus-one generators. We compute the framed functor category over arbitrary \(D_{\mathcal T}\), including unbounded negative degrees.

3.640. The full odd tensor-derivation calculation

Under GZR.8 a framed functor in GZR.16 is a \(B_\Omega\)-action on each \(\underline V\otimes\mathbf1_{\mathcal T}\). The generator is closed, of degree minus one. Its primitive coproduct is exactly the tensor derivation rule; naturality means it preserves all representation intertwiners. The complete reconstruction RSC.28 can be applied to this entire derivation complex.

Explicitly extend the operator to the regular coefficient algebra by its finite rational subrepresentations. It obeys the graded Leibniz rule and commutes with the regular right coaction. Evaluation at the identity determines the invariant derivation by its value on the augmentation cotangent \(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2=\mathfrak h^\vee\). On every representation this gives \[ u_V=d\rho_V(\alpha),\qquad \alpha\in Z^{-1}(\mathfrak h\otimes D_{\mathcal T}). \tag{GZR.19} \] Conversely these formulas have the tensor derivation rule and preserve every intertwiner, so reconstruct the same operator. This argument works with every shifted coefficient module. The square-zero test \(1+\epsilon u\), together with the regular Hopf identities, identifies its full derivation complex and mapping homotopies, not just its closed vertices.

There is no relation \(u^2=0\) to impose. The free graded Lie algebra on an odd generator has that generator and its even bracket square; graded Jacobi makes the square central. Its enveloping algebra is precisely \(B_\Omega\). The free-action bar therefore retains all powers of the generator and their entire coherent mapping resolution. The calculation gives \[ \operatorname{Fun}^{L,\otimes} (\mathcal R_{\mathcal Q}^{\mathrm{fr}},\mathcal T) \simeq \operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{CAlg}}(A_0,D_{\mathcal T}). \tag{GZR.20} \] For a connective commutative DG algebra \(A\), the full free-module bar identifies tensor functors \(\operatorname{Mod}_A\to\mathcal T\) with algebra maps \(A\to D_{\mathcal T}\), by taking the unit to the unit. This is RSE.19 and includes all transformations. Comparing with GZR.20 and using its actual universal coefficient yields \[ L_{\mathcal Q}^{\mathrm{fr}}: \mathcal R_{\mathcal Q}^{\mathrm{fr}} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Mod}_{A_0}. \tag{GZR.21} \] To check that this is an equivalence of categories, take \(\mathcal T=\mathcal R_{\mathcal Q}^{\mathrm{fr}}\) in the functor-space comparison to produce an inverse, then take \(\mathcal T=\operatorname{Mod}_{A_0}\) and use full faithfulness to identify the other composite. Thus this is not a test only on scalar affine targets.

3.641. The finite exterior algebra forces actual curve torsion

Choose a basis \(e_1,\ldots,e_d\) of \(\mathfrak h\) with dual odd coordinates \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_d\). Then \[ A_0=\Lambda(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_d),\qquad |\xi_i|=-1,\quad d\xi_i=0,\quad \alpha_{\mathrm{univ}}=\sum_i e_i\xi_i . \tag{GZR.22} \] In particular \(H^0(A_0)=\mathbf C\) and its underlying complex has degrees \([-d,0]\). The universal framed coefficient of a finite representation \(V\) is the actual internal module \[ E_V^{\mathrm{fr}}=A_0\otimes V,\qquad u=d\rho_V(\alpha_{\mathrm{univ}}). \tag{GZR.23} \] Its full action is the free \(B_\Omega\)-action bar on that operator. Every coefficient of the \(r\)-th power of this matrix is a product of \(r\) of the \(\xi_i\)'s. Consequently, with \(m=\lfloor d/2\rfloor+1\), \[ u^{d+1}=0,\qquad v^m=u^{2m}=0 \quad\text{on }E_V^{\mathrm{fr}} . \tag{GZR.24} \] The even power is a \(B_\Omega\)-linear map, since \(v\) is graded central. Its displayed nullhomotopy is the zero polynomial matrix. All tensor and intertwiner comparisons retain it.

This is also direct membership in \(\operatorname{Mod}_{A_0}\otimes\mathcal I\), with the entire scalar action. Indeed the cofiber \(B_\Omega/(v^m)\) has a finite word filtration with augmentation-module layers. Its scalar extension has the same filtration. The localization fibre argument RSC.23, applied to the commuting \(A_0\) and \(B_\Omega\) actions, says \[ \operatorname{Mod}_{A_0}\otimes\mathcal I =\ker\!\left[ \operatorname{Mod}_{A_0\otimes B_\Omega} \longrightarrow \operatorname{Mod}_{A_0\otimes B_\Omega[v^{-1}]} \right]. \tag{GZR.25} \] The tensor of the localization triangle is exact on every unbounded module. GZR.24 makes its localized term zero. This proof does not bound the eventual automorphic input or replace its Postnikov tower by a direct colimit.

3.642. Full frame descent and the genuine restricted target

Changing the frame sends \(\alpha\) to its adjoint transform. In regular matrix coordinates this is the same conjugation as the original tensor frame change: apply the regular coaction to GZR.19. Iterating gives the same maps over \(\mathcal O(H)^{\otimes s}\); coproduct, counit and antipode give every face, degeneracy and inverse comparison. Thus GZR.21 is equivariant for the full algebraic frame nerve.

The conservative Hopf descent RSE.15–RSE.18, applied to this equivariant framed equivalence, gives the actual unframed tensor equivalence \[ L_{\mathcal Q}:\mathcal R_{\mathcal Q} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{QCoh}([\,\operatorname{Spec}A_0/H\,]) =:\mathcal A . \tag{GZR.26} \] The last stack is exactly the projective-line restricted stack RSC.29. In particular this argument has not substituted the completed coefficient category for the restricted spectral stack. It computed their universal tensor coefficient comparison.

The universal coefficients in GZR.23 descend with their full tensor maps and frame nerve. Since \(\mathcal I\) is dualizable and its embedding is full, the same limit descent retains the ind-connection coefficient and every map. Hence \[ E_V\in\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal I \subset\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal Q . \tag{GZR.27} \] This is the actual universal coefficient BLI.16: framing both constructions gives the identical operator GZR.23 and the same regular coaction. Conservative full frame descent identifies their whole functors. The polynomial zero in GZR.24 is equivariant, so descends as well.

For a finite set \(J\), the universal coefficient is its external tensor product with the prescribed representation multiplications at collisions. The full comparison is therefore \[ E_{\vec V}\in\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal I^{\otimes J}, \qquad v_j^mE_{\vec V}=0\quad(j\in J). \tag{GZR.28} \] The maps of GZR.26 carry precisely these coefficients, their frames and all collision and unused-coordinate maps. This follows from the representing calculation GZR.16–GZR.21, not from equality of field-valued points.

3.643. The actual Hecke action has ind-connection coefficients

Transport the full action GZR.15 along GZR.26. We obtain a continuous unital action \[ \mathcal A\otimes\mathcal C_F \longrightarrow\mathcal C_F . \tag{GZR.29} \] Its universal coefficient action is exactly the original completed Hecke action: this is how GZR.26 was defined on each full finite-point stage. With \(\mathrm{act}\) denoting GZR.29, \[ \widehat{\mathsf H}^{\,F}_V(M) \simeq(\mathrm{act}\otimes\operatorname{Id}) (E_V\otimes M). \tag{GZR.30} \] The equality is in \(\mathcal C_F\otimes\mathcal Q\) and includes every original Hecke comparison. GZR.27 consequently refines it to the actual full subcategory \(\mathcal C_F\otimes\mathcal I\). Apply its continuous inclusion into \(\mathcal M\) and the normalized geometric realization: \[ \mathsf H_VF\in\mathcal M\otimes\mathcal I . \tag{GZR.31} \] The same argument with GZR.28 proves the statement for every finite set, with all its original action maps and higher relations. No compactness, boundedness or input regularity has been assumed.

The universal polynomial nullhomotopy gives more than individual local nilpotence. In the lifted completed coefficient of each Hecke operation, \[ v_j^m\widehat{\mathsf H}^{\,F}_{\vec V}=0,\qquad m=\lfloor\dim H/2\rfloor+1 . \tag{GZR.32} \] This is a specified natural nullhomotopy of the even central action. It is inherited from GZR.24 under the actual module action, and persists for arbitrary unbounded \(M\in\mathcal C_F\). It is not obtained by imposing a degree bound on \(M\). The existence of this refinement for every \(F\in\mathscr S_Y\) proves the unrestricted genus-zero Hecke-lisse inclusion.

3.644. The full complex nilpotent projector image in every genus

For genus zero, GZR.31 supplies \(\mathscr S_Y\subset\mathcal N_{\mathrm{Hl}}(Y)\). For positive genus the inclusion is NHT.31. In every genus GFP.55–GFP.56 give the reverse inclusion and chartwise ind-regularity. Thus, over the original complex coefficient field, \[ \operatorname{Dmod}_{1/2,\mathcal N}(\operatorname{Bun}_G) =\mathcal N_{\mathrm{Hl}}(\operatorname{Bun}_G) =\operatorname{EssIm}(\Pi_{\mathrm{res}}) \subset\mathscr R_\infty(\operatorname{Bun}_G). \tag{GZR.33} \] This holds for every connected reductive \(G\), every genus and every bundle component, with both infinite cohomological tails. The full restricted projector and its original normalization are those of RSE.37–RSE.38 and NTR.16. In particular its given natural identity on the full Hecke-lisse category becomes \[ \Pi_{\mathrm{res}}|_{\operatorname{Dmod}_{1/2,\mathcal N}} \simeq\operatorname{Id}. \tag{GZR.34} \] The assertion is equality with the independently defined cohomological support category NU.1–NU.4. It is not only an equality on bounded objects.

The envelope argument deliberately uses a set of arbitrary supported Hecke words. It proves neither ordinary compactness of those words nor the chartwise supported compact factorization criterion AIC.17. The supported ind-Riemann–Hilbert identification requiring that criterion retains its hypothesis. Other geometric ground fields, derived tempered Satake and the stated additional categorical foundations also retain their requirements.

Figure 3.76. GZR.4–GZR.11 use a fixed-point-Hecke-invariant presentable envelope for each arbitrary supported input. The full frame algebra and its universal odd operator are GZR.18–GZR.24. The finite exterior coefficient gives an actual equivariant central-power nullhomotopy, and GZR.26–GZR.34 transport the complete action to the restricted target and identify the full supported image.

Free further reading for the completed-to-ind coefficient refinement is AGKRRV, The stack of local systems with restricted variation and geometric Langlands theory with nilpotent singular support, §14.3, especially Remark 14.3.9. The arguments above use the explicit projective-line tensor derivation and its actual categorical frame comparison.

3.645. A nonzero square in the universal \(SL_2\) coefficient

Exercise 3.HS. For \(H=SL_2\) and its standard representation, use odd exterior variables \(a,b,c\), each of degree minus one, and write \[ A_0=\Lambda(a,b,c),\qquad U=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-a\end{pmatrix}. \tag{GZR.35} \] View \(U\) as the degree-minus-one operator on the free rank-two \(A_0\)-module, with coefficients on the left and the graded \(A_0\)-linearity rule. Compute \(U^2,U^3,U^4\). Determine the least positive power of \(v=u^2\) that is zero in this universal coefficient.

Solution 3.HS. Exterior anticommutation gives \[ U^2= \begin{pmatrix}bc&2ab\\-2ac&-bc\end{pmatrix}\ne0 . \tag{GZR.36} \] For example the upper-right entry is \(ab-ba=2ab\). Multiplying once more, \(bca=abc\) and \(acb=-abc\), so \[ U^3=3abc\,I_2,\qquad U^4=0 . \tag{GZR.37} \] The last equality holds because every resulting monomial repeats an odd generator. Thus \[ v\ne0,\qquad v^2=0 \quad\text{on this universal module}. \tag{GZR.38} \] For \(d=3\), the exponent \(m=2\) in GZR.24 is attained. Replacing the associative loop algebra by an odd graded-commutative algebra would incorrectly erase the nonzero matrix GZR.36.

3.646. Unbounded scalar coefficients and the localization test

Exercise 3.HT. For \(H=\mathbf G_m\), let \(r\ne0\) be an integer weight. Use the connective DG algebra and its unbounded module \[ A=\Lambda(\xi)\otimes\mathbf C[z],\quad |\xi|=-1,\quad |z|=-2,\quad d=0,\qquad M=A[t,t^{-1}],\quad |t|=2 . \tag{GZR.39} \] The scalar map from the universal framed algebra sends its odd generator to \(\xi\). Compute the coefficient action of \(u\) on the weight-\(r\) pullback tensored with \(M\). Show directly that it is an ind-connection coefficient despite the two infinite tails of \(M\). Compare the Laurent word module \(B_\Omega[v^{-1}]\).

Solution 3.HT. The weight derivative is multiplication by \(r\), so the full coefficient operator and its central square are \[ u(m)=r\xi m,\qquad v(m)=0 . \tag{GZR.40} \] The graded rule is respected: \(\xi a=(-1)^{|a|}a\xi\). All degrees of the input are retained. Localization is the telescope of multiplication by \(v\). Since its maps are zero on this module, its cohomology localization vanishes; equivalently the cone of \(1-\mathrm{shift}\) on the direct sum of the zero-transition system is acyclic. Thus \[ B_\Omega[v^{-1}]\otimes_{B_\Omega}^{L}M=0, \qquad M\in\mathcal I . \tag{GZR.41} \] This calculation uses the universal odd exterior relation, not a lower degree bound on \(M\).

On the other hand the free Laurent word module has invertible central action and a nonzero constant word: \[ L=B_\Omega[v^{-1}]\ne0,\qquad B_\Omega[v^{-1}]\otimes_{B_\Omega}^{L}L\simeq L,\qquad L\notin\mathcal I . \tag{GZR.42} \] It is an object of the completed category \(\mathcal Q\). The genus-zero Hecke theorem does not identify it with an ind-connection; it proves that independently supported inputs have the actual universal coefficient refinement GZR.30–GZR.32.

4. Betti, constructible, and tempered categories

Now suppose \(k=\mathbb C\), and choose a coefficient field \(E\) of characteristic zero. The large Betti category consists of complexes of \(E\)-sheaves on the analytic stack, with no finite-dimensional stalk requirement. Its automorphic subcategory is

\[ \operatorname{Shv}^{\mathrm{Betti}}_{1/2,\operatorname{Nilp}}(Y) \subset\operatorname{Shv}^{\mathrm{Betti}}_{1/2}(Y). \tag{4.1} \]

Here singular support is the microlocal support on smooth analytic charts. The zero-support condition on a smooth space says that a sheaf is locally constant as a derived sheaf. “Derived” is essential on a stack: local systems include higher coherent monodromy, not just representations of its ordinary fundamental group.

There is also a chartwise ind-constructible theory: on each finite-type affine chart, ind-complete the category of bounded complexes with algebraically constructible finite-dimensional cohomology, then descend. This is the theory denoted \(\operatorname{Shv}^{\mathrm{Betti,constr}}\) in GLC I. Its nilpotent subcategory is the restricted automorphic variant. It can be smaller than the large category. Compact objects of the large category are not defined by finite-dimensional stalks; §7 gives a rank-one example.
